title: ‘Absolutely manic’: hot weather puts unprecedented pressure on Greater Manchester police | Police | The Guardian
description: Force has seen busiest month in its history, with heatwaves putting added strain on criminal justice system
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Force has seen busiest month in its history, with heatwaves putting added strain on criminal justice system
Content: Officers patrol in the town centre of Ashton-under-Lyne on a ‘day of action’ enforcing an alcohol-free zone.Photograph: Joel Goodman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOfficers patrol in the town centre of Ashton-under-Lyne on a ‘day of action’ enforcing an alcohol-free zone.Photograph: Joel Goodman/The GuardianPolice‘Absolutely manic’: hot weather puts unprecedented pressure on Greater Manchester policeForce has seen busiest month in its history, with heatwaves putting added strain on criminal justice systemHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn England’s hottest day of the year so far, Ashton-under-Lyne inGreater Manchesterwas thronging with pedestrians, many clutching ice-creams or cold drinks as they passed through the town centre.Officers from GreaterManchesterpolice were also out in force, some in plainclothes, some stationed by a facial-recognition van, apprehending wanted suspects and stopping persons of interest. In total, officers made 54 arrests across the borough of Tameside as part of Operation Avro, GMP’s blitz on local crime which runs in a different district each month.For the past two months, the demand on officers here has been greater than ever, and GMP received a record-breaking 152,000 contacts from the public in July – the highest number ever recorded by the force in a single month.View image in fullscreen‘Every day is a busy period,’ said the Tameside neighbourhood sergeant Rob Froggatt, here posing for a selfie in Ashton market.Photograph: Joel Goodman/The GuardianThe World Cup is likely to have played a part, but the main driver, officers said, was the continued hot weather, which is putting an added strain not just on health services but also on the criminal justice system.And GMP is not alone – according to data from the NationalPoliceChiefs’ Council, which includes all the Home Office’s forces, British Transport Police and Police Scotland, emergency call volumes increased by about 11.5% year on year during July.Digital contact with the public also increased. Online reports submitted through Single Online Home, the platform used by most police forces, increased by about 10% year on year.The Met Office has confirmed that July was the hottest and the driest month on record, while heatwaves have continued into August. “These factors bring people outside, there’s an increase in alcohol consumption, an increase in people going into reservoirs, into water,” said Tameside’s neighbourhood chief inspector, James Grundy. “So that does increase the demand for police.”Grundy said there had been an increase in calls on everything from off-road bike use to antisocial behaviour and people taking disposable barbecues to locations prone to wildfires.View image in fullscreenNeighbourhood chief inspector James Grundy waits in the Hyde police station car park before carrying out dawn raids.Photograph: Joel Goodman/The Guardian“It is challenging,” Grundy said. “Obviously we have to attend incidents based on the threat, harm and risk, so we have to prioritise certain incidents over others, which means that some people don’t often receive the level of response that they deserve. We have officers that are pulled from different areas to support that demand on the frontline at times.”“At the moment in Greater Manchester police every day is a busy period,” said the Tameside neighbourhood police sergeant Rob Froggatt. “Every day police officers are being run ragged.”He said his neighbourhood officers were often pulled on to response policing when those teams needed more support in order to do their jobs safely. “It’s a fine balance,” he said, “but I’d say we deal with it quite well.”Tameside response officer PC Daniel Bragg has been in his job for seven years, and said with the exception of perhaps New Year’s Eve, this summer had been the busiest he had ever known.“Over the last few months, obviously with the World Cup, the sun, it’s just non-stop,” he said. “Due to the football you have more people jumping in cars after pubs, so we had a lot more crashes. When it gets warm, naturally with older people you have a lot more deaths occurring.”View image in fullscreen‘It was absolutely manic again last week,’ said PC Daniel Bragg, a response officer.Photograph: Joel Goodman/The GuardianBragg said domestic incidents and mental health crises were also two big drivers of 999 calls. “It was absolutely manic again last week, non-stop,” he said, adding that senior officers were being sent out on jobs in order to meet response targets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOfficers attended 14,991 grade 1 incidents (where there is an immediate emergency) in July, achieving an average response time of seven minutes and 54 seconds, and 10,266 grade 2 (serious incidents lacking immediate danger), with an average response time of one hour and two minutes.In the last month, Bragg said, the team had been responding to up to 40 calls in a night shift; typically that number would lie somewhere between 10 and 20.“You’re doubling or quadrupling that in one night,” he said. “You are out of the station from 9 o’clock when a job comes in, and then you’re coming back in at 7 o’ clock really, just going job to job.”With more hot summers on the horizon, Bragg said: “I do think if it continues like this over the years to come, there would have to be a change just in terms of staffing. It’s kind of impossible to police what we’re policing at the minute.”View image in fullscreenThe repeated heatwaves were ‘a very serious issue that as a police service we need to consider’, said Arif Nawaz, the Tameside district superintendent.Photograph: Joel Goodman/The Guardian“When I look at the three-month period and compare it to the same three months last year, it’s been a really significant increase,” said the Tameside district superintendent, Arif Nawaz. “We’re looking at around an extra 572 grade 2 incidents and an extra 272 grade 1 incidents. So that effectively means my response teams have to deal with an extra seven grade 1s and 2s every single day.”As well as the weather, Manchester’s rapid development brought more people to the city, which in turn placed additional strain on policing, Nawaz said. “The economic development around Manchester is brilliant for the region but it’s also contributing. The Co-op Arena is a new site attracting 20,000 people each event. That’s in addition to the AO Arena. So that’s just one simple example of something that’s great for the economy, but there’s a policing demand.”The repeated heatwaves were, Nawaz said, “a very serious issue that as a society we need to consider, as a police service we need to consider”.“The government’s looking at it as well, so who knows what the future will bring?” he added. “Clearly it is in our thinking around how we prepare ourselves for this.”Explore more on these topicsPoliceGreater ManchesterEmergency servicesExtreme heatUK weatherManchesterNorth of EnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations? | Women | The Guardian
description: There are more than 70,000 hysteroscopies every year in England alone. The NHS calls them ‘low complexity’ – yet a shocking number of patients complain of inadequate pain relief and medical staff who refuse to take them seriously
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: There are more than 70,000 hysteroscopies every year in England alone. The NHS calls them ‘low complexity’ – yet a shocking number of patients complain of inadequate pain relief and medical staff who refuse to take them seriously
Content: Illustration: Hélène Blanc/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Hélène Blanc/The GuardianWomen‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations?There are more than 70,000 hysteroscopies every year in England alone. The NHS calls them ‘low complexity’ – yet a shocking number of patients complain of inadequate pain relief and medical staff who refuse to take them seriouslyAnna MooreSun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February this year, Beth Harris sat in the day surgery waiting room of her local hospital and tried to steady her nerves.She was there for a hysteroscopy, in this case to remove a fibroid. A thin surgical instrument with a lens, a light, a blade and an irrigation system for pumping saline solution would be inserted through her vagina and cervix, into her womb. The saline solution would widen the womb and the fibroid would be shaved away. Her hospital had advised taking paracetamol or ibuprofen an hour before the appointment, which Harris had done. However, the appointment was for 1pm, and by 4pm, she was still waiting in her hospital gown, surrounded by other patients.Hysteroscopies are common procedures – classed by the NHS as “high volume low complexity”. In 2021, 71,000 took place in England alone. This was Harris’s third. “I’d been shocked by how painful the first two were,” she says. They had been “diagnostic” only – examinations of the inside of the womb – because years of breast cancer medication had led her womb lining to thicken. When she learned that she had a fibroid that needed removing, Harris’s first question was: “Will it be painful?” Her gynaecologist assured her that she would be given local anaesthetic and “wouldn’t feel anything”. He compared it to “going to the dentist”.Any doubts Harris harboured while awaiting that procedure were multiplied by the two patients treated ahead of her. “The first woman was hysterical when she came out,” she says. “The nurse had to get the consultant to talk to her. The second collapsed in the recovery room. Nobody came to her, so a little old man in his gown and slippers, a random patient, got involved and found a nurse. They took her away on a trolley.”View image in fullscreen‘It feels as if someone is sweeping a knife around inside you,’ said one patient.Photograph: Posed by model; Twenty47studio/Getty ImagesWhen Harris was finally called in, there were several people in the theatre. “There was the gynaecologist, nurses, an anaesthetist behind me, although he didn’t do anything. They were talking to each other throughout – no one was sitting with me. It was very casual.” The gynaecologist administered local anaesthetic – a small injection near the cervix – but there was no pause to see if it had worked. “There was no gap, no questions,” she says. “The injection itself was painful, but the procedure, with this spinning blade inside you, was unbelievable. The pressure, the pushing of the machine, the manipulation – it was barbaric. I’ve never experienced anything like it in my life. I felt as if I’d been assaulted. By the end, I was crying my eyes out.” A nurse led her, sobbing, to the recovery room. “There was no dignity, no privacy,” says Harris. “I said to her: ‘There must be a better way of doing this.’”Katharine Tylko, a founder member of the campaign groupHysteroscopy Action(HA), has been saying the same thing for 16 years. HA was formed in 2010 to demand that all hysteroscopy patients are fully informed about the procedure, including the risk of severe pain, and given a full range of pain relief choices – local anaesthesia, gas and air, conscious sedation, epidural, and, for those who need it, general anaesthetic. “In short, we want parity with colonoscopy patients, half of whom are men,” says Tylko. In April, therenewed Women’s Health Strategyset out by the then health secretary Wes Streeting seemed a major breakthrough. Action 7 of the strategy called for informed consent and a choice of pain relief for hysteroscopies. “We were thrilled,” says Tylko, “but there’s been nothing since. Just silence.”Many conditions might require a hysteroscopy. By far the most common is heavy or unexplained bleeding. In 2018, guidelines from the National Institute forHealthand Care Excellencemade them the primary diagnostic tool for this. A hysteroscopy’s “inside view” of the womb makes them the gold standard for ruling out any sinister pathology such as endometrial cancer. They are also used to investigate cases of unexplained infertility or recurrent miscarriage, to remove uterine fibroids, polyps or scar tissue.Once hysteroscopies required a general anaesthetic, but this changed through the 2000s and 2010s after clinical audits and trials established that outpatient hysteroscopies were safe, much faster and more cost-effective. (Present NHS targets are that 90% of diagnostic and 50% of operative hysteroscopies take place in an outpatient setting.) Pain relief options vary wildly across the country. Too often, says Tylko, there is nothing beyond a nurse to hold your hand and supply a constant stream of “hairdresser chitchat”.Tylko, 71, a musician and translator, required a hysteroscopy 23 years ago, because of unexplained bleeding. “It was late-stage womb cancer which took two years to be diagnosed,” she says. “By then, I was bleeding so much, I was sleeping on bath towels.” After numerous GP appointments, Tylko asked why she wasn’t being referred for investigation. “My GP told me that I would ‘freak out’ at an NHS gynae clinic,” says Tylko. The GP had reached this conclusion partly because Tylko hadn’t had a baby, so her cervical canal had not been stretched, and also because she found smear tests difficult (she now knows this was almost certainly because of undiagnosed endometriosis).View image in fullscreen‘There was no dignity, no privacy,’ said a patient.Photograph: Posed by model; SDI Productions/Getty Images“That night was probably the worst night of my life,” says Tylko. “I thought: ‘She thinks I’ve got something – and she thinks I probably won’t be able to stand the test for it.’ I went privately and still had to jump through lots more hoops, but I finally got a hysteroscopy under general anaesthetic.”Through her subsequent cancer treatment, Tylko met many women who had been traumatised by their hysteroscopies. “I’d been told that only 2% of women had problems with them,” she says. “I was given the message that if I was ‘normal’, if I’d had children, I wouldn’t be complaining. Then I met women who’d had children with no pain relief but who’d fainted after their hysteroscopies.” The penny finally dropped that she wasn’t the only one who struggled with gynecological procedures.More than 13,000 women have completed HA’s online survey, which set out to learn more from women’s experiences, and itspetitionis nearing 70,000 signatures. The comments make harrowing reading. In 2020, abenchmark multicentre studyfound that mean pain scores for outpatient hysteroscopies were 5.2 (that’s “moderate” on a hospital ward and would merit codeine) and 35% of women had a “severe” pain score of seven and above.“As a campaign, we’ve had real difficulty treading a rational path between trying to effect change but not putting women off something that can predict cancer,” says Tylko. “We’ve always put the caveat that two-thirds of women do not experience severe pain.” Equally though, outpatient hysteroscopies have a failure rate of around 10%, with pain as the predominant reason, points out Richard Harrison, lecturer and co-lead of pain research at Reading University. “That, too, can lead to a whole lack of engagement with future medical procedures, which could be lifesaving.”Harrison worked on a recently publishedstudythat analysed data from nearly 5,000 women who had undergone hysteroscopies. For Harrison and his co-authors, the issue sits within a wider body of research on the gender pain gap – it’s already well established that women presenting in health care settings with pain areprescribed less analgesic than men, and are more likely to begiven antidepressants instead. In this hysteroscopy study, they identified a “gynaecological pain gaslighting” where women were repeatedly told: “It can’t be that bad” and: “Most women tolerate this procedure well.”Helen Garnett, 56, from North Lincolnshire, was so certain that she would be “gaslit” that she secretly recorded her outpatient hysteroscopy and later released it online (with voices altered). “I’d already had two hysteroscopies for heavy bleeding which had been so horrendous, I’d almost passed out,” she says. This time, she called her GP and clinic in advance to request pain relief – and was told her consultant would discuss it on the day. The recording is excruciating to hear. Garnett is nervous, clearly but apologetically asking for pain relief – “I’m not wimpy but this I find so painful” – but is swept through with none. Instead she was left with patronising chatter from nurses: “Do you think we should have some music in here? I could sing to you!”; “You’re doing amazing!”; “Well done you!”“It feels as if someone is sweeping a knife around inside you,” says Garnett. “I have three daughters, I run my own business, I thought I’d be able to advocate for myself more, but I just couldn’t. It’s crazy. You lose all sense of being an adult as they treat you in such a childlike manner. I’m surprised they don’t give you sweets and a sticker on the way out. As soon as I got away, I burst into tears. I didn’t want them to see me crying like a baby.”Some gynaecologists are determined to make changes. Dr Gail Busby, a consultant gynaecologist for 26 years, admits it has been a “learning curve”. “A long time ago, I don’t think we were aware how painful an outpatient hysteroscopy can be,” she says. “As a gynaecologist, you’re so focused on the procedure. We thought it was period-like, crampy pain, which is the case for a lot of women, but it is absolutely undeniable that some women have severe pain and they need to be listened to.”View image in fullscreenSome hospitals now offer deep sedation administered by an anaesthetist.Photograph: Posed by models; andresr/Getty ImagesTwo incidents forced Busby to reevaluate. The first was learning through a patient about HA and its campaign. The second was her own experience of a colonoscopy. “It was with sedation, but for me, it was the most hideous, painful thing ever. Some people have no problems with them. I had tears running down my face.” Busby has had a hysteroscopy, too, with no pain relief, and for her, that was fine. “I just think people are wired differently and there’s no way you can predict if you’re going to fall into the one-in-three women who have severe pain,” she says. Busby now offersdeep sedation– administered by an anaesthetist and the patient will sleep through most of the procedure – to her hysteroscopy patients at her private Spire clinic and her NHS practice at St Mary’s Hospital in Manchester. “Not everyone needs it, but the women who say they need it really need it.”Consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist Richard Flint offers conscious sedation – a combination of analgesia and sedative via a needle in your arm – at his clinic in Chelsea and Westminster hospital. “I’ve been performing hysteroscopies for eight years now, and though many patients are fine with outpatient hysteroscopies, there is a large proportion for whom it is agonising,” he says. “From my point of view, I stop immediately and those procedures are really heart-sink moments. You feel you’ve failed the patient.”In 2023, Flint introduced conscious sedation at C&W, one day a week. They are now expanding it to a five-day service (the only hospital currently offering it for hysteroscopies). They also offer it for other outpatient procedures such as cystoscopies (examinations of the bladder), IUD insertions and manual vacuum aspirations after miscarriage. At the same time, the clinic is trialling theWid-easy test, a vaginal swab that checks for womb cancer in women with abnormal bleeding. It is already in routine use in Austria and Switzerland, has been introduced in Germany, and is on trial for NHS use in various clinics across the UK.“That is massively reducing the number of hysteroscopies we need to do,” Flint says. He now has data on more than 300 hysteroscopies performed under conscious sedation, which he is releasing shortly. “The pain scores are so much better. The average is two out of 10,” he says. “What has sealed it for me is seeing patients whose previous hysteroscopies had to be abandoned. They usually say: ‘Why didn’t I have this before?’”There are other small signs of progress. The British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy has recently appointed a female president – the first in decades – consultant gynaecologist Rebecca Mallick. This month, Mallick and Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) president Dr Alison Wright met with members of HA. “Alison and I were shocked and have a lot of things to think about,” says Mallick. At present,RCOG guidelinesstate that outpatient hysteroscopy patients should be fully informed about the procedure first, and “made aware” that there are other settings and pain relief offerings, including a general anaesthetic or intravenous sedation. “We could do a deep dive into why best practice isn’t always happening,” says Mallick. “We’ve got half a million people on the gynae waiting list, so clinics want to see as many people as possible. Are we giving enough time to talk through all the options or just trying to firefight numbers? We need to look at how we can support hysteroscopists to offer all types of analgesic. We also need to advocate for more funding and resources so we can tackle the backlog and improve care.”Tylko sees this as part of a much bigger picture. “We’re a gathering snowball made up of all sorts of gynae-women’s groups,” she says. “Endometriosis UK,Sling the Mesh, women fighting for better maternity care, better IUD fittings. We are getting together and saying: ‘This has to end.’”For Harris, any hard-won changes will come too late. She has chosen to have a hysterectomy. “I’ve found a gynaecologist I trust and she is the only one I will let do it,” she says, “but I’m on the waiting list to see a psychologist first to help me get through it. At the moment, since that last hysteroscopy, every medical appointment makes me cry and panic.” Harris is taking this route partly so that she will never need another one. “I will not undergo any more tests, no more procedures, no more examinations. I’ve reached my red light. This is how I’ll bring it to a close.”Explore more on these topicsWomenHysterectomyHospitalsCervical cancerHealthHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t always go full banana!’ From the yellow man to a playful shrink, stylish people on what they wear every day – and why | Fashion | The Guardian
description: How does a rabbi choose her shoes? Why does a psychoanalyst like slogan tees? And why does a doctor avoid wearing scrubs at work? Seven striking dressers share their surprising style stories
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: How does a rabbi choose her shoes? Why does a psychoanalyst like slogan tees? And why does a doctor avoid wearing scrubs at work? Seven striking dressers share their surprising style stories
Content: Photograph: Emma Stoner/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Emma Stoner/The GuardianFashion‘I don’t always go full banana!’ From the yellow man to a playful shrink, stylish people on what they wear every day – and whyHow does a rabbi choose her shoes? Why does a psychoanalyst like slogan tees? And why does a doctor avoid wearing scrubs at work? Seven striking dressers share their surprising style storiesEllie Violet BramleySun 16 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Wearing yellow spreads a bit of love’Andrew Geldart, 65, retired engineer, CornwallFor 30 years as a civil engineer I wore conventional grey and navy, then I retired at 55, moved down to Bude in Cornwall with my wife, Lynn, and the sun came out. Bude is a positive place, where you can be yourself. Everyone is friendly; it’s paradise.I first started down the yellow route 10 years agowhen we moved to Bude with a camper van called Primrose. People gave me yellow accessories for it and the seed was sown – I thought I might wear yellow myself. Now it’s a mainstay of my wardrobe. I wear it practically every day. I have everything from yellow caps to yellow shoes. I prefer sunflower yellow rather than mustard tones: it’s bright and cheerful.I don’t always go “full banana”! I dress according to the situation. I wouldn’t wear yellow to a Remembrance Day parade, but I would to a funeral of a friend, as I’m known for wearing it and I would be honouring them. If I want to go under the radar, I wear beige. I’m a church leader and help run the food bank: usually people know me there and adjust their behaviour accordingly, but when they don’t recognise me because I’m not in yellow, I can blend into the background and hear what the community really want.There are practical benefits. My grandchildren can easily spot me in a crowd. In fact, they walk past me if I’m not wearing yellow, and ask: “Where’s Pops?” But the main reason I choose to stand out is to connect with people, to show that I am friendly and approachable, even if I’m not smiling.Someone says, “I like your glasses”, nearly every day (I have a jazzy, stripy, bright yellow summer pair and a more muted, translucent yellow winter pair), and that opens the door to a conversation. There are so many isolated people looking down at their phones, and if I can encourage someone to talk, I’m happy. I want to spread a bit of love in the world and to show that it’s safe to say how you really are, to get past just “Good morning”. A coffee and a chat can be a little glimpse of sunshine.I have toyed with changing to red or green, and that would be a new conversation – “What happened? Why aren’t you wearing yellow?” It’s a colour that works for me, but never say never: men’s fashion is quite limited when it comes to yellow, so I may be forced to change to another bright colour one day.Sometimes the old conventional and staid engineer part of me thinks, “Can I get away with this? Is this too much?” But I saw a picture of the late David Hockney in his yellow glasses recently and thought, “Maybe I’m not ridiculous.” I want to give people the courage to step outside the box – let’s make life enjoyable.As told to Emily Cunningham‘I like tosubvert the expectations of how a shrink ought to dress’Anouchka Grose,56,psychoanalyst, LondonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianI don’t want to dress too conservatively as I don’t want to look like an authority figure, or like someone who believes that “analytic neutrality” – the idea that the therapist is a blank slate – means some kind of John Lewis cosplay. “Neutrality” can’t mean aligning with a dominant norm – psychotherapists need to be critical thinkers. But what I wear also can’t be so unusual that the client is distracted. Overall, I’m aiming for a kind of quiet surrealism – a balance between comfortable, pleasurable and characterful.So I have a vague uniform of a genderless jumper or jacket – a strict-looking black jacket with pointy shoulders, say – with a man’s shirt or T-shirt, big trousers (I’m currently loving a stripy pair from Maison Margiela I found on eBay) and ugly shoes, usually Uggs I buy secondhand. Most things are outsized, or loose.Very often my T-shirts will have a slogan – my favourite is “Dress for the male gays”. It references Laura Mulvey’s theory that there could be a male gaze that things are constructed around, which was one of the first ways into psychoanalysis for me. But it’s also a funny wordplay referencing the post-Freudians, who thought of homosexuality as a kind of sickness to cure. I see that T-shirt as a sort of apology for the past homophobia of psychoanalysis. Plus it makes clients laugh, which is allowed. (Freud took jokes extremely seriously.)Subverting the expectations of how a shrink ought to dress has been a real theme for me. A patient once asked me: “Are you allowed to wear those trousers to work?” They were balloonish red and white checked ones. And sometimes when I’ve given papers at analytic conferences, the other shrinks will be, like, “Yeah, but what do you wear for work?” (It is no different from what I am wearing at the conference.)I’ve always loved clothes and the way they transmit meaning. I love the crazy semiotics of them – communicating social signals to other people who know those signals. That seems very psychoanalytic to me.They always say that as a psychoanalyst you get the patients you deserve. I really like that idea. There have been some people I frightened away because of how I looked, and that’s good.Maybe that’s why I don’t spend too long worrying how people will perceive me. Psychoanalysis teaches you that associations are fractured and kaleidoscopic. So you can’t really control the meanings that other people make; any garment could mean anything to anyone.‘My love of vintageisa rejection ofcapitalism’Annastasia, 62, author, DevonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Emma Stoner/The GuardianWhat I wear is an integral aspect of my identity. I am what I wear, and what I wear is secondhand, sometimes reproduction, clothing that dates between the 1920s and about 1966. It stops there because I think the mid‑60s is when life started to change from being a very ordered, slow society to something else. I was born in 1964, so I’ve pretty much lived in the something else period; I’ve always rejected the current timeline I live in.Seeing The Wizard of Oz when I was four was the starting point. I was born into a poor, working-class family, and everything seemed really grey. That film, with its heightened colours, fired my imagination as to what clothing – and the world – could look like. Then, when I was about six, a friend of my mother’s dropped round a pile of what she thought were dressing-up clothes – 50s ball gowns and cocktail dresses. When I put them on, I felt completely myself, which I didn’t in the functional, ubiquitous clothes of the day. I saw then that getting dressed could become a creative thing. At 12, I began dressing like this. Now, every day the first creative choices I make are what to wear. It’s ritualistic.My love of vintage clothing is an outward rejection of advanced capitalism and the tyranny of its desperate buy, buy, buy culture, which results in so much clothing being sent to landfill. I like colours that are more muted, which you get in vintage fabrics. The last thing I would buy as a winter coat would be a puffer jacket that makes you look like a caterpillar. It would be wool, 1950s, cinched in.Through my clothing, I am expressing that attire can be inexpensive, ethical, well made and, to me, aesthetically pleasing. I like the values of vintage clothing: care, attention, consideration and slowness. But that isn’t to say that I’m about nostalgia or traditional values. I would hate anyone to think I was espousing tradwife values via the way I dress. Quite honestly, in my 60s, I can dress the way I want to.I have faced criticism for what I wear. When I was working alongside women and girls in Birmingham in the 70s and 80s, feminist organisations used to be very judgmental towards me. It was as if I had to prove my credentials more than other women because I wasn’t wearing jeans and Dr Martens. By contrast, the people I visited as part of the community outreach I was doing used to say how impressed they were that I had made such an effort to dress nicely for them.I now write time-slip fiction – where present-day characters get entangled with those from the past –under the pen name Pearl Fane. The pivotal character lives in England in the 50s. It’s so useful because I can relate to how she might have experienced the world by how clothing felt on her.People are surprised I dress like this every day – but I wouldn’t know any other way of being.‘I’m a rabbi, and I like to coordinate my shoes with the 12 Hebrew months’Arielle Stein, 35, rabbi, New YorkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Maegan Gindi/The GuardianI have been figuring out my style for a long time. I started out as a visual artist; now I’m a congregational rabbi, and I’ve been working to meld the more formal with the more alternative. The result is a quirky mix of some business-casual, some downtown hipster, and then truly random things that delight me.Style has always been a way to communicate my identity; I think of it as a form of storytelling. As a rabbi, there are definitely norms around how you should present. But I think being on the younger side, and a woman, freed me from a lot of that; no matter what, I wasn’t going to look like the traditional model. Plus, I deeply love to subvert a norm: for me it’s about adding to the mosaic of what’s possible.I have a role in a lot of important life-cycle moments and I think it’s vital I don’t take centre stage. But people are drawn to me either on an artistic or creative level, or on a peer level. So the style element is important.Our generation has had a lot of struggles connecting to religion and spirituality, and I think for people to meet a rabbi who looks like them definitely creates a sense of comfort. My style often functions as an invitation: I get a lot of emails that start with something about style and then get into something that person has wanted to talk about and hasn’t yet found a way that felt comfortable to them.There are a few occasions when I have more of a uniform. At the synagogue I work at, we’re a pretty traditional Reform congregation, and so we all wear a mandated robe on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. But, at the same time, because we are a progressive denomination, we all select our own shoes.Shoes in general are a nice way of bringing that alternative personal flavour. I like to coordinate mine with the 12 Hebrew months: for instance, wearing low-key Birkenstocks for the contemplative month of Tammuz; freaky jelly sandals for Adar, which is the month of Purim and the craziest time of the year; and Vibram five-toed Mary Janes for Nisan, the month of exodus and the Passover story, as they’d be perfect for getting through the desert. In fact, I wear different shoes for each night of Passover, from studded Madewell mules on night five, when I’m thinking about plagues and boils, to blood-red Tory Burch mules on night six, when I’m thinking about the Passover sacrifice.We often get stuck in an idea that Judaism is one way or one thing only, and that’s exceedingly not true. I think we’re living in a visual culture right now, so this type of representation helps people remember that. It creates an opportunity for people to come as they are and to feel as if they can be Jewish in a way that feels authentic to them.Key for me is showing the Jewish community and the world that multiplicity is a deep part of who we are, and caring about style doesn’t mean that you don’t have a place in the Jewish world.‘My bright clothes are welcoming to my patients’Dr Bhasha Mukherjee,30, GP,LondonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThere aren’t really any rules for how to dress as a GP. One of my first bosses used to wear a full suit, and another would dress in a band T-shirt and jeans. I think you can take those liberties when you have been around long enough and developed a relationship with patients.I tend to wear something that is a cross between expressing how I’m feeling and being comfortable. I exercise every day, so part of my outfit is usually sportswear, but it’s a little bit glam, a little bit sexy, and I might wear it under a blazer. I love wearing a blazer; it’s power dressing. But it’s not going to be a boring black blazer. It’s going to be patterned, maybe even fuchsia pink. I love colour – dopamine dressing is a core theme for me.Jewellery is also important – I’ve got autism and ADHD, and I use it as a tactile, fidgeting thing. I will fidget with my necklace as I’m talking to patients because it helps me stay focused on what they’re saying.There’s evidence for trust levels in doctors being dependent on what they wear. But it’s not always simple. I remember one day I turned up in scrubs and my boss was, like, “Don’t be looking so scruffy at work.” I think Covid changed scrubs. They were definitely a dress code during the pandemic – they became the norm – but since then they have been hijacked by non-medical people on social media, a status symbol for influencers trying to gain the public’s trust. It confuses patients. I don’t need scrubs and a stethoscope to showcase my professionalism. Plus, I like to express myself more – I feel as if that’s more welcoming to patients, anyway.A part of me likes being a rebel. All through medical school, as a woman, I got shamed for wearing certain things at work. I would get called out by female colleagues who said my lipstick shade was too dark and unprofessional. Now I don’t feel like anybody can tell me that. I grew up consuming fashion magazines in the 00s – I do not walk out of the house without lipstick on.One thing I won’t wear in a professional setting is Indian dress. When I dress in that way I’m very maximalist and I will wear the full outfit: the sari, the head jewellery, neck jewellery. I can’t pare it back, so I’ve never dressed that way for work.‘Grunge feels like a form of quiet rebellion’Lorenzo Tondo,44,international correspondent, SicilyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alessio Mamo/The GuardianI can pinpoint the exact moment when my obsession with workwear began. It was the winter of 2018 and I was heading to the frozen mountains of Bosnia to cover the refugee crisis. Thousands of Syrian, Iraqi and Afghan refugees were moving along the Balkan route, hoping to reach Europe after weeks of walking through snow, mud and dense forests.I needed clothes that were practical and forgiving. That was when I remembered a pair of old Carhartt trousers buried in a cupboard. I had worn them heavily in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Wide-cut and designed to take a beating, they were faded now, tighter than I remembered, but still comfortable. I decided to take them with me. I needed trousers I wouldn’t mourn if they ended the day soaked through, caked in mud or torn. Their approachability was a plus, too: I’ve reported on thewar in Ukraine, in the occupiedWest Bankandin Syriafor the last six years and know that a blazer, however well intentioned, can quietly reinforce distance.Ever since then, I’ve hunted down loose-fitting vintage pieces: early-90s Carhartt jackets and at least three pairs of wide-leg trousers not unlike the ones I used to skate in as a teenager. I have worn them on the frontlines of the warin Ukraine, in cities flattened by theearthquake in Turkey, and amid the chalkydust of Idlib, in rebel-held north-west Syria. But also at home in Italy: for shopping, or heading out for a day trip with my children, or going out for dinner with friends.This was the style I had grown up with in the 90s, in a small town on the south-western coast of Sicily. Grunge originated in the Pacific north-west of America – a place of rain and lumber towns. I might have belonged to a very different community nearly 10,000km away, but I felt a shared sense of values. In my town, people dressed in Dolce & Gabbana and Gucci on Sundays. Wearing old clothes felt like a form of quiet, necessary rebellion against the superficial aesthetics of luxury fashion.As I got older, I started drifting towards something more conventional. Then grunge came back into fashion, along with the bands I used to listen: Pearl Jam, Nirvana and Rage Against the Machine. Call it Peter Pan syndrome if you like, but slim jeans, tidy knitwear and carefully tailored coats have never felt like home. Grunge is a style that helps me feel rooted, wherever I am. Last year, I attended a press conference that the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was giving in Jerusalem. Most people were in suits and ties. I was wearing baggy, faded jeans and a loose beige shirt. Being one of the only people dressed differently brought back that feeling of rebellion that had fuelled my youth.Lorenzo Tondo‘My motto now I’ve lost my eyesight is:if they’re gonna look, make them stare’Lucy Edwards,30, disability activist, near BirminghamView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ayesha Jones/The GuardianWhat I wear has changed a lot over the years. I lost my eyesight nearly 14 years ago – the sight in my right eye at 11 and left eye at 17. I don’t wear the clothes “sighted Lucy” used to wear – I’ve come so far and if I were to dress as her that would be weird. Sighted Lucy had a lot of internalised ableism. She wore things that might have made her feel amazing because she looked in the mirror – they were a lot more skin-tight – and now blind Lucy prioritises things that are flowy and tactile. It’s been a long journey to get here.I feel happiest when I feel the most comfy, which isn’t necessarily what looks the best, and I’m OK with that. I had this little voice in my head for so long, saying, “A sighted person has to tell you whether it looks good, whether it flatters your body”. Whereas now what I wear is just what I feel the best in, and often that is sequins, feathers, velour, silk – things that feel nice.When I was planning my wedding, all the girls in my life came down and watched me try on dresses, but it was really important that I put the dress on alone first and asked myself, “Do I want to show this to my family? Do I want their sighted opinion, or do I just want my opinion here?” So that was a big part of me choosing. The dress I picked was so lovely that I didn’t have to have that visual affirmation – I knew in myself it was right. Although I did love their reaction when I came out in it.I do still ask my sighted family about colour, and my sister is my mirror when I need one. She has autism, and because her world is black and white she will say directly, “No, you can’t wear that” or “Yes, you can.” That provides so much comfort. Often, if I dress in colour it tends to be the same colour top and bottom, which is why I end up wearing a lot of co-ords.When it comes to what I wear, my voice has definitely got louder the older I’ve become. My motto is: if they’re gonna look, make them stare. So I make sure to have a glittery harness for my guide dog, Miss Molly, or a glittery cane for me. I also make sure me and Miss Molly match. I see it as part of my activism. For so long I hated being a guide-dog user. But now I’m, like, “No, Lucy, that is so much internalised ableism, absolutely effing not.”I get dressed more for myself now than ever. I still wear heels, which surprises some people. I’m less likely to go for stilettos, but if I do I just change my cane height to match. I put on makeup and get dressed. People will ask why, given it’s so visual. But I’m seeing the non‑visual elements of it. It’s a ritual and it grounds me. What I wear has to feel happy. Getting dressed now is freeing – I can just be myself.Explore more on these topicsFashionMen's fashionVintage fashionBody imageHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I see the incredible promise’: on set of an AI film shoot as new studios embrace controversial tech | Film industry | The Guardian
description: Amid fears for jobs, some film-makers say AI could enable them bypass studio giants and take more creative risks
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Amid fears for jobs, some film-makers say AI could enable them bypass studio giants and take more creative risks
Content: Actor Tori Thomas on set at the AI studio Promise in Los Angeles filming the studio’s newly announced AI-enabled horror film, Touch Grass.Photograph: Alex Welsh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenActor Tori Thomas on set at the AI studio Promise in Los Angeles filming the studio’s newly announced AI-enabled horror film, Touch Grass.Photograph: Alex Welsh/The GuardianFilm industry‘I see the incredible promise’: on set of an AI film shoot as new studios embrace controversial techAmid fears for jobs, some film-makers say AI could enable them bypass studio giants and take more creative risksRobert BoothSun 16 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNear the collonaded entrance to Sony Pictures’ historic Culver City film studio, a tech-powered rival has sprung up this summer. The artists at Promise, a new studio feeding off the potential of AI, can glimpse the lots where Singin’ in the Rain and Men in Black were shot, but no longer do they need to get beyond the studio’s high walls to make their visions come true.From far more modest premises, they are making movies with rapidly accelerating AI models that create backgrounds, special effects and even “synthetic performers” – using US models but also driven by market-leading Chinese AI.Backed by Google, Silicon Valley venture capitalists and Disney, Promise is one of a rising number of AI film studios now taking root in Hollywood, with the result that traditional studios’ vast sound stages and financing are becoming less necessary.It is a controversial trend. Leading directors including Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro have criticised generative technology, actors and writers are fearing for their jobs, and the Democratic congresswoman Laura Friedman, who represents Hollywood’s actors, writers and directors, warned last month: “We can’t wait until we see tens of thousands of American workers displaced.”But the excitement and energy about AI’s potential was palpable this week at Promise’s new base when a human actor, Tori Thomas, waited for her call amid rows of computers for early shooting on the studio’s newly announced AI-enabled horror film, Touch Grass, with a budget in the low millions of dollars.The sound stage was little more than a corner of the office hung with white sheets. A small camera followed Thomas as she scrambled in a chase scene, then the AI did the rest. It superimposed her movement in real time on to a field of swaying grass generated by a Chinese AI model, Seedance 2.5, released this month, which looks set to dramatically slash production times.Whole scenes – actor and backdrop – were instantly visible on the director’s handheld monitor, as if they were filming in real locations. Even the seedheads in the AI-generated meadow moved as Thomas appeared to brush past. In another take, the field was easily replaced by a nightmarish underground cavern. With a glance at the screen, Thomas could immediately see the backdrop she was acting with.Promise is not alone in embracing the technology, which Netflix last week said it had used in 300 of its 1,000 titles in 2026. Ron Howard, the veteran director of the Da Vinci Code and A Beautiful Mind, is set to release an AI-enabled animated documentary feature about prisoners of war in Vietnam, working with another new AI studio, Obsidian. Brad Pitt said this week that while there was a lot of pushback, “AI is going to be the very thing that, if used as a tool, is going to help these mid-budget films, $40m- to $90m-budgeted films, get made.”Filming crew at Promise studioThat chimed with predictions from a new wave of AI native film-makers, such as Kavan “the Kid” Cardoza, 37, who has set up the Phantom X studio. He predicted a creative renaissance circumventing the studio giants not seen since Quentin Tarantino and Spike Lee’s breakthroughs more than 30 years ago.Why are respected film-makers suddenly embracing AI?Read moreThe Promise shoot involved veteran film-makers including Joel Hynek, an Oscar winner who worked on the manual special effects for Arnold Schwarzenegger’s 1987 action-horror film Predator.“When we went from optical to digital film, we thought we’d gone to heaven,” he told the Guardian. “It’s like that again. So many things are easy to do. I am an embracer of AI. Some people are wary of it, a little afraid of it, but I see the incredible promise.”Others, like Nolan, voice concern. “I’ve never seen a technology advancing so rapidly, so completely rejected by the public,” the Odyssey director has said. “Everybody’s suspicion of it is so extreme, particularly young people.”There has been a backlash against anAI resurrection of the late actor Val Kilmerto star in a new feature and the emergence of the AI “actor” Tilly Norwood, with the actor Emily Blunt calling it “really, really scary” and pleading: “Please stop taking away our human connection.”But the new AI studios are undeterred. Dave Clark, the director of Promise’s Touch Grass – who is also working on an animation, Hardcore 94, set to an early 1990s LA hip-hop soundtrack – said that with “great dialogue and backstory”, AI-generated characters could become interesting and believable.The US actors’ union Sag-Aftra will no doubt beg to differ, but Cardoza predicted: “Next year [AI actors will] be just as good as real actors.”George Strompolos, a co-founder and the chief executive of Promise, estimated that hybrid AI films – human actors alongside AI technology – would prove 20% to 50% cheaper than conventional production. That could free film-makers from requiring major studio investment.View image in fullscreenDave Clark, co-founder of the AI studio Promise.Photograph: Alex Welsh/The Guardian“We’re at the beginning of a golden era of independent, highly empowered creative companies – call them small studios, micro studios – that will lead to more creative risk-taking,” he said.Joanna Popper, a producer and an adviser on AI to production companies, said the positive view on AI in film and TV was that it “empowers anybody with a talent and a discipline for storytelling to be able to go make what they want to make”. But she said: “The concern is … if five tech companies suck all of the financial gain out of the industry.”Imagine, the 41-year-old studio run by Howard and Brian Grazer, now has an AI studio, Obsidian, operating from space in its Beverly Hills HQ. It has partnered with Obsidian to make The Code, an AI-enabled, Howard-directed animated feature based on drawings made in Vietnamese captivity by US prisoners of war.D Ryan Reeb, an executive producer at Obsidian, estimated the technology delivered a 30% to 40% cost saving. He said he had met with dozens of top production companies interested in the technology and predicted all would use it. But AI in Hollywood has drawn comparison to plastic surgery: everyone’s doing it but nobody wants to talk about it. “It’s 100% like that,” Reeb said.An AI native film-maker such as Cardoza, who makes films in his spare bedroom in Playa Vista, has no reason to downplay his AI use. It has helped him reach 28m YouTube views for his Chronicles of Bone fantasy universe series launched online last autumn, featuring his versions of Robin Hood, Peter Pan, King Arthur and Tinkerbell and a lucrative deal with the Magnific AI platform. Cardoza believes AI film-makers are attracting audiences because, ironically, their direct authorial voice has greater authenticity than in Hollywood where “they turn writing into algorithms”.View image in fullscreenKavan ‘the Kid’ Cardoza at his home in Los Angeles.Photograph: Alex Welsh/The Guardian“I’ve had meetings with studios where [they say] a horror movie has to have X amount of jump scares … Why can’t I just write the story? And if there’s two jump scares, there’s two. If there’s 10, there’s 10. Why are we hitting markers? That’s not creativity – that’s manufacture.”He said the growth in AI-led film-making “reminds me more of the 90s era when you got Tarantino, [Robert] Rodriguez and all these guys popping off … You put on any one of their movies and you will know that it’s theirs without their name being shown because of the style and voice.” Now, he said, films in cinemas “all look the same”.Cardoza highly rates the models made by Chinese tech companies who are “smoking everybody on everything – the image generation models, the video generation models.”He assumes the Chinese models are so powerful because they have been “trained on everything under the sun”, in a way that US models cannot be because of intellectual property restrictions. But with Washington considering restrictions on Chinese open-source AI models, Cardoza opposes a ban on such powerful tools, which have allowed him a creative flourishing.“I’ll move to China,” he said. “I’m not even lying.”View image in fullscreenTori Thomas filming a scene from Touch Grass.Photograph: Alex Welsh/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsFilm industryAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘Why did it become personal?’: furore over plans to expand Kent oyster shack | Kent | The Guardian
description: James Green’s oyster company owns a chunk of Whitstable’s shoreline but success has not brought affection from residents
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: James Green’s oyster company owns a chunk of Whitstable’s shoreline but success has not brought affection from residents
Content: James Green wants to build decking and a pergola for a seating area on the beach.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJames Green wants to build decking and a pergola for a seating area on the beach.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianKent‘Why did it become personal?’: furore over plans to expand Kent oyster shackJames Green’s oyster company owns a chunk of Whitstable’s shoreline but success has not brought affection from residentsDaniel Boffeyin WhitstableSun 16 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe clink of glasses and the lapping of the tide was punctuated by giggling toddlers and the slurp of oysters at tables populated by people gently sizzling on a baking day on theKentseaside.But James Green, of the Whitstable Oyster Fishery Company, had the demeanour of a man who had found grit in his mollusc. “I don’t like to use the term but it is nimbyism,” he said. “Why did it become personal? I don’t know really. Because we’re a family business, it’s a relatively small town?”Green, 58, is the director of the WOFC, a company he inherited from his father and whoserootscan be traced back to 1793. He has become embroiled in a battle over his plans for a seafood empire.The WOFC harvests about 2m oysters a year from Whitstable’s seabeds, half of which stay on the south coast to be sold in the company’s hotel and the four restaurants it runs on the front.View image in fullscreenThe Forge seaside oyster shack that Green wants to extend on to a patch of beach.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianIt is Green’s application to extend the seating of one of those restaurants, the Forge oyster shack, on to a patch of beach used to store boats belonging to members of the Whitstable Yacht Club, that has caused a furore and which he says highlights a national problem.Green is battling, he says, to grow a business that employs 200 people but could take on more, and which has cemented Whitstable’s reputation as “Britain’s Oysteropolis”. The new seating for the Forge would allow visitors to enjoy “half a dozen oysters and a glass of muscadet” on the sand, he said, and offer further reason to visit the town.In 1865, more than 100 boats in Whitstable harvested about 80m oysters for sale at the Billingsgate fish market each year. By the 1970s, overfishing, pollution and the arrival of introduced diseases with imported stock resulted in the collapse of the industry.Green’s father, Barrie, bought the WOFC in 1976. The company had one employee and was barely functioning. It was Green’s sons, James and Richard, who started the industrial-scale farming of non-native Pacific rock oysters in 2008, helping to make Whitstable’s reputation what it is today. But the Greens had to fight a lengthy and expensive campaign nearly a decade ago for the right to maintain the thousands of metal racks off the beach on which they grow.View image in fullscreenThe WOFC harvests about 2m oysters a year from Whitstable’s seabeds, half of which stay on the south coast to be sold in the company’s hotel and four restaurants.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianThe company’s success – it is the owner of a considerable chunk of the town’s beach and its shoreline – has not brought affection. The planning application in June for extra seating space and a pergola for the Forge has already attracted more than 200 opposing submissions, including from the Environment Agency which is concerned about the impact on flood defences.Some Whitstable residents called it “a carbuncle” and a “horrifying visual, physical and commercial intrusion”. “Disastrous,” said another of the intention for the cafe to serve alcohol and seafood to customers’ tables on both sides of the King Charles III coastal path that traces the outline of the coast.Paul McNally, speaking on behalf of the Whitstable Beach Campaign, a group that was at the vanguard of the attempt to block the metal racks in 2018, said there was no justification for the Forge’s extension on to the beach.“Our remit, for many years, has been a simple one – to protect the unspoilt nature of Whitstable beach and maintain public access to it. Both of which would be compromised by the current development proposal.”View image in fullscreenA Green party councillor, who opposes the extension plans, said people were ‘highly protective’ of the beach.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianGreen, who spent £1m on his planning application for the racks, and who unsuccessfully sought a licensing application for a similar extension of the Forge five years ago, detects a “general antipathy” towards his company as well as a lack of realism about the economic challenges facing the area and the UK.“I think this country has a problem with commercial enterprises and expansion maybe,” he said. “And people don’t like change. Maybe we are perceived as quite a big company in a small town.”Five years ago, when asked to consider an appeal against Canterbury city council’s rejection of the company’s plans, a district judge noted that Green – an “able and determined businessman who through force of will and personality drives forward his projects to commercial success” – had “generated some public animosity towards him personally”.Green and his company had become the “source of tension, even open hostility, with some within the local community”, the judge added.Stuart Heaver, a Green party councillor in Whitstable who opposes the extension plans for the Forge, said it was an unfortunate side to the dispute. “People are highly protective of the beach, and it’s a maritime town,” he said. “It is a close-knit community and people get very excited when people try to alter things.“I have met James Green a few times, a perfectly sensible and nice fellow, but there is a history in the town of a little bit of friction between the company and local residents.”View image in fullscreenThe Whitstable Yacht Club, which leases the area of beach from the WOFC that Green wants to expand on to, now says it has no objection to the expansion.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianGreen remains unabashed. The licensing application failed last time in part due to the scale of opposition to it, including fromWhitstable Yacht Club, which leases the beach from the WOFC to store its boats.This time the club, after being offered a better lease in return for giving up some space, has said it has no objection. “The Whitstable economy is based on tourism, like it or lump it,” said Green. “In this day and age you have to do things that are going to make it somewhere people want to go.“To me, it is completely bonkers that it shouldn’t be supported. I am not looking to build flats on the beach – it’s decking and a pergola, for fuck’s sake.”Explore more on these topicsKentSeafoodFood & drink industryFishRestaurantsFoodLocal politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Destroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the Danube | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: The Guardian travelled 100 miles along the EU’s longest river, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking water
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: The Guardian travelled 100 miles along the EU’s longest river, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking water
Content: The Hungarian parliament building on the banks of the Danube is not being lit as normal at night owing to energy-saving measures being imposed during drought conditionsView image in fullscreenThe Hungarian parliament building on the banks of the Danube is not being lit as normal at night owing to energy-saving measures being imposed during drought conditionsThe Sunday readClimate crisisDestroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the DanubeThe Guardian travelled 100 miles along the EU’s longest river, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking waterLorenzo Tondoin Hungary. Photographs byDavid LeveneSun 16 Aug 2026 06.37 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareFor centuries, the rock was seen as a warning. When it began to emerge from the Danube, beneath Gellért Hill in Budapest, it meant the river had fallen so low that floating mills could no longer operate, crops were probably failing, and hunger would almost certainly follow. That is why, in the Hungarian capital, where over time the boulder became little more than a legend, it was namedÍnség-szikla– the Rock of Starvation.Today, amid record-low water levels on the Danube, the rock has not only emerged from the water, but surfaced almost in its entirety, along with the sandy riverbed on which it rests, astonishing geologists and government scientists sent to examine it. And, much as the rock was said to warn, Hungary is now facing an unprecedented energy crisis that has forced the countryto shut down all but one of its Danube-cooled nuclear reactorsfor the first time in 44 years.The Guardian travelled for more than 100 miles (160km) along the banks of the Danube, the EU’s longest river, which sustains the 10 countries it crosses, visiting villages and towns where residents are struggling to secure drinking water and farmers are fighting to keep their crops alive.PócsmegyerLast week, the Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar,warnedthat the economic damage caused by this year’s drought was expected to surpass that of the historic dry spell that devastated Hungary’s farmland in 2022.View image in fullscreenIstván Somogyi has lost nearly 50% of his harvest this yearWhile the full extent of the losses is still difficult to assess, István Somogyi, a 56-year-old farmer from Pócsmegyer, a village on the Danube, in Pest County, has already done his calculations.View image in fullscreen“I’ve lost nearly 50% of my harvest this year and it could go up to 70%,” he said. “It’s gone. Everything has dried up. Since I started farming this land after the end of communist rule, I’ve never seen a catastrophe like this.”Somogyi said the unprecedented crisis did not come out of nowhere, and that the heatwaves and droughts of previous years had already offered a warning. Scientistssaythat human-caused climate breakdown is making every heatwave in the world more intense and more likely to happen.“You could see this coming,” he said. “The harvest was already poor last year. But we were lucky because the Danube stayed high. Despite the intense heat, there was still enough water in the soil. This time, there is no hope of saving our crops.”On the near-deserted roads running alongside the river, families with children sought relief in the Danube’s shallow waters, while, not far away, military water tankers were siphoning water from rural wells, hauling vital supplies to the storage pools that feed the local grid.SzentendreView image in fullscreenLow water levels in the Danube at SzentendreAcross the river from Pócsmegyer, on the opposite bank of the Danube, lies Szentendre, a town known for its community of artists. During the most intense days of the heatwave, some evening performances have been held by candlelight in an effort to reduce electricity consumption.View image in fullscreenAerial view of a long boat filled with people in shallow waterHere, in recent weeks, vast, desert-like islands have emerged. The exposed riverbed is cracked like a mosaic of hard, dry clay, baked by suffocating heat that has pushed temperatures in Budapestclose to 42C, with overnight temperatures hitting a high of 28C. Europe is warming faster than any other continent, with intense summer heat and prolonged drought being amplified by the deepening human-caused climate crisis. Extreme conditions continue to fuel wildfires and strain water supplies.View image in fullscreenJózsef Gulyás stands in front of stocks of bottled water being kept at the town hall in case of supply shortagesIn some stretches of the Danube near Szentendre, it is now possible towalk through itwith the water barely reaching above your ankles.“Swimming and navigation are banned here,” said László Balázs, 44, head of the local river rescue service. “But people escaping the heat still enter the water, unaware it can suddenly drop into deep pools where they risk drowning.”At the end of June, Budapest police (BRFK) saidthree people had gone missingin the Danube over a single weekend. Water police later recovered one body near Iváncsa, while searches continued downstream for the other two missing swimmers.The drought and resulting disruption to energy supplies have also left some Hungarian towns struggling with shortages of drinking water. In a room inside Szentendre’s tourist information office, thousands of bottles of water are stored ready to be distributed, particularly to elderly and vulnerable residents.“About 4,000 to 5,000 households were left without water,” said József Gulyás, 62, Szentendre’s deputy mayor. “We distributed 25 tonnes of water and received about 100 emergency calls a day. We had never experienced anything so serious. Elderly women would hug the officers delivering water and burst into tears.”BudapestView image in fullscreenA geologist takes advantage of the low water levels to view the ‘Rock of Starvation’Driving from north to south, towards the Hungarian capital, Budapest, where the level of the Danube under normal conditions reaches an average height of 2 to 3 metres, and can rise as high as 8 metres, intense summer heat and continuing drought conditions caused the river to fall to a record low of just14-19 cmon 4 August.Average daily water level, cmThe water levels have fallen so dramatically that, as the Danube has retreated, it has revealed a succession of relics long hidden beneath its waters, including the remains of awoolly mammoth, abridgedestroyed after the second world war in Budapest, aNazi warshipand anunexploded British bomb.View image in fullscreenTourists and passersby look down over the side of the Liberty bridge in Budapest. The remains of an older bridge can be seen the shallow waters below.The water is so low in the capital that on 28 July, at about 4.30pm, Gábor Kürti, president of the Magyar Kerékpárosklub (Hungarian cyclists’ club) and owner of a cargo bike company, left his office in central Budapest, jumped on his bicycle and, in an unprecedented feat, rode for 30km along the exposed bed of the Danube, with his journey quickly going viral onsocial media.View image in fullscreenKürti rode for 30km along newly-exposed beds of the Danube“I wanted to show that if you can cycle along the bed of the Danube for 30km, it means that, because of this climate emergency, we have literally hit rock bottom,” he told the Guardian.Riding his KTM X-Strada 20 gravel bike, Kürti set off from the mouth of the Szilas stream (Szilas-patak) and made his way across fine gravel, large pebbles, hard-packed sand and mud, eventually reaching the ferry terminal at Vác about three hours later.“For many people it was an extraordinary adventure. For me, it was heartbreaking,” he said. “Cycling through parts of the river where, as a child, I used to swim or go kayaking, and which I could now cross on a bicycle, filled me with an indescribable sadness. It was like looking at the scene of a terrible accident. Throughout that journey, the scale of the catastrophe was unfolding before my eyes.”NagytétényView image in fullscreenThe Kis-Háros-sziget island nature reserve is usually only accessible by boat but is now reachable by foot, as low water levels in the Danube have exposed the river bed connecting the island to the mainlandKürti took the Guardian into what, until only a few months ago, was the striking floodplain forest in Nagytétény named Kis-Háros-sziget, a protected area home to climbing plants, wild vines and several families of European beavers.The river is reached by walking across ground that would normally lie several metres beneath the water. Here, one branch of the Danube has receded so dramatically that it came to an abrupt halt, blocked by an exposed riverbed left behind by the drought.Its dry, clay-like surface looks like an image from a future shaped by the escalating human-caused climate crisis. Yet this is happening now. Passersby walk across what was once the river, their feet sinking into patches of mud. Kayakers struggle to make their way through the remaining shallow channels; many eventually give up, lift their kayaks on to their shoulders and walk home.Hungarian authorities have beenpumping water into large areas of the country’s nature reservessuch as the one in Nagytétény, to keep marshlands from drying out as the drought intensifies.PaksView image in fullscreenHungary’s only nuclear power station, in Paks near to the banks of the river DanubeContinuing south, the road finally reaches Paks, home to Hungary’s nuclear power plant, its towers rising above the horizon. Here, municipal workers have been working weekends to keep more than 700 threatened trees alive and water the town’s flowerbeds.View image in fullscreenSzilvia Farkas: ‘I have never seen so much vegetation dry out in all my years doing this job.’“I’ve been doing this job for 18 years,” said Szilvia Farkas, 39, who is employed by Dunakom Zrt in Paks, owned entirely by the municipality, to plant and water trees and plants. “I have never seen so much vegetation dry out in all my years doing this job, and I have never worked as hard as I have this year to try to keep it alive.”Dunakom Zrt uses its own drilled well for water extraction. In addition, the company is able to extract water from a decantation basin. The public is not permitted to use tap water for irrigation at the moment; instead, residents collect greywater and use it to water their gardens.In the country’s more marginalised and deprived areas, the water crisis has compounded longstanding problems for thousands of people who were already living in difficult conditions before the drought, struggling with inadequate access to running water and sewage systems.Géza Orsós Renáta, 43, who lives with her four children in a small farmhouse on the outskirts of Paks, has never had access to running water. Orsós, who also works for Dunakom Zrt, helping to water public green spaces drying out in the heat, has long relied on water from a neighbour.View image in fullscreenGéza Orsós Renáta is helping to water public green spaces drying out in the heat“Even in winter, we have to pump water and heat it in large bowls so we can wash,” she said. “Now a friend brings us water once a week. But it is becoming unbearable.”Driving back from Paks, tall, swollen clouds occasionally gather on the horizon in the clear skies above Budapest, appearing to promise the return of rain, only to fade by evening, dashing the hopes of an entire country.For now, people can do little but cling to the hope that the Rock of Starvation will disappear once more beneath the currents of the Danube, returning to the depths of the river and becoming little more than a legend again.But Somogyi, who grew up hearing the story of the boulder passed down through generations, and who is now witnessing the consequences of the warning it was said to foretell, knows it will not.“The drought will return next year,” he said. “That is the trend. And there isn’t much that we can do.”Zsuzsa Borbély contributed to this reportThis article was amended on 16 August 2026. An earlier version included a map which placed Croatia in Serbia’s location; this has been corrected.

title: Turbocharge special needs internships to help tackle UK youth jobs crisis, says Milburn | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Government review led by former minister to recommend huge expansion of onsite schemes for those who need support
Author: Claudia Efemini
Headline: Exclusive: Government review led by former minister to recommend huge expansion of onsite schemes for those who need support
Content: Alan Milburn, who is leading a government review of young people and work, said supported internships should be scaled up to combat ‘devastating’ joblessness rates.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlan Milburn, who is leading a government review of young people and work, said supported internships should be scaled up to combat ‘devastating’ joblessness rates.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianYouth unemploymentTurbocharge special needs internships to help tackle UK youth jobs crisis, says MilburnExclusive: Government review led by former minister to recommend huge expansion of onsite schemes for those who need supportPatrick ButlerandClaudia EfeminiSun 16 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpecialist internships designed to secure work for young people with special educational needs should be put on “turbocharge” to help tackle the growing youth jobs crisis, a government review is to propose.Alan Milburn who isleading a reviewof young people and work, said supported internships should be scaled up to combat “devastating” joblessness rates for young people with a learning disability, autism or mental illness.Nationally, as few as 5% of some groups of young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) move into permanent jobs. However, employment rates among those who complete supported internship schemes can be as high as 70%.Nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are classified as Neet (not in employment, education or training), a 10-year high that Milburn – a former minister in the Tony Blair government – has said represents a moral crisis and is economically unsustainable.Number of young people out of work or training in UK could hit 1.25m by early 2030sRead moreIn May, his first report warned that Britain risked a 25% rise in the number of Neets to 1.25 million by the early 2030s without urgent government action. Central to the recent growth of Neets is an increase in young people diagnosed at school with neurodevelopmental conditions or mental illness who do not make the transition into work, leaving them at high risk of becoming economically inactive.Milburn said the UK had to move away from the idea that people with a diagnosis were unable to work. They can work, he said. “The question is: are the opportunities there and is the support there?“Supported internships have got such an effective track record. With the best ones around 70% of the people on them end up in paid employment. In my view we have to turbocharge support – and at the moment the system is not set up to do that.”Milburn dismissed “myths” about 18- to 24-year-olds being a “snowflake generation”, saying: “The problem isn’t shortage of effort on the part of young people. It’s a shortage of opportunities, jobs, support.”He added: “There are two views about [the rise in youth ill health]. You can either say it’s fake or you can decide its real. It’s a real phenomenon. So we’ve got to deal with it and we have got to adjust our systems to deal with it.”The Guardian recently reported that English primary schools could berequired to identify childrenat risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job as part of the Milburn review.“The warning signs are there from a very early, early age,” he told the newspaper. “You know, frankly from preschool.“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”The year-long internships provide tailored onsite work experience and job coaching for 16- to 24-year-olds with education, health and care plans (EHCPs) who face high barriers to the job market. Employers involved include the NHS, Asda and Amazon.Callum Beeston, a 20-year-old from Doncaster who has autism, recently completed a supported internship at Amazon with job coach support fromAspirations Doncaster. This month he started a full-time job there as a warehouse operative, and has been praised for his work from his bosses.Beeston said his family’s expectations of him finding work after he finished school were low and he was “unsure what to do next”. His grandmother used to say she would leave her will to him because she was worried he would never get work. “In the last 12 months I’ve become a very confident young fella,” he said.View image in fullscreenCallum Beeston, right, with Alan Milburn. Beeston recently completed a supported internship at Amazon and now works there as a warehouse operative.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianKim Patterson, the finance director at Aspirations Doncaster, said school-based ECHP support often “drops off a cliff” once students leave. Some autistic young people find it hard to manage job applications and interviews, and can struggle to adapt to work routines without specialist support.In England there are just 4,500 supported internships. About 48% of supported interns found paid work, according to anofficial evaluationpublished this year by the Department for Education, although some internship providers report job success rates as high as 70%.Milburn said capacity shortages meant there was no guarantee a young person with Send could access a supported internship in their local area. He believed that while the model worked it lacked the resources to be delivered at scale, and there was low awareness of the scheme among parents, employers and schools.He was tight-lipped on how such an expansion might be paid for, with fears funding might be taken from young people’s disability benefits. His final recommendations are expected to be delivered to the government in the autumn.Milburn said the system was geared too much towards paying health and disability benefits and not enough towards supporting young people to enter the job market.“If you are a young person today and you apply and get a health and disability benefit, there’s a 50% chance that in 15 years’ time you will still be eligible. You’ll still be out of work. That is neither a good outcome, frankly, nor is it a progressive cause,” he said.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentSpecial educational needsAutismMental healthYoung peopleCareersUnemploymentShareReuse this content

title: Reform accused of targeting the most vulnerable with £50bn benefit cut | Benefits | The Guardian
