description: Robert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Robert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’
Content: Robert Jenrick said it was ‘just plain immoral’ to pay social security to non-British people.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert Jenrick said it was ‘just plain immoral’ to pay social security to non-British people.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesBenefitsReform accused of targeting the most vulnerable with £50bn benefit cutRobert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’Rowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 16 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been accused of excluding the most vulnerable from society and punishing non-Britons living in the UK as it prepared to outline £50bn of cuts to benefits for disabled people and foreign nationals.Robert Jenrick, Reform’s finance spokesperson, will detail the plans for £20bn of cuts to disability benefits overall, as well as another £21bn from stopping foreign nationals – including EU citizens with settled status – claiming almost any benefits, among other cuts.The party said the plans were aimed at reducing the welfare bill by a quarter, with personal independence payments (Pip) replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”.It said “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by councils and mayors.In relation to foreign nationals, the plans extendproposals set out by Nigel Faragelast year in which he claimed that banning migrants from claiming some benefits and scrapping indefinite leave to remain would save £234bn over several decades.Jenrick’s policy paper goes further by stopping foreign-born households claiming universal credit, housing benefit, pension credit, jobseeker’s allowance, child benefit, free childcare, free school meals or disability benefits.The paper says the change would save the taxpayer £21bn a year by the fifth year of the policy, and would also apply to those with EU settled status. However, foreign-born parents with British-born children would still be eligible for child benefit and free school meals.Best for Britain, the pro-EU campaign group, said denying benefits to those with indefinite leave to remain would tear up Britain’s EU withdrawal agreement.Tom Brufatto, the executive director of policy at the organisation, said: “Ourpollingshows that people do want to renegotiate our relationship with Europe, but by moving closer, not by damaging ties with vital allies and punishing our neighbours, colleagues and friends who have settled status here.”Disability benefits system ‘not working’ Timms review findsRead moreJenrick claimed paying benefits to non-British people was “plain immoral” – even though many would have paid into the tax system through working. He also wrote in the Telegraph over the weekend that the amount spent on disability benefits was “not generosity … it is suicidal empathy”.However, Jenrick was accused by campaigners of making life harder for disabled people and of not understanding that it would not save money.Rachael Maskell, the Labour MP who led the campaign against previous disability benefit cuts under Keir Starmer, said: “When Pip helps people go to work, play a role in our society and simply live, threatening to remove Pip demonstrates that Reform do not want disabled people to play a full role in our society.“Instead, Labour is working with disabled people throughthe Timms reviewto optimise the impact of Pip to ensure both taxpayers and disabled people get real value out of the system.“Instead of making it harder for disabled people, who already experience significant financial deprivation, they should spend time learning of the benefit it brings.”Linda Burnip, the co-founder of Disabled People Against Cuts, said previous attempts to replace disability benefits with cheaper options had not been successful.“Originally the Tories scrapped disability living allowance and replaced it with Pip, aiming to save 20% from the social security bill,” she said.“However, this obviously has failed and the major problem with Reform’s crude plans to save money by denying payments to disabled people is that they fail to understand that a relatively small payment, which supports someone, could result in a massive saving overall from the public purse.“It could, for example, mean someone with a mental health condition is able to remain living safely in the community rather than needing to spend weeks or even months in a hospital for which private firms often charge around £12,000 per person a week.”Labour described the plans to cut disability benefits as “fantasy economics” that would “strip support” from disabled people and shift the costs of employing people with sickness or a disability on to employers through an insurance-based model.Mothin Ali, the Green party deputy leader, said the “establishment parties are all trying to outdo each other when it comes to who can be the most xenophobic, who can punch down the hardest to the most vulnerable in our country, and who can cut the most support from disabled people”.He added: “It is cowardly to take from the most defenceless when we should be taxing the super-wealthy, including those who are in the privileged position of accepting £5m donations,” he added, referring to Farage, the leader of Reform UK.Meanwhile, the Conservatives, who are trying to show they are taking a tough stance on welfare, said Reform’s announcement was “cobbled together” and claimed only the Tories had a “credible plan to save £23bn from welfare alongside our root and branch review of sickness benefits”.Explore more on these topicsBenefitsReform UKDisabilityRobert JenrickNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason Arday | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: University says it continued to provide support after resignation of academic, who was found dead on Friday
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: University says it continued to provide support after resignation of academic, who was found dead on Friday
Content: Jason Arday quit his role as professor of sociology of education this month.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday quit his role as professor of sociology of education this month.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason ArdayCambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason ArdayUniversity says it continued to provide support after resignation of academic, who was found dead on FridayRachel HallSun 16 Aug 2026 10.09 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUniversity of Cambridgehas defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday.The university said it had continued to provide Arday with extensive mental health support and security measures, including installing panic alarms and screening racist emails and post, after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education this month.He quit after widespread press coverage ofaccusations of plagiarismandinconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.A University of Cambridge spokesperson said: “Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time.”Arday, 41, waspronounced deadafter emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, south London, on Friday.When he was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge at the age of 37 in 2023, he was the university’s youngest ever black professor.A vigil in Arday’s memory organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. The group’s co-convener Weyman Bennett said in a statement that Arday’s death was the “result of a racist witch-hunt”.He added: “For more than a week, the rightwing press, politicians and the far right have hounded Jason with the most vicious racism. They are spreading the far-right lie that black people are only appointed because of the colour of our skin, rather than our ability.”View image in fullscreenProf Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her top priority was ‘supporting our community through this tragedy’.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianArday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. He denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.When allegations surfaced in the UK media in July, Cambridge said it had investigated the claims and found no wrongdoing, describing Arday as the victim of a “vile smear campaign to undermine his credibility”.This month, the university announced it wouldopen a fresh investigationafter it said it received “new information” about Arday’s qualifications and career.Other elements of Arday’s life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal until the age of 11, as well as being illiterate until 18.It is understood Cambridge has paused the investigation while Arday’s family are grieving, and will consider whether to reopen it in due course.Academics and politicians have cast doubt on whether Cambridge took Arday’s vulnerability seriously when he was appointed to the ­senior public-facing role in 2023. At the time, the university had been facing criticism for its lack of diversity in senior roles.Prof Simon Baron-Cohen, Arday’s friend and former colleague, told Times Radio he thought the university should proceed with the investigation. “We should see what we learn from it. This is the whole purpose of investigations,” he said.He also questioned whether the media had failed in its duty of care towards Arday, as a vulnerable person with disabilities. He said Arday faced racist abuse and was used as a “lightning rod for a culture war on [diversity, equity and inclusion]”.Simon Woolley, the principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and Arday’s former mentor, has called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.In a statement on Saturday, Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her “thoughts and deepest condolences” were with Arday’s family, as well as with colleagues and students in the faculty of education and at Jesus College where he was a fellow.“Supporting our community through this tragedy is the single most important priority for me and my leadership team right now. We will be reaching out to many of you directly, and we are committed to ensuring that no one feels they must face this alone,” she said.A fundraiser launched by the Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon on Saturday afternoon has raised more than £65,000 to contribute towards funeral and memorial costs and support for Arday’s family.On the crowdfunder’s webpage, Vernon said: “I was one of the people who publicly supported Jason during the recent controversy because I was deeply concerned about the nature and intensity of the attacks directed towards him. I was also subject to media scrutiny for signing the letter of support and challenged in supporting Jason.”Andy Burnham, the prime minister, described Arday’s death as a “tragedy on so many levels” and urged a “moment of reflection”.In a statement issued via Simon & Schuster, which published Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, in the US this week, Arday’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.They added: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him. The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeAcademicsHigher educationUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jared Kushner meets with Hamas ahead of talks with Netanyahu on Gaza | Jared Kushner | The Guardian
description: Trump’s son-in-law and envoy held rare meeting with Hamas chief in Egypt in push for progress on ceasefire
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump’s son-in-law and envoy held rare meeting with Hamas chief in Egypt in push for progress on ceasefire
Content: Jared Kushner speaks during the 56th annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on 22 January 2026.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPAView image in fullscreenJared Kushner speaks during the 56th annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on 22 January 2026.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPAJared KushnerJared Kushner meets with Hamas ahead of talks with Netanyahu on GazaTrump’s son-in-law and envoy held rare meeting with Hamas chief in Egypt in push for progress on ceasefireAssociated PressSun 16 Aug 2026 18.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy,Jared Kushner, held a rare meeting withHamas’s political chief on Sunday inEgypt, in a new diplomatic effort to make progress in the stalled Gaza ceasefire. Kushner will meet on Monday with Benjamin Netanyahu, who is under pressure after rejecting the new 15-point, US-backed road map.The talks aim to salvage the plan for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw from the Palestinian territory shattered bywar.At stake are the lives of some 2 million people in Gaza and reconstruction of the crowded enclave now largely controlled by Israeli forces, more than 10 months since the ceasefire ended major military operations. Ameetingbetween Kushner, fellow envoy Steve Witkoff and Hamas leaders in Egypt last yearhelpedclinchthe ceasefire, whose progress until now had been stalled over the key issue of Hamas’s disarmament.The over two-hour meeting inEgyptwith Hamas’s political chief, Khalil al-Hayya, was confirmed by a regional official and a Hamas official, both speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to reporters. Kushner was one of a trio of envoys meeting with al-Hayya, with officials from mediating countries Egypt, Qatar and Turkey also there.Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his alliesRead moreHamas in a statement later called on mediators and the US-createdBoard of Peaceoverseeing the ceasefire to “compel” Israel to approve the road map for next steps.Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, last weekrejectedthe 15-point plan in a rare publicshow of defianceagainst the Trump administration, Israel’s closest ally.Kushner; Tony Blair, the former British prime minister; and Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace director, are to meet with Netanyahu on Monday, according to a source familiar with the plans and a diplomatic source. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.Several regional powers including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates issued a joint statement condemning Israel’s rejection of the road map, saying: “Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza.” Other signers included Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia and the ceasefire mediators.View image in fullscreenEgyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi receives Jared Kushner in New Alamein, Egypt, on Sunday, in the presence of foreign minister Badr Abdelatty and general intelligence service chief Hassan Rashad.Photograph: Egyptian President Office/APAImages/ShutterstockThe foreign ministers’ statement called on the Board of Peace and the US to take “immediate and concrete measures” to keep any party from obstructing the plan’s implementation.Kushner’s meeting with theHamasleader aimed at ensuring the militant group’s commitment to the road map, particularly disarmament, before his meeting with Netanyahu, the regional official said.The Hamas official said the group is committed and waiting for mediators to start the 14-day negotiation period to work out a timetable for implementation. That period requires all parties’ approval of the road map to begin.The Hamas official also said the Hamas leader demanded that Israel halt its attacks onGazaand withdraw to the so-called “yellow line” dividing the territory before beginning implementation. The yellow line was never precisely defined. Israeli forces have moved beyond it and now control about 60% of Gaza.In May, Netanyahusaidthe next step was to move to 70% control, with Israel “tightening the grip” on Hamas “from every direction”.Israel has killedmore than 1,200 Palestiniansin Gaza, and wounded more than 4,100 sinceagreeingto the ceasefire on 10 October 2025, according to Gaza’s health ministry.The White House referred questions about Kushner’s meetings to the Board of Peace, which did not immediately comment. The Tony Blair Institute did not comment.BBC seeks to subpoena Trump children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuitRead moreUnder the road map, Hamas would hand over weapons to the Palestinian technocratic committee meant to oversee daily operations in the territory. The committee has not yet entered Gaza. But Hamas has linked the surrender of its heaviest weapons to the creation of a Palestinian state, something Israel’s current government rejects.The road map involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. But Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed.That stance leaves other elements of the ceasefire on hold, including reconstruction and the deployment of international forces to separate Israeli forces from committee-controlled areas.Netanyahu faces a challengingelectionon 27 October as he tries to hold on to power with a coalition that includes ministers taking a harsh line on Gaza, and it’s not clear whether he will take decisive steps on the ceasefire before then. Also coming up is the three-year anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October.Netanyahu’s Likud party on Sunday responded to the statement by regional powers by claiming “Arab states want to topple” Netanyahu so that centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot and center-left party leader Yair Golan “will give them everything they want. That will not happen.”Robert Mackey contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsJared KushnerHamasIsrael-Gaza warTrump administrationGazaIsraelEgyptnewsShareReuse this content

title: Five teenagers killed after car driven on wrong side of Irish motorway  | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Head-on collision between two vehicles on M9 in County Kildare also injured four other people, say police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Head-on collision between two vehicles on M9 in County Kildare also injured four other people, say police
Content: Emergency services at the scene of the collision, which happened at junction 3 of the motorway near Athy.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenEmergency services at the scene of the collision, which happened at junction 3 of the motorway near Athy.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAIrelandFive teenagers killed after car driven on wrong side of Irish motorwayHead-on collision between two vehicles on M9 in County Kildare also injured four other people, say policeNadeem BadshahSun 16 Aug 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive teenagers have died and four other people have been seriously injured in a crash involving a car driving in the wrong direction on a motorway in the Republic ofIreland, police said.Gardaí confirmed the bodies of the youths, all male, had been removed from the scene of the two-vehicle collision, which happened at about 3am on Sunday on the M9 in County Kildare.The force said the occupants of the second vehicle involved, three women, two in their 30s and one in her 20s, and a boy, all remained in hospital with serious injuries.The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, described the head-on collision between the two cars as “horrific” and said “in some cases” vehicles were being driven on the wrong side of motorways for social media likes.Last weekend, nine people were injured in a head-on collision on the M50 in Dublin involving a car travelling in the wrong direction.Describing Sunday’s crash, Kelly said: “These family members were travelling innocently when they were struck by a vehicle being driven the wrong way down the motorway.“This horrific incident, after the recent collision on the M50, shows how irresponsible and dangerous driving on the wrong side of the motorway is.“That, of course, should be self-evident, but what makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes, regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves.”He added: “As this particular incident has been referred to Fiosrú, the police ombudsman, I am constrained in what I can say in detail about this incident, but I know that gardaí do what they can to stop such vehicles while also taking into consideration all other road users.“Gardaí are put in a really challenging situation dealing with such incidents.”Officers are investigating the circumstances of the crash, which happened at junction 3 of the motorway, near Athy, at about 3am on Sunday.Emergency services had been alerted to reports of a vehicle travelling southbound on the M9 northbound carriageway.Earlier, a Garda Síochána spokesperson said the female driver and front-seat passenger of the second car had been taken to Tallaght university hospital, and were in a critical condition.A female rear-seat passenger, in her 20s, was taken to St Luke’s general hospital in a serious condition.The third passenger, a child, was taken to the Children’s Health Ireland at Crumlin in Dublin, also in a serious condition.The bodies of the teenagers who died were taken to Naas general hospital, where postmortem examinations were due to take place.Gardaí appealed for anyone who witnessed the collision or has dashcam footage to come forward.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeRoad safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: Water companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during drought | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Suppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumption
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Suppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumption
Content: Thames Water are among the five companies looking into the new pricing model.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThames Water are among the five companies looking into the new pricing model.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesWater industryWater companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during droughtSuppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumptionJoanna PartridgeSun 16 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater companies could be allowed to raise bills for customers during periods of drought under proposals being considered by the sector’s regulator for England and Wales.Suppliers would be permitted to factor “water scarcity” into bills as part of efforts to reduce consumption under Ofwat’s plans, which are being likened to surge pricing – the practice where private hire firms raise taxi fares at times of higher demand.The proposals come just a few days after the prime minster, Andy Burnham,said he was angrywith water companies and accused them of treating their customers like a “blank cheque” after more than a dozen firms were given the green light to raise water bills even higher.It emerged last Thursday that five companies – Southern Water, Thames Water, Severn Trent, Wessex Water andSouth East Water– would be allowed to raise bills more than originally planned before the end of the decade to allow for billions of pounds of extra spending on repairs and infrastructure.The surge pricing proposals, first reported by the Sunday Telegraph, come after the 30 July conclusion of Ofwat’s consultation on changing the rules relating to wholesale charging, with the regulator due to share its final decision shortly.Public anger over the behaviour of water companies hassoared in recent yearsas bills have continued to climb even while sewage has flowed into the nation’s waterways andfirms have increased bosses’ payand handed out millions of pounds in dividends to shareholders.View image in fullscreenSurfers Against Sewage, seen here in Brighton, England last year, are one of many protest groups who have taken aim at the water industry.Photograph: Charlotte Coney/Getty ImagesDuring an exceptionally hot and dry summer, leading to almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales being declaredofficially in drought, suppliers have also come under fire for failing to save water lost through leaky pipes, whichcampaigners say far outstrips the amountthat could be saved through a nationwide hosepipe ban.An Ofwat spokesperson said: “The efficient use of water is in the best interests of everyone, including businesses. The options we are progressing would support greater consideration of water scarcity and efficiency by water companies when setting their charges, and encourage more tariff innovation.”Several water companies have beencarrying out charging trialsover the past few years aimed at making bills more affordable and, potentially, reducing demand.South West Water, which supplies water to about 1.8 million customers across south-west England, including Cornwall and Devon, is trialling a “rising block tariff”, where about 500 household customers are charged a cheaper rate for using a lower amount (or “block”) of water and progressively higher prices for higher consumption.The company said 90% of its customers would see lower bills on this trial, according to its assessments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUniversity spinout to launch water quality app for UK and US watersRead moreAnglian Water, which supplies 7 million customers across the east of England, the UK’s driest region, and South West Water are also trialling charging customers more for water used in the summer than in the winter months.The Guardian understands there are no government plans for nationwide surge pricing for water bills.A government spokesperson said: “Water companies are trialling new charging structures which must, as promised, make bills fairer and more affordable while encouraging greater water efficiency.”They added: “We have already ringfenced money earmarked for new infrastructure so it can only be spent on fixing the problems, and will go further by fundamentally reforming the water sector so that it works for the public, keeping bills as low as they can be.”Andy White, a senior lead for social policy at the Consumer Council for Water (CCW), a government-sponsored body that represents customers’ interests, said water companies were right to explore new tariff structures that could help manage demand and give customers more control over their bills.He said: “Any new approach must be fair and protect customers who are already struggling with rising water costs. None of the schemes currently being trialled are designed to generate additional revenue for water companies, and many are structured so that most customers will pay less overall.”White added that companies should give consumers smart meter data to give them a clearer picture of how they use water.A spokesperson for Water UK, the industry’s trade association, said companies were working to cut down on leaks, adding: “We also need to consider whether we could help people save water by rewarding people through their water bill. This might include eliminating standing charges or expanding discounts for customers who save water.”Explore more on these topicsWater industryUtilitiesWater billsHousehold billsThames WaterSevern TrentSouth East WaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Summer jobs bounce back in UK thanks to busy calendar of sport and music | Hospitality industry | The Guardian
description: Industry tracker finds ‘exceptionally warm weather’ has helped boost job listings in hospitality and tourism sector
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Industry tracker finds ‘exceptionally warm weather’ has helped boost job listings in hospitality and tourism sector
Content: Typical entry-level jobs for young people, such as catering or bar work, have seen a slight uptick over this summer in the UK.Photograph: Martin Bennett/AlamyView image in fullscreenTypical entry-level jobs for young people, such as catering or bar work, have seen a slight uptick over this summer in the UK.Photograph: Martin Bennett/AlamyHospitality industrySummer jobs bounce back in UK thanks to busy calendar of sport and musicIndustry tracker finds ‘exceptionally warm weather’ has helped boost job listings in hospitality and tourism sectorJoanna PartridgeSun 16 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe summer job has staged a comeback this year thanks to the hot weather and a packed calendar of events such as the men’s football World Cup, new UK figures show.Recent months have seen a significant increase in seasonal hiring in sectors such as hospitality and tourism compared with summer 2025, said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC), which runs a monthly labour market tracker.It said that this time last year “there was concern about the death of the great British summer job”, but added: “This is the summer when the seasonal summer jobs market started to come back.“Exceptionally warm weather and a busy calendar of sporting, music and cultural events … has helped boost demand for workers.”Unemployed young people to join AI boot camps to get job-readyRead moreA dip in postings for summer jobs last year fuelled concerns that squeezed employers would continue to cut back on seasonal hiring, which has traditionallygiven young people their first experienceof the world of work.However, this year there has been a double-digit rise in hospitality and tourism job advertisements over the summer period.But there was a slight dip in the number of active job postings and new job postings in July this year when compared with the previous month.Maxine Bligh, the REC’s chief membership and innovation officer, said: “It is not totally straightforward for young people to earn wages just yet, with many entry-level jobs still not bouncing back as much as we would like.“But there are undoubtedly more opportunities across hospitality, tourism and construction than last year.”She added that “the prospect of an Indian summer in much of the UK may mean many of these opportunities last longer than usual”.There were just under 1.67m active job postings in the UK in July this year, which is up 7.7% on a year earlier but a 2.6% drop from June.Explore more on title: ‘It’s been very tough’: hope of progress in gruelling battle against south Wales wildfire | Wales | The Guardian
description: Efforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the future
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Efforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the future
Content: Military personnel cut fire breaks to minimise the spread of the flames.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMilitary personnel cut fire breaks to minimise the spread of the flames.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianWales‘It’s been very tough’: hope of progress in gruelling battle against south Wales wildfireEfforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the futureBethan McKernanWales correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than three weeks after it began burning and two days after the military deployed to the area, there is hope that the huge wildfire on the hillside above the Ebbw valley village of Blaenavon may finally be coming under control.Emergency workers and soldiers described a gruelling battle against the deep-seated peat fire that has spread over 4,000 hectares (9,800 acres), putting lives, farmland and property at risk.At least 13 other fires have blazed across the valleys this weekend, prompting SouthWalesfire and rescue service to ask for military support – the first UK military deployment to deal with wildfires since 2018.Nationally, approximately 36 fires are still burning, 11 of which have been declared major incidents. Extreme heat and a lack of rain, supercharged by the climate crisis, have made this summer the busiest on record for wildfires in the UK, placing significant pressure on crews and resources.Wildfire breaks out in Ebbw valley, south WalesJamie Windsor, a group commander at Ebbw Vale station, said underground layers of peat beneath the orange and purple heather on the Blaenavon hillside had made the fire harder to put out.“It burns very deep, the peat, and because it’s been so hot, it’s not cooling down at night. You think you’ve got a handle on it but it’s burning underground and it just pops up again somewhere else,” he said. “We’re got a lot of wildfire experience here in south Wales but I’ve never seen anything like it in 30 years.”During the Guardian’s visit to the scene on Sunday, soldiers from the Queen’s Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment tirelessly dug firebreaks and turned over smoking soil to minimise the spread of fire. Small flames licked around the base of blackened trees a few metres away as they worked, while in another part of the woods several trees lit up quickly with no warning.View image in fullscreenA helicopter drops water over the land.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianOn the ridge of the hill, a civilian-contracted helicopter picked up water from a huge plastic pool fed by a local dam and circled again and again to dowse reigniting pockets of the smouldering hillside.Smoke from the area has been visible as far away as Cardiff and Gloucestershire.Firefightersfrom services around the UK have come to help improvise how to get water to hard-to-reach places, using an old steel mill on the edge of town as a temporary headquarters. New thermal camera drones and specialised response vehicles designed by the South Wales fire service came online this summer.“Just in time,” said Darren Cleaves, the group manager for the service, as he radioed a colleague at the perimeter of the fire to report what he could see on the drone screen. “The drone means we can be much more accurate with pinpointing where we need to go, and it keeps our teams safer.”View image in fullscreenDarren Cleaves operating the drone.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe combined efforts have worked, saving houses in Blaenavon a few hundred metres away. For weeks, residents on Llanover Close, a road on the village boundary, have watched a steady stream of fire engines, water tankers, tractors and other emergency vehicles and equipment go back and forth to the forestry track above their homes.Cindy Rogers, 60, lives in the last house on the road where Blaenavon meets the hillside. A fire in 2004 that began on the top of the mountain almost reached her house, she said, pointing from her back garden to where the fire line is still visible.View image in fullscreenCindy Rogers: ‘It’s a worry that this is going to get worse with climate change.’Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian“It’s a worry that this is going to get worse in the future with climate change, but I wouldn’t move unless I really had to,” she said. “All it takes is the wind to change direction and that’s it.”By Sunday afternoon, the Blaenavon fire was showing signs it may be slowing, said Fin Monahan, the chief fire officer of South Wales fire and rescue.“It’s been very tough, but I’m so proud of the professionalism of these teams and how hard they are working,” he said. “Morale is still high, everything is calm and controlled … It’s just the scale of what we’re dealing with is unprecedented. We normally get about 1,000 999 calls a week, and at the moment it’s 7,000.”View image in fullscreenA fire engine hits the road.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianArson had been a major contributor to this summer’s fires, Monahan said. “Not every investigation has been completed yet but we can already see it’s been a significant issue this year in south Wales. Fire safety education is another key area we focus on … Driving home last night, I saw smoke and I went and found a guy burning tires and other stuff in his garden, under a tree. I had to tell him to put it out.”The cause of the Blaenavon fire is still unknown, but across the country arson arrests have been made in relation to this summer’s fires. On Saturday, four teenage boys from Porth in the Rhondda valley were detained on suspicion of arson and later released on bail.In Stoke-on-Trent, a man and woman have been arrested in connection to a fire that destroyed four homes, and a man in King’s Norton and another in east London have been arrested on suspicion of arson to endanger life.The UK has experienced multiple heatwaves this summer, as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The whole of Wales and almost three-quarters of England were declared officially in drought last month, and the Met Office said this week that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature.View image in fullscreenIt is hoped the fire may finally be coming under control.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe Blaenavon fire and many others across the country may only finally settle with cooler temperatures and rain, but the onset of autumn and more rainfall is not guaranteed to reverse the drought conditions, the Met Office said on Saturday.In Blaenavon, flash flooding has plagued residents in recent years. Asupercharged El Niñois now predicted to bring wet and stormy conditions to the UK this winter.An 89-year-old resident of Llanover Close, who did not want to give his name, said he had lived on the street since it was built. “It’s the flooding that worries me. My basement flooded last winter,” he said. “Fire and flood … I never thought it would come to this.”Explore more on these topicsWalesFirefightersMilitaryWildfiresUK weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: The five-year plans that turned into lifetimes: Windrush elders’ stories ‘open door’ for young people | Commonwealth immigration | The Guardian
description: Collecting first-hand accounts of older generation’s struggles is opportunity for Hackney’s children, says leader of pioneering project
Author: Faisa Mohamed
Headline: Collecting first-hand accounts of older generation’s struggles is opportunity for Hackney’s children, says leader of pioneering project
Content: Yvonne Straughn (left) and Lucy Bubb, participants in the Hackney archives project.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYvonne Straughn (left) and Lucy Bubb, participants in the Hackney archives project.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianCommonwealth immigrationThe five-year plans that turned into lifetimes: Windrush elders’ stories ‘open door’ for young peopleCollecting first-hand accounts of older generation’s struggles is opportunity for Hackney’s children, says leader of pioneering projectFaisa MohamedSun 16 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are faces young and old around a table in Hackney library as people share a meal of curry goat, rice and peas and sorrel cake. There are photos of the smiling faces of Windrush elders scattered around. They will soon become permanent fixtures of the Hackney Archives.There is a feeling among the group that somebody is missing.Lessept Saunders, the founder of the Hackney Caribbean Elderly Organisation, died in April aged 107. He had been the second-oldest known living man in London and the oldest contributor to Stories of Windrush. Saunders was part of the Windrush generation, having arrived in London from Jamaica in 1944 after hearing stories about higher wages and hope from returning friends who had served in the second world war.“Saunders had a five-year-plan, like many of the elders who came to the UK,” saysPaul Anderson, the CEO of Voyage Youth, a social justice charity leading the archival project. “They would tell themselves ‘I’m only going to be here for five years and go back’ but many were not able to do that. The cost to travel back home was such a barrier that many just stayed.”Stories of Windrush is one of the first projects in the UK to document first-hand accounts from Windrush elders collected entirely by young people. The accompanying book and photographs and its digital counterparts will have a permanent place in the Hackney Archives.View image in fullscreenProject participants at the Windrush Archives in Hackney.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianZainab Awonoki was 15 when she first started working on the archive four years ago. “I never grew up with my grandparents so speaking to elders has been so eye-opening,” she says. Despite learning briefly about the Windrush generation in her Hackney secondary school, it was only through the archives that she learned about the struggles these elders had faced. “Hearing their stories first hand lets you see that they practically fought for us to actually stay here. It tells our elders that they’re not alone with their past and trauma.”Researchhas found that giving young people access to archives can improve educational attainment and increase awareness of local decision-making. It seems to resonate with Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, who wrote aforewordfor the book. She wrote: “For all those who form part of the Windrush generation, and many who have been subject to scandalous impositions by state agencies, we must not forget their lives, their struggles, their achievements and their legacy are worth celebrating.”Claudette Barned arrived in the 1960s from Jamaica at the age of nine and was immediately struck by the freezing temperatures in Clapton, east London. Today, the 74-year-old fans herself in the scorching heat, wearing a pink summer dress and recently having dyed her hair blue. “My mother passed away before I could ask her about history,” she says. “Talking to the young people means that when we die our stories are shared and when they’re old they can repeat the cycle.” Now retired, she has not forgotten the loneliness of her first few years inEngland. She socialises at elderly clubs with other Windrush elders and has passed on her Caribbean traditions to her grandson, who has nicknamed her “Reggae Grandma”.Through the archives, Anderson hopes to address the youth unemployment crisis, starting with Hackney’s children whoexperiencesome of the highest rates of child poverty in England. He says: “For many, it opened a door they had not known was there: a route into the heritage sector, a reason to consider higher education, and a genuine change of pathway into a field where African and Caribbean communities remain significantly under-represented, despite so much of the history held within it being their own.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYvonne Straughn was born in Barbados in 1941 as the only girl among five brothers. “I was rebellious,” she told the young archivists, recalling how she would refuse to do chores unless she was paid. At 85, her rebellious spirit seems to live on. As Anderson describes the legacy of the archives, she is quick to remind the elders that none of them will be around to see it.Straughn’s tale is a classic Windrush story. In 1966 she arrived in England to work in a hospital, treating patients who were often hostile to the sight of a black nurse. Awonoki says it is a big responsibility to be entrusted with stories such as Straughn’s, particularly in the rollback of diversity initiatives. “You need their stories to realise this isn’t something new,” she says. “The older generation had a massive impact on life. They gave us the Equality Act and now we’re talking about getting rid of it?”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth immigrationWindrush scandalImmigration and asylumLondonEnglandRacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can exercise really help improve my sex life? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Here’s what experts say about how sex and exercise are linked, and whether the type, timing and intensity of movement matter
Author: Keren Landman
Headline: Here’s what experts say about how sex and exercise are linked, and whether the type, timing and intensity of movement matter
Content: While the links between physical activity and having great sex might seem obvious, they are not as linear as you might expect.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhile the links between physical activity and having great sex might seem obvious, they are not as linear as you might expect.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesCall the doctorWell actuallyCan exercise really help improve my sex life?Here’s what experts say about how sex and exercise are linked, and whether the type, timing and intensity of movement matterKeren LandmanSun 16 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s a reason to put your sneakers on: exercise can improve your sex life.It’s not necessarily about changing how your body looks, or being strong enough to swing from the chandelier. Regular movement improves smaller, less visible bodily functions that increase your desire and capacity for sex – like the release of arousal-promoting hormones and enhanced circulation in the nether regions. Perhaps just as critically, it gets your mind in the right frame to do it.While the links between physical activity and having great sex might seem obvious, they are not as linear as you might expect.Here’s what you need to know.How can exercise improve sexual function?Two of the main ways exercise canupgradeyour sex life are that your body gets better at arousal and your mind less likely to interrupt it.The physical impacts relate largely to circulation. Good blood flow underpins arousal: it promotes the function of fluid-secreting glands and sensation-conducting nerves in women, and facilitates erections in men.Wellness culture is trying to sell you products your vagina doesn’t needRead moreExercise also improves rest, which leads to increased energy levels. Certain types of activity can strengthen pelvic floor muscles, which boosts sexual satisfaction in bothmenandwomen, and positively affects the levels of hormones and neurotransmitters tied to sexual response.Scientists measure sexual function inmanydifferent ways, including the subjective sense of desire and arousal, the presence of lubrication (in women) or erection (in men), the ability to achieve orgasm and overall satisfaction with one’s sex life. Arecent review of multiple studiesfound that across those domains, women who engaged in various forms of exercise – including cardio, yoga and pelvic-floor work – scored significantly higher than women who did not. (These studies were randomized controlled trials, which differentiate between exercise effects and sex habits likely to already be present in people who exercise.)Otherstudieshave found similarly positive effects in men, although their quality and the effects they have measured have been a little spottier.The psychological effects relate to exercise’s tendency to improve mood, energy and body image. Both chronic stress and a busy, self-critical mind interfere with arousal, although that plays out differently for women and men, said Debby Herbenick, a psychologist and researcher who directs Indiana University’s Center for SexualHealthPromotion.To be clear, exercise is not a magic fix for anxious thoughts about appearance and performance. But, Herbenick says, it can “decrease cognitive distractions and enhance arousal and orgasm”.Does the type, timing or intensity of exercise matter?What type?When it comes to physical benefits for your sex life, aerobic exercise – the kind that makes you sweat and increases your heart rate – has the best evidence, in part because it is what has been studied the most.But for the psychological benefits, it’s less important to focus on what the movement is than on how it makes you feel. Exercise that you do because it makes you feel healthy and fit ismorelikelyto make you feel good about yourself. In turn, that positive self-image helps your brain minimize arousal killers such as stress and anxiety. It’s best for people to “choose the exercises that they enjoy rather than try to choose an exercise just to enhance arousal or orgasm”, said Herbenick.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen?Workouts can act as an aphrodisiac for some women – but not straight away. Cindy Meston, a sex researcher and professor at the University of Texas at Austin, ranlabstudiesin the 1990s and 2000s aimed at understanding how the timing of exercise affected sexual function. She found women’s genital blood flow was actually suppressed right after vigorous exercise, then rose above baseline 15 to 30 minutes later, once hardworking muscles had stopped hogging the body’s blood supply.Skip the run: here are six joint-friendly cardio alternatives suggested by expertsRead moreHerbenick’s research has corroborated this finding, but structuring your sex life around your workouts “is not realistic for everyone”, she says.What about intensity?Workout intensity seems to matter more than timing. In Herbenick’s research, low-intensity or low-repetition exercise had little effect on arousal or orgasm – but push too hard, and the exercise can backfire. Stick to the middle of the range; if it makes your entire body ache, it’s less likely to turn you on.How can I apply this in real life?You don’t need to sweat the details to enjoy the sexual benefits of exercise. For most people, it’s enough to move regularly, with some effort, in a way that feels good and sustainable. Real life is messy, and exercise might mean swimming laps or walking the soccer fields while your kids are in the pool or at practice, said Herbenick.Exercise has been proven to improve sexual function in womentaking anti-depressantsand those who have hadhysterectomies. People who exercise for other health reasons may also earn sexy dividends. Diabetes and heart disease can impair the same blood vessels and nerves that arousal depends on, so exercise prescribed to manage those conditionsoftenimprovessexualfunctionas a side effect.If you’re an athlete training hard for something demanding, good communication with your partner is key, said Herbenick. Talk to your partner honestly about when you actually have the energy and comfort for sex, rather than assuming your body will cooperate on cue.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCall the doctorSexHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ariana Grande Eternal Sunshine tour review: pop illusion at its most effective – for good and bad | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: On her last live dates before she steps back from the public eye, Grande holds her own – but it’s also impossible to avoid feeling concerned for her wellbeing
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: On her last live dates before she steps back from the public eye, Grande holds her own – but it’s also impossible to avoid feeling concerned for her wellbeing
Content: ‘A show that wants us to see one thing and experience another’ … Ariana Grande on stage in Austin on 27 June.Photograph: Julian DakdoukView image in fullscreen‘A show that wants us to see one thing and experience another’ … Ariana Grande on stage in Austin on 27 June.Photograph: Julian DakdoukAriana GrandeReviewAriana Grande Eternal Sunshine tour review: pop illusion at its most effective – for good and badThe O2, LondonOn her last live dates before she steps back from the public eye, Grande holds her own – but it’s also impossible to avoid feeling concerned for her wellbeingKate SolomonSun 16 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a thrum of excitement in the air as an eight-minute countdown starts and Ariana Grande’s unmistakable silhouette appears on a giant backlit curtain on the stage of the O2. Is it actually her? Posing there for eight minutes before the show starts? It can’t be. But is it? It’s the first time we question what is and isn’t real at this Eternal Sunshine tour stop, a 10-night residency and a robust arena show that ultimately wants us to see one thing and experience another.Collectively, we’ve been scolded for talking about it – the “endless, ongoing public scrutiny” of Ariana Grande’s body has pushed her to “[take] a step back from visibility” when this tour ends. It can’t be nice or fun to have your body examined and discussed for any reason but it is impossible to witness the 33-year-old’s frame on stage and not be gripped by genuine concern for her. Two songs in, a lump forms in my throat, which is not the intended effect of Positions, the zippy title track of her 2020 album. As the set around her is engulfed in digital flames, Grande sings about her infinite flexibility vis a vis relationship boundaries and sexual olympics and all I can think is: she looks like a little kid.But you put it aside, of course. That’s how this all works: you’re powerless in the face of it, so you get on with enjoying the show, which is grand and sincere and slick, and full of songs that are so huge they rattle the rafters of the O2. There’s no pyro but who needs it when you have a voice as explosive as Ariana Grande’s? Her diva-era belters like Break Free and One Last Time are peaks amid the troughs of her newer, more subdued sounds. Dangerous Woman is punctuated by drums that sound like firecrackers as she drags the mic stand around the B-stage to belt the chorus directly to as many fans as possible. The songs from Petal, her eighth album released weeks ago, are largely packed into the final portion and forgo the juddering choreo of the rest of the show for something more gig-like. Pogoing through the live debut of Bad Thing and swishing her Victorian nightie around through a ferocious Petal, Grande cries: “It’s such a fucked situation.” Well, yes.View image in fullscreenGrande performing in Atlanta on 6 July.Photograph: Katia TemkinThe energy of the show is buoyed by a gaggle of dancers who orbit around her, and you never feel Grande wane even as she struts up and down the runway on impossible stilettos. Her vocals are supple and astonishing, ad libs that scamper and swandive over songs – at the climax of Safety Net, she kneels at the edge of the stage casually emitting sounds that her peers would envy. When she speaks, her words run together like her thoughts are racing to get out of her mouth first: “I’msohappyfortheconnectionwe’veshared,” she says. “You’resuchabeautifulpresenceinmylife.”Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answerRead moreMuch of Grande’s music has been created in the face of painful adversity but it – and she, in this moment too – carries a lightness with it. She has a smile playing around her lips for most of Thank U, Next, which is a laundry list of romantic misadventures and regret, and a song that had the capacity to feel like a diary entry you cringe at years later. She throws her arms open to the crowd and flicks her long ponytail around with whip-like precision and all the sass of the woman who sees it and wants it and wants it and gets it.Every so often that illusion of lightness breaks. She turns on the mid-stage and leans sort of forward as she sings Past Life, a move to communicate her earnest romantic pain, a plea for empathy. The angle she’s standing at and the lighting collude to knock the breath out of me for a second: I shouldn’t be able to see this person’s skeleton.Those moments are deeply conflicting and in them I wish she had cancelled this run of dates rather than wait for them to wrap up. The show is a good testament to her 13-year pop career and worthy of being enjoyed, but that is hard to do when you feel that someone spectacular might be slipping through our fingers right in front of us. I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons: I hope it ends up a four-star aside in a long and rich life.Explore more on these topicsAriana GrandePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘At one point she said, “I don’t want to offend you, but you seem quite privileged”’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A trainee accountant and a company director had differing views on opportunities for young people, but could they find common ground on the new prime minister?
Author: Erica Buist
Headline: A trainee accountant and a company director had differing views on opportunities for young people, but could they find common ground on the new prime minister?
Content: Margaret and Clare. All photographs: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMargaret and Clare. All photographs: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘At one point she said, “I don’t want to offend you, but you seem quite privileged”’A trainee accountant and a company director had differing views on opportunities for young people, but could they find common ground on the new prime minister?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howErica BuistSun 16 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMargaret, 22, LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationTrainee accountant and part-time arts producerVoting recordGreen in the past and is now a Labour memberAmuse boucheIn 2024 she was president of the Cambridge Footlights student comedy societyClare, 64, LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationDirector of a healthcare services company and part-timebloggeron health and urban planningVoting recordDemocrat when she was in the US, Conservative in the UKAmuse boucheShe is very into the River Thames. She rows and swims in it, and regularly spots seals and egretsView image in fullscreenFor startersClareI was really looking forward to it. We clicked on the fact that we both love the idea of dining across the divide.MargaretI was a bit nervous, as all I knew about her was that she was a “Kemi [Badenoch] fan”. I know Conservatives, but don’t know anyone who would say that about themselves. But I found it really interesting hearing someone voice those opinions, and we agreed on a lot.ClareI had a watermelon carpaccio, mint and feta salad, then mussels with chips and, for dessert, a peach sorbet with chantilly. It was very nice.MargaretI’m vegan, so my options were limited. I had a mock sushi dish made from watermelon, and some fries, then a divine blackcurrant sorbet. We shared a bottle of orange wine.View image in fullscreenThe big beefClareI thinkKemi Badenochis very courageous, focused and honest. Her party’s been decimated and is facing some of the biggest challenges they’ve ever had. It’s brave of her to take the role and stick to her convictions.Dining across the divide: ‘He didn’t change my mind on anything – but he did give me a lift to my car’Read moreMargaretI think Kemi Badenoch is a contrarian. When she said the UK should support the US and Israel in the conflict in Iran, I felt it was “let’s just go to the other side of what the government is saying”.ClareShe seemed genuinely excited aboutAndy Burnhamcoming into leadership. Believe it or not, I feel positive about that, too. I’m not a basher; I’m always an optimist.MargaretI think she was more excited about Burnham than I was, which surprised me. It’s great to have someone who’s making the left and centrists so excited, but I’m always cautious when I feel myself getting excited about a political figure. I was a teenager in very left-leaning Liverpool when Jeremy Corbyn was the leader of the Labour party and it was almost a cultish fever. But I don’t know if he would have been a good leader, on reflection.View image in fullscreenSharing plateClareBeing involved with the Conservative party, I never really felt any discrimination as a woman. But you look at data and see that women earn less than men, so clearly women face discrimination.MargaretI would have thought that someone who had Clare’s level of success, and especially someone with her political stance, might think women have an easier time, but we talked about how so many of the core features of our society were built by men, for men. Women are getting into those spaces now, and some might see that as positive discrimination – but that’s not such a bad thing.View image in fullscreenFor aftersClareThe situation young people are in, particularly with housing, is awful. She lives in a warehouse with a couple of people. She says it’s a lovely warehouse and a great setup, but I campaign actively for more housing.MargaretFor me it’s less about housing and more about opportunities for young people. At one point she said, “I don’t want to offend you, but you do seem to be quite privileged.” I wasn’t offended, but I do disagree. Being from Liverpool and ambitious, I had to work very, very hard to get down to London as it’s where all the opportunities seem to be.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysClareit’s getting harder to meet someone with a different view – especially if you’re 22 and you’ve grown up online. So my takeaway is that everybody should do this. There is common ground in everything.MargaretClare came from the US as a Democrat and then aligned with the Conservatives, and there can be an ingrained dismissiveness of someone like that. But I really enjoyed speaking to her. There are so many different kinds of people in the world, and most are wonderful and well-meaning when you actually get down to it.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeClare and Margaret ate atThe Bull and Last, London NW5Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt’s ‘dream comes true’ with fourth European Championships gold | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The British sprinter became the first to win four titles at a single event while Dina Asher-Smith hit a record 11 European medals total
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British sprinter became the first to win four titles at a single event while Dina Asher-Smith hit a record 11 European medals total
Content: Amy Hunt is in dreamland after winning her fourth gold medal of the European Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt is in dreamland after winning her fourth gold medal of the European Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAmy Hunt’s ‘dream comes true’ with fourth European Championships goldBritish sprinter first to win four titles at single eventDina Asher-Smith hits record 11 European medals totalSean Ingleat Alexandra Stadium, BirminghamSun 16 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf there was any remaining doubt that this has been Amy Hunt’s summer, it was dispelled over 10 seconds of controlled fury at the European Championships, as Britain’s newest sporting superstar completed an unprecedented quadruple.When the baton was slapped into the 24-year-old’s hand on the anchor leg of the mixed 4x100m relay, she was a fraction behind Gina Lückenkemper of Germany. But then Hunt became the hunter, and a record-breaker.European Championships security scare keeps fans and athletes stuck at stadiumRead moreIn no time those long legs began to whir, her vast stride started to widen, and she found her wings. First Lückenkemper was chased down. Then Hunt ran into history.As she crossed the line, she stuck her tongue out, stretched her arms in triumph, then held four fingers to the camera. And just like that the Cambridge graduate had completed the quadruple.“It’s just a dream come true – I’ll remember this week for the rest of my life,” said Hunt after becoming the first athlete in the 92-year history of the European Championships to win four gold medals in a single event.To make things even sweeter, Britain’s time was a European record 39.97sec, with Germany taking silver in 40.11 and Spain claiming bronze.“I think it surpassed my expectations for myself at these champs,” Hunt said. “Not in terms of not just the goals, but how I’ve handled myself, how I’ve handled the pressure, the attention, the recovery, the discipline of it all.”“It was a bit like when you’re queueing for a rollercoaster and you’re a little nervous and you’re seeing the drops and stuff,” Hunt said when asked about the craziness of her past week. “Then when you get off you want to do it again. So it was that adrenaline kick certainly. I loved the event.”To run seven races in seven days is difficult enough. To win all seven, across heats and finals, not only takes talent and guts but a hefty dose of chutzpah too.But while Hunt certainly has main character energy she quickly ensured that her teammates – Jeremiah Azu, Dina Asher-Smith and Zharnel Hughes – were hailed as well.“To do it all together is incredible, especially because that was the first time we did that changeover about an hour ago in warm-up,” said Hunt. “And look how smooth it was. Such professionals.”View image in fullscreenDina Asher-Smith, with Amy Hunt, Zharnel Hughes and Jeremiah Azu, also made history with her record 11th European gold.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesIt was hard to argue with that. This was the first time the mixed 4x100m relay has taken place at these championships and with the men and women alternating changeovers the difficulty level was increased to the highest. No wonder the Netherlands and Italy were disqualified. But Britain looked smooth throughout – at least to the untrained eye.“I’m going to be completely frank with you, I was absolutely terrified,” said Asher-Smith. “When the gun was going, I was like ‘Dina, please relax, it’s only going to go well if you relax’. When I gave that baton to Zharnel, I was so happy, I can’t lie. That’s exactly how I feel. Very unfiltered. I was just like ‘get this out of my hand – bye’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHunt was not the only record holder on the night as Asher-Smith made it a record 11 European medals in total – surpassing Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska – with this victory.“It hasn’t sunk in at all,” she said. “I just don’t think it’s something that when you start your career you ever think is going to be attached to you. Just want to run faster and get better. So I feel very humbled and blessed.”“At this point in my career, I’m just having fun,” Asher-Smith said. “I’m just seeing what can be maxed out because I’m fortunate enough to stand on the line, and I don’t really have much to prove. I’d like an Olympic gold, but that’s kind of the only thing that’s on my bucket list.”Earlier on Sunday there was more British success in the women’s marathon, as Abbie Donnelly overcame bringing different sized running shoes to Birmingham to take a surprise bronze medal.However her race was saved when her boyfriend Shane dashed up in the morning with the right shoe. “I actually bought two different size shoes by accident to this race,” said Donnelly, who became the first British woman to win a European Championships marathon medal.“I tried them on last night and I was like ‘the right one does not feel right’”, added Donnelly, whose time of 2:27.33 was just over five minutes behind Finland’s Alisa Vainio, who set a championship record.“So then I had to call my parents and my boyfriend. It was half an hour beforehand that my boyfriend Shane put the [tracking] chip on because I was so flustered.”Britain also won the women’s team event through Donnelly, Rose Harvey, Louise Small and Clara Evans-Graham, while Germany’s Amanal Petros took the men’s marathon in a championship record 2:09.11.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s the standard’: Mikel Arteta hails Arsenal’s desire on blue day for Maresca  | Mikel Arteta | The Guardian
description: The champions delighted their manager by ‘winning the first trophy’ while Enzo Maresca wants Manchester City signings to arrive soon
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: The champions delighted their manager by ‘winning the first trophy’ while Enzo Maresca wants Manchester City signings to arrive soon
Content: Mikel Arteta lifts the Community Shield, the ‘first trophy’ win for Arsenal this season.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta lifts the Community Shield, the ‘first trophy’ win for Arsenal this season.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesMikel Arteta‘That’s the standard’: Mikel Arteta hails Arsenal’s desire on blue day for MarescaChampions delight manager by ‘winning the first trophy’Maresca wants Manchester City signings to arrive soonBen Fisherat the Principality StadiumSun 16 Aug 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta said his Arsenal players demonstrated their hunger to defend the Premier League title in theirCommunity Shield triumphover Manchester City. Arsenal, who ended their 22-year wait last season and are seeking to win back-to-back top-flight titles for the first time since 1934-35, beat City 3-0 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff in Enzo Maresca’s first significant match in charge.Riccardo Calafiori opened the scoring after 24 seconds, the fastest goal in the competition since Bobby Owen’s strike for City in 1968, before Kai Havertz doubled Arsenal’s lead and their captain, Martin Ødegaard, completed the scoring on 48 minutes. The 3-0 defeat represented the joint-heaviest loss for a City manager in their first game in charge, with Harry Newbould the most recent to suffer a three-goal opening defeat – 4-1, also toArsenal, in 1906. It is also Maresca’s joint-heaviest defeat as a manager in England.Calafiori’s fast start inspires Arsenal to big Community Shield win over Manchester CityRead moreArteta was delighted with Arsenal’s convincing display. “I am obviously extremely happy with the performance, the result and winning the first trophy,” he said. “We talked about the desire we have to start the season and to show ourselves how much we want it and I saw a lot of positive things against a top opponent. I’m very impressed in the manner that we played, in the manner that we competed. That’s the standard for us. If we drive the standards at this level, I’m sure that we’re going to be really, really competitive.”Asked about the desire displayed by his team, he said: “Because we want to go straight again. The desire comes [because] I want to live that moment again. I want to live other moments, even bigger than them … we know what it’s going to take. We know the difficulty of the task. We’ve never done it at this club, to win it again. We know that it’s going to demand something special and we are ready for it.”Arteta praised the performance of Christos Tzolis, who was involved in all three goals. “He is a really intelligent boy and he has a massive quality, which is when he is in the last 20-30m [of the pitch] he is so composed to pick people out in and around the box,” said the Arsenal manager. “And also to finish actions and he has shown that again two or three times. He was decisive.”View image in fullscreenNew signing Christos Tzolis was involved in all three of Arsenal’s goals.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPAØdegaard said the team’s performance was evidence they are capable of winning back-to-back titles. “We played some brilliant football,” said Arsenal’s captain. “[It was a] great performance and a great way to start the season. I always want to help the team as much as possible with goals and assists. I want to score more goals. We showed our level today. We’ve shown we’re ready. We’re serious and we want to do it again. We want to attack it. We want to do it again. When you get a taste of how nice it is you want to do it again. We want to win everything.”Maresca acknowledged City, who are closing on a deal to sign Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi as they prepare to sell Rodri to Barcelona, would welcome new arrivals before their league opener at home to Bournemouth on Sunday. Rodri did not travel to Cardiff, where Elliot Anderson started in midfield, and Jack Grealish arrived from the substitutes’ bench for his first City appearance since May 2025. “Any new signing, the sooner they arrive the better because we are starting the Premier League in one week and if they start to work with us as soon as possible it’s better that they can also understand the way we want to play,” he said.Maresca said he was not alarmed by the manner of the defeat. “In general I’m always concerned, even when we win games so imagine how [concerned] that we didn’t win the game,” said the Italian, who succeeded Pep Guardiola this summer. “It’s just the beginning, we have many things that we need to do better, I think the reaction was good after conceding the first goal and now try to reset and analyse the game and think from Tuesday about the next game.”Explore more on these topicsMikel ArtetaCommunity ShieldArsenalManchester CityEnzo MarescanewsShareReuse this content

title: Rodri set to complete Barcelona move after Manchester City accept £65.4m bid | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Rodri looks set to complete a move to Barcelona after Manchester City accepted a bid of £65.4m
Author: Mark Dobson
Headline: Rodri looks set to complete a move to Barcelona after Manchester City accepted a bid of £65.4m
Content: Rodri has won four Premier League titles in seven seasons at Manchester City.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenRodri has won four Premier League titles in seven seasons at Manchester City.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PATransfer windowRodri set to complete Barcelona move after Manchester City accept £65.4m bid30-year-old said to favour a move back to SpainMaresca chasing Lille’s Bouaddi as replacementMark DobsonSun 16 Aug 2026 16.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRodri looks set to complete a move to Barcelona afterManchester Cityaccepted a bid of £65.4m from the Spanish club.The 30-year-old World Cup winner had entered the final year of his contract at the Etihad Stadium and made it clear he would like the opportunity to move toBarcelona. City, who are now closing in on a deal to sign Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, were reluctant sellers but had little choice with the Spanish international out of contract next summer.Calafiori’s fast start inspires Arsenal to big Community Shield win over Manchester CityRead moreCity had already rejected Barcelona’s bid of around €60m (£51m) for Rodri last week after an initial offer of €45m (£38.5m) but have now accepted the latest bid.Speaking after City’s 3-0 Community Shielddefeat by Arsenalon Sunday, Enzo Maresca called Rodri a “top player” and said “all the teams need Rodri”, but City have been unable to persuade their linchpin to stay and sign a new contract. Rodri had only returned to the club on Friday, having undergone back surgery after the World Cup, with Maresca saying he had given him a “big hug” when he first met up with him.Rodri has spent seven seasons with City, winning the Premier League four times and scoring the only goal when they beat Inter in the2023 Champions League final. The following year he won the Ballon d’Or but, by the time he was presented with the trophy, he was sidelined with an anterior cruciate ligament which ruled him out of most of the 2024-25 campaign, while hamstring and groin problems limited him to 33 appearances in Pep Guardiola’s final campaign in charge.City have already undergone major changes in midfield this summer, spending £116m on Elliot Anderson, while agreeing a deal to sell Tijjani Reijnders to Al Qadsiah. They are now ready to seal a move for the Morocco star Bouaddi.The teenager impressed at the World Cup and Lille had initially wanted any potential move to include a 12-month loan deal back to the French side. However, with City losing Bernardo Silva and now Rodri, Maresca is keen to bulk up his midfield options for the new campaign and want Bouaddi available for this season. City have also been linked with Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández and retain an interest.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowBarcelonaManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Djokovic’s medical malaise in Cincinnati exposes fraying edges of ageing great’s game  | Novak Djokovic | The Guardian
description: First-round exit for 24-time grand slam winner made for a difficult watch but there is an emerging pattern of saving his best for the big occasion
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: First-round exit for 24-time grand slam winner made for a difficult watch but there is an emerging pattern of saving his best for the big occasion
Content: Novak Djokovic receives medical treatment courtside during his opening match defeat in Cincinnati.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic receives medical treatment courtside during his opening match defeat in Cincinnati.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockNovak DjokovicDjokovic’s medical malaise in Cincinnati exposes fraying edges of ageing great’s gameFirst-round exit for 24-time grand slam winner made for a difficult watch but there is an emerging pattern of saving his best for the big occasionTumaini Carayolat the Lindner Family Tennis CenterSun 16 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNovak Djokovic walked from the ­stadium court in Cincinnati to the corridor reserved for post-match press interviews practically without breaking stride. The 39-year-old had been cruising up a set and well on his way to a seemingly comfortable victory when he began to feel the full force of the elements.
