Djokovic woulddevote much of his time during the final two setsto crouching on all fours between points, vomiting into towels and desperately struggling to perform.Such was his disappointment with his ageing body failing him once again that Djokovic, who is usually one of the most loquacious on the tour, briskly answered four questions in about a minute before offering his thanks and striding to the locker room. He wanted nothing more than to get out of there.There was once a time when an opening-round loss for Djokovic at the final Masters 1000 event would send alarm bells ringing, but ­perhaps the most interesting part of this defeat is how familiar such results have become. This year, his results in the paltry three non-slam events he has played were losses in his opening match at the Cincinnati and Italian Opens and a fourth-round defeat at Indian Wells. His last quarter-final at a Masters 1000 tournament came in October at the Shanghai Masters.Novak Djokovic suffers in Cincinnati heat as Thiago Agustín Tirante inflicts shock defeatRead moreThere have been numerous issues during those reverses, from injuries to other physical ailments or difficult preparation, but Djokovic’s motivation in these tournaments has clearly been a factor. He has spent his entire career finding a way to drag himself through impossible situations, even when things have been physically or mentally awry. Such ­recoveries require an immense amount of ­commitment, something he clearly does not have in these tournaments of less importance. Djokovic has long identified the grand slam tournaments and ­Olympics as his priorities at this point in his career, and his results have reflected those convictions. For the past year and a half, Djokovic has been the most consistent player at the grand slams beyond Carlos Alcaraz or Jannik Sinner. He has reliably found his way through nearly every other obstacle.View image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic shakes hands with a victorious Carlos Alcaraz after the Spaniard beat him in the Australian Open final in February.Photograph: Aaron Favila/APPerhaps the most striking part of Djokovic’s fleeting one-minute press conference came when he was asked whether he envisioned himself being back at Cincinnati. He issued a sober response: “I certainly hope so, but it looks more likely not, unfortunately. But let’s see what the future brings.”The tennis world has spent the past few years trying to anticipate when Djokovic might retire, and his tendency to cast doubt on his future after tough defeats has often looked an indicator. In this case, it is totally reasonable that he never wishes to compete in the Ohio humidity again. Otherwise, as long as he remains competitive at the grand slams, it does seem like he is content with his current life. While he stresses the importance of not looking too far forward at his age, when everything can change quickly, he has also been clear about wanting to compete in one final Olympics in Los Angeles, where he will be the defending champion.For those reasons, it does not feel that much has changed for him ahead of the US Open, the final grand slam tournament of the year. Time and again, he has shown that he will raise his game and find a way through to the latter rounds at the majors, even when he is barely competitive elsewhere. At his age, it is only a matter of time before he also loses his edge in the biggest events, but it remains to be seen when that shift will occur.In some ways, the final stretch of Djokovic’s career has been quite a confusing time. He has never hesitated to recognise the superiority of Sinner and Alcaraz at this stage in their careers, but he also remains one of the top four players in the world in both his own mind and according to the rest of the field.View image in fullscreenA defeated Novak Djokovic departs the court after losing 2-6, 6-4, 6-4 to Argentine Thiago Agustín Tirante, who capitalised on the 39-year-old’s struggles.Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty ImagesHe has repeatedly stressed that he is not fixated by the prospect of winning a 25th grand slam title and that pursuit is not the primary motivation for his longevity, but his standards have been high for so long that he still cannot help but feel the same amount of immense disappointment when he fails to live up to them as if he was still No 1. He knows that his ­performances and level are rare for a player of his age, that he should be proud of what he is achieving in the latter stages of his career, but he still wants more.The one certainty, though, is his enduring love for this sport. Despite how much his reality has changed compared with the years when he was the best player in the world and racking up titles from grand slams to 250s, he continues to show up, compete and find meaning and enjoyment in the success. Long may it continue.Explore more on these topicsNovak DjokovicTennisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Seifert demolition job sets up Manchester Super Giants for maiden men’s Hundred title | The Hundred | The Guardian
description: Manchester Super Giants triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Manchester Super Giants triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets
Content: Manchester Super Giants’ captain Jos Buttler (centre) holds the men’s Hundred trophy aloft at Lord’s.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester Super Giants’ captain Jos Buttler (centre) holds the men’s Hundred trophy aloft at Lord’s.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThe HundredSeifert demolition job sets up Manchester Super Giants for maiden men’s Hundred titleManchester Super Giants, 162-5 beat Trent Rockets, 158-8 by five wicketsOld Trafford-based side win men’s final at third attemptTaha Hashimat Lord'sSun 16 Aug 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new name has done the trick. The Manchester Super Giants – once known as the Originals, now part of the tournament’s IPL-ification – triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets. Tim Seifert set up victory with 72 off 38 balls; Liam Dawson completed it with two balls remaining, a six to seal it.New Zealand’s Seifert turned Jos Buttler, his captain, into a support act in a chase of 159, his scarily high backlift producing seven sixes and a 23-ball half-century. The 31-year-old launched far higher than any of the Rockets, their innings defined by useful cameos. Noor Ahmad fizzed the ball down for the Super Giants, taking three for 33, but this was Seifert’s night as the Manchester side won the tournament for the first time after two previous runners-up finishes.Trent Rockets soar over Sunrisers Leeds to bring home maiden women’s Hundred titleRead moreThe Rockets, who were going for a doubleafter their women’s side had triumphedearlier in the piece, did offer a scare at the close. Seifert departed with 22 balls remaining, 23 still required – and the Super Giants stumbled. Mohammad Amir removed Heinrich Klaasen and Michael Bracewell and, with three required off the last over, Dawson struck air with his first two balls. It would be third time lucky, Ben Sanderson sent over deep midwicket to finally finish it.It closed a season defined by team reboots and a drop in overall attendance. There has been Jude Bellingham in the ground, the introduction of the illogical name that is MI London and the persistence of a key problem: the cricket is yet to dominate conversation. Of course, a final allows the actual sport to breathe a little and a last-over end was welcome after Seifert had threatened to complete it much earlier. “It was a little bit [more] stressful than it needed to be,” said a relieved Buttler.Lord’s was a psychedelic place before the start. Ella Eyre had the thankless task as musical guest while the two sides warmed up yards away, daytime fireworks in full flow. This was a second consecutive men’s final for the Rockets but they had just the one survivor from last year: Sanderson. Ben Duckett’s runs had helped on their progress to this point while the Super Giants had enjoyed the fruits of an England pace triumvirate: Josh Tongue, Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson. With Buttler deciding to bowl, Duckett against the quicks – what felt like the key battle at the start of the day – was first up.View image in fullscreenManchester’s Liam Dawson (right) celebrates hitting the game-winning shot, a six over midwicket, with teammate Leus du Plooy (left).Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesDuckett got the scoop out against Atkinson and Baker, and was grateful for a drop; the left-hander reverse-swept the ball to Tongue, who erred at short third. Duckett looked on for a big one, having hit 141 against India at this ground last month.Ahmad decided otherwise. The left-arm wrist-spinner struck with his first ball, to Finn Allen, and the delivery to Duckett moments later would not have been out of place in a red-ball game. A wrong’un caught the inside-edge before finding Buttler’s gloves, Duckett gone for 31. Another Ahmad googly later in the innings accounted for Australia’s Tim David, whose difficult tournament – 90 runs from eight knocks – ended with a first-ball edge to the sharp Buttler, leaving the Rockets on 91 for four after 59 deliveries.In a match packed with internationals it was the uncapped Aneurin Donald who gave the Rockets their biggest lift. His 19-ball 38 included a mix-up with Sam Billings, prompting the captain’s run-out, but the Rockets could call upon a strong lower order for the finish. Mitchell Santner’s unbeaten 20 took him to a season’s batting average of 146. Lewis Gregory was brutal with a 16-ball 32.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt looked like a decent score but Seifert was in a hurry, taking 14 off Amir’s first over and pulverising the leg-side. He appeared a goner on 33 after finding Allen by the leg-side rope; the Rockets man leaped beyond the boundary before flicking it back into play for Calvin Harrison to complete the catch. The decision went upstairs and was adjudged not out due to Allen brushing the rope in the buildup.Seifert moved to his half-century by slogging Harrison into the Mound Stand, with the Super Giants reaching 87 for one off 50 balls. Their control grew when Buttler went stratospheric against Harrison with back-to-back sixes, but an attempt at a third cost him when he found long-off. Would this be a gamechanging moment? It was nearly the case, but Dawson got it right at the end.Explore more on these topicsThe HundredCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scotland appoint Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approach | Scotland | The Guardian
description: The Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli, sacked by Monaco in June, is Scotland’s second non-Scottish manager after Berti Vogts
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli, sacked by Monaco in June, is Scotland’s second non-Scottish manager after Berti Vogts
Content: Sébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAView image in fullscreenSébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAScotlandScotland appoint Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approachBelgian is the first non-Scot in role since Berti VogtsSFA welcomes ‘aggressive, front-foot style of play’Ewan MurraySun 16 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Scottish Football Association has appointed the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002 to 2004.Clarke’s abrupt departurecame afterScotland were knocked out of the World Cupat the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager with the Danes Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand being linked with the position.Pocognoli, a left-back who played for Brighton and West Brom, will probably be welcomed byScotlandfans seeking a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, including appearances at three major tournaments, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief football officer, said Pocognoli “will bring an aggressive, front-foot style of play that will excite supporters”.After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France. The former Everton and Belgum winger Kevin Mirallas is expected to join him in the dugout.Pocognoli said: “When I first heard of the interest, I was immediately excited about the opportunity. Scotland’s supporters are famous for their passion – most recently at the World Cup in the USA - and I have experienced it myself as a player for Belgium when we played in 2013.“Along with my coaching staff, I will do everything I can to give them a team to be proud of and build on the success that has been achieved already by my predecessor.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland begin their Nations League campaign with a trip to Slovenia on 26 September. Pocognoli’s first home game in charge will be Switzerland’s visit to Glasgow three days later.Explore more on these topicsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cyclists criticise ‘catastrophic’ safety measures after Finlay Tarling’s death | Cycling | The Guardian
description: The riders’ union, the CPA, is ‘furious’ with safety measures on Tour, two days after the death of Finlay Tarling following a collision at the Volta a Portugal
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The riders’ union, the CPA, is ‘furious’ with safety measures on Tour, two days after the death of Finlay Tarling following a collision at the Volta a Portugal
Content: The classifications leaders observed a minute's silence to honour Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal on Sunday.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPAView image in fullscreenThe classifications leaders observed a minute's silence to honour Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal on Sunday.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPACyclingCyclists criticise ‘catastrophic’ safety measures after Finlay Tarling’s deathRiders’ union expresses fury about Volta a PortugalTarling died after collision with non-race vehicleJeremy WhittleSun 16 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe professional cycling community has reacted with fury to thedeath of the teenage Welsh rider, Finlay Tarling, in the Volta a Portugal, with a leading former professional describing the race’s safety measures as “catastrophic”.Tarling, the younger brother of the Netcompany Ineos professional Josh Tarling, was in collision with a non-race vehicle driving towards the peloton while he competed in the Portuguese race’s eighth stage. The 19-year-old’s death on Friday has led to a surge of anger, with the riders’ union, the Cyclistes Professionnels Associés (CPA), describing itself as “furious”.British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies in Volta a Portugal accidentRead more“We are speechless and filled with anger after the news of Finlay Tarling’s death at the Tour of Portugal,” the CPA posted. “It is not right that a young athlete’s life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents.”The former French professional Jérôme Pineau was one of those to criticise the levels of security in place at the race, which he labelled “catastrophic”.Pineau, who rode multiple Grand Tours between 2002 and 2015, described the lack of other incidents in the race as “a constant miracle” and added that “the finishes are not worthy of a race of this level”.“It’s the result of the lack of resources to organise major cycling races which are becoming increasingly expensive,” Pineau said.“All of this should primarily concern the authorities in charge,” he said, referencing the sport’s governing body, the UCI. “They must implement approval processes, and if security is not guaranteed, if the organisers are not capable of it, they should not be authorised to organise the event.”Both the Volta a Portugal organisers and the UCI have been contacted for further comment.The circumstances of Tarling’s death are now subject to a police investigation, but the Portuguese police stated that while “more evidence will be gathered,” it is thought unlikely that the driver will face criminal charges.The Volta a Portugal does not benefit from full road closures, as is the case with Grand Tours such as the Tour de France, and instead uses a rolling road closure, effectively a “bubble” of security that encloses the race convoy, from front to back.Carlos Catanario, of the Portugese police, told RTP that Tarling was racing to catch up on a downhill section, with the peloton ahead of him and split into three groups. The “broom” wagon, the van signifying the rear of the convoy and the end of the rolling road closure, was behind him.Catanario said that the GNR (National Republican Guard) police escort “could not keep up with Tarling”. Further ahead, the driver involved had been stopped at the roadside for some time, to allow the race to pass.After waiting, the driver is understood to have asked bystanders if he could join the road, and then drove on to the course, before the broom wagon had passed. “In that specific location, we know there were no officers present because it was not one of the locations prioritised in the assessment that had been carried out,” Catanario said.“The vehicle was going in the opposite direction to the direction of the race. The cyclist [Tarling] cut across the curve on the left lane – as is natural, as [racing] cyclists do – and that is what caused the cyclist and the vehicle to collide.”Tarling’s loss is the latest in a sport increasingly beleaguered by safety issues. As racing speeds increase and traffic intensifies, costs for event security rise, meaning race organisers are coming under increasing pressure to implement more effective measures.“It’s becoming increasingly expensive to organise races, and some organisers are abandoning the safety principles that govern the entire cycling bubble,” Pineau said. “The Volta a Portugal is a second-tier race; they have to find race officials, staff to organise it, and funds for the police.”View image in fullscreenA memorial for Finlay Tarling before the ninth stage of the Volta a Portugal on Sunday.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPATarling’s team, NSN Development, withdrew from the race on Saturday, but the race otherwise completed its final stages over the weekend as planned. Riders observed a minute’s silence at the start of the ninth stage, the leader’s jersey worn by Alexis Guérin was changed from yellow to black and the peloton wore black armbands.Tributes were paid and black armbands worn at other races including the Czech Tour and the Arctic Race of Norway.On Sunday Tarling’s father, Michael, posted a message on social media. “This has been the hardest couple of days of our lives and it’s taken us a bit of time to be able to post this. Hearing how lovingly and fondly Fin was thought of has been a huge help to us. We simply can’t thank you all enough for the support we’ve had.“I don’t know how we carry on from here, but we’ll figure it out with the support of all our family, friends, and community. Whilst our broken hearts will never be fixed, he was not only our son and brother but our best mate. Gentle, loving with the driest sense of humour, we will miss him terribly.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxury | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: A worker in London shields himself from the sun.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA worker in London shields himself from the sun.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersOpinionExtreme heatAndy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxuryJohn HarrisNurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plansSun 16 Aug 2026 07.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIdon’t think I have ever written before about a British strike directly related to the climate emergency. But that’s exactlywhat began late last weekin north London, with a zeitgeisty connection to Andy Burnham’s fixation on buses: picket lines outside depots and massed walkouts, while the temperatures in the relevant parts of the capital and its suburbs hovered at about 34C (93F).Last Friday, more than 1,500 drivers employed by the transport giant Arriva begana planned run of 26 stoppagesthrough to October, affecting bus routes spread between London and Essex. Everything is being led by the union Unite, whose recent grievances include alleged company union-busting and assaults by the public on staff. But the fundamental basis of the dispute is at the heart of the national condition: the near-impossibility for millions of people of working through another insanely hot summer.Most of Arriva North London’s buses, says Unite, have old-fashioned air cooling systems rather than air conditioning, which means that onboard temperatures have come down by only two or three degrees during this year’s five heatwaves. On other such vehicles, it insists,the air-con is broken. The cabs where drivers sit are essentially compact greenhouses, and can easily reach 40C or higher. And there is another grim twist: union members complain of a shortage of toilets on too many routes, meaning they refrain from drinking water. Unite has been warning about all this since the phases of intense heat that began back in May; its members, the union says, have experienced “heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration”.Arriva’s last financial figuresshowed a pre-tax profitof £133m.The company insiststhat it has “introduced short-term measures to protect drivers”, and is now also spending money on “longer-term fixes, including cab air-conditioning upgrades and our ongoing investment in new fleet”. But the root of its current problems seem clear. There is a longstanding failure, which runs across the UK’s public and private sectors – and also transcends national boundaries – to understand the mounting everyday effects of global heating, and to engage in what so many 21st-century companies and institutions remain so bad at: protective investment, with both eyes fixed not just on the searing inevitabilities of the future, but realities that are already here.Arriva places tight restrictions on its drivers talking to the media, so Unite pointed me instead to Mo, who has worked for another London bus operator for over 15 years, and had come to a picket line to show the strikers his support. “When it’s very hot, it’s very difficult to concentrate,” he told me. “Imagine the heat you feel when you put your hand near an oven. That’s what it’s like.” What, I wondered, had happened when these problems were raised with management? “Sometimes, we don’t want to raise this stuff, because they don’t want to hear it. If you say, ‘I’ve got a hot cab, I want to come out,’ they’re like, ‘Well, we’re going to lose mileage; we’re going to get penalised by TfL [Transport for London].’ I know the mayor’s put the message out” – in June,Sadiq Khan saidhe was committed to improving working conditions for drivers – “but the company says, ‘He doesn’t employ you. We do.’”There are no end of similarly unsettling reports from other occupations. The Royal College of Nursing says some of its members working in the health servicehave recently collapsed, while others have reported dizziness, nausea and dripping with sweat “from head to toe”, along with profound concerns about NHS patients’ most basic welfare.Recent research into the building tradefrom the University of Reading showed that 44% of the construction workers it contacted had experienced a heat-related illness, such as heatstroke, heat exhaustion or dehydration. Moreover, 57% said they had received no compulsory training on how to deal with heat.View image in fullscreenPeter Crane, who has driven for Arriva for 22 years, shows a temperature reading from inside of his cab of 44C as he takes part in strike action in north London.Photograph: Tom Jeffreys/PAAlmost exactly a year ago, I wrote aboutthe tragic story of Montse Aguilar, a 51-year-old woman who worked as a street cleaner in Barcelona, and returned home from a working day in which the city’s temperatures had reached 35C, only to collapse, hit her head and die. Soon after, people marched carrying banners that read “Extreme heat is also workplace violence”, and street cleaners demanded better summer workwear and more breaks. Much to her family’s distress, the city councilhas still not recognised her deathas a workplace accident, and there has yet to be an autopsy.This year, Barcelona’s authoritieshanded out about 1,400 braceletsfor staff working outdoors – including street cleaners, park workers and refuse specialists – which measure workers’ body temperatures and go into alert mode if they sense that the wearer is at risk: as and when that happens, the person concerned has to stop working. But despite Spain’s reputation for comparatively stringent heat regulations, unions continue to draw attention to a supposed system of protection still full of gaps. Late last month,the CGT union filed official complaintswith Barcelona’s labour inspectorate about what it deems deficient management of those wristbands, a lack of air-con in working vehicles and pledges from the city council being applied “late and halfway”.Across the world, every hot season inevitably brings more victims. In the US, official figures suggest thatmore than 550 workers die annuallyfrom heat exposure across the country. One recent story is that of Umeshkumar Thakkar, a 58-year-old postal worker who lived in Little Elm, Texas – who, though the cause of his death has yet to be officially established,has been citedas the third such employee in three years to die in the Dallas area amid extreme heat. Amazingly,Texas has barred its cities and countiesfrom passing local heat protections – while,to quote the New York Times, “The Trump administration is moving to rewrite Biden-era rules that would mandate breaks and access to water and shade for workers.” Hydration, it seems, is that bit too woke.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe UK’s position, it is a relief to say, is not nearly as dreadful, though there is still much work to do. For people working indoors,official guidancesuggests a minimum temperature of 16C, which falls to 13C for “physical work”, but there are no maximum temperatures for either indoor or outdoor labour. Things do finally seem to be moving: last month, the Department for Work and Pensions said that the Health and Safety Executive will soon launcha public consultationon improvements to safety-at-work rules that will cover levels of heat at work. There again,the official linefrom the prime minister’s spokesperson sounds bleak: “We have no plans to introduce a mandatory maximum workplace temperature.”In the wake of the Green MP Hannah Spencer’s private member’s bill toestablish exactly that, Unite is loudly making the case – as are the TUC and the independent advisory Climate Change Committee,which wants employersto “ensure that workplaces and working practices are safe for employees, including for those working outside”. Meanwhile, having planned for a late summer talking about the cost of living, Burnham did not mention the climate crisisuntil last Friday, in a country where brown fields are so starved of water they are now turning a scorched yellow,homes have been engulfed by wildfires, and far too many workers are finding the once-simple business of earning a living physically impossible. Like many people – including, I would imagine, plenty of those north London bus drivers – my guarded optimism about the new prime minister and his government endures. But the last of those issues needs as much urgent action as the others, before another boiling summer takes an even grimmer toll.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsExtreme heatOpinionIndustrial actionAndy BurnhamTrade unionsTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: Move over, Odysseus: time for the women of ancient Greece to have their moment in the sun | Natalie Haynes | The Guardian
description: The hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiences, says writer Natalie Haynes
Author: Natalie Haynes
Headline: The hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiences, says writer Natalie Haynes
Content: Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss (on screen) during rehearsals for Electra/Persona.Photograph: Monika Rittershaus/National Theatre/PAView image in fullscreenCate Blanchett and Nina Hoss (on screen) during rehearsals for Electra/Persona.Photograph: Monika Rittershaus/National Theatre/PAOpinionTheatreMove over, Odysseus: time for the women of ancient Greece to have their moment in the sunNatalie HaynesThe hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiencesSun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt feels like a very Greek summer here in the UK. The ground is scorched, it last rained months ago, and the giant publicity machine for Christopher Nolan’sbillion-dollar-grossingThe Odyssey – from red-carpet frocks to professorial disapproval – is a Charybdis, swallowing all other cultural events in its gaping maw.Mere Mortals– San Francisco Ballet’s astonishing work inspired by the story of Pandora – runs in Edinburgh this month before going to Sadler’s Wells in September. And Greek tragedy continues to fill London’s theatres.Last week, I went to seeSimon Stone’s reworkingof Aeschylus’s Oresteia at the Bridge theatre in south London, and it was packed. Even on a Thursday afternoon, there was a huge audience for the story of a family who turn on one another, wreaking intergenerational violence until their whole house lies in tatters and madness. Partly that is because of the excellent cast: David Morrissey and Mary-Louise Parker play Christopher and Montie – a modern Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, their marital squabbles fizzing back and forth until he cracks and she snaps. Their children are the ones who will have to try to reconcile the impossible: duty to their murdered father, respect to their murderous mother.Partly it is because Stone has earned his audience for Greek tragedy. Hisversion of Phaedrawith Janet McTeer at London’s National Theatre in 2023 blended Euripides, Seneca and Racine. And his adaptation ofEuripides’s Medea, starring Marieke Heebink at the Barbican in 2019, remains one of the best things I have ever seen. This modern-day version began with Medea leaving the asylum where she has spent the past year, after attempting to kill her ex-husband for his infidelity to her and their children. The dread piled up like bodies as the play moved to its wrenching conclusion. These very different plays posed a similar question: what do women do with their rage, if speaking it goes unheard?View image in fullscreenLiv Ullmann as Elisabet, left, and Bibi Andersson as Alma in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 film, Persona.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyThe hottest Greek ticket of the year, though, is surely for Cate Blanchett in the upcomingElectra/Persona by Benedict Andrews. Electra is a fascinating choice, not least because we have three different versions of her story: Sophocles and Euripides each wrote one, and Aeschylus’s Choephoroi covers the same part of the myth. There are plenty of variations between the three, not least because Euripides takes potshots at Aeschylus’s version, mocking a recognition scene that depended on Electra identifying her long-absent brother from a lock of hair and a footprint, both of which (implausibly) resemble her own.But the essential beats of her story are these: Agamemnon is murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra, and her lover, Aegisthus. Clytemnestra feels wholly justified in her actions, because Agamemnon had killed her older daughter 10 years earlier. She has spent the whole Trojan war waiting for the chance to take her revenge. But her surviving children – Electra and Orestes – cannot forgive her for killing their father, no matter the reason. Orestes has grown up away from home, biding his time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChristopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epic | Charlotte HigginsRead moreSophocles’s Electra has nowhere else to go: she cannot leave home, because she is a young woman and ancient Greek mores require that she live in her father’s house until she marries. Which she cannot do, because Aegisthus and Clytemnestra know she hates them, so any husband (or son she may have) would be turned against them. Electra is essentially imprisoned in the home of the people who killed her beloved father, with no hope of parole.This is the role that was being performed by Elisabet (played by Liv Ullmann) in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 psychological drama,Persona, before she has a breakdown and stops speaking. Alma (Bibi Andersson) is the guileless young nurse tending to her, sharing stories of her own life to fill the silence, until she finds that Elisabet is studying her. It is a film that has perplexed critics, unable to decode the women’s strange, strained relationship.But Electra is always a perplexing character, with warring emotions: love for her father, disregard for her late sister, loathing of her mother, and her pulsing heartbeat of rage. One reason these Greek tragedies keep finding an audience is that they give voice – and terrible action – to unheeded female anger. Medea doesn’t accept her abandonment, she destroys everything her husband has and wants in a single day. Clytemnestra doesn’t accept her daughter’s murder, she avenges it. And Electra doesn’t accept her father’s killing, but (like Hamlet) she doesn’t have the strength to act alone against her mother. These women are extremists – like many characters in Greek tragedy – but their rage is more powerful because they have been silenced and ignored. If modern theatre audiences are anything to go by, their days of silence are behind them.Natalie Haynes is presenter of Natalie Haynes Stands Up for the Classics on Radio 4, and author of books including Stone Blind and Pandora’s JarExplore more on these topicsTheatreOpinionThe OdysseyWomenCate BlanchettcommentShareReuse this content

title: My lovely French husband has made the ultimate sacrifice for me – he’s now officially British | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: In Leeds Civic Hall, I watched 20 new citizens pledge their allegiance to King Charles and his heirs, writes Emma Beddington. But it wasn’t patriotism that brought tears to my eyes
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: In Leeds Civic Hall, I watched 20 new citizens pledge their allegiance to King Charles and his heirs, writes Emma Beddington. But it wasn’t patriotism that brought tears to my eyes
Content: Emma Beddington and Olivier, after he received his British citizenship.Photograph: Courtesy of Emma BeddingtonView image in fullscreenEmma Beddington and Olivier, after he received his British citizenship.Photograph: Courtesy of Emma BeddingtonOpinionImmigration and asylumMy lovely French husband has made the ultimate sacrifice for me – he’s now officially BritishEmma BeddingtonIn Leeds Civic Hall, I watched 20 new citizens pledge their allegiance to King Charles and his heirs. But it wasn’t patriotism that brought tears to my eyesSun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTShareIhaven’t felt great about asking my husband to become British. There was theidiotic Life in the UK testthat every applicant has to pass; the cost; the faff; and the uncertainty, which still hasn’t ended. I found out his application had been accepted when he came into the kitchen in June with a face like thunder. “But that’s brilliant! You’ll never need to know how many Scottish ski resorts there are again!” I said, puzzled. He explained that, because we’re going on holiday before he can get a British passport to go with his French one, he’ll be inan immigration grey areathat could mean he gets refused re-entry.He should, theoretically, be OK, but it’s confusing.Why would he even want to come back to this place with its threadbare services,toxic waterways, obsession with “picky bits” and ridiculous politics? His Home Office email arrived just after the Makerfield byelection and that night the news showedthe returning officer’s poker-faced declarationagain: our future prime minister flanked by a politely clapping Binface and an oversized, blank-eyed fox. I started laughing, hysterically, guiltily. What have I done to him? “Will the world go a different colour when I’m British?” he asked on the train to the ceremony. “Yeah, reverse Wizard of Oz – everything goes grey.”But if you are becoming British, because you really love your wife or for any other reason, Leeds Civic Hall is a good spot for it. We admired the outside, embellished with large, golden owls, from the terrace of Wetherspoons, where another set of ceremony attenders – a south Asian couple our age, smartly dressed, finishing up an appropriate full English – were taking a “before” pic. We exchanged shy congratulations, then headed inside, where there was dark wood and stained glass, a proper sense of historical gravitas and a brief panic about the travel issue.An inadequate fan moved stifling air around feebly as the registrar explained people shouldn’t plan trips abroad before getting their British passports, to some overheated consternation. An intensive-care doctor decided to defer, unwilling to risk missing her shifts, but after some shrugging and a few fingers-crossed gestures, everyone else went ahead.I’m so glad we did. It was kind, laid-back and gently funny in a way that almost made me feel patriotic. There was a warning from the registrar not to laminate citizenship certificates (“You do not want to give the Home Office any more money!”), plus one for my husband that she’d probably say his name, Olivier, “with a Yorkshire twang” (she did; it was lovely). At one point, the whole team decided to move the table with the draped union jack for better photos, propping King Charles, in his clip frame, against the speaker used for a single mumbled verse of the national anthem.The business part of becoming British was very brief. Olivier had practised affirming allegiance back home (“No, you’re not pledging loyalty to his hair – itsheirs”), worried about speaking solo, but it was a group effort. Everyone swore or affirmed, then pledged, then the registrar said simply they were all citizens now – and I found myself crying.It had been such an act of love for us – I hugged him, whispered my thanks – but also it was impossible not to be moved by everyone else. The frail, stooped woman who left her walker to go up, proudly unaided, for her certificate. The radiant teen in a white minidress who was getting her A-level results the same day, adulthood unfolding in the dazzling sunshine. The tiny mother photographed by her giant, bashful teenage son in a sharp suit and blinding-white trainers. The grey-haired Chinese woman in wire-rimmed glasses, attending alone, who asked me to take her beaming picture. The guy who ducked out apologetically before group photos, saying he had to get to work. The 20 people from Spain, Bahrain, Bangladesh, China, Eritrea, France, Ghana, India, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Pakistan, Poland, Romania and South Africa, who had done something hard for love, safety or a different life.An hour later, we were back on the train. The world hasn’t gone grey for my husband, he says – wait until he finds himself stranded in a foreign airport – and, for a moment, for me, it felt quite golden.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumOpinionBritish identity and societycommentShareReuse this content

title: Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as Trump | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: Marco Rubio at the Munich Security Conference, 14 February 2026.Photograph: Giuseppe Lami/EPAView image in fullscreenMarco Rubio at the Munich Security Conference, 14 February 2026.Photograph: Giuseppe Lami/EPAOpinionMarco RubioMarco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as TrumpSimon TisdallAs chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignoreSun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareViewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaignconclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this weekflatly rejectedhis latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’sattacks on Nato alliesgrow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His bossmocked himas “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.Or maybe not.Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice:become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. Helamented the declineof “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump hasattacked eight countriesin the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession,could be next.View image in fullscreenMarco Rubio looks on as Donald Trump speaks at an American Mining Industry roundtable, Washington, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Matt Kaminsky/EPARubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding.This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer,Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now hetoes Trump’s ingratiating lineon Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, hasgutted USAIDand seeks todismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, hetravelled to Romeand set the pope straight.The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losingon the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy isshort of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu –faces defeatin October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMillions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that? | Arwa MahdawiRead moreRubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. Heknows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out.The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becomingTrump’s chosen successorand heir to the Maga brand.Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsMarco RubioOpinionUS foreign policyTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: A positive new report raises the question: was Reeves undermined by dodgy data? | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Assessment’s finding of a jump in UK productivity emphasises urgent need to appoint a national statistician
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Assessment’s finding of a jump in UK productivity emphasises urgent need to appoint a national statistician
Content: When the former chancellor Rachel Reeves returns to the backbenches this autumn, she will have some right to wonder if she was let down by ONS figures.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenWhen the former chancellor Rachel Reeves returns to the backbenches this autumn, she will have some right to wonder if she was let down by ONS figures.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAEconomics viewpointProductivityA positive new report raises the question: was Reeves undermined by dodgy data?Heather StewartAssessment’s finding of a jump in UK productivity emphasises urgent need to appoint a national statisticianSun 16 Aug 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe keen new chancellor, John Healey, responded to last week’s better-than-expected economic news by claiming the government was “bringing hope back”. Growth did not plunge as feared after Donald Trump unleashed war on Iran – with GDPexpanding at a pretty decent 0.4%in the second quarter.But what if we should have held on to a bit more hope all along? Anew assessment of the UK’s recent productivitysuggests this critical measure of the country’s economic strength may have been systematically underestimated.Instead of stagnation, it points to a “meaningful pickup” in productivity since mid-2024, with annual growth of about 1.6% – up from an average of 0.3% in the previous decade.This has very much not been the prevailing narrative since Labour came to power. Indeed, Rachel Reeves spent months last year scrambling to respond to a downgrade in productivity projections from theOffice for Budget Responsibility(OBR) – from 1.3% annual growth to 1% – with a knock-on effect for the public finances.Other things being equal, weaker productivity means weaker growth, which broadly translates to lower tax revenues and a bigger public deficit.The OBR rethink didn’t reflect anythingLabourhad done, resulting instead from the long-term failure of productivity growth to bounce back after the 2008 global financial crisis. And part of the reason it became so pivotal was because Reeves had left herself so little room for manoeuvre.But the productivity downgrade contributed to the gloomy sense that Labour was overseeing an economy beset by intractable long-term challenges. And it increased thesize of the tax grab Reeves neededto make at last year’s budget to rebuild the headroom against her fiscal rules and pay for Labour’s welfare U-turn.The new estimates, from the Centre for Economic Performance at the London School ofEconomics(LSE), where former Reeves advisers John Van Reenen and Anna Valero have now returned to their desks, paint a markedly different picture.Productivity is defined as how much output each worker produces, but the UK has been botching the job of sizing up the workforce now for several years. The beleagueredOffice for National Statistics(ONS) withdrew the status of accredited official statistic from its labour force survey (LFS) in 2024 as it struggled with plunging response rates from consumers.Instead of using the LFS, which the OBR has to rely on, the LSE co-authors, including Van Reenen and Valero, together with Niki Barbas, use estimates made by the Resolution Foundation thinktank.Resolution’s approach relies on an alternative dataset published by the ONS, based on what companies tell the tax authorities through the PAYE system (augmented with other sources to account for the self-employed).The differences are wide. While the LFS records a 377,000 increase in the number of employees since mid-2024, the tax-based measure shows a decline of 133,000.Of course, depending on what’s happened to those missing workers – retirement, unemployment, sickness, childcare – this may be a different cause for concern. Reeves has been accused of depressing hiring by piling costs on to employers.But using the smaller estimate for the number of employees suggests that far from flatlining, productivity has jumped. That raises the intriguing possibility that, with better data, the OBR downgrade, and the massive headache it created for the then chancellor, could have been avoided.Van Reenen says that “the best current guess does suggest we are getting more out of our workers than we used to”.He dismisses the idea that what has happened is just layoffs among low-skilled workers, pushing up average productivity. “I don’t think that’s the main story: a chunk of this appears to be real.”It’s too early to say what may be driving an uplift in productivity, let alone whether it will be sustained – but one hypothesis is that AI is starting to bear fruit in some sectors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s certainly a possibility that we are seeing the first signs of that starting to happen,” Van Reenen says.UK heatwaves may have cost economy £4.4bn in lost output so far this year, analysis findsRead moreNot surprisingly, he points to his former boss Reeves’s policies – including a significant increase in public investment and the stripping back of planning rules – as reasons to hope the improvement could continue.The latest official GDP figures showed business investment – widely seen as one determinant of productivity – rising strongly, though experts were quick to caution that it could be reversed as high energy prices take their toll.Whatever the future brings, the wide discrepancy with the official figures underlines how urgent a priority it should have been to fix the gaping holes in the UK’s jobs data earlier, and more effectively.The poorly resourced ONS has been doggedly developing a new, online version of the LFS. Instead of the cumbersome 40-45 minute phone call needed to complete the existing questionnaire, it takes about 15 minutes.Inan update last week, the ONS acknowledged that the refreshed survey design appeared to be turning up slightly different results – including, for example, lower levels of long-term sickness. It also confirmed that it would be November next year at the earliest before it could switch over to the new version.The UK has had no national statistician, the head of the ONS, for more than a year since Ian Diamond resigned in May 2025. The vacancy hardly speaks of burning urgency in Whitehall.Some of Labour’s worst domestic struggles over the past two years, from winter fuel tothe welfare row, were self-inflicted. But as Reeves returns to the backbenches this autumn, she could be excused for feeling her challenges at No 11 were exacerbated by dodgy data.Explore more on these topicsProductivityEconomics viewpointOffice for National StatisticsEconomic growth (GDP)Office for Budget ResponsibilityEconomic policyEconomicsRachel ReevescommentShareReuse this content

title: Ali came to me seeking help for disordered eating. The real issue was a relationship built on control | Ahona Guha | The Guardian
description: She second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someone
Author: Ahona Guha
Headline: She second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someone
Content: ‘He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts,’ writes Dr Ahona Guha.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA WireView image in fullscreen‘He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts,’ writes Dr Ahona Guha.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA WireThe modern mindEating disordersAli came to me seeking help for disordered eating. The real issue was a relationship built on controlAhona GuhaShe second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someoneThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTShareAli* initially came to therapy for disordered eating. She was a young and diffident woman. She described recurrent cycles of restricted eating followed by attempts to exercise it away. We usedcognitive behavioural therapy for eating disordersto unpick her “food rules” – the underlying beliefs which can drive eating disorders, such as “the less I eat the better” or “carbs are bad”.As we worked on understanding and shifting her beliefs and behaviours around food, we noticed that most of her assumptions around eating, shape and weight coincided with the start of her relationship with her ex-partner. She told me he was a “gym junkie” and spent hours working out and encouraged her to do the same. “He got angry if I ate carbs,” she said, “and created a couples meal plan for us so I could shred and look hot when we were out together.”Slowly, she spoke of other forms of control: encouraging her to dress in a “sexier” manner than she felt comfortable with, jealousy if he saw her talking to another man, watching her bank transactions to see where she was going, and insisting on going to all her social events so he could get to know her friends. “But he’d always start an argument, or would say he didn’t like them,” she told me. “And then I had to stop seeing them to prove my loyalty to him.” He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts, telling her that what he wanted was “normal” and she was not being a good partner if she refused.I’m seeing more people in therapy struggling with war-related anxiety. Here’s what helps | Ahona GuhaRead moreAs she spoke to me, I saw the shift in her eyes when she realised the pattern which had slowly emerged over three years:coercive control.After this realisation, her eating stabilised. Food was one of the initial mechanisms of control he used to start shaping her body and personality, and her difficulties with eating were a symptom of the trauma she had experienced.Unlike physical violence, coercive control can be easy to miss as it is a pattern of repeated subtle behaviours and usually inflicted with the victim’s seeming agreement. At other times the coercion is more overt and can involve threats such as taking away children, or inflicting violence if sexual demands are not met. Regardless of the level of severity of this behaviour, the impacts can create psychological harm for victims.Like many other victims of coercive control, Ali had very poor self-esteem and was racked with anxiety. She second-guessed herself and was overly deferential and eager to please, reporting she “felt frozen” when she believed she displeased someone. Her beliefs about herself and about relationships were distorted (“I have no radar”, “all relationships are unsafe”). These are all typical responses demonstrated by people who have experienced coercion or violence in intimate relationships.Our work together encompassed a few stages. First, we worked together to understand what coercive control is, and used a simpleABC model derived from CBTto help Ali understand how certain statements or behaviours by her ex bypassed her instinctive radar and influenced her to give in to him by creating feelings of insecurity and anxiety. We looked at the way she experienced his approval as a potent reinforcer for compliance as it signalled that the danger of relational rupture or loss was over.We named the distinction between her emotions/thoughts and reality, allowing her to separate from the belief that she was “not enough”. We also adaptedcognitive processing therapy for PTSDtechniques to help her understand and reframe her “stuck points” (eg the trauma of her distorted beliefs about how she failed herself through her “poor radar”). We also looked at the characteristics of healthy relationships, and helped her create a checklist for herself of the signs of healthy relationships so she could date with more confidence.Together, we also worked on Ali’s anxiety. This predated her former partner though had considerably worsened after the relationship. We utilised a cognitive behavioural approach and looked at the beliefs which fuelled her anxiety (“my friends don’t like me because I withdrew from them while with my ex”) and how she responded to these beliefs, such as by refusing to go to gatherings or engaging insafety behaviourslike drinking. We did some behavioural “experiments” to challenge her beliefs and to learn new ways of coping, and also brainstormed ways she could talk to her friends about the relationship with Ian. She was pleasantly surprised to find that her friends understood and were supportive of her once they knew the context.Recovery was not a linear journey, but these small steps allowed Ali to stop blaming herself, to feel more confident in her body and to show up in the world just as she was, without focusing on pleasing a partner.*all clients are fictional amalgamsIn Australia, theButterfly Foundationis at 1800 33 4673. In the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In the US, help is available atnationaleatingdisorders.orgor by callingANAD’seating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. Other international helplines can be found atEating Disorder HopeDr Ahona Guha is a clinical and forensic psychologist, trauma expert and author from Melbourne. She is the author of Reclaim: Understanding Complex Trauma and Those Who Abuse, and Life Skills For a Broken WorldExplore more on these topicsEating disordersThe modern mindMental healthRelationshipsDomestic violenceAnxietycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the changed world of job interviews: missing the human factor | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Andy Burnham’s doubts about Zoom interviews apply more widely to a hiring process being transformed by AI
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Andy Burnham’s doubts about Zoom interviews apply more widely to a hiring process being transformed by AI
Content: ‘For young people especially, experiencing repeated rejection without interacting with a single human being is alienating as well as disappointing.’Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreen‘For young people especially, experiencing repeated rejection without interacting with a single human being is alienating as well as disappointing.’Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAOpinionJob huntingThe Guardian view on the changed world of job interviews: missing the human factorEditorialAndy Burnham’s doubts about Zoom interviews apply more widely to a hiring process being transformed by AISun 16 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTShareAlmost half of UK jobseekers have found themselves pitching to an AI bot, according to recentresearch, leading many to give up in frustration. As one despairing applicantlamentedin the pages of the Guardian a few months ago: “The hiring process has become so mechanised, both figuratively and literally, that it’s hard to believe that the people who end up getting hired aren’t merely the best at gaming the system.” For young people especially, experiencing repeated rejection without interacting with a single human being is alienating as well as disappointing.It was encouraging, therefore, to hear Andy Burnhamvoiceconcerns about online recruitment processes on a recent employment-focused podcast. Describing the jobseeking environment for young people as “harsh”, the prime minister criticised the widespread use of interviews on Zoom and Microsoft Teams, and questioned whether applicants could properly convey their personal qualities without a face-to-face meeting.There is another side to the story, as Zoom executives wereswiftto point out. Online interviewing cuts out travel costs, for example, giving a chance to applicants who may not be able to fund long journeys and possible overnight stays. But Mr Burnham is right to identify a dangerous drift towards selection processes that undervalue the worth of conversations between people in the same room at the same time.The increasingly used “one-way” video interview – in which applicants are given fixed periods of time to plan and deliver responses to prerecorded questions – seems to offer a particularly disorientating experience. Interviewees, in effect, speak into a void, unable to process feedback or interpret body language.The sorting processes deployed in AI interviews have been rightly criticised for their opacity, and susceptibility to algorithmicbias. A lack of transparency in relation to the programming of recruitment software means that an unlevel playing field may be suspected but difficult to prove. The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission settled an age discriminationcasewith a company that came to light only when a failed applicant reapplied, changing just her age, and miraculously passed through to the next round.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty ImagesIt could hardly be claimed that traditional recruitment processes were bias-free. Used in the right way, new technologies can play their part in opening up possibilities for applicants rather than simply screening them out with minimal explanation or feedback. But while it may be convenient for businesses to rely on tech to do the work, the struggle even to present one’s credentials to another human being is adding insult to injuries already inflicted by an exceptionallyunforgivinglabour market. A recent report from the Institute for Public Policy Research found that young people in England were increasingly “losing faith in their futures”.The Information Commissioner’s Office has been tasked by parliament with producing acode of practiceon AI and automated decision-making. In a recentreportit found that when companies claimed that AI-generated hiring recommendations were subjected to human review, that was often only partially true, if at all. Applicants deserve better. The use of digital technologies is already changing the face of the entry-level jobs market. Interviewees should be protected from the downsides of their growing dominance in the recruitment process.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every year | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The provision of homes needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded. It is vital economic infrastructure, so let’s make it affordable for all
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The provision of homes needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded. It is vital economic infrastructure, so let’s make it affordable for all
Content: Mixed housing in Poplar, east London … ‘Designed in recognition that a city could not function without healthy employees living nearby.’Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyView image in fullscreenMixed housing in Poplar, east London … ‘Designed in recognition that a city could not function without healthy employees living nearby.’Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyOpinionSocial housingThe Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every yearEditorialThe provision of homes needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded. It is vital economic infrastructure, so let’s make it affordable for allSun 16 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareLondon’s city centre has long been a place where rich and poor live side by side, while so many other metropolitan equivalents – Paris, New York, San Francisco – remain the preserve of the rich. It maintains its mix today: in many inner London boroughs, between20% and 40%of households live in social housing. Asmall but steady declinein social housing in these areas leaves many fearing that the city’s diversity is under threat.What happens when cities become less socially mixed? The G15 group of housing associations, which provide social and affordable homes for about one in 10 Londoners,commissioned researchrecently on the economic contribution of those living in social housing. It found that they contributed £27.8bn to London’s economy in 2024, even after housing benefit was taken into account. Its methodology involved comparing the lives of people in social housing with those without a stable and affordable place to live. The conclusion was that stable and affordable housing reduces spend and demand on public services, promotes better physical and mental overall health, and results in a higher likelihood that tenants stay in work and contribute economically.The idea that social housing is an economic investment is not new. England’s municipal housing was designed in recognition that a city could not function without healthy employees living nearby. Gordon Brown and Tony Blair revisited this idea in the early 2000s, arguing that England’s public services would deteriorate if hospital workers and police officers were pushed out of major urban centres. They framed social housing not as a charitable act, but as critical economic infrastructure.The G15 report finds that key workers such as nurses and care and retail workers account for about 65% of London’s social housing population (compared with 40% of London’s population). Not so long ago, these same workers were clapped in the streets for keeping cities functioning during the Covid-19 pandemic; they were the reason that people could buy milk and elderly people remained cared for while others had to stay at home. But many such workers would not be able to afford to live in big cities without the help of social housing. Even moving to the outer bounds of the city would add thousands to their commuting bill, as well as hours to their working days, according to the research.View image in fullscreenNye Bevan, postwar Labour minister and deputy leader.Photograph: Joseph McKeown/Getty ImagesViewed through that lens, housing that average-wage earners can afford becomes a vital asset for the country’s resilience. Social rents are proof that housing costs need not bea key driver of poverty– and yet our current building targets aren’t being pursued urgently enough to fix the problem. Housing charities say that90,000 social homesa year are needed in England. No major party has plans for anything like that number.Mr Blair shifted social housing from councils towards housing associations, and the coalition commercialised that model. Andy Burnham now appears to want to put councils back at the centre. In an interview with theLondon Review of Booksin 2024, Mr Burnham said: “If you read Nye Bevan’s speeches, as I do, if you read his speech that was the postwar Housing Act, second reading, he talked about how housing needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded and sold, a wealth creator. Everybody needs it, it’s an essential service. And it was interesting how he positioned it like the NHS. And so that’s the philosophy that we need.” Amen to that.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Women should not have to travel for hours to give birth  | Pregnancy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers reflect on how hospital closures are putting pregnant women’s lives at risk
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers reflect on how hospital closures are putting pregnant women’s lives at risk
Content: ‘An ambulance may do it quicker, but there is often a two-hour delay before one becomes available.’Photograph: Jinli Guo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘An ambulance may do it quicker, but there is often a two-hour delay before one becomes available.’Photograph: Jinli Guo/Getty ImagesPregnancyLettersWomen should not have to travel for hours to give birthReaders reflect on how hospital closures are putting pregnant women’s lives at riskSun 16 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe situation facing pregnant women in Devon and Cornwall following the closure of North Devon district hospital is not unique (‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in Devon, 10 August). Many rural areas have already seen the distances travelled in labour increase due to the closure of local units over the past two decades. In south Cumbria, first-time deliveries are only available at Lancaster or Barrow-in-Furness. If you live in Ambleside, the distance to Royal Lancaster infirmary could be done in an hour, but you can face long delays due to traffic.An ambulance may do it quicker, but there is often a two-hour delay before one becomes available. As someone who had to drive their partner to hospital following a heart attack, I am more than aware of ambulance delays in Cumbria.Once upon a time Kendal had a wonderful maternity unit, sadly now closed. It was midwife-led, so now possibly deemed unsafe. But being supported by an experienced midwife was the best outcome for me – certainly far better that being in the second stage of labour on the hard shoulder of the M6.Pat GibsonKendal, CumbriaThis is an issue experienced at the other end of the UK too, where for over a decade mothers-to-be in Caithness have had to travel for more than two hours to give birth at Raigmore hospital, as services were downgraded at Caithness general hospital. This is an issue that makes young professionals think twice about accepting posts in teaching and healthcare in the north Highlands.At the other end of the scale, that distance from a major hospital led me and other colleagues who had lived and worked in Caithness for four decades to decide not to retire in the far north.Julie AdamsArbroath, AngusMy parents lived in Lynton in north Devon when my mother was pregnant in 1978, and she hoped to give birth in the local cottage hospital where my father was born. However, she was told that she would have to travel to Barnstaple. Now, 46 years later, women in north Devon are being told that they need to travel to Taunton or Exeter for “spontaneous” births. Or they can stay at home and hope for the best. It’s horrifying.Cars may be radically different compared with the 1970s, but congestion on the local roads only gets worse. What next? Plymouth? Bristol? Working-age people are already being priced out by holiday lets and second homes, and now they can’t give birth safely either.Name and address suppliedAlthough it is good news that Yvette Cooper, our new health secretary, plans to reintroduce binding national maternity standards (6 August), I was dismayed to discover while on a visit to my old home town of Barnstaple, north Devon, that women will have to travel to Exeter, 40 miles away along narrow country roads, while in labour to deliver their babies. To anyone who knows north Devon this is sheer madness. Women might well end up having to have their babies by the roadside.I had quick labours and one of my children had the cord around his neck. He would not have survived if we had not been safely in hospital. I hope Cooper can act quickly to address the chronic shortage of midwives in this country.Sarah SheilsYorkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
