title: How surrogacy helped my sister and friends | Surrogacy | The Guardian
description: Letter: Hazel Davis responds to a letter about the regulation and ethics of surrogacy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Hazel Davis responds to a letter about the regulation and ethics of surrogacy
Content: ‘I became an auntie via surrogacy when my sister’s friend carried her third child.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘I became an auntie via surrogacy when my sister’s friend carried her third child.’Photograph: GettySurrogacyLettersHow surrogacy helped my sister and friendsHazel Davisresponds to a letter about the regulation and ethics of surrogacySun 16 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareI wish to respond to Lexi Ellingsworth’s letter (Regulation cannot eliminate surrogacy risks, 23 July). I gave birth to a baby for my friends in January. While the baby is living with its parents, my husband and I are the legal parents. We are waiting for our family court date in September to recognise the baby’s biological parents as legal parents.My surrogacy story started when my sister suffered complications following the birth of her first child. After a second difficult birth, the doctors told her that it wouldn’t be safe for her to carry any more children. I became an auntie via surrogacy when my sister’s friend carried her third child. Now my niece is a determined five‑year-old, just as much a part of the family as her older siblings, and I see no evidence that her origins have any impact.In 2023, some friends confided they had joined SurrogacyUK as they hoped to start a family, but needed some help. David had been my husband’s best friend since primary school, and my friend since university, and is now our daughter’s godfather.They were very surprised when I offered to be their surrogate. I was aware of the risks, but I was surrounded by support. During the pregnancy, our friends recorded children’s stories. I played these through little speakers on my belly so the baby would recognise their parents’ voices from birth.The legal challenges were highlighted when their baby became extremely unwell at only 11 days old. My husband and I – as legal parents – were glued to our phones in case the hospital needed us to consent to medical tests. His parents were at his bedside, ready to make those decisions. The law is not acting in the best interests of the children.To those who wish to protect me by denying me the choice to use my body to help my friends, your concern is misguided. Susan Golombok, professor emerita of family research at the University of Cambridge,wrote in Aprilthat a 20-year study of UK surrogacy families had “found no evidence of widespread psychological harm to children, parents, or surrogates”.Our friends’ baby will grow up knowing where they came from, how much they were wanted and how much they are loved.Hazel DavisTrustee,SurrogacyUK FoundationHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: To protect babies from abuse, we need CCTV in nurseries | Child protection | The Guardian
description: Letter: Cameras would help catch perpetrators earlier and save children from harm, says Tulip Siddiq MP
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Cameras would help catch perpetrators earlier and save children from harm, says Tulip Siddiq MP
Content: ‘I am urging Andy Burnham to take heed of our campaign, to strengthen the safety and regulation of nurseries.’Photograph: Alex Hinds/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I am urging Andy Burnham to take heed of our campaign, to strengthen the safety and regulation of nurseries.’Photograph: Alex Hinds/AlamyChild protectionLettersTo protect babies from abuse, we need CCTV in nurseriesCameras would help catch perpetrators earlier and save children from harm, saysTulip Siddiq MPSun 16 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTShareFor seven years, my youngest constituents were abused at Bright Horizons nursery in West Hampstead, London. Earlier this year,Vincent Chan was jailedfor 18 years for his horrific crimes.It is every parent’s worst nightmare to discover that their child has been subject to abuse. For this to have happened in a nursery, where parents trusted their children would be safe, is truly abhorrent. Tragically, many families will probably never know whether their child was a victim. The lack of evidence about what was happening in the nursery, in the rooms where Chan was in charge, means that some parents have been left only with questions.A group of 200 locally affected parents have come together to call for mandatory CCTV in nurseries, as well as requiringOfstedto review such footage in all inspections. Together we have met the previous education secretary and the previous early years minister, and gave evidence to an expert panel to assess the feasibility of mandatory CCTV in nurseries. With none of these ministers still in post, we must not lose momentum.All the parents I have met are truly inspirational, given everything that they’ve been through, and are doing all they can to stand up for their little ones.Alongside the parents of Genevieve Meehan in Manchester (Parents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across England, 9 August), and the Lullaby Trust, I am urging Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, to take heed of our campaign, to strengthen the safety and regulation of nurseries.With20,000 reportsof serious childcare incidents in English nurseries in the past five years, we need mandatory CCTV to tackle this. While it may not be the magic bullet, in several cases across the county – from Bristol and Manchester to Twickenham in London – CCTV would have caught the perpetrators earlier and saved children from harm.More broadly, parents are calling for an improved inspection and accountability framework of early years settings after concerns were repeatedly ignored by nursery staff and regulators. Babies and toddlers are the most vulnerable people in our society, and we must do all we can to protect them from harm.Tulip Siddiq MPLabour, Hampstead and HighgateExplore more on these topicsChild protectionEarly years educationChildcareOfstedChildrenParents and parentingTulip SiddiqlettersShareReuse this content

title: If you’re working class, you’ve got little chance of a career in classical music  | Class issues | The Guardian
description: Letter: Diversity schemes that ignore class will keep mistaking a handful of border-crossers for structural change, says one reader, whose son was judged too privileged
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Diversity schemes that ignore class will keep mistaking a handful of border-crossers for structural change, says one reader, whose son was judged too privileged
Content: ‘Many UK recital venues insist on conservatoire-trained performers, but refuse to pay them.’Photograph: Vadim Ponomarenko/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Many UK recital venues insist on conservatoire-trained performers, but refuse to pay them.’Photograph: Vadim Ponomarenko/AlamyClass issuesLettersIf you’re working class, you’ve got little chance of a career in classical musicDiversity schemes that ignore class will keep mistaking a handful of border-crossers for structural change, says one reader, whose son was judged too privilegedSun 16 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTShareSymeon Brown’s argument that class is the elephant in the room in conversations about race (Interview, 9 August) is nowhere more visible than in classical music.Celebrated black classical musicians held up as evidence of progress are very often solidly middle class: children of professionals who could afford the instruments, tuition, exam fees and travel that serious musical training demands. Their success is real, but is mainly evidence that class opens doors.My son is white, working class, was on free school meals until he was 12, and still lives in one of England’s most deprived areas. He won a scholarship to a specialist music school and went on to a top conservatoire. His closest friend, a black working-class classical musician, followed an almost identical path. Both were judged too privileged for widening-participation support at master’s level because they had attended independent schools, ignoring their bursaries, or that their families could not fund exam entries, let alone two years of postgraduate fees and living costs. In interviews, conservatoires even vigorously disputed the extent of their exclusion.Reinforcing the class barrier, many UK recital venues insist on conservatoire-trained performers, but refuse to pay them, even declining to share an often substantial retiring collection, claiming that the experience is reward enough – and thus excluding anyone who must work for a livingDiversity schemes that ignore class will keep mistaking a handful of border-crossers for structural change, leaving the poorest musicians of every colour stranded.Name and address suppliedExplore more on these topicsClass issuesClassical musicRaceDEI policiesSocial mobilitylettersShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow | Russia | The Guardian
description: Kyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capital
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Kyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capital
Content: 0:56Warehouse near Moscow on fire after Ukrainian drone attack – videoRussiaUkrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says MoscowKyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capitalDan Sabbaghin KyivSun 16 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine has launched one of its largest drone attacks since the start of the war, causing a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow and killing at least six people overnight, according to Russian authorities.The defence ministry in Moscow said it had shot down 1,478 Ukrainian drones in the past 24 hours – the highest ever total claimed – in an escalating air war in which seven Ukrainians were also killed asRussiabombed 13 locations inside the country.A huge fire engulfed a 250,000 sq metre building near Podolsk, 25 miles south of Moscow’s city centre, belonging to the Wildberries distribution company. The facility was disabled as a result, Ukraine’s military said.Sergei Sobyanin, the mayor of Moscow, said 600 drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, of which 201 were destroyed. One person was reported killed in the region, while Ukraine said a second warehouse at nearby Domodedovo was also targeted.MapThe Russian news agency RIA Novosti reported that the figure was the largest daily total claimed by the defence ministry, exceeding a record that had been set only the day before, though the figure is probably exaggerated and could not be verified.Experts said Russian numbers needed to be treated with caution but added that the scale of damage caused overnight nevertheless demonstrated how rapidly Ukraine had expanded its long-range attack capabilities in 2026.Serhii Kuzan, the chair of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a thinktank, said Russian authorities “deliberately inflate their figures” to make exaggerated claims about the effectiveness of their air defence.But he said that “against the backdrop of increased production of Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles, both the number of strikes and the scale of Ukrainian weaponry’s deployment are on the rise” as the war continues.Kuzan argued that it was “quite possible” it was the largest-scale attack on the Moscow region, and it was “at least on a par” with theMay strikes on an oil refineryin the Kapotnya area near Moscow.View image in fullscreenFirefighters try to extinguish a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesA rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including theFlamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing dronefrom Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles from its border.Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv faces missile barrage after Zelenskyy targets Russian satellite networkRead moreUkraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it still does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles fired frequently by Moscow.At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to a rise in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter.Kuzan said: “With every successful strike, Russia’s economic and military capabilities are diminished, and the Kremlin faces a new dilemma: how to counter this in a war of attrition.”In the past month, Kyiv has shifted focus to attacking facilities linked to Wildberries, used widely by businesses to support online retail. Ukraine says the warehouses are used by the military for logistics, though they also store stock sold by large and small Russian businesses.Ukraine’s military said on Sunday it had disabled seven out of 10 of the company’s largest warehouses in an effort to hurt the Russian economy and affect ordinary citizens financially, in a strike conducted with FP-1 drones.View image in fullscreenA Wildberries employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire.Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty ImagesFive people were reported to have been killed in Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, and the local governor said a further 150 incoming drones had been destroyed. Ukraine said it had targeted a factory that produced rocket fuel in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, causing a fire there.Russian drone and missile attacks killed two people in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, while a Spanish F-18 jet shot down what appeared to be a Russia drone that had crossed over the border into Romania.The Spanish fighter was part of a Nato patrol mission and shot down the drone at about 5am after it crossed into Romanian airspace. “The drone appears to be Russian,” a Nato military spokesperson said.Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region, said the assault on the region was “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory”. Video footage on social media showed a fast fire raging across the Wildberries warehouse complex.Russian attacks on Ukraine also killed two in the Sumy border region and three others across the country. A ballistic missile attack on Kyiv shortly before 3am injured six and caused several fires in the capital.A blaze caused by the attacks destroyed a large part of the Petrovka book market in the Obolonskyi district in Kyiv overnight, with some booksellers reporting they had lost their entire stock in the incident.View image in fullscreenFirefighters work to put out a fire at a book market in Kyiv.Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP“There is nothing. Nobody has anything left,” said Natalya, a bookstore owner who was interviewed by Ukraine’s Hromadske website. “Everything burned down. I was selling foreign language [textbooks] for schoolchildren. We were waiting for September so that everyone would have textbooks … But what happened happened.”Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, praised the work of the country’s emergency services and accused the Russians of attacking ordinary people. “Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” he said in a social media post.Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles at Ukrainian cities and communities over the past week, most of them ballistic missiles of various types.Though Ukraine is effective at stopping slower-moving drones, it has little to no defence against high-speed ballistics, its stock of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles – the only weapons capable of knocking them out – having been run down.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Wildfires kill two in Greece and torch Belgian nature reserve | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Couple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near Liège
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Couple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near Liège
Content: A firefighting helicopter drops water over a wildfire on the island of Salamina, near Athens.Photograph: Yannis Panagopoulos/Eurokinissi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighting helicopter drops water over a wildfire on the island of Salamina, near Athens.Photograph: Yannis Panagopoulos/Eurokinissi/AFP/Getty ImagesWildfiresWildfires kill two in Greece and torch Belgian nature reserveCouple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near LiègeAngela Giuffridaand agenciesSun 16 Aug 2026 17.27 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn elderly couple died in fires on the Greek island of Salamis on Sunday and Belgium is battling its largest modern-day wildfire at an inaccessible area nearGermany, in the latest wave of European wildfires.The couple died outside their home in the Peristeria beach area of Salamis, Greece’s coastguard said. More than 500 people were ordered to evacuate.Map of Greek wildfireIn Spain, a soldier died on Sunday while helping efforts to extinguish a large wildfire in Aragon, authorities said. French reinforcements were due to help contain the wildfire in the north-eastern region, which has raged for a week and threatened a 1,000-year-old monastery.View image in fullscreenA wildfire in the area of Las Peñas de Riglos in Aragon, Spain.Photograph: UME/AFP/Getty ImagesInBelgium, a wildfire that broke out on Friday in the High Fens, a large nature reserve popular with hikers, had ravaged about 3,000 hectares (7,400 acres) of land and was encroaching on the border with Germany by early Sunday morning.About 600 people in the municipalities of Waimes and Bütgenbach, in Liège province, were told on Saturday to evacuate from their homes, and tourists were also advised to leave, as winds shifted and smoke spread.Of those who followed the order, about 20 spent the night in a sports hall, while others sought refuge with family and friends.Hervé Jamar, the governor of Liège, said more than 250 firefighters and emergency staff were involved in the operation, including firefighters from Germany.Map of Belgian wildfireFarmers have also been helping to battle the blaze, using their tractors to pull in water from Lake Robertville.Air support, provided by two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden and four helicopters – two from Belgium and two from the Netherlands – is crucial owing to the nature reserve’s complex and fragile terrain, which is made up of dense forest, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy firefighting vehicles risk sinking.Access to Lake Bütgenbach was prohibited on Sunday to allow the aircraft to refill.View image in fullscreenAir support in fighting the fire in the High Fens nature reserve is crucial owing to the complex terrain where heavy vehicles risk sinking.Photograph: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/ShutterstockAuthorities described the conditions as still challenging, although two fire fronts towards Jalhay and Monschau were now under control, said Belgium’s interior minister, Bernard Quintin, after visiting the crisis centre in Vottem on Sunday afternoon.“On this third day of fighting the fires, all resources remain mobilised on the ground,” he wrote on X, and he thanked all those involved.“We can also count on the solidarity of our European partners … thank you to everyone who mobilised to fight the fires. United, we are stronger.”Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?Read moreThe fire, described by officials as the largest in Belgium’s modern history, began in an area that in 1911 was badly affected by massive wildfires during a drought.In Portugal, hundreds of firefighters were battling a series of blazes. At a wildfire near Dine, a village close to the border with Spain, five firefighters were injured when their vehicle caught fire, local media reported. Other fires were burning near the Spanish border, including at Boticas and Chavez.Human-caused climate breakdown issupercharging extreme weatheraround the world, driving more frequent and deadlier disasters from heatwaves to floods to wildfires.Much of Europe is experiencing a new period of intense heat, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.On Friday a fire engulfed ⁠homes in a Croatian holiday resort, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of “very extreme” wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.Hundreds more people were evacuated from villages in western Germany and south-west France, while stranded holidaymakers were picked up from beaches threatened by flames in Greece and the army rescued historical relics in Spain.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresEuropeExtreme weatherGreeceBelgiumGermanynewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham urged to crack down on gig economy firms to protect 4m workers  | Gig economy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Campaigners say millions are missing out on key rights including sick pay and protection against unfair dismissal
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Exclusive: Campaigners say millions are missing out on key rights including sick pay and protection against unfair dismissal
Content: Labour is facing intense lobbying from business over its Employment Rights Act, which includes a ban on exploitative zero-hours contractsPhotograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLabour is facing intense lobbying from business over its Employment Rights Act, which includes a ban on exploitative zero-hours contractsPhotograph: WPA/Getty ImagesGig economyBurnham urged to crack down on gig economy firms to protect 4m workersExclusive: Campaigners say millions are missing out on key rights including sick pay and protection against unfair dismissalRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 07.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is being urged to protect 4 million gig economy workers by prosecuting companies that use widespread “bogus” self-employment practices to deny people their rights.As the prime minister fleshes out his agenda, the Fabian Society and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation have warned that millions of workers are missing out on key statutory rights including parental leave, redundancy pay and protection against unfair dismissal.Publishing a joint report calling on Burnham to take action, the Labour-linked thinktank and the anti-poverty charity said changes were essential to make work pay amid the cost of living crisis.The report calls on the government’sFair Work Agency– launched in April as a powerful watchdog for workers’ rights – to use its civil proceedings powers to prosecute companies suspected of engaging in “widespread bogus self-employment”.It also urges ministers to push ahead with changes to employment law to combat longstanding misuse of the system.Britain’s employment laws are unusual among leading economies for including three classifications of employment status. An employee has the most rights and responsibilities, while a self-employed person has limited protections but fewer obligations. There is also an intermediate “worker”, or “limb (b)” status, with fewer rights and obligations than a full employee.According to the report, as many as 4 million workers – including hairdressers, personal trainers, delivery workers and drivers for gig economy platforms – work in this gap. Experts say many have been hired by gig economy companies in this way to avoid granting them employment rights.Labour had promised to create a single “worker” status for all but the genuinely self-employed, before rowing back on the plan to fend off Conservative attacks on its approach to business before the 2024 general election.Once in power, the policy was not included in Labour’s shake-up of employment rights, and though it promised to consult on “moving towards a single status of worker”, this has not materialised.Labour faces intense lobbying from business over its sweeping Employment Rights Act, which includes aban on exploitative zero-hours contractsand day-one rights to statutory sick pay.Last week, official government analysis showed the planned changes would help to support economic growth and offer workers more protections, though they would cost businesses an estimated £350m to £2.9bn.In his first week in office, Burnhamspoke to business leadersto state his determination to push ahead with the plan for the biggest shake-up of employment rights in a generation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, the Fabian Society and Joseph Rowntree Foundation said changes to address employment status were needed to ensure gig economy workers would benefit from these upgraded protections.The report calls for the burden of proof for whether someone is an employee, worker or self-employed to be shifted from the worker to the employer. This would help people to avoid fighting lengthy legal battles to secure basic rights such as the minimum wage and holiday pay.Luke Raikes, the deputy general secretary of the Fabian Society, said: “The government must ensure those who play fast and loose with employment law can’t undercut the majority of good employers who play by the rules.“If it looks like employment then employers should be treating people as employees by default and should expect enforcement action if they aren’t complying. Insecure workers should not have to take on a company’s lawyers – sometimes all the way to the supreme court – just to establish the basic rights they are owed.”A government spokesperson said: “Our plan to make work pay will boost secure employment, improve job security and deliver stronger, higher living standards. The Fair Work Agency is already helping workers get the rights they are entitled to. We’ve committed to consult on employment status and will consider how the Fair Work Agency can use its civil proceedings power alongside that.”Explore more on these topicsGig economyEmployment lawZero-hours contractsWork & careersAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Todd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White House | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: US attorney general says no one in his role ‘should ever’ make this vow amid concern over Trump steering DoJ
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: US attorney general says no one in his role ‘should ever’ make this vow amid concern over Trump steering DoJ
Content: Todd Blanche, the US attorney general, speaks before Donald Trump at the David Mack Center for Training and Intelligence in Garden City, New York, on 14 August.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreenTodd Blanche, the US attorney general, speaks before Donald Trump at the David Mack Center for Training and Intelligence in Garden City, New York, on 14 August.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APTrump administrationTodd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White HouseUS attorney general says no one in his role ‘should ever’ make this vow amid concern over Trump steering DoJMichael SainatoSun 16 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS attorney generalTodd Blancheon Sunday declined to assure that the federal justice department he helms would always act independently of the White House andDonald Trump.“No, I’m not going to pledge that,” hesaidwhen asked about the topic by NBC’s Meet the Press host, Kristen Welker. “And no attorney general should ever pledge that.”Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crosses an ethical or legal line – after the president dismissed his predecessor,Pam Bondi, having become frustrated over insufficient action from the justice department against Trump’s political foes.“The president will never ask me to do something unethical or legal or illegal,” Blanche told Welker. “He never has. He never will. And no, I have – I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done.“And so, this narrative that’s mostly pushed by the left and pushed by the media that the president’s going to pull me aside and ask me to do something illegal is completely a false narrative, not true, will not happen and hasn’t happened.”Todd Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, sworn in as US attorney generalRead moreIn response to his demurring on the questions of always acting independently of the White House,Barb McQuade, a University of Michigan law professor, wrote onsocial mediathat Blanche’s stated position was “an appalling departure” from the justice department’s mission after the Watergate scandal that prompted Richard Nixon to resign from the presidency in 1974.The justice department, “as we once knew it, is no more”, McQuade wrote. “Blanche has turned it into Trump’s private law firm. What a complete disgrace.”Blanche’s comments to Welker on Sunday came days after he was only narrowlyconfirmedby the US Senate in a 50-49 vote to succeed Bondi, with all Democrats voting against him. Hepreviously servedas Trump’s criminal defense lawyer when a New York state jury convicted Trump between his two presidencies of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in connection with payments to adult film starStormy Daniels.In April, Blanchesaidhe would tell Trump, “I love you, sir,” if the president decided to fire him and nominate someone else to replace Bondi.Blanche, meanwhile, in Decemberdefendedmoving Ghislaine Maxwell, the convicted child sexual trafficker and Jeffrey Epstein associate, to a minimum-security prison. And Blanche has also continuedfacing scrutinyover his handling of the so-called Epstein files andhis treatmentof those victimized by the sex-trafficking network built by Epstein.While speaking with Welker on Sunday, Blanche also defended Trump’spardoningof 1,500 supporters who were convicted of attacking the US Capitol toward the end of his first presidency in early 2021.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’m not opining or in any way saying what President Trump did was wrong,” Blanche said when asked about the pardons, which included more than 170 people who pleaded guilty to assaulting police officers. “That is the president’s right.”Blanche declined to say whether any of the pardoned attackers might still receive settlements from the federal government – though they attorney general alsoclaimeda$1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fundfor allies whom Trump considered to be unfairly prosecuted was dead.“Well, anybody can file a claim against the federal government, not just anybody associated with [the Capitol attack],” Blanche said. “I’m not going to sit here and say on a news program whether a litigation that may or may not happen will result in money. I can’t do that.”He alsoaffirmedthe justice department would not drop “election integrity” efforts despite more than 20 consecutive court defeats connected to efforts to try to force states to turn over voter rolls ahead of themidterm electionsin November, when the president’s Republican party is projected tolose seatsin Congress and favored to lose the majority in the US House.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS justice systemUS politicsLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his way | Brazil | The Guardian
description: President, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: President, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’
Content: Lula said he would dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare, and go after organised crime bosses.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLula said he would dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare, and go after organised crime bosses.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesBrazilBrazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his wayPresident, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’Tom Phillipsin São Bernardo do CampoSun 16 Aug 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s leftwing president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has launched his campaign for a historic fourth term and vowed that as long as he lived he would not allow the “shameless” right to return to power.Addressing a sea of supporters in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, the 80-year-old politician reminded voters of the chaos and violence that unfolded duringthe 2018-22 presidency of his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whose sonFlávio Bolsonaro will face Lula in October’s presidential election.Lula recalled how hundreds of thousands of citizens died during a Covid outbreakJair Bolsonarowas accused of bungling with his anti-science policies. Gun ownership soared as laws were relaxed, allowing criminal groups to expand their arsenals. “They handed out … more than a million weapons,” Lula said, promising to dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare as well as developing Brazil’s rare-earth deposits, the world’s second largest after China’s.View image in fullscreenLula launched his re-election campaign at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his rise to the presidency began in 1979 as a union leader.Photograph: Sebastião Moreira/EPALula also said he would improve security by targeting the rich organised crime bosses who lived in luxury apartments. “It’s easy to kill a crook in a favela. But the guy running the show lives in a penthouse … and we need to stop this,” Lula said. He also told his far-right rivals to “show some shame”.Lula was speaking at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his astonishing rise to the presidency began in 1979 when, as 33-year-old union leader, he spearheaded two historic strikes that helped end the military dictatorship. Those strikes made Lula a household name and in 2002, after three failed attempts,he won a landslide victoryto become his country’s first working-class president.‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaignRead moreDuring Lula’s first two-terms, from 2002 until 2010, he was credited with fighting hunger, dramatically expanding social welfare programmes and access to higher education, and improving Brazil’s global standing, although his administration was blighted by corruption scandals. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, became Brazil’s first female president but led the country into a severe economic recession beforebeing controversially impeachedin 2016.In 2018, Lula was jailed for alleged corruption and he spent 580 days in prison before the supreme courtquashed his conviction. Lula’s imprisonment allowed Bolsonaro to win that year’s election, ushering in four years of environmental destruction and international isolation.In 2022 Lula won his third term, defeating Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin and vowing to rescue the country from “one of the worst periods in Brazilian history”. “This nightmare is over,” Lula declared at his January 2023 inauguration. A week later, far-right radicals rampaged through the capital, Brasília, ina botched attempt to bring Bolsonaro back.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro and his wife, Fernanda Bolsonaro, arrive for his campaign launch event at Rio’s Copacabana beach.Photograph: Silvia Izquierdo/APBolsonaro wasjailed in 2025 for 27 yearsfor plotting that failed post-election power grab. Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, launched his campaign on Sunday with an event on Rio’s Copacabana beach, previously the scene of huge rallies in support of his father. “I am going to be Brazil’s next president because I’m going to fight this system,” Bolsonaro, who wore a bullet-proof vest under a yellow Brazil shirt, told a crowd far smaller than those his father used to attract.Polls suggest Lula holds a slender advantage over Bolsonaro, with 43% of intended votes to his rival’s 40% in a run-off which will take place on 25 October if, as expected, no candidate secures 50% of the vote in the 4 October first round.André Pagliarini, the author of a book about Lula called A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, said the showdown would be “the single most important electoral contest this year in the world”.Pagliarini said he believed a Bolsonaro victory would be a significant boost for thepro-Trump “reactionary block”that has won elections across Latin America, from Argentina and Chile to Colombia, where the far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella recently took office.Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly asserted its leadership over the region, launching deadly military operations against alleged “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific,threatening to “take back” the Panama canaland, in January,abducting Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro. Last week, the US state department publishedan incendiary videodeclaring that “American dominance in the western hemisphere will never be questioned again”.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch event on Sunday. Donald Trump’s administration has increasingly asserted its leadership over the region and recently designated Brazil’s two biggest organised crime groups as terrorist organisations.Photograph: Bruna Prado/AP​In recent months Trump has turned up the heat on Brazil, designating its two biggest organised crime groups, the Red Command and the PCC, as terrorist organisations. That has kindled fears of a US military intervention on Brazilian soil or interference in Brazil’s presidential election.During a visit to a jungle training camp in Panama on Friday, Trump’s defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said Washington planned to use the military to “ruthlessly” pursue Latin American drug traffickers, “just like [they did with] Isis and al-Qaida” during the “war on terror”.The idea, Hegseth said, was to “do bad things to bad people – because for too long, bad people did bad things to good people inside the United States of America and across Central and South America”.There was anger at the US outside Lula’s campaign launch on Sunday, where some activists handed out stickers that read: “Fuck Trump.”Seixas Alves, a 33-year-old Lula supporter, said he worriedthe decision to classify Brazilian drug factions as terrorist groupscould be used as a pretext for a US attack. “Just like they [did with] Saddam Hussein,” Alves added, referring to the Iraqi dictator’s supposed development of weapons of mass destruction.In Rio, Flávio Bolsonaro praised Trump’s decision to target the Brazilian crime groups and said he was the only politician capable of “sitting down with the US”.In Vila Euclides, Simone Tebet, a centrist Lula ally, urged voters to do everything they could to stop Brazil falling back into the hands of far-right politicians who wanted “to kill Brazilian democracy” and create “a country of hate”.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If only people knew’: the fascinating lives of flies | Environment | The Guardian
description: Most people associate the insects with filth, but they are vital to the food cycle and sometimes even pretty
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Most people associate the insects with filth, but they are vital to the food cycle and sometimes even pretty
Content: Bee-mimicking hoverflies are just one of the 108 families of flies found in the British Isles.Photograph: Martin Lelievre/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBee-mimicking hoverflies are just one of the 108 families of flies found in the British Isles.Photograph: Martin Lelievre/AFP/Getty ImagesInvertebrate of the year 2026Environment‘If only people knew’: the fascinating lives of fliesMost people associate the insects with filth, but they are vital to the food cycle and sometimes even prettyVote for your favourite invertebrateErica McAlisterSun 16 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 08.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery spring, billions of flies commute thousands of miles in a huge web around the world. They may begin life in Iran and then spend the rest of it in the UK. They may hatch in India but undertake seasonal migrations to the fertile regions of Mongolia, China and Siberia.Most of us assume that bees carry out pollination. But look closely at the creatures flitting around our gardens and parks, and you will see that many of those “bees” aren’t bees at all. They fly differently, sound different and, indeed, on closer inspection, look a bit different.They are often bee-mimicking hoverflies, one of the 108 families of flies found in the British Isles. Now that we have at least some proper research, we’ve found that more than half of those families have pollinator species in them. Even the biting midges (Ceratopogonidae) have species that might get a bit more respect if only people knew they pollinated the plant from which their beloved chocolate is made.Nominate your invertebrate of the yearRead moreThe charismatic adult hoverflies may be some of our most important pollinators, but their larvae have jobs too. You might not see them, but they work away, camouflaged – some resemble bird droppings – busily recycling organic waste or predating species that eat our flowers and crops.And therein lies the true ecological beauty of flies: the ways in which, throughout their life cycles, they interact deeply with the environment. I know most people think of the fly as a creature that loves faeces and filth, or that spreads terrible diseases. And I can’t lie: a very few species do. But do we tar all mammals with the same brush just because one mammal – humans – inflicts such damage to our world? Of course not. So maybe it’s time we gave the other species of flies a chance.View image in fullscreenA tachinid fly (Prosena siberita) from theTachinidaefamily.Photograph: Andy Sands/NPL/AlamyTake the punk flies (Tachinidae) – the name hints at their appearance – whose larvae eat lots of creatures that blight our landscape, such as the oak processionary moth (Thaumetopoea processionea). This species of moth only arrived in 2006, but its caterpillars rapidly started making a nuisance of themselves, stripping oaks of their leaves. Their needle-thin defensive hairs also easily snap off these marauding munching machines, floating on the wind and causing rashes, conjunctivitis and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis. Never fear, though, for the punk fly larvae love eating them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘The eww holds power’: why disgust shapes how we see nature, queerness and each otherRead moreThis isn’t the only example of its kind. In the US, fire ants, having hitched on a boat from South America, have flourished away from their natural predators, causing havoc among native populations – and their venom is toxic to humans. But one of their natural predators, a species of ant-decapitatingPhoridae, has been shipped over and deployed to great effect. These flies are very species-specific, leaving all the native species alone. Incidentally, thePhoridaeand punk fly families contain some fantastic-looking species – the former having some incredibly rotund, hairy species that look like small, flying hedgehogs, the latter including a species named after Arnold Schwarzenegger because of its bulging legs – if somewhat smaller than its namesake at a third of a millimetre in length.View image in fullscreenThe furry bee-fly is one of the more attractive fly species.Photograph: Andrew Greaves/AlamyThe same good looks apply to the bee flies (Bombyliidae). I have yet to meet someone who, when first discovering one of the more hirsute species, has not let out a small squeak of pleasure. Again, the adults will be playing their part in pollinating flowers, while the larvae feast on other immature insects. Before you condemn them as parasites, consider that they are a natural part of the food web, and their presence indicates a healthy host population and a balanced system.Flies can look hairy, or metallic, have eyes on the end of stalks, or paddles on their legs, or even have no wings at all – but they are all something worthy of more consideration. The world would be a duller and smellier place without them.It’s invertebrate of the year! title: Gorging on bearcam: the livestream of big beasts eating that draws millions | Animals | The Guardian
description: Ahead of Fat Bear Week, avid fans are glued to the spectacle of brown bears devouring salmon at Brooks Falls in Alaska
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Ahead of Fat Bear Week, avid fans are glued to the spectacle of brown bears devouring salmon at Brooks Falls in Alaska
Content: Brown bears at Katmai national parkThe age of extinctionAnimalsGorging on bearcam: the livestream of big beasts eating that draws millionsAhead of Fat Bear Week, avid fans are glued to the spectacle of brown bears devouring salmon at Brooks Falls in AlaskaThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentMatthew PearceSun 16 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of this summer’s biggest onscreen hits has had big beasts, great escapes and choppy waters, but it’s not Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey – it’s a livestream of Alaskan brown bears catching salmon.TheBrooks Falls bearcamat Katmai national park in the US was watched 7.3m times between 22 June and 4 August – up 70% from the same period last year and more than double the views it attracted in 2024.The cameras, run by the wildlife networkExplore.org, show brown bears gathering at Brooks Falls waterfall to catch sockeye salmon as they make their way upstream. More than a dozen bears at a time can be spotted prowling around the rocky waters and chomping on the fish.Candice Rusch, Explore.org’s director of new media, said the surge in viewers appeared to be driven by the bears returning to the falls in large numbers after a less concentrated season last year.“Last year was a really high salmon run, which meant there was salmon all over the river and the bears didn’t need to congregate at the falls the way they’re doing right now,” she said.“This year we’ve just had very good views of large congregations of bears.“It’s like the whole world discovered they could put bearcam on their TV at the same time,” she said. “Maybe people just have it on while they’re cooking dinner.”View image in fullscreenBrown bears at Brooks Falls eating sockeye salmon in Alaska’s Katmai national park.Photograph: John Moore/Getty ImagesThe cameras were first installed in 2012 as part of an effort to bring remote wildlife into people’s homes. Rusch said the idea was that people were more likely to protect animals and landscapes they had come to know and care about.Dr Jeffrey Skibins, an associate professor at East Carolina University, said: “Recent studies have shown that nature-based webcams are beneficial to both wildlife and people. They benefit wildlife by improving conservation attitudes, behaviours and awareness.“This is not to suggest they are replacements for getting out in nature, but rather serve as viable additions,” he said.The stream has developed a dedicated fanbase. Viewers can identify individual bears from features such as their ears, noses and body shape, and some keep detailed records of their feeding habits.‘I was watching osprey for five hours a day’: how the world fell in love with nature live streamsRead moreOne dedicated fan reported watching a bear called Otis eat 42 salmon over several hours, which Rusch said could equate to more than 100,000 calories.The bears’ gorging will take on added significance next month, when Katmai’s annual Fat Bear Week begins in the autumn. The public votes in a knockout-style competition to crown the park’s fattest bear, as the animals pile on winter weight in preparation for hibernation.“The bears are great,” Rusch said. “This is an amazing place and it deserves all the love it’s getting.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsAnimalsThe age of extinctionWildlifeAlaskaMammalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida sets record for sea turtle nests but Trump move could stall recovery | Marine life | The Guardian
description: Loggerhead turtles abound this season but rollback of Endangered Species Act protections could threaten future
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Loggerhead turtles abound this season but rollback of Endangered Species Act protections could threaten future
Content: A nesting sea turtle in 2026.Photograph: Adrienne McCracken/Loggerhead Marinelife CenterView image in fullscreenA nesting sea turtle in 2026.Photograph: Adrienne McCracken/Loggerhead Marinelife CenterMarine lifeFlorida sets record for sea turtle nests but Trump move could stall recoveryLoggerhead turtles abound this season but rollback of Endangered Species Act protections could threaten futureRichard Luscombein MiamiSun 16 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWildlife groups inFloridaare celebrating record numbers of sea turtle nests this season, but experts warn Donald Trump’srecent guttingof the Endangered Species Act (ESA) could reverse decades of their recovery from the edge of extinction.With more than two months of the summer nesting season still to run, loggerhead turtles have already made13,770 nests, hundreds more than recorded in any previous year, along an 8.5-mile stretch of shoreline monitored by the Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach, on Florida’s Atlantic coast.The same record has fallen on Sanibel island, on the Gulf coast, where loggerheads have laid922 nestsso far this year, surpassing the 2023 total of 878, according to the Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation.The numbers reflect theongoing revivalof sea turtles since the 1970s, when overhunting, poaching and habitat loss pushed several species to the brink, including the loss of about 95% of the Caribbean’s population of green turtles.View image in fullscreenA sea turtle is prepared for a CT scan at the Loggerhead Marinelife Center.Photograph: Loggerhead Marinelife CenterThe ESA, passed in 1973, enshrined protections that are paying dividends now because sea turtle hatchlings take years to decades to reach reproductive age. The loss of those safeguards, from Trump’s“death sentence” repeallast month of sections of the law to favor oil drilling, mining, logging and development interests, has some experts fearful that the recovery might have reached the high-water mark.An alliance of environmental and wildlife groups issuing the Trump administrationin part over a rule giving outsized deference to “economic considerations” when determining protections for endangered species and critical habitat.“What we’re seeing is the result of several decades of sustained protection of these species under the ESA and various other measures to protect their habitat in different ways,” said David Godfrey, executive director of the Sea Turtle Conservancy, an advocacy group that is not a plaintiff in the lawsuit, but is supportive of it.“It takes just about any species of sea turtle 20, 30 years to reach maturity, to come back and nest, to return to beaches where they were first protected as eggs or as hatchlings and afforded the opportunity to live without ending up in a fisherman’s net and on a table in a nice restaurant.“So the recovery’s going on largely due to the ESA, which is one of the reasons why we’re all very concerned about the setbacks to the legislation.”The ESA is credited with safeguarding more than 1,700 species and their habitats,preventing 99%of those listed from going extinct.Godfrey said: “The detractors of the ESA sometimes say, ‘Oh, this thing is a failure. Look at all these animals that are still on the list. We haven’t removed a lot from the list.’ And I come right back and say, yeah, but look at all these animals that are on the list that we haven’t lost.View image in fullscreenA sea turtle nest excavation.Photograph: Marisa Marulli“They were put on the list because they were creeping toward extinction, and sea turtles certainly are still here because of the act and they are growing in numbers.“The levels of nesting numbers of turtles aren’t quite where we would want them to be to completely take them off the list, but they’re going in that direction unless we reverse things.”Justin Perrault, vice-president of research at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, said this year’s elevated nesting figures were the result of the years of those protections, as well as favorable environmental conditions, reduced pollution and education around marine conservation.“It’s incredibly exciting and encouraging because the world needs some good nature stories, and it’s important to celebrate that we are doing some things well,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘God squad’ waives endangered species law to allow US drilling in Gulf of MexicoRead more“Being a mother sea turtle is very difficult, they do all the work, they don’t lay just one nest every season, they lay multiple nests, and that is very energetically costly and they usually take about two, three or four years off in between each time they come back to nest.“And we are seeing increases across the years right now. We’re still cautiously optimistic about saying that they’ve recovered, but we can say stability.”His center, a marine life hospital that treats and rehabilitates sick and injured turtles, has partnered with numerous groups and organizations around the country to share research data and collaborate on education efforts.One of its most successful projects has been theResponsible Pier Initiative, in which anglers in particular are equipped with knowledge and tools to rescue stranded or injured turtles, or those entangled in fishing lines.To date, 79 piers around the country, including in Virginia, Texas, North Carolina and Puerto Rico, have signed up, and more than 1,200 turtles have been rescued.Valerie Tovar, the center’s conservation manager, said the program had saved the lives of multiple species of sea turtle.“We’ve seen loggerheads, green turtles, olive ridleys, hawksbills,” she said. “We had two reports of hooking a leatherback sea turtle, and obviously that line broke very quickly, they’re massive animals.”As well as the pier initiative and establishing protection zones, Tovar said other conservation projects under way, or planned, can help further fuel the sea turtles’ recovery.View image in fullscreenLoggerhead turtle hatchlings head for the sea.Photograph: Loggerhead Marinelife Center“We’ve expanded our horizons. We’re getting into the world of water quality, habitat restoration, and outreach and advocacy, to really find the connections between water quality, human health and sea turtle health,” she said.Perrault said that, as a conservation organization, Marinelife does not comment on politics or policies. But he said: “We support the Endangered Species Act here, and we believe in the Endangered Species Act.“Every single animal we take into this facility is on the endangered species list so obviously we believe that the animals should be protected and continue to be protected in the ways that they have been since the ESA was enacted.”He also pointed toFloridastate regulations still in place that he said were “beneficial”.“We’re starting to see record years more often, and that’s incredibly encouraging,” he said.Explore more on these topicsMarine lifeReptilesWildlifeFloridaEndangered speciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Torrential rain and flood kill nine in Japan amid wettest month in decades | Japan | The Guardian
description: Downpours in Japan’s east have snarled roads, caused power outages and destroyed homes in Chiba prefecture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Downpours in Japan’s east have snarled roads, caused power outages and destroyed homes in Chiba prefecture
Content: Abandoned cars on a flooded road in Sakura in Chiba prefecture after ‘unprecedented’ heavy rain.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbandoned cars on a flooded road in Sakura in Chiba prefecture after ‘unprecedented’ heavy rain.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesJapanTorrential rain and flood kill nine in Japan amid wettest month in decadesDownpours in Japan’s east have snarled roads, caused power outages and destroyed homes in Chiba prefectureAgence France-PresseSun 16 Aug 2026 01.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeavy rain that battered eastern Japan has left nine people dead, the public broadcaster NHK said on Sunday, afteran “unprecedented” delugethat flooded more than a thousand homes and snarled up roads and rail services.Torrential downpours that started late on Thursday have triggered landslide warnings and power outages, with forecasters issuing the highest-level heavy rain warning for the Chiba region for the first time.A weather station in the prefecture recorded 300mm (nearly 12 inches) of rain in 24 hours, making it the area’s wettest August in six decades.By Friday morning, the city of Chiba had logged more than three times the rainfall typically seen in the whole of August, Tokyo’s land ministry said.Nine people have since died in the rains, NHK reported Sunday morning, citing its own tally.View image in fullscreenA flooded 7-Eleven store in Oamishirasato.Photograph: Issei Kato/ReutersChiba’s disaster management office as of Saturday evening listed eight dead, some trapped inside submerged cars and others found on flooded streets.More than 70 houses across the Chiba region were partially destroyed by the rain, the prefecture’s latest tally showed.More than one thousand households reported being flooded, nearly 600 of which had water surge above the floorboards.An estimated 1,200 cars also remain abandoned on roads, local media said, with authorities working on towing them away or using jacks to move them.An official from Japan’s meteorological agency told a news conference on Thursday that it was “shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain”.Scientists say human-driven climate change is making extreme weather more frequent, prolonged and intense.Explore more on these topicsJapanFloodingAsia PacificExtreme weatherShareReuse this content

title: King Charles and Prince William face £10m energy upgrade bill for estates | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: New rules could affect nine in 10 rental properties in duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster and at Sandringham
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: New rules could affect nine in 10 rental properties in duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster and at Sandringham
Content: King Charles and Prince William are likely to face criticism if their estates fail to meet the new government standards.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenKing Charles and Prince William are likely to face criticism if their estates fail to meet the new government standards.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyMonarchyKing Charles and Prince William face £10m energy upgrade bill for estatesNew rules could affect nine in 10 rental properties in duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster and at SandringhamNick SommerladSun 16 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Charles andPrince Williamcould be forced to spend up to £10m upgrading hundreds of rental properties on their private estates to meet planned energy-efficiency rules.The government has announced that landlords will need to ensure their properties have energy performance certificate (EPC) ratings of C or higher by 2030 – up from the current requirement of an E.EPCs are documents that provide an energy-efficiency score for properties, in relation to their running costs.Introduced in 2007 amid growing concern about carbon emissions, they help to estimate energy bills and environmental impact. The most energy-efficient properties are awarded an A rating, and the worst are given a G rating.A Guardian investigation has found that almost nine in 10 domestic properties on the duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster and the Sandringham estate have had EPC ratings of D or lower.King Charles’s tax bill: what did we learn, and what is still in the dark?Read moreBoth Charles and William have been praised for their environmental advocacy. They are likely to be criticised if the estates fail to meet the new government standards as fears about soaring energy costs and the climate crisis intensify.They face spending up to £10,000 to upgrade each property, and could be fined £30,000 for every home they continue to rent without carrying out the necessary work.A government spokesperson said: “Everyone deserves to live in a warm, comfortable home. Our plans for private rental homes to be EPC C by 2030 could lift up to half a million households out of fuel poverty by 2030, cutting bills to give families across the country the breathing space they need.”Nationally, just over half of all rental properties currently have an EPC rating below C, but the Guardian has found that properties on the three large royal estates are more poorly insulated and expensive to heat than average.The king inherited the Sandringham estate and theDuchy of Lancasterfrom his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, after her death in 2022. He did not pay inheritance tax on either estate because assets passed between monarchs are exempt.The Duchy of Lancaster was established in 1265 to provide a private income for the sovereign and its profits soared during the late queen’s reign. It spans about 18,000 hectares (44,000 acres), stretching from the north-west of England to parts of London.View image in fullscreenA Duchy of Lancaster property, which rated G.Photograph: Nick SommerladThe income generated by Sandringham, bought by Queen Victoria in 1862 and set over 8,000 hectares (19,000 acres) in rural Norfolk, has not been disclosed.When Charles became king after his mother’s death, he passed theDuchy of Cornwallto William. Founded in 1337 to generate money for male heirs to the throne, it too became significantly more profitable in recent decades. It covers about 55,000 hectares (135,000 acres) and is concentrated mainly in the south-west of England.The Guardian examined more than 700 domestic EPCs across the three estates and found that 630 would fail to meet the government’s proposed requirements.This analysis revealed that 99% of the rental properties on the Sandringham estate had an EPC rating of D or lower. The figure was more than 90% for the Duchy of Lancaster and about 80% for the Duchy of Cornwall.The investigation excluded properties that appear to have been converted into holiday lets or those with separate leasehold titles, as it is unclear how the new rules will apply to them.Is Cornwall’s newest high street an inspiring model, or a threat to nearby Newquay?Read moreThe precise number of domestic properties across the three estates is also unclear because they do not publish lists of their landholdings, though the figure is believed to exceed 1,200.In the past, aides working at the two duchies have gone to great lengths to obscure details of their property portfolios, withholding the information even from parliament.However, if this sample of more than half is representative, then more than 1,000 properties could fall foul of the new rules, requiring improvement if they are to be rented out.The renovation costs could exceed £10m, similar to the annual combined residential rental income of the duchies. The duchies pay out about £50m a year to Charles and William. They are exempt from most business taxes, which helps them maximise their profits.The details of how landlords will be required to upgrade their properties from a minimum of an E to a C from 2030 are yet to be published by the government.This week, the Guardian revealed that more than 100 domestic properties on royal estates have EPC ratings of F or G.Some have exemptions from the minimum energy efficiency standards regulations, while others are outside the scope of the rules as they are farmhouses or because the tenancies pre-date the current regulations. It is unclear if these loopholes will remain in place when the rules are amended.View image in fullscreenMarsh Farm in Norfolk, where Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor now lives, is among the properties that may be affected.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesA Whitehall source said: “We recently consulted on reforms to the energy performance of buildings regime and will update in due course.“Some buildings, such as historic or mixed tenure, may not be able to upgrade to the new standard and some limited exemptions are in place on this basis. About 48% of privately rented properties are already at a current EPC C standard. We will consider further guidance for mixed-use buildings, ahead of the new standards coming into force.”The royal estates are less energy efficient than most privately rented homes because they are mainly older rural properties, often heated by oil, coal or wood.Only the Duchy of Cornwall’s newer builds at Poundbury, in Dorset, andNansledan, in Cornwall,consistently meet the new planned targets for efficiency. However, of more than 300 Duchy of Cornwall EPCs the Guardian examined, just 11% were rated B and 8% rated C.The rest were D or lower, and if this is typical of the rest of the Duchy of Cornwall’s 600 or more rental properties, then the total improvement bill could reach up to £5m – or about one quarter of the estate’s annual profits.On top of a previously announced £500m investment over the next decade, the Duchy of Cornwall said that “an additional £50m is planned for improving the condition and efficiency of our existing properties”.The Duchy of Cornwall said it had a “unique portfolio, including many historic buildings located in isolated rural and island locations”.“While this confers a special character, it also brings some unique challenges which we have started to address systematically through our retrofit programme,” a spokesperson said.“We recognise that these challenges mean work does not always happen as fast as we would like, but we will continue to work closely with our tenants to identify effective and practical energy-efficiency improvements as quickly as possible.”The duchy added that it had spent £11m on home improvements since 2022, and in the last year had delivered 150 “modern, energy-efficient homes, all of which are EPC A or B”.However, in response to follow-up questions from the Guardian, it confirmed that only six of the new properties were duchy private rents, with most having been sold.View image in fullscreenOnly newer builds, such as those in Poundbury, Dorset, part of the Duchy of Cornwall, are likely to meet the new standards.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/Rex/ShutterstockThe Duchy of Lancaster’s annual report states that it operates more than 300 domestic rental properties, but the precise figure is not known.The Guardian found more than 200 properties on the estate that have domestic EPCs. More than 90% of them have ratings of lower than C. Nearly half are rated E and over a quarter are rated D. The total potential bill for improvements could top £2m.The Duchy of Lancaster said it placed “great importance” on “being a responsible landlord”.“Any tenant with concerns is encouraged to contact us directly and can be assured we will address these issues promptly and constructively,” a spokesperson added.“Over the last year, the Duchy of Lancaster has invested more than £3m in residential property repairs and upgrades as part of our ongoing commitment to provide well-maintained homes compliant with all legislation.“While improving the energy efficiency of some historic buildings is challenging, we continue to work to improve their EPC ratings.”The Guardian has seen EPCs for more than 150 properties on the Sandringham estate, understood to be about half of the total. None were rated A or B, with just one rated C. Almost all could need work to meet the new regulations, with 99% rated from D down to G.The biggest group – 120 properties, equivalent to 75% of those analysed – are rated E, the minimum EPC rating allowed for rented properties since new rules in 2018.This includes Marsh Farm, where Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor now lives. It has an EPC produced in 2019, which rated it as a low E, just two points above an F. If our findings reflect the wider Sandringham estate, the total bill for energy-efficiency improvements by 2030 could come to £3m.A spokesperson said Sandringham has “a mixture of property and tenancy types, which are fully compliant with MEES regulations”.“We continue to invest significantly in an ongoing programme of maintenance and improvement works on all properties, including those out of scope of the regulations, to upgrade energy efficiency across the estate,” she added.“While we do not comment on individual cases, these regulations do not apply to every property on the estate, and exemptions are necessary on a small number of properties.”Jonathan Bean, a spokesperson for campaign group FuelPovertyAction, said: “The royal duchies should be leading the way in upgrading all their properties to a minimum EPC of C by 2030 to protect people’s health and the environment.“Instead they are dragging their feet and looking for loopholes. If even the richest landlords are allowed to get away with it, what hope is there of getting the rest to do the right thing?“The government must act now to close all loopholes and increase enforcement efforts.”A duchy of Cornwall spokesperson said it was unable to confirm the accuracy of our findings as the Guardian did not provide the estate with a list of properties we had inspected, to protect the tenants who spoke to us on condition of anonymity.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyDuchy of CornwallDuchy of LancasterFuel povertyEnergy efficiencyHousingEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: Man under threat of deportation to Jamaica wins right to rejoin his British family | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Mark Nelson released from immigration detention on bail after lawyers challenge decision to remove him
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Mark Nelson released from immigration detention on bail after lawyers challenge decision to remove him
Content: Mark Nelson has lived in the UK since 2000 but has faced deportation since 2022.Photograph: Mark NelsonView image in fullscreenMark Nelson has lived in the UK since 2000 but has faced deportation since 2022.Photograph: Mark NelsonImmigration and asylumMan under threat of deportation to Jamaica wins right to rejoin his British familyMark Nelson released from immigration detention on bail after lawyers challenge decision to remove himDiane TaylorSun 16 Aug 2026 07.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Jamaican man who has lived more than half his life in the UK and was facing imminent deportation has been allowed to reunite with his British family after a legal challenge.Mark Nelson, 47, came to the UK in 2000 and later set up his own car-mechanic business. He has five British children and a British partner. He faced deportation in 2022 after serving a four-year prison sentence for possession with intent to supply a class B drug, abstracting electricity and two offences of racially aggravated intentional harassment. He had not committed any further offences.The deportation was later cancelled and instead he was tagged and told to report weekly at aHome Officecentre. But last month – almost 10 years after his original conviction – Nelson was arrested, detained and told that the government again planned to deport him to Jamaica.The Home Office gave him a ticket for a flight on 7 August, but after reading about his casein the Guardian, lawyers offered to represent him pro bono to challenge his deportation.After they made an 11th-hour application for a judicial review theHome Officebacked down on the deportation and cancelled his ticket. This week he was granted bail and can return to the home he shares with his partner, Rachel Derbyshire, in the north of England and see his children again.Nelson said he was overjoyed to to have left the immigration detention centre near Heathrow where he had spent several weeks in hot and crowded conditions.“I’ve spoken to my kids, my partner and my brother,” he said. “Everyone is so excited about my release. If it hadn’t been for the lawyers who got in touch after reading the Guardian article I would be back in Jamaica by now, separated from my family, not knowing when I would see them again.“I have no family members there and believe my life would be at risk.”Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors, who contacted Nelson after reading about his case, lodged the judicial review application. He has also lodged an appeal relating to his immigration case in the first-tier tribunal and a referral has been made for him to the national referral mechanism as a potential victim of modern slavery.Kandiah said: “He committed his offences in 2017 and served his sentence. Yet nearly a decade later he continues to endure the threat of deportation, with the devastating possibility that he could be permanently torn away from his British children and partner. A prison sentence should not become a life sentence by another name.“Vulnerable people can struggle to secure legal representation when they need it most. When a person facing removal cannot access timely legal advice, the risk is that the Home Office can remove them before their case has been properly scrutinised.”Nelson wrote anopinion piecefor the Guardian in 2022 about being under threat of deportation. He said Jamaica was a place where he no longer knew anyone after his great-grandparents, who brought him up there, died when he was 16.A Home Office spokesperson said:“All foreign national offenders who receive a prison sentence in the UK are referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity.“We have removed or deported almost 70,000 people who were here illegally since the last election, an increase of 41%.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeJamaicaCommonwealth immigrationCaribbeannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our rota crew have the best summer’: parents share how they get through the school holiday | School holidays | The Guardian
description: As research suggests six weeks of childcare can cost £1,145, parents are relying on spreadsheets, savings and sharing the load
Author: Nicola Slawson
Headline: As research suggests six weeks of childcare can cost £1,145, parents are relying on spreadsheets, savings and sharing the load
Content: With children off school for about 13 weeks a year, but most employees entitled to far less annual leave, parents say the sums simply do not add up.Photograph: SolStock/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWith children off school for about 13 weeks a year, but most employees entitled to far less annual leave, parents say the sums simply do not add up.Photograph: SolStock/Getty ImagesSchool holidays‘Our rota crew have the best summer’: parents share how they get through the school holidayAs research suggests six weeks of childcare can cost £1,145, parents are relying on spreadsheets, savings and sharing the loadNicola Slawsonand Amee JoshiSun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe summer holidays are in full swing, bringing the annual challenge many parents face in balancing work and looking after school-age children. With children off school for about 13 weeks a year, but most employees entitled to far less annual leave, parents have told the Guardian that the sums simply do not add up.New research suggests arranging six weeks of holiday childcarecan cost working parents up to £1,145 a child, while almost three-quarters of parents say the summer childcare juggle candamage their career.We spoke to parents about the creative, and sometimes costly, ways they are making it work.In Northern Ireland, Emma Willis, 35, relies on flexible working as a stock processor for a charity and her husband’s ability to work from home to get through the summer holidays with their three children, aged 15, 13 and 10.View image in fullscreenEmma Willis says her children spend much of the holidays at home.Photograph: Emma WillisWillis, who works part-time on minimum wage, says if her husband lost the ability to work from home she would probably have to give up her job.“I long to work a better job with more hours to enhance all of our lives but right now I have to sit on my hands and keep the plates spinning,” she says. “At the moment, it’s just about getting by. I think that’s what a lot of families are doing – just doing the best they can.”While the family can manage without paid childcare, she says the children spend much of the holidays at home and she wishes they had more opportunities for activities and trips.“I feel like our arrangement isn’t great for the kids. They are stuck at home most of the summer and we don’t have the money to engage them in many extracurricular activities.”double quotation markThere was no point wasting your annual leave just to get through the summer when there’s a creative solutionIt can be harder for those with younger children who are less likely to be able to entertain themselves. Melany Rose, 39, from east London, came up with a radical plan after realising that all her parent friends were taking annual leave on the same day only to meet up in the park.This inspired her to set up a community childcare rota with nine families.“There is no point wasting your annual leave allowance just to get through the summer when there’s a creative solution.”The rota involves 14 children from nine families, though never all at once because families dip in and out depending on trips away and other childcare arrangements.
