Using a shared spreadsheet, parents take turns, with at least two adults taking the children on adventures to museums, splash parks and other free or low-cost attractions.View image in fullscreenThe ‘rota crew’ has eliminated the need for holiday clubs and saved families thousands of pounds.Photograph: Melany RoseThe system has eliminated the need for holiday clubs, which can cost £60 a day, and saved families thousands of pounds since they first began.“Our rota crew have the best summer ever and as adults, we’ve really all bonded. It’s the base of our friendship group now,” she says. “No one gets parent burnout either … six or seven weeks is a long time to be with your kids while you’re trying to juggle working.”double quotation markWe negotiate the summer holidays a few months in advanceJoe*, from Birmingham, is part of a blended family. He and his wife have a four-year-old together, while he has two other children under 12 who stay with them about 30% of the time, and his wife has a preteen who is with them about 80% of the time.To cover the six-week summer break, the couple work compressed hours and alternate their non-working days to plug gaps in childcare, using paid holiday clubs only where they feel they are most needed.He says the biggest challenge is the constant planning. “We have two shared calendars … and we negotiate the summer holidays because we have to work out how we all work, live and keep the kids safe. That’s normally a conversation a few months in advance.”Diane, 45, from Horsham in West Sussex, gave up her 17-year career in accounts after having children, as she realised the cost of childcare for her son, now 10, and daughter, 7, would leave them financially worse off. Instead she retrained as a school kitchen lead, allowing her to work only in term time, supplementing this with a Saturday retail job.“I left the profession I worked and trained for and took a complete sidestep into working in school kitchens. It’s less pay, but we’re better off financially.”double quotation markI left the profession I worked and trained for and took a complete sidestepKeeping two children entertained still takes weeks of planning, however. Diane relies on free and low-cost council events, booking activities as early as possible before places disappear.Her son has special educational needs, adding another layer of complexity: “There are a lot of holiday clubs that just won’t take a Send child full stop … Finding support or activities for your child that’s appropriate for your child, it’s an ongoing battle.”For those who work full-time, the summer holidays can be a huge expense. Jenny, 45, from Newark-on-Trent, and her husband rely on flexible working, annual leave and a patchwork of holiday clubs and activities with their two children, aged six and nine.To keep track of it all, she has created what she describes as an “epic colour-coded Excel spreadsheet”, mapping out nine different clubs. “Because we’re all over the place I frequently panic that I’m not where I should be,” she says.When they can, the family useschildcare vouchers, a legacy salary sacrifice scheme not currently open to new applicants that allows participants to pay for registered childcare from pre-tax income. The vouchers covered almost half their paid childcare, but the rest costs about £50 to £60 a day. “We’re dipping into savings,” Jenny says, “but we want them to feel like they’re having a proper holiday.”*Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsSchool holidaysChildcareChildrenParents and parentingFamilynewsShareReuse this content

title: Taliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identity | Afghanistan | The Guardian
description: UK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisals
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: UK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisals
Content: Hamid (not his real name) worked for the Afghan national police unit alongside the British military.View image in fullscreenHamid (not his real name) worked for the Afghan national police unit alongside the British military.AfghanistanTaliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identityUK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisalsHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by aMinistry of Defenceleak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in anaccidental 2022 leakby an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.Hamid said he had received a number of threats from theTaliban, including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements.View image in fullscreenTaliban security personnel in Kandahar. It is nearly five years since the group retook political power in Afghanistan.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty ImagesThe MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal.Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme.“Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.”Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on15 August 2021after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed.View image in fullscreenHamid lives in hiding and says the emotional impact has been ‘devastating’.Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said.Abbas fought the Taliban alongside US and Australian troops. Now exiled in Iran, he feels abandonedRead more“Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.”After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain”.“It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said.Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said.“The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship.“I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.”An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission inAfghanistan, and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria.“Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.”Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsAfghanistanTalibanMinistry of DefenceSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in small Polish village | Poland | The Guardian
description: Hundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa
Content: The 55.6-metre statue of the Virgin Mary towers over the village of Konotopie, Poland.Photograph: Adam Burakowski/East News/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe 55.6-metre statue of the Virgin Mary towers over the village of Konotopie, Poland.Photograph: Adam Burakowski/East News/ShutterstockPolandEurope’s tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in small Polish villageHundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech WałęsaAssociated PressSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe’s tallest was inaugurated on Saturday in a small Polish village, in the presence of the anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa.Hundreds of people took part in the consecration of the monument, which towers 55.6 metres (182ft) over Konotopie in centralPoland, a village of fewer than 150 people.While helicopters scattered miniature red roses over the crowd, priests in white robes celebrated mass and the Mazowsze folk ensemble sang and danced to traditional Polish music.The statue is taller – if less dramatically located – than the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which measures 38 metres including its pedestal. The Polish monument’s height includes a crown-shaped 15-metre pedestal.It also surpasses another large-scale religious monument in Poland, the Christ the King statue in the western town of Świebodzin, which was revealed in 2010 and, with the mound it stands on, is 52.5 metres tall.There is a taller statue of the Virgin Mary in the Philippines, which measures 98 metres. But the new one in Poland is believed to be the largest of its kind in Europe.View image in fullscreenThe statue was paid for by a wealthy couple who live nearby.Photograph: Agnieszka Bielecka/EPAWałęsa, who won the Nobel peace prize for his leadership of the Polish anti-communist resistance as the head of the Solidarity trade union and was later Poland’s president, had a front-row seat during the inauguration ceremony.“This is the end of my path,” said Wałęsa, 82, suggesting the causes he had long championed, including democracy and the Catholic faith, were now completed. “I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary.”During his Solidarity days, Wałęsa famously wore a Black Madonna pin and he has often credited his faith in God with giving him the strength to fight against communism.Most Poles identify as Catholic. The church played a powerful role in public life after the fall of communism in 1989, benefiting from the prestige it earned through its support of the anti-communist opposition.The country is the homeland of Saint John Paul II, who was pope from 1978 until his death in 2005. A huge statue of him – but much smaller than the one of Mary – was revealed more than a decade ago in the city of Częstochowa.The influence of religion in public life has gradually declined in recent years, particularly among younger people and in urban areas. However, the Catholic church remains influential, especially in rural communities and among older generations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWiesław Mering, a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who attended the ceremony, said: “I cannot help but notice the weakening of the institution of the church, a withdrawal of specific social categories from Catholicism, and this hurts me. The history ofChristianityhas ups and downs, but this place is a reminder that Mary won’t give up on Poland.”View image in fullscreenVisitors descend from the viewing platform inside the statue.Photograph: Adam Burakowski/East News/ShutterstockThe statue was commissioned by Roman Karkosik, a wealthy Polish businessman, and his wife, Grażyna. The couple live in a small palace a few miles from Konotopie.Roman Karkosik, an entrepreneur whose ventures included plastic bottle manufacturing in the 1990s, amassed a fortune through investments on the Warsaw stock exchange to become one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals.The couple have said the monument is an expression of their gratitude to God. “The statue will be for all people,” Grażyna Karkosik said. “Each of us coming to see it will think more deeply about their own lives, not only about God.”Local authorities hope the monument will become an important pilgrimage site and a tourist destination. The statue has a viewing platform built inside its pedestal.Explore more on these topicsPolandCatholicismChristianityReligionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: At least six people dead from days of storms and record flooding in Indiana | Indiana | The Guardian
description:
Indiana public safety officials say at least six people have died during days of storms and historic flooding in the state
At least six people dead from days of storms and record-setting flooding in Indiana
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Indiana public safety officials say at least six people have died during days of storms and historic flooding in the stateAt least six people dead from days of storms and record-setting flooding in Indiana
Content: Flooding in northern Indianapolis, Indiana, on Saturday.Photograph: Indianapolis Fire Department/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlooding in northern Indianapolis, Indiana, on Saturday.Photograph: Indianapolis Fire Department/AFP/Getty ImagesIndianaAt least six people dead from days of storms and record flooding in IndianaFour-year-old boy, two men and three women among those who died since storms began on 11 August, officials sayAssociated PressSun 16 Aug 2026 15.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDays ofstorms and flooding in Indianaleft at least six people dead as flood waters peaked in Indianapolis’s White River – and rains were expected to ease in the state capital region and other parts of the state on Sunday.A four-year-old boy, two men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began on 11 August, state homeland security department spokesperson Liz Woods said.Officials in Jennings county, in the southern end of the state, said the boy was killed on Tuesday when a tree crashed through his bedroom during strong winds.“This is obviously unexpected,” Jennings county deputy chief Cody Low told the local ABC affiliate. “There’s nothing we can say that is going to make it any better. We’re going to push through this as a community.”View image in fullscreenFloodwater inside the Yorktown Public Library in Yorktown, Indiana, on 13 August 2026.Photograph: Yorktown Public Library/AFP/Getty ImagesThe other victims included a 19-year-old man whose body was recovered on Saturday. Officials in Delaware county, located east ofIndianapolis, said Matthew Morey had jumped off a bridge into the rushing waters of the Mississinewa River with friends three days earlier.Family and friends gathered earlier in the week at the bridge to remember the recent high school graduate, who was headed to Purdue University, and warn of the dangers of swollen rivers.Delaware county officials also said they recovered the body of Stephanie Sallee and her dog in a cornfield on Saturday, not far from her car. They believe the 58-year-old had been driving on a flooded road when the vehicle was swept away. In a statement shared with local news outlets, her family remembered her as a compassionate and loving person who adored her grandchildren and other young relatives.InIndianapolis, flooding from the White River peaked early on Sunday morning, with high water levels expected to hold for a few hours before beginning to recede, according to the city public works department.The agency said it would reopen the city’s floodgates on Sunday and that emergency shelters remained open after hundreds of homes along the river and its canals were evacuated. First responders used boats to rescue people stranded by rapidly rising flood waters.View image in fullscreenFirst responders helping a resident in flood waters in Indianapolis, Indiana, on 15 August 2026.Photograph: Indianapolis Fire Department/AFP/Getty ImagesRecovery efforts, meanwhile, started in earnest as northern parts of the state began drying out.“I must admit it is a good morning,” Christine Altman, president of the Hamilton county board of commissioners, said during a Sunday briefing. “It’s not raining, and the water is receding.”She said the county, located just north of Indianapolis, escaped without any loss of life, though officials were assessing whether a significant bridge damaged in the flooding could be repaired or if it needed to be completely replaced.Heavy rain and flash flooding were still possible across portions of the central part of the state throughout the day, the National Weather Service (NWS) warned.The NWS urged residents to check river and weather forecasts and “stay out of dangerous, fast moving waters” as heavy rain has led to significant flooding along most rivers and creeks across centralIndiana. Roads and bridges across the state have also been seriously damaged or washed out entirely by the powerful rushing waters.Nearly 130,000 utility customers statewide remained without power by midday Sunday, down from a peak of about 300,000, according to Woods and the online utility tracker PowerOutage.us.Heavy rains have hammered Indiana over the past week, causing rivers to crest and setting new records.The White River crested at more than 24 feet (7.32 meters) in the communities of Anderson and Noblesville, surpassing records set in 1913.Indianapolis mayor Joe Hogsett said the flooding was the worst the capital city has seen in more than 30 years.Governor Mike Braun’s office said more than 350 evacuations and scores of rescue and welfare checks have occurred elsewhere in the state, including at a senior mobile home community north of Indianapolis.Donald Trump on Saturday approved Braun’s request to the president for federal disaster assistance to help with flooding response and recovery efforts.The drenching rains and destructive flooding were among the effects of severe storms that have wreaked havoc across the US midwest and beyond in recent days.Tornadoes, heavy rains and flash flooding brought serious damage to communities from Illinois to western Pennsylvania.Explore more on these topicsIndianaIndianapolisUS weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in Virginia State University shooting found hiding in dorm closet | Virginia | The Guardian
description: Suspect, 19, who is not enrolled at the university arrested in connection with shooting of five people, authorities say
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Suspect, 19, who is not enrolled at the university arrested in connection with shooting of five people, authorities say
Content: Police investigate the scene of a shooting on the campus of Virginia State University on Saturday, in Petersburg, Virginia.Photograph: WWBT/APView image in fullscreenPolice investigate the scene of a shooting on the campus of Virginia State University on Saturday, in Petersburg, Virginia.Photograph: WWBT/APVirginiaSuspect in Virginia State University shooting found hiding in dorm closetSuspect, 19, who is not enrolled at the university arrested in connection with shooting of five people, authorities sayMichael SainatoSun 16 Aug 2026 15.39 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA young man suspected in connection with theshooting of five peopleon Saturday on the campus of Virginia State University (VSU) hid in a dormitory closet for more than 14 hours before being found and arrested, according to authorities.The suspect – identified as 19-year-old Camron Harris – was found in Seward Hall on VSU’s campus at 4pm, local police Lt James Lamb said, according to theVirginianews outletWTVR. The shooting occurred at about 1.30am on Saturday.Harris, who is not a student enrolled at the university, was taken to the Chesterfield county jail to be booked on four counts each of malicious wounding and use of a firearm in the commission of a felony. The Henrico,Virginia, resident was being held without bond, and police said additional charges may be filed against him.Chesterfield county police said officers discovered five people with gunshot wounds when they arrived on scene outside campus dormitories. The five victims were transported to local hospitals, with one victim reported to be experiencing life-threatening wound and in a critical condition.The other four victims had non-life threatening wound,accordingto police. At least one of those victims, a 20-year-old, was confirmed to be a student.Police did not immediately release details about a possible motive, saying the investigation remained ongoing.VSU initially saidin a statement the shooting involved “multiple suspects”. The campus was temporarily put on lockdown.VSU latersaidthat authorities did not believe there was any additional, immediate threat to the safety of the school community after the mass shooting.“We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends, and the broader VSU community,” VSU said in thestatement. “The safety and wellbeing of our students remain our highest priority.”VSU is a public university about 20 miles (32km) south of Richmond that has about 5,700 students, most of whom are undergraduates.Many students on Saturday had just completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students, an event alluding to the nickname for the school’s athletic teams.‘She is a hero’: 13-year-old survivor of Michigan shooting rampage called 911Read moreAs of Sunday morning, there had been more than 300 mass shootings reported across the US so far for the year, according to theGun Violence Archive.The archive, a nonpartisan reference resource, defines mass shootings as cases in which at least four victims are wounded or killed.The US has perennially registered high numbers of mass shootings, with a considerable portion of those occurring at school and university campuses or activities. Those grim numbers have prompted calls for more substantial federal gun control, though Congress over the years has not implemented such restrictions.In a separate, high-profile mass shooting reported in the US on Saturday evening, one person was killed and four more were wounded at Charles Young Park in Lexington, Kentucky.Local news outlets reported that Lexington police chief Lawrence Weathers said two children, aged four and 14, were among those shot.Weathers declined to share any information about a suspect or possible motive but told reporters he did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsVirginiaUS crimeGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina stolen from Sicilian museum | Art | The Guardian
description: Theft of four works on national holiday described as wound to historical memory and cultural identity of city of Messina
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Theft of four works on national holiday described as wound to historical memory and cultural identity of city of Messina
Content: The five surviving panels of Antonello’sPolittico di San Gregorio –three of which were stolen on Saturday.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe five surviving panels of Antonello’sPolittico di San Gregorio –three of which were stolen on Saturday.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/ReutersArtRenaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina stolen from Sicilian museumTheft of four works on national holiday described as wound to historical memory and cultural identity of city of MessinaLorenzo Tondoin PalermoSun 16 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour of the most important works of art by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.Thievesgained access to the Regional Museum of Messina, or MuMe, on Saturday evening, possibly capitalising on attention being focused on La Vara, a huge religious festival that takes place in the city on 15 August, when Italy marks the Ferragosto national holiday.Bypassing the alarm systems, the gang broke into a security display box and stole four wood panels painted by Antonello, who is widely credited withchanging the course of Renaissance art.Thieves took three of the five surviving panels that made up an altarpiece known as thePolittico di San Gregorio, one of the Sicilian painter’s most important works.View image in fullscreenThe fourth, smaller stolen work, which depicts Virgin and Child.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/Reuters“It is an extremely serious and significant loss,” said Marisa Mercurio, the director of the museum. “They have stolen works of enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance, not only for Messina but for Sicily as a whole. All we can do now is hope they are recovered as soon as possible.”Originally composed of six panels created for the Monastero di San Gregorio, which was destroyed in the 1908 Messina earthquake, the altarpiece was the only work by the Sicilian painter never to have left his home city.A fourth work was taken from a secure display case: a small double-sided painting depicting the Virgin and Child with a Franciscan monk on one side and Christ on the other.The painting had belonged to the Wilhelm Soldan collection and was sold by Christie’s to the Sicilian regional government in 2003, the year it was attributed to Antonello.The haul could have been even greater: six paintings were stolen in total, but, inexplicably, two of the panels were abandoned on a low wall outside the museum.Born around ​1430, Antonello trained in Naples where he studied the works of Provençal and Flemish artists, whose influence is apparent in his works.“Antonello was instrumental in bringing Flemish oil-painting techniques toItaly, making possible a new softness, delicate glazing and subtle shading,” said Valentina Certo, an art historian affiliated with the University of Messina and author of the illustrated children’s book The Workshop of Antonello da Messina. “Even on very small panels, he was capable of extraordinary precision and detail.”View image in fullscreenThe grounds of the Regional Museum of Messina.Photograph: Danilo Arnone/Reuters“The overnight theft is a wound inflicted on the historical memory and cultural identity of the city of Messina,” she added. “These were works that had survived the earthquake, destruction and five centuries of history. To see them taken from the public in this way makes the loss impossible to measure in purely economic terms.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn 28 December 1908, the city of Messina was struck by what is still considered the deadliest natural catastrophe in modern European history: a 7.1-magnitude earthquake lasting 37 seconds that killed half its population and levelled much of the city.Along with homes, churches and monuments, invaluable historical sources and documents were lost, including works by Antonello.In February, the Italian government secured a rare Antonello masterpiece at auction in New York,spending $14.9m (£11m) on his Ecce Homo. The painting, sold at Sotheby’s, is an intenselyhuman portrait of the suffering Christ, believed to have been completed in about 1460.Prosecutors in Messina have opened an investigation into the theft. Police sources said the museum was fitted with several surveillance cameras and that the works were protected by a sophisticated alarm system. Investigators are examining several lines of inquiry, including whether the paintings were stolen for the illicit art market.According to the state news agency Ansa, investigators are also considering the possibility that the theft was carried out on commission for an art dealer.The theft took place after Italian police on Friday hadrecovered three paintingsby the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that werestolen earlier this yearfrom a private museum near the northern city of Parma.Explore more on these topicsArtItalyEuropePaintingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Interest rate dilemma for central banks as inflation rises but growth slows | Inflation | The Guardian
description: The Federal Reserve, the ECB and the Bank of England appear unclear on how to tackle inflation amid the Iran war
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: The Federal Reserve, the ECB and the Bank of England appear unclear on how to tackle inflation amid the Iran war
Content: Up and down fuel prices from the on-off Iran war are making it even more difficult for central banks to predict inflation rates.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUp and down fuel prices from the on-off Iran war are making it even more difficult for central banks to predict inflation rates.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesInflationAnalysisInterest rate dilemma for central banks as inflation rises but growth slowsPhillip InmanThe Federal Reserve, the ECB and the Bank of England appear unclear on how to tackle inflation amid the Iran warNew UK cost of living crisis looms as rising energy bills lift inflationSun 16 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTShareInflation rates have been falling across the industrialised world, but fears that the Middle East war will raise oil prices means central banks are sitting on their hands when they should be raising interest rates to subdue inflationary pressures.The US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and theEuropean Central Bankare still smarting from the criticism of their inaction in 2022 when inflation soared above 10% in the UK and eurozone, and over 9% in the US.Central banks were plagued by accusations that they moved too slowly to confront inflation in the months after the Ukraine war started, when post-pandemic consumer spending was already stoking prices on everything from food to construction materials.Trump Fed chair’s inflation strategy: leave it to the market | Eduardo PorterRead moreIt’s now been five years since they all met their 2% inflation target and now they are asking themselves whether the continuing blockade of the strait of Hormuz will mean a sixth or seventh year of target-busting prices growth?The Federal Reserve seeks helpUS inflation edged lower to 3.4% in July from 3.5% in June and 4.2% in May, largely in response to falling petrol prices.Since the Bureau of Labor Statistics collected the data, the price of a barrel of Brent crude has risen again to about $90 – a figure that will push up the price of energy and transport across the US in the second half of the year.Fed officials are asking whether US inflation will climb back towards 4%, double its target.The US central bank’s new boss, Kevin Warsh, has instigated an all-embracing review of the Fed’s operations based on the advice of 15 outsiders that he says are among the most eminent experts and economists of the age.Many analysts have applauded him for recognising that a series of inflation shocks dating back to the arrival of Covid-19 have undermined the integrity and durability of central bank forecasting.Mohamed El-Erian, an economist and professor at the Wharton Business school, said Warsh recognised that many of the shibboleths of monetary policymaking had proved flawed.“The key issue for me is having someone there who’s committed to long-overdue Fed reforms. This is essential for future Fed effectiveness, credibility and political independence,” El-Erian says.Chief among the tools Warsh has already ditched is forward guidance – the explicit signalling of the likely future path of interest rates. He also declined to join other Fed policymakers in creating dot plots on a graph showing how the economy and inflation are expected to develop over the next couple of years.View image in fullscreenThe US central bank’s new boss, Kevin Warsh, has instigated an all-embracing review of the Fed’s operations.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAAmong Warsh’s 15 appointments to five subject committees is Lord Mervyn King, the former governor of theBank of England, considered a founding father of inflation forecasting, but who has since argued that trying to predict the future is a fool’s game.In King’s 2022 book Radical Uncertainty, he argues that central banks should drop the idea that consumers and businesses act like atoms in a physics experiment because it strips out emotional responses to economic events.King says central banks should take more account of uncertainty in how people react and ditch a heavy reliance on economic models that claim to predict what is likely to happen.He describes forward guidance as “silly” when no central bank knows what the interest rate will be in six months or two years’ time. “It will depend on what is happening in the economy,” he says.El-Erian calls forward guidance “spurious accuracy”. What financial markets and the public need to know is the “reaction function”. In other words, how the central bank will respond to different types of events.Charlie Bean, a professor at the London School ofEconomicsand a former deputy governor of the BoE, says that, so far, Fed watchers don’t have guidance on either the path of rates or the central bank’s likely reaction to developments in the economy.“Warsh is getting in a bit of a mess in the way he is not giving a guide to where rates are going and also not talking about how changes in the economy will affect rates,” said Bean. “It means he is not saying anything of substance.”The Fed held rates in July and financial market betting expects a hold again in September, though a rise is thought possible. Markets anticipate at least one, and possibly two, quarter-point increases by the middle of next year, taking the Fed’s target rate from its current 3.5-3.75% range to 4-4.25%. Will market betting prove reliable? Nobody knows.The Bank of England suffers a post-Covid hangoverWhile the BoE is widely considered to have acted consistently since the start of the Iran war – saying it will raise the cost of borrowing should there be any signs of persistent inflation. However, the decision to hold the Bank Rate steady at 3.75% so far this year could come under pressure.The UK consumer price index (CPI) dropped to 2.6% in June, but some analysts expect it to rise to 2.9% or even 3% when July’s figures are published by the Office for National Statistics on 19 August.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA majority of the nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) are wary of increasing interest rates when it will have little effect on global oil prices, aware that higher borrowing costs could depress an already weak UK economy.Bean says the MPC is also under pressure from even more fundamental trends, including high and rising government debt.View image in fullscreenPeople pass the Bank of England building in London.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersThe difficulty arises when governments are highly indebted and a central bank wants to raise interest rates to control inflation. A rise in the cost of borrowing increases the government’s debt financing bill. Central banks must decide whether to cripple the government’s finances or let inflation remain high for a longer period above its target.This is a problem for the Fed’s Warsh, too – after the US paid the highest borrowing costs to sell 30-year bonds since 2001, in an debt auction this month..Neil Shearing, chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, says he has argued for many years that central banks will preside over high inflation for as long as western governments cannot control their debt-fuelled spending.“The conceit is that central banks need to maintain 2% as their target while at the same time tolerating a slightly higher level of inflation. They cannot say it publicly, or even privately, because they would be accused of trying to dupe the public and more importantly, the financial markets,” he says.Making matters worse, most inflationary shocks come from global events and restrictions in the supply of essential goods. Interest rate rises dampen consumer spending with little effect on the price of imported goods.Nevertheless, financial markets predict the BoE will raise rates this year, possibly from as early as its next meeting in September on the path to pushing rates as high as 4.25% by late 2027.The ECB goes rogueUnlike the Fed and BoE, the ECB has raised the cost of borrowing this year. Critics say it moved too quickly.While the eurozone’s central bank has freed itself from forward guidance, critics say the ECB remains confused about how to react when inflation begins to climb.Itraised interest rates in Juneafter only a modest rise in inflation caused by the Middle East war and rising oil prices.Many economists said the move was too early when much of the eurozone economy continues to be devastated by the energy shock that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.View image in fullscreenJoggers pass the European Central Bank building in Frankfurt, Germany.Photograph: Wolfgang Rattay/ReutersShearing said: “The ECB was clearly fighting the previous war and prematurely raising rates. The underlying picture in the eurozone is one of weakness.”Shearing is among many analysts who believe financial markets are wrong to expect the ECB will raise its main deposit rate by a quarter-point to 2.5% at its next meeting in September and possibly act again with a further quarter-point increase next year.He says that while high oil prices put pressure on inflation, they act as a brake on economic activity, as a rise in interest rates would also do. A rate rise would be like kicking the economy when it is already down, and the ECB wouldn’t win any plaudits for doing that.Explore more on these topicsInflationFederal ReserveEuropean Central BankBankingEconomicsUS economyEurozoneanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought – if I die, I’ve had a good innings’: producer James Ford on life, death and making an album from his hospital bed | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was Britain’s most in-demand producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he says
Author: Nosheen Iqbal
Headline: The Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was Britain’s most in-demand producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he says
Content: James Ellis Ford in his home in London.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJames Ellis Ford in his home in London.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianPop and rockInterview‘I thought – if I die, I’ve had a good innings’: producer James Ford on life, death and making an album from his hospital bedNosheen IqbalThe Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was at the height of his powers as Britain’s most in-demand music producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he saysSun 16 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a moment outside the door of a recording studio in rural France, staring at a half-eaten apple that he believed possessed psychedelic properties, when James Ford knew things had really got out of hand. He was stood with Klaxons; all of the band members were hypnotised by this rotting fruit which throbbed on the floor with kaleidoscopic intensity. They were convinced that its blooming mould was in fact their spiritual guru.The band had been riding the wave of their huge, scene-defining debut album, 2007’sMyths of the Near Future– which was produced by Ford – and were now trying to record the interminably difficult follow-up, aided by daily doses of a concoction they’d taken to calling “the five-star general”.“It was a huge bag, five drugs mixed together, probably ketamine and speed, I don’t know what else, but it was quite a psychedelic powder and they were doing it every morning and throughout the day,” says Ford. He realised he couldn’t rein things back in. “And after a two-and-a-half-week period … things got fucking weird.”So weird, in fact, that the head of the UK record label came over on the Eurostar carrying a bell jar at the band’s request, only to find out it was to cover an apple that had been chewed up and spat out by a passing dog and was now being called Mr Tabernacle. Klaxons, it’s fair to say, had lost their minds a little bit. The album was aborted.View image in fullscreenFord’s home studio.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The Guardian“We thought we were making The Dark Side of the Moon,” says Ford with a giggle, now sitting in the studio in his east London home. Instead, that “ill-fated second record” became the only project that Ford has never finished in a career that has since established him as the music industry’s go-to magic weapon.It is quite the trajectory. Ford went from tearing up 00s dancefloors as one half, alongside Jas Shaw, of Simian Mobile Disco – musicians and DJs who elevated the electro-rave era of the decade – to becoming the most sought-after ear in music. In the last decade, with little in the way of hype, he has quietly become the pre-eminent producer of his generation.Ford is who you call when you’re trying to make a career-defining album (Arctic Monkeys; Florence + the Machine; Jessie Ware; Fontaines DC), who you trust to realise a stunning comeback (Pulp; Blur; Gorillaz; Depeche Mode) and who you need to help translate critical buzz into commercial success (Geese; The Last Dinner Party; Black Country, New Road).“It’s a very broad term ‘producer’,” he says, trying to explain his role. “It doesn’t really describe what happens; I’m trying to get to the bottom of someone else’s vision and pull that out there.” Be it Pet Shop Boys or Jessie Ware, artists agree that Ford doesn’t produce in a conventional sense. “I think if you try to imprint your sound, it seems a weird ego-y thing to do, to try to do a Phil Spector on everyone’s record.” And so he doesn’t impose a sound or vibe on to the room so much as mediate, and draw artists in and out of whatever creative pattern they’re in.View image in fullscreenJames Ellis Ford photographed in his home in London, July 2026.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianAt home, surrounded by synths, guitars and all manner of recording equipment, Ford seems relaxed and is softly spoken, with a light touch of the Staffordshire accent he grew up with. The heyday of his hedonism may be behind him, but it’s obvious that he still loves what he does. It is this and a general sense of ease that has earned Ford a level of trust from artists at their most vulnerable. A gracious, nice guy in an industry famously short of decency, it’s easy to understand why the world’s biggest artists are knocking down his door to work with him.Still, it’s a minor miracle we’re even meeting today. On Christmas Eve 2024 Ford was with his wife and young son at his in-laws’ in Folkestone when he got “hit like a ton of bricks”. He was laid out on the sofa, unable to get up with a fever that wouldn’t break and a flu-like illness that refused to let up. He had worked flat out all year, and in the weeks running up to December had felt unusually fatigued. He wondered whether he was heading for burnout, but this was something entirely new.He was admitted to the local A&E; his blood tests were “all over the place”. Having travelled to India with Damon Albarn some weeks earlier, doctors initially suspected he had picked up a tropical disease. “There were a lot of red herrings,” he says. “It took ages to get any kind of diagnosis because my bloods had to get sent to London, so I spent weeks in this horrible state, and just felt I was going to die. It was awful.”double quotation markNo-one was supposed to visit me in hospital, but Jarvis came. The staff let him inWeeks later, on a Friday night, “someone unceremoniously came in and said: ‘We’ve found leukaemia. You need to go to a cancer ward.’” And that was it. If his life had flashed before him, Ford, who had just turned 46, could admit it had been a good one. A great one, even. “I’ve got a wonderful family with my wife and little boy, I’ve got a great relationship with my parents, a good career, I’ve travelled a lot, done a lot of things with a lot of people that I’ve dreamed of working with,” he says. And he has partied hard, I joke, having borne witness to multiple Simian Mobile Disco sets and afterparties. “I’ve partied really hard,” he says. “I’ve had some great times, I’ve got a lot of good memories and I’ve made some things I’m really proud of. I think I’ve been a generally good person in the world. And so I was almost at the point where I was like, if I die, I’ve had a good innings. I wouldn’t be that scared of it.”View image in fullscreenFord’s US platinum disc for Arctic Monkeys’ AM.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianFord was eventually transferred to St Barts hospital in London and pummelled with rounds of drugs. He spent the early weeks of 2025 obliterated by the illness. Then came the second round of chemotherapy, and something of a breakthrough. He asked his wife Sereen, whom he met as a student at Manchester University, to bring in his laptop, an Ikea fold-up table, some synthesisers, a microphone and a guitar to his hospital room. Supported by staff at the hospital, who could see it cheered him up and got him out of bed, Ford began making music. Nurses got used to administering their daily medical care while Ford messed with drumbeats and sang, locked in his creative flow state. In two weeks, Ford wrote and recorded his new album, Lost in Another World, which would be remarkable enough on its own – were it not for the fact that it is also stunning.Despite being sung and recorded by Ford in a creative jag while contemplating life and death, the record feels like his signature sound – melodic, electronic, art-pop. It’s joyful where you expect it to be bleak. Over the course of nine months, Ford went through two more rounds of chemotherapy, a stem cell transplant, sepsis – three times – and a stay in intensive care. To say it has been an unremittingly traumatic year sells it short, but he – and the album – wear it lightly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t know if nervous is the right word,” he says of Lost in Another World’s impending release. “It’s more odd because it takes me back to that moment of being ill. And I’d intentionally left it, but now I’m having to talk about it. At first, even hearing it back for the first time, I was like ‘Ugh!’” I insist we don’t have to talk about the depths of his illness.“I always felt pretty invincible, though,” says Ford, reflecting on it. “And then suddenly, you’re like: ‘Oh, I’m not.’ And it was that thing: two or three years before this, I started running. I was going to the gym regularly. I was eating well. I’d lost weight, I’d given up drinking, given up all drugs, blah blah, the full cycle. And then I fucking get leukaemia!”Despite the toll the cancer took, Ford still somehow managed to produce two more major albums when he was really ill. One for Gorillaz, the other for the Mercury prize-nominated War Child album,Help(2), where he was producing the likes of Olivia Rodrigo and Beth Gibbons from his hospital bed. “Remote producing a session [going on] at Abbey Road while having a blood transfusion was not on my 2025 bingo card,” he posted on Instagram at the time.View image in fullscreenFord’s home setup.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianFord was not allowed any visitors for long stretches in hospital, Sereen excepted, because his immunity was so shot. “Funnily enough, Jarvis [Cocker] came in when he wasn’t meant to. But he’s so recognised, they were bamboozled and let him in and he’d very sweetly bought me some of his favourite books and wrote little things in them of what he liked and stuff. It was wonderful but I was a bit: ‘Wow, OK!’”Mentally at least, music saved him. “It was amazing to have something to focus on that made me feel good, to get into that zone where I shut down everything else on the outside. The lyrics [for Lost in Another World] literally just fell out. Obviously I had a bunch of stuff to process, but it was the easiest music-making process I’ve ever had.”‘Some artists thought it was too political’: can Jarvis, Damon, Olivia Rodrigo and Arctic Monkeys reboot the biggest charity album of the 90s?Read moreHow is he doing now? “I’m still not fully out of it.” Ford will have his bloods closely monitored for the next few years and attend regular checkups to track whether the cancer comes back. For now, he is gearing up for a number of live shows following the album’s arrival into the world and rehearsals are under way.“The obvious thing that has come out of all of this is that it does make you recognise what and who the important things in your life are and that life is exceptionally fragile,” he says of his renewed work-life balance. “Not to spend any time with people who aren’t worth spending time with and on projects that aren’t worth spending time on. Just being really selective and intentional about every choice you make. And that can be as simple as ‘spend more time in nature’, ‘spend more time with my family’, ‘maybe not work so hard’.”He smiles at the last one. “None of that is particularly groundbreaking. It’s stuff you see every day on the internet, but it’s different when you live through it. I definitely had read about the value of gratitude and all of those things, but I could never really take it on board in a way that I have now.”Lost in Another World by James Ellis Ford is out now; he plays Rough Trade East, London,17 August; and the Horse Hospital, London, 17 September.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Four Walls and a Roof review – fascinating tale of Brecht, the red scare and today’s émigrés | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Rabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie explore the playwright’s life, and their journey from Beirut to Berlin, in an absorbing show at the Edinburgh international festival
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Rabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie explore the playwright’s life, and their journey from Beirut to Berlin, in an absorbing show at the Edinburgh international festival
Content: Pointed parallels to today … Four Walls and a Roof.Photograph: KFDA Sybille CornetView image in fullscreenPointed parallels to today … Four Walls and a Roof.Photograph: KFDA Sybille CornetEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFour Walls and a Roof review – fascinating tale of Brecht, the red scare and today’s émigrésStudio Theatre, EdinburghRabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie explore the playwright’s life, and their journey from Beirut to Berlin, in an absorbing show at the Edinburgh international festivalMark FisherSun 16 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBertolt Brecht termed it “cold execution”. He was thinking of the way the US government, in the era of theHouse Un-American Activities Committee(Huac), could murder its opponents not by directly killing them but by cutting them off from what kept them alive. Where the cold war was waged without bullets, these cold executions were enacted, for example, on any blacklisted artist who could no longer work in Hollywood.It is an idea picked up by Lebanese artists Lina Majdalanie and Rabih Mroué who use the story of the playwright in exile as a way of thinking about displacement in our own era. Brecht, no doubt seeing the writing on the wall, got out of his native Germany soon after the burning of the Reichstag in 1933. It took him several countries, eight years and a journey across land and sea to reach the US. As Majdalanie and Mroué wryly point out, getting back to Europe after the US questioned his communist affiliations took only a day.View image in fullscreenAn absorbing illustrated lecture … Rabih Mroué in Four Walls and A Roof.Photograph: KFDA Sybille CornetIn an absorbing illustrated lecture, accompanied by pianist Henrik Kairies singing songs by Brecht and Hanns Eisler, the pair use the playwright’s life away from home as a way of asking questions about place and identity. As émigrés from Beirut to Berlin, they have a personal interest in the idea of homeland: however you define it, it means more than the four walls and a roof of the title.Reading from their script in a casual, un-actorly way, they gently prod Brecht’s story towards today. The Huac wanted yes-or-no certainty and did not allow the playwright to readhis prepared statement. Had they heard his commentary on the early Nazi crackdown on free speech perhaps they would have spotted parallels with their own intolerance. With the far right on the rise again, they are parallels that speak to us ever more pointedly.AtStudio theatre, Edinburgh, until 17 August.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalBertolt BrechtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Have I tried having sex to my own music? God, no!’: Natalie Imbruglia’s honest playlist | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The singer was wooed with some knocked-off Joni Mitchell and might even be persuaded to sing Torn at karaoke. But what fan comment winds her up the most?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer was wooed with some knocked-off Joni Mitchell and might even be persuaded to sing Torn at karaoke. But what fan comment winds her up the most?
Content: Natalie Imbruglia … ‘I’m not the most confident party playlist DJ.’Photograph: RankinView image in fullscreenNatalie Imbruglia … ‘I’m not the most confident party playlist DJ.’Photograph: RankinHonest playlistPop and rock‘Have I tried having sex to my own music? God, no!’: Natalie Imbruglia’s honest playlistThe singer was wooed with some knocked-off Joni Mitchell and might even be persuaded to sing Torn at karaoke. But what fan comment winds her up the most?As told toRich PelleySun 16 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withMy dad gave me California Dreamin’ by the Mamas & the Papas on vinyl for my fifth birthday. I said: “Oh thanks, Dad,” but really, I thought: “Who is this weird bunch of people?” Obviously, the present was really for him.The first single I boughtI remember begging my mum to buy me Beat It by Michael Jackson at a record shop in the ’burbs of Sydney. I mean – he’s Michael Jackson.The song I do at karaokeWhen you’re a singer, it’s really awkward: you don’t want to throw a tantrum, sound too good or show off, because then everyone is like “Ugh.” I might do Torn, but only at parties, when I’m drunk and my friends make me.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toYou’re the Voice by John Farnham – because it’s a bit of a tour bus anthem after a show and a couple of gins.The song I can no longer listen toWhen I was 17, this guy wrote out the lyrics to Coyote by Joni Mitchell and told me he’d written a poem about me. I thought: “My God, he’s a poet.” But years later, I was listening to this album and thought: “I recognise those words!” So now I just think: “What a creep!”The best song to play at a partyAny time it’s afters at mine, I always think: “What am I gonna put on?” I’m not the most confident party playlist DJ. But, no matter the mood or the crowd, I can put on Genius of Love by Tom Tom Club, and everyone loves it.The best song to have sex toPass! Have I tried my own music? God, no!The song that changed my lifeI have to say Torn, don’t I? Even though it’s a cover, which I’ve been tortured over ever since. People say: “You didn’t write Torn.” I think: “So what? I know I didn’t.” There was a meme that said: “The way you feel when you find out Torn’s a cover,” and it all started again! I thought: “For fuck’s sake, I just got over that!”The song that gets me up in the morningI’m not good in the mornings, so it has to be something gentle, like Little Blue by Jacob Collier.The song that makes me cryA Song for You by Donny Hathaway is just the most incredible love song. The tone of his voice is so pleasing.The song I’d like played at my funeralAnother One Bites the Dust by Queen, segued into Don’t Stop Me Now.Natalie Imbruglia’s album Algorithm is out on 4 September.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockHonest playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It is not only a future certainty – the disaster is already here’: why we need climate fiction | Books | The Guardian
description: As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisis
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisis
Content: A firefighter in Galicia, Spain.Photograph: Brais Lorenzo/EPAView image in fullscreenA firefighter in Galicia, Spain.Photograph: Brais Lorenzo/EPABooks‘It is not only a future certainty – the disaster is already here’: why we need climate fictionAs wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisisTara MenonSun 16 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. Everywhere I went, the heat broke records. In Italy, Germany and Spain, I sought refuge from the afternoon sun in air-conditioned hotels. In normally temperate Zurich, it averaged 37 degrees. I jumped into the Limmat for relief. On my final day in Warsaw, Poland had never been hotter – one of 14 countries to hit a historic high. In June, when I left to return to the US, Europe was scorching. At the end of July, as I write this, it is burning.Since the heatwaves began, there have been more than 10,000 excess deaths. Yet for many, myself included, the high temperatures brought nothing more than inconvenience – uncomfortable commutes, heat rash, less time outdoors. This seems to be a defining feature of today’s climate crisis; deadly for some, banal for others. Even when the world is on fire, it somehow doesn’t feel like an emergency for everyone.This disparity cast my mind back toHurricane Sandy in 2012. I was living in New York, one of millions ordered to shelter in place. (I was lucky – hundreds of thousands were ordered to evacuate their homes.) I followed instructions. I stayed in my warm, dry apartment on the Upper West Side, watching trees swaying violently against the dark sky. The next morning, the rain had stopped; the sun was out, the air was still again and the power was still on. When I went outside to survey the damage, there was little to see except a few broken branches. The mood in my neighbourhood was jovial. The subways were closed, schools were shut, work was called off. Brunch was on.In other parts of the city, it was a different story. Whole fleets of taxi cabs submerged in water, their canary yellow roofs peeking out; a huge midtown crane snapped cleanly in half; the collapsed wall of an apartment building. I watched and rewatched a video of a power plant exploding. Half a million people, including most of the residents of lower Manhattan, were now without electricity. The American news outlets focused almost exclusively on New York. The international news sites told a more complete story: Sandy killed 233 people in eight countries and caused $70bn in damage.Several days after the storm, I volunteered in Chinatown, distributing basic goods – batteries, canned food and bottled water – to elderly people who lived on the highest floors of public housing buildings and hadn’t yet ventured outside since the storm. (the lifts weren’t working and they weren’t able to take the stairs). The apartments smelled of rotting food and unflushed toilets. The national guard rolled through the streets in tanks; rats brazenly stalked the pavements and Red Cross workers posed for photographs with locals. Research labs at NYU lost their lab animals during the storm; the news reported them dead, but rumours spread that the rodent population of the city had grown by 10,000 transgenic mice and rats.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIn the weeks after Sandy, I was struck by the disparity between those who could escape the city to second homes and those who had nowhere else to goNew rules governed downtown life. Bars served free drinks by candlelight, neighbourhood people with handmade signs offered water to passersby, small shops offered free charging stations. The roads around Ground Zero stayed flooded for weeks; the water was green and brackish. Amid the darkness, one building stayed lit, its squares of gold stretched into the sky. Goldman Sachs would not be stopped.In the days and weeks after Sandy, I was struck by many disparities: between downtown darkness and uptown light; between those who were able to escape the city to second homes and those who had nowhere else to go; between the countries with a quick, organised disaster response and those that relied entirely on community help. I also found myself thinking about the natural disasters I had heard about as a child and teenager growing up in Singapore: the 1999 Odisha cyclone, the 2003 heatwave across India, the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, the 2006 Southern Leyte mudslide in the Philippines, the 2007 cyclone in Bangladesh. These were disasters with much higher death tolls that I realised many people had never heard about.When Sandy made landfall in 2012, I had just begun my PhD in English literature. For work, I read canonical 19th-century realist novels; for pleasure, I read contemporary literary fiction. I searched for novels about the environment but often found myself disappointed. In many, the severe consequences of the climate crisis were packaged as a future possibility – something to come, one day. But the climate crisis is not only a future certainty, it is past and present truth. The disaster is already here.double quotation markCan literary fiction capture both the freak event and the mundane truth of the climate crisis?Several years after Sandy, I read Amitav Ghosh’s The Great Derangement, in which he argues that literary fiction has failed us. Ghosh perfectly articulated my disappointment about the climate fiction, or cli-fi, I had read. But he went further. Ghosh listed the reasons the modern novel was unsuited to the challenge of representing the climate crisis. One, contemporary western novels had become “ever more radically centred on the individual psyche”. Two, unlike other genres, novels can’t range freely over space and time. Three, our literary imagination had become “radically centred on the human”. And four, the climate crisis is defined by improbable events and “probability and the modern novels are twins”.When I first read The Great Derangement, I agreed with Ghosh that “the climate crisis is also a crisis of culture, and thus of the imagination”. But I also wondered whether it would be possible to write what he said didn’t exist but should: serious literary fiction that captures both the freak event and the mundane truth of the climate crisis.Ghosh laid down a gauntlet; I thought I’d try to pick it up. Over the next eight years, I wrote a novel that moves towards two cataclysmic events – Hurricane Sandy and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami – but also documents the slow violence that unfolds in both New York and Thailand. My debut novel, Under Water, seeks to represent climate change in the very form Ghosh suggests is ill-suited to the task: a realist novel centred on a single individual.It is true, as Ghosh notes, that, unlike epics, novels do not usually bring multiple universes into conjunction. But a realist novel centred on a bourgeois subject in today’s globalised world can in fact move across space and time. A single individual might, as my protagonist Marissa does, grow up on a barely inhabited island in south-east Asia and then, a decade later, live as an adult in a large metropolis on the east coast of the United States.My book also responds to Ghosh’s striking claim that the modern novel was “never forced to confront the centrality of the improbable”. In Under Water, I try to imbue Hurricane Sandy, a highly improbable event, with expectation. Because of her childhood and her past, Marissa experiences the approach of Sandy differently from other inhabitants of the city.Under Water is a riposte to Ghosh’s claim that the contemporary realist novel is destined to fail us. A single novel cannot show everything, everywhere, all at once. But it can, more effectively than any other cultural form, wield what I think is still one of our best weapons against this or any other crisis: the determination to pay close, careful attention to the people and places we are losing, every day.Under Water by Tara Menon is published by Summit(£16.99).
