title: Blackbox review – a legendary escape from slavery is told with magic tricks | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The story of Henry ‘Box’ Brown, who succeeded in mailing himself out of bondage, is recounted rather than fully dramatised
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: The story of Henry ‘Box’ Brown, who succeeded in mailing himself out of bondage, is recounted rather than fully dramatised
Content: Jada Evelyn Ramsey and Josiah Alpher in Blackbox at Underbelly, Edinburgh.Photograph: Jason SullivanView image in fullscreenJada Evelyn Ramsey and Josiah Alpher in Blackbox at Underbelly, Edinburgh.Photograph: Jason SullivanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBlackbox review – a legendary escape from slavery is told with magic tricksUnderbelly, EdinburghThe story of Henry ‘Box’ Brown, who succeeded in mailing himself out of bondage, is recounted rather than fully dramatisedMark FisherSun 16 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry “Box” Brown is wrapped up in chains when he has an idea to claim his freedom. As inspiration hits him, actor Josiah Alpher flexes his muscles and, miraculously, the chains appear to pass through his neck. Magic!It is a neat visual metaphor for a true story that seems miraculous in itself. In 1849, Brown made a break to flee slavery near Richmond, Virginia, by posting himself in a wooden crate to Philadelphia, a state where ownership of human beings had been phased out by the Gradual Abolition Act of 1780. Alpher describes a painful journey, squashed, upturned and knocked about, beforeBrown’s happy delivery.Rickerby Hinds’s staging of his own play uses the language of stage magic, from the glamorous magician’s assistant (Jada Evelyn Ramsey) to the knotted rope trick, to emphasise how extraordinary this escape was. Brown gets into the box as if he were Harry Houdini performing a stunt.Hinds shows too how the bonds of US slavery were not just represented by physical chains: they extended to a church that sanctioned the practice and to the constant threat of whipping, a nagging psychological burden.Not for Glory review – folk dance and bagpipes, but not as we know themRead moreAll this is duly itemised in a script that tells Brown’s story before his break for freedom, not only the callous treatment at the hands of his owner, but also accounts of conditions even worse than his own.It is weighty material but it is lessened in three ways. The story is recounted rather than dramatised and were it not for the magic tricks would seem theatrically flat. The actors hit an impressively breakneck speed, but perform without tonal variation, making it hard to keep up. And the story ends where you might expect it to begin, with Henry “Box” Brown’s entry into a new life.At Underbelly, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalFestivalsMagicSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Last Drop review – everything is rotten in this dark domestic comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Dante Passarelli’s play, part of the Edinburgh fringe’s São Paulo Showcase, is an atmospheric hour borrowing themes from Hamlet
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Dante Passarelli’s play, part of the Edinburgh fringe’s São Paulo Showcase, is an atmospheric hour borrowing themes from Hamlet
Content: A sense of individual lives adrift … The Last Drop by Manás Theatre Lab.Photograph: Di Scapino/Jammil BubrukView image in fullscreenA sense of individual lives adrift … The Last Drop by Manás Theatre Lab.Photograph: Di Scapino/Jammil BubrukEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Last Drop review – everything is rotten in this dark domestic comedyZoo Playground, EdinburghDante Passarelli’s play, part of the São Paulo Showcase, is an atmospheric hour borrowing themes from HamletChris WiegandSun 16 Aug 2026 03.36 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year’s fringe variously puts Hamlet inthe Big Brother housewith Lady Macbeth, makes him “Prince of Sweden” in an Italian two-hander and grinds the play into what Polonius might call a “tragical-comical”swipe at the meat industry. Dante Passarelli’s The Last Drop, part of the festival’sSão Paulo Showcase, borrows the opening and closing lines of Shakespeare’s masterpiece and pursues similar themes of madness, revenge and surveillance in a story where everything, not just something, is rotten.The opening tableau resembles a murder scene: has death-stare Cynthia (Fernanda Zancopé) done away with her husband, Gilberto (Ernani Sanchez), who lies sprawled on the floor? Apparently not: as he rises, and they resume their bickering, you realise wider crimes are at play in this densely packed city where new buildings rise around them and construction often involves corruption. Suspicion is rife: they have lived for years in this apartment block with its peeling wallpaper and hold their upstairs neighbour, so wasteful with water, responsible for the mouldy stain on their ceiling.Sniff, sniff … Drip, drip. What exactly are all those other appalling smells and sounds invading their home? Directed to claustrophobic effect by Passarelli and Zancopé for ManásTheatreLab, with English surtitles and a suitably queasy lighting design, the play unfolds against a backdrop of social and environmental unrest. Its stark commentary about class and inequality at times brings to mind Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite.Joseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70 review – a dork’s last day at school is one to rememberRead moreThe 60-minute play crams another hour’s worth of plot into its final minutes which rather dilutes its richly oblique atmospherics, often playing on the notion ofthe memory of waterand giving it a sinister, rather than cleansing, quality. There is a sense of nature watching on, judging our behaviour.A black domestic comedy which adds some hilariously unerotic marital foreplay to the mix, it gives a sense of individual lives adrift in the social system. Somewhere within its extremes you will recognise everyday experiences of the housing industry’s venality. You wouldn’t want to live at this address, but it’s well worth a visit.AtZoo Playground, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)HousingCommunitiesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Singer review – come on feel the noise with KT Tunstall’s glowing gig theatre | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: In Cora Bissett’s highly enjoyable and accessible production, a deaf man reintroduces a busker to the joy of music
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: In Cora Bissett’s highly enjoyable and accessible production, a deaf man reintroduces a busker to the joy of music
Content: Dab hands with a song … Jamie Rea (left) and Dylan Wood in The SingerView image in fullscreenDab hands with a song … Jamie Rea (left) and Dylan Wood in The SingerEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Singer review – come on feel the noise with KT Tunstall’s glowing gig theatreTraverse theatre, EdinburghIn Cora Bissett’s highly enjoyable and accessible show, a deaf man reintroduces a busker to the joy of musicMark FisherSun 16 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘There are other ways to listen,” says Joe (Jamie Rea) to his new friend Andy (Dylan Wood), a busker he has discovered on the street and invited home for a drink. He takes off his shoes, the better to feel the vibrations through the floor, and straps on a gadget called aSubpac. He gets Andy to lean his full height against a towering speaker stack. Only then does the rumbling bass kick in.Little, perhaps, to distinguish them from two drum’n’bass enthusiasts, but this is something else. Joe is less singer than signer, a BSL speaker whose disability has been no impediment to his love of music. He tells an incredulous Andy that he appreciates sound by feeling it and puts his hand on the musician’s acoustic guitar to demonstrate. They form the least likely of songwriting partnerships.View image in fullscreenWe all delightedly join in … The Singer.Photograph: PRStaged by Cora Bissett, who made a 20-minute film of the same name with Rea, The Singer is gig theatre with a difference. Midway through, the house lights come up and they teach us how to sign the chorus of Find My Feet, the kind of feelgood morale booster you can imagine on the soundtrack of a children’s movie. We all delightedly join in. The song is written byKT Tunstall, whose indie folk rock score lends an authentic edge to the story, complemented by Joe’s beats, under the musical direction of Michael John McCarthy.Flamenc Oh!! review – frills, flirting and fierce footwork in breezy Spanish comedyRead moreThat story, also written by Bissett, is not the production’s chief strength. Staged by Dundee Rep and Solar Bear, it is a simple tale of a tested friendship in an exploitative music industry. But as Andy goes from faithful to fickle and back again, it finds room to make salient points about the exclusion of d/Deaf people and the lower status accorded to BSL culture.It wears its politics lightly but unmistakably on a set by designer Jenny Booth that ensures written, spoken and signed languages are always available. Adding a ribald running commentary are Hannah Jarrett-Scott and Peter Dobre as Andy’s can-do grandparents, an excellent Jarrett-Scott giving Tunstall’s songs a soulful boost alongside Wood’s earthy singer-songwriter vibes. Whatever your language, it is a highly enjoyable show.At Traverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Touring until 26 September.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreKT TunstallDeafness and hearing lossDisabilityreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Not for Glory review – folk dance and bagpipes, but not as we know them | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jack Anderson and Charlotte Mclean began as champions of classic Irish and Highland steps. Here, with piper Malin Lewis, they give them a new form
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Jack Anderson and Charlotte Mclean began as champions of classic Irish and Highland steps. Here, with piper Malin Lewis, they give them a new form
Content: A cracking dancer … Jack Anderson in Not for Glory at Assembly @ Dance Base.Photograph: Brian HartleyView image in fullscreenA cracking dancer … Jack Anderson in Not for Glory at Assembly @ Dance Base.Photograph: Brian HartleyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewNot for Glory review – folk dance and bagpipes, but not as we know themAssembly @ Dance Base, EdinburghJack Anderson and Charlotte Mclean began as champions of classic Irish and Highland steps. Here, with piper Malin Lewis, they give them a new formLyndsey WinshipSun 16 Aug 2026 03.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Anderson was once a champion Irish dancer who toured the world in popular shows. But when he later enrolled at contemporary dance school, he hid his past like a shameful secret. Charlotte Mclean also tried to leave behind her childhood legacy as a competitive Highland dancer. She never liked Highland dance anyway (she just liked winning competitions) but as an adult, is she finally changing her mind?These are just two of many talking points in this anarchic dance-theatre gig from Anderson, Mclean and piper Malin Lewis. The trio are all coming to terms with their artistic inheritance, by means of distortion, deconstruction and downright mockery, then reclaiming it on their own terms. (Lewis has arguably already done this, with the acclaimed albumHaloclinein 2024 which saw them tagged “the future of Scottish folk”).View image in fullscreenReel ambition … Malin Lewis (left) and Charlotte Mclean in Not for Glory.Photograph: Brian HartleyThere’s a lot here to ruminate on: lost histories, the tyranny of competition, the dance’s links to class, the military, misogyny and political resistance; what makes a particular style of dance cool or worthy. Most classical and traditional dance forms have been reinvented by this point, but I’ve never seen Highland dance get that treatment before.So what would a new vision of these Celtic dances look like? Dancing a reel to a banging bass beat? Melting the strict lines and shapes into something gloopier? We see both, but the slightly wild-eyed, on-the-edge Mclean isn’t interested in creating a new set of rules. This show has gone freeform, somewhat unhinged in persona and direction. (It could benefit from tighter focus, a bit more meat and really honing the gags.)Flamenc Oh!! review – frills, flirting and fierce footwork in breezy Spanish comedyRead moreWhile Anderson explores what you can do with Irish dance’s sharp hinges and segmentation of the body, Lewis performs CPR on their pipes. Not for Glory is about resuscitating these performers’ love for their art as much as remaking the art forms themselves. The best bit is when the three talk honestly about their pasts and demonstrate their renewed affection. Anderson, especially, is still a cracking dancer, and Lewis’s haunting piping might make you reconsider everything you think about bagpipes. I can’t wait to see what they all do next.AtAssembly @ Dance Base, Edinburgh, until 23 August. title: ‘The kids were right’: 30 years of Pokémon, from school-wide bans to multimillion-dollar trading cards | Pokémon | The Guardian
description: Pokémon outlived the moral panic of its early days in Australia and its staying power has proved that simple joy can cross borders
Author: Patrick Marlborough
Headline: Pokémon outlived the moral panic of its early days in Australia and its staying power has proved that simple joy can cross borders
Content: ‘Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, for me, that made my life in Perth feel a little less isolated,’ writes Patrick Marlborough.Photograph: James D Morgan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, for me, that made my life in Perth feel a little less isolated,’ writes Patrick Marlborough.Photograph: James D Morgan/Getty ImagesPokémon‘The kids were right’: 30 years of Pokémon, from school-wide bans to multimillion-dollar trading cardsPokémon outlived the moral panic of its early days in Australia and its staying power has proved that simple joy can cross bordersPatrick MarlboroughSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a generation of Australians for whom Cheez TV was a religion. Every morning before school, I’d sit in my little white plastic chair about three feet from our big wooden television and watch 90 minutes of cartoons“curated”by the show’s teenage hosts, Jade and Ryan.Premiering in 1995, Cheez TVdominated the children’s breakfast market by 1998,stealing the crown from Channel Seven’s bogan-muppet icon Agro. A daily dose of Cheez TVwas such an important ritual to methat I remember feeling active resentment towards Princess Diana’s death because the news coverage bumped Earthworm Jim.View image in fullscreenCheez TV: ‘I remember sitting there, tinned spaghetti-soaked toastie in hand, gripped by a feeling of meteoric magic and wonder.’Photograph: YouTubeBut in September of 1998 my world was rocked when Jade and Ryan introduced something unlike anything I had ever seen – a Japanese cartoon called Pokémon. I remember sitting there, tinned spaghetti-soaked toastie in hand, gripped by a feeling of meteoric magic and wonder as the opening bars of the theme song rolled over me:“I want to be the very best / like no one ever was.”Yes, I thought,yes! I want that more than anything!But it wouldn’t be long before Pokémania became a moral panic in the Australian media – not so much a kids’ cartoon as a national security threat.View image in fullscreenTsunekazu Ishihara, the chief executive of the Pokémon Company, at the 2025 Gold Gala.Photograph: JC Olivera/Variety/Getty ImagesCelebrating its 30th anniversary this year, Pokémon was created by zinester turned game designerSatoshi Tajiri, developed by his company Game Freak and released in Japan by Nintendo as a sort of swan song for the ageing Game Boy. In Japan, it rapidly transformed from a schoolyard phenomenon to a national one, but it would take two years before it arrived in the west and became as omnipresent asZubats in a dark cave.It crash-landed in Australia via Cheez TV and, within a month of its debut, my life (and an entire generation of lives) revolved around the singular quest to “catch ’em all”.When the Game Boy games hit Australian shelves, they were an instant sensation too, jointly selling more than 400m worldwide.For the uninitiated, these games asked the player to explore a region called Kanto to collect, research and battle an enormous variety of creatures known asPokémon.View image in fullscreenGame Boy Pokémon games sold more than 400m worldwide.Photograph: AlamyI became so immersed in the world they presented – mythical animals and explorable forests and caves – that I felt my sense of what was possible, from my imagination to life itself, actively shift and expand. Pokémonwas beautiful.So of course, my school, the media and Australia at large responded to it like it was a plague devouring the hearts, souls and minds of the nation’s youth.‘Turning our children to witchcraft and violence’“The most popular toy this Christmas could be turning our children to witchcraft and violence,”began a Channel Seven news feature on Pokémon in 1999, citing the concerns ofSunshine Coast pastor Chas Gullo.“It’s short for ‘Pocket Monster,’”opined another Seven news anchor, “and when you discover the cost, it’s not a bad description.”On ABC radio, Mark Colvin warned:“The slogan is ‘gotta catch ’em all’, but many parents would be wondering whether that refers to the characters or the company’s aims for every primary school child in Australia”.He handed over to a reporter who called it “a worldwide craze over a collection of odd-looking creatures. One hundred and fifty-one, to be precise. With names like Pikachu, Meowth and Giber”.View image in fullscreenPikachu mascots.Photograph: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images(There is no Pokémon that goes by the name “Giber”.)The release of the Pokémon Trading Card Game midway through 1999 turned recess and lunch into something resembling the two-up game from Wake in Fright. The trading card game was and is a beast unto itself – a loose adaptation of the video game’s mechanics that also revolves around battling, trading and collecting them all – and Australians spent $11m on the trading cards inthe first two months of their release. They invited lunchbreak drama, which led to school-wide bans.View image in fullscreen‘The release of the Pokémon Trading Card Game … turned recess and lunch into something resembling two-up from Wake in Fright.’Photograph: Mael Ghazi/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesThese bans were met at some schools with protests. At my own, we led a sit-in at the special school assembly to debate the matter, with appointed representatives tasked with explaining the concept of Gengar to our beleaguered principal.How Pokémon Go encouraged me to find wonder in the worldRead moreIn this early wave of media hysteria, which was not contained to Australia, Pokémonwas seen as something between a vice,an addictionand, according to Peta, a past-time thatcould lead to animal abuse and dogfighting. There were reports of robberies, fraud and counterfeit, andold wives’ tales of kids jumping off buildingsbecause they thought they’d evolved into Pidgeotto.Undercutting a lot of these Australian news stories of a“dangerous craze”,however, was the footage that accompanied it: of children playing amicably in large groups, smiling at the camera and excitedly explaining to puzzled journos why Alakazam can easily defeat Machamp, despite the latter’s muscles.Lost in the reactionary responsewas a misunderstanding of its genius: to catch ’em all, you had to interact, befriend and trust your fellow players. Pokémonnot only encouraged community, it required it.View image in fullscreen‘Pokémonnot only encouraged community, it required it.’Photograph: Martin Lelievre/AFP/Getty ImagesPokémon was also my first taste of places and people beyond my own sphere. I remember one of my cousins coming back from Japan with a boxful of Japanese Pokémon cards; a Canadian exchange student swapping US-exclusive toys for rare Yowies; sharing the language of Pokémon with Sri Lankan kids, none of whom spoke English.Young fans knew that Pokémania was not an affliction but a shared, communal experience that linked you to people all over the globe. Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, for me, that made my life in Perth feel a little less isolated.Today Pokémon remains bound up in the national zeitgeist while still attracting controversy:there’s currently a wave of hobby-shop burglaries around the country,sparked by the insane inflation of the value of Pokémon trading cards, which have almost become their own currency –the most valuable of these auction for $16.5m.But despite the earnest wishes of my teachers, parents and the Australian media, Pokémon’s staying power has proved that the kids were right all along. It is now the single largest media franchise in the world, with countless games, media, toys, a new theme park andeven crockery.Pokémonremains at the top of the food chain because of its emphasis on simple joys; it will always be a franchise thatunites peoplebecause it continues to ask one simple question: do you want to have some fun?Explore more on these topicsPokémonGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Olga Soffer obituary | Anthropology | The Guardian
description: Professor of anthropology whose approach to archaeology centred on crafts executed by women 40,000 years ago
Author: Mike Pitts
Headline: Professor of anthropology whose approach to archaeology centred on crafts executed by women 40,000 years ago
Content: Olga Soffer compared Palaeolithic tailoring to ‘something from Donna Karan or Calvin Klein’.Photograph: Bill Wiegand/University of Illinois Urbana-ChampaignView image in fullscreenOlga Soffer compared Palaeolithic tailoring to ‘something from Donna Karan or Calvin Klein’.Photograph: Bill Wiegand/University of Illinois Urbana-ChampaignAnthropologyObituaryOlga Soffer obituaryProfessor of anthropology whose approach to archaeology centred on crafts executed by women 40,000 years agoMike PittsSun 16 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlga Soffer, who has died aged 83, brought a revolutionary idea into the conversation about prehistoric ice age people: women mattered. Inspired when working on archaeological excavations in the former USSR, and by remains from a dig in Moravia, in the 1990s she presented a case for women as makers of textiles, baskets and nets, critical to survival in bleak northern conditions 30,000 years ago.Her achievement was the more remarkable for her career path. By then a professor of anthropology at the University of Illinois, she had obtained her three degrees over three decades, partly while also working as a cosmetics buyer and fashion promoter for a New York department store.Since the 20s, Soviet Russia, looking to historical materialism, generously funded large archaeological excavations. Unlike most of her colleagues in the west, Soffer, whose family had fled Tito’s Yugoslavia and settled in Brooklyn in 1955, could read the reports. In 1977 she began years of travel and research, supported by grants from the US government, the National Geographic Society and many others. Among 30 sites she worked on, four stood out: Mezhyrich, Ukraine; Avdeevo, Russia; and Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov, Moravia (now in Czechia).At such places, people built tent-like houses with mammoth bones. At Mezhyrich, 160 kilometres south of Kyiv, male archaeologists credited the remains to heroic male hunters. To Soffer there were too many mammoths – one house was assembled from 95 jaws. She argued instead that the bones had been collected from natural death sites, while noting that archaeologists had overlooked remains of smaller animals. “Maybe they killed one mammoth every 10 years,”she commented, “and never stopped talking about it.”Already doubting the existence of male-dominated ice age communities, in 1990 she noticed marks in a few tiny clay fragments excavated decades before at Pavlov. She showed them to James Adovasio, an archaeologist at Mercyhurst College, Pennsylvania, who had been digging with her at Mezhyrich, and who knew about basketry and textiles. He recognised impressions of woven threads. They went on to identify 79 such marks among thousands of clay scraps, from Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov, with explosive implications.Adovasio saw evidence, fortuitously imprinted in clay, for cordage, plaited basketry and woven textiles, made from plants, not animal sinews or hides. Soffer found indications of dress and headgear, previously overlooked in favour of attention to breasts and buttocks (characterised by Soffer as “paleoerotica”), on small female figurines, many of which were found at Avdeevo (carved from mammoth ivory and stone) and Dolní Věstonice (ceramic), similar to the Venuses of Willendorf, west of Vienna, and Kostenki, south of Voronezh, in Russia. Sofferlater wrotethat the head of the Willendorf figurine offered the clearest depiction of a fibre-based woven cap or hat, “rather than a hairdo, as posited by scholars”.View image in fullscreenThe Venus of Willendorf, with a fibre-based woven cap or hat, ‘rather than a hairdo, as posited by scholars’.Photograph: Heritage Image Partnership Ltd/AlamyWith Adovasio and his colleague David Hyland, Soffer conjured a world featuring mats, wall hangings, blankets and bags, shawls, shirts, skirts and sashes. Knotted string suggested nets, used by women to hunt small animals. She compared Palaeolithic tailoring to“something from Donna Karan or Calvin Klein”. A figurine’s beaded string item was a “skirt … to die for”. “We’re not talking protection from the elements here,” she told the New York Times.The sophistication of the weaving and cord-making prompted Adovasio to suggest a history that went back at least 40,000 years. Noting more recent practices, they believed the crafts would have been invented and executed by women.In 2007 Soffer and Adovasio co-authored, with the science writer Jake Page, The Invisible Sex: Uncovering the True Roles of Women in Prehistory, in which they addressed a perceived male bias. It was widely reported, but the public narrative of ice age life was led byJean Auel, whose multi-million-selling Earth’s Children novel series was to end in 2011. Soffer was consulted on two titles (The Mammoth Hunters and The Plains of Passage), but the protagonist Ayla, a blond, blue-eyed modern human who challenges the patriarchal world of Neanderthals, nonetheless wears animal skins. Soffer’s wider message, that what survives from the ancient past is a tiny and often misleading representation of reality, has yet to be absorbed, even by many archaeologists.Olga was born in Nazi-occupied Belgrade. As an infant she was taken with her maternal grandparents to a labour camp: she was treated favourably by the camp commander, she was told, due to her Aryan colouring and looks.Her parents, Galina (nee Girs) and Alexander Shabunin, came from Russian migrant families scattered after the 1917 Bolshevik revolution. In New York, reached via Yugoslavia and four years in a displaced persons camp in Italy, her father assembled window blinds and her mother worked as a seamstress, while Olga went to Thomas Jefferson high school in Brooklyn.After obtaining a BA in political science (1965) at Hunter College, City University of New York, she began working at Abraham & Straus, a Brooklyn-based department store chain, first as an assistant buyer for cosmetics, then special events coordinator for fashion. In the latter role she created a gourmet festival featuring the television chef James Beard, and hired a young Brooke Shields as a model.Bored with work, she took night courses in art history at Hunter, which led to an interest in archaeology and ethnography, and her eventual MA in anthropology there (1975).In 1978, having gone part-time at the store, she became an adjunct instructor of anthropology at Hunter, moving to Lehman College, then the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee. After a PhD on the archaeology of eastern Europe at the Graduate Center, City University of New York (1984), Soffer joined the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as assistant professor of anthropology. She rose to professor, with stints as visiting archaeology professor at the Centre de Recherches Archéologiques, France (1992), and heading the department of Slavic languages and literature at Illinois (1993–98). She retired in 2008 as professor emerita. Her awards included an honorary doctorate from the Russian Academy of Sciences.Both her marriages, to Mark Soffer, a history teacher, in 1962, and Dmitry Bobyshev, a poet and professor of Russian literature, in 1979, ended in divorce. She is survived by her daughter from her first marriage, Alex, and two grandchildren, Jake and Mena.Olga Soffer, archaeologist, born 9 September 1942; died 20 June 2026Explore more on these topicsAnthropologyAnthropology and archaeologyArchaeologyobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Joy in Hollywood as historic Cinerama dome to reopen: ‘People still want to go to the movies’ | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Sony Pictures in July announced that the celebrated theater, built in 1963 and shuttered during Covid, will reopen in 2028
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Sony Pictures in July announced that the celebrated theater, built in 1963 and shuttered during Covid, will reopen in 2028
Content: The Cinerama dome featuring Despicable Me characters in Los Angeles, California, on 30 June 2015.Photograph: Jim Steinfeldt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Cinerama dome featuring Despicable Me characters in Los Angeles, California, on 30 June 2015.Photograph: Jim Steinfeldt/Getty ImagesLos AngelesJoy in Hollywood as historic Cinerama dome to reopen: ‘People still want to go to the movies’Sony Pictures in July announced that the celebrated theater, built in 1963 and shuttered during Covid, will reopen in 2028Matthew Cantorin Los AngelesSun 16 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrive down Sunset Boulevard inLos Angeles, along the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and you’ll see a movie theater straight out of The Jetsons.Built in 1963, the Cinerama dome is instantly memorable: a white,geodesic construction that looks like a giant golf ball cut in half and plopped down in the middle of the city.In recent years, however, it’s served as a sad memorial to better times in the movie business – the cinema closed in 2020, with no certainty that it would ever open again.This summer, things finally changed. Sony Pictures in July announced that the Cinerama dome would reopen in 2028, thanks to a new agreement with its owners. It’s great news for cinephiles, as well as fans of LA architecture; the building was designated as ahistoric cultural monument in 1998.The closed Cinerama dome “has become a symbol of everything that went wrong during Covid”, says Adrian Scott Fine, president and CEO of the LA Conservancy. “To have this come back is really, really good news,” he adds, saying it’s perhaps an indicator that LA is “getting back to where it once was”.The reopening comes amid more good news for the movie industry: between blockbuster successes like The Odyssey and tiny-budget hits like Obsession, cinemas are experiencing their biggest year since before the pandemic. Is the Cinerama dome’s reopening a hopeful sign of the times?The fight to save the domeThe story of the cinema’s fall and rise tracks the story of filmgoing in recent years. Like movie theaters across the US, the dome closed as Covid took hold; unlike many of those theaters, it never reopened. That felt like a tragedy to many Angelenos, who inundated the conservancy with calls asking about its future.The original films presented in the Cinerama widescreen format featuredthree projectors and a curved screenfor immersive viewing. Many cinemas were adapted to show the movies, but the dome,constructed of 316 concrete hexagons and pentagons, was purpose-built for the Cinerama experience. “There’s nothing else like it in the world,” says Fine. “Every Angeleno loves this building.”Among them is Benjamin Steinberg, a 26-year-old film-maker and activist who led the push for reopening. “I think it’s one of the most important movie theaters in the world, and to have it sitting abandoned for over literally five years and zero contact from the owners was extremely frustrating,” Steinberg says.He created a petition to save the dome “within five minutes” of hearing the closure would be permanent. The petition, directed at the cinema’s owners, the Decurion Corporation, quickly gottens of thousands of signatures– to little effect. Steinberg eventually opted for more aggressive tactics, including rallies outside the theater and, finally, projecting pictures of the owners on to the side of the dome in April. “That went extremely viral,” he said. It alsoresulted in a police response.After apublic hearinga few weeks later, Sony announced the deal.View image in fullscreenThe Cinerama dome, on 13 April 2021.Photograph: Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images“Hot damn! We’re bringing the Dome back, baby,” said Tom Rothman, the CEO of Sony Pictures,in a statement on 22 July. “We believe in moviegoing down to our soul, and no venue on earth stands more for that than the one-of-a-kind Dome.”Under the new arrangement, Alamo Drafthouse – a dine-in theater chain Sony Pictures bought in 2024 – will operate the venue. Sony plans to maintain its historic feel and its name, which comes from the film technology it was originally built to show.Since the Cinerama technology faded in the 1960s, the dome has shown traditional films on a curved screen, which will remain in use at the 956-seat, single-screen movie palace. Meanwhile, in good news forElijah Woodand others infuriated byAlamo’s recent policyrequiring patrons to order food on their phones, the dome will offer traditional concessions rather than meals. (Reopened screens next door will be dine-in theaters.)The Cinerama dome is one of several LA theaters that have lately been rescued. The Westwood Village theater, built in 1930, closed in 2024 but will reopen in 2027 after a collective of directors, including Jason Reitman, Steven Spielberg and Guillermo del Toro, purchased it. The nearby Bruin theater, which closed the same year,is expected to reopenin the autumn.Kristen Stewart recently purchasedthe century-old Highland Park theater.View image in fullscreenThe Highland Park theater in Highland Park, California, on 3 October 2019.Photograph: Araya Doheny/Getty Images“This is a town that’s very passionate about their favorite movie theaters and root for them like baseball teams, and they’re happy to see an old favorite come back,” says Amy Nicholson, film critic for the Los Angeles Times.Signs of resurgence – but struggles remainIt all comes amid a hopeful year for filmgoing.The pandemic “was the most serious gut punch that the industry had seen”, says Jason Squire, host of the Movie Business Podcast and professor emeritus at the University of Southern California’s school of cinematic arts, saying it had been more transformative for cinema “than the coming of sound”.But on Tuesday, the summerbox office hit $4bnfor only the second time since 2020 – the previous mark was in 2023, fueled by the “Barbenheimer” phenomenon, and this time the milestone has come weeks earlier. Revenues areexpected to reach $10bnfor the year for the first time since Covid hit, according to Variety.“It’s been a fabulous summer, and all movie lovers and all executives are celebrating the fact that people have not stayed at home on their couch,” says Squire. “Every couple of years, there are stories about the demise and death of movie theaters, and it’s just not a valid assumption.”What, exactly, is driving the apparent resurgence? Critics and analysts have a number of theories, beginning with the quality of the films themselves. “It’s been a year that I, as a critic, have been looking forward to a long time,” says Nicholson. “The year that Hollywood finally starts to trust in younger film-makers and younger audiences enough to pass them the camera.”View image in fullscreenMoviegoers buy tickets from the box office at the Regal theater in Los Angeles, California, on 21 April 2017.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThat was most evident in horror films like Obsession and Backrooms, both of which were directed by twentysomethings. “We have a generation of talent that is growing up learning how to not only write, direct and edit their own shorts, but they’ve also learned by posting them online and getting instant feedback on what audiences like,” Nicholson says.Maybe it’s working: younger audiences are today’s biggest filmgoers, according to arecent Fandango study, which found that 87% of gen Zers and 82% of millennials had gone to the movies in the past year, versus 70% of gen Xers and 58% of baby boomers.Social platforms like TikTok andLetterboxd, the app where users share their own film reviews, are also driving a “culture of moviegoing” among younger people, says Carlos Aguilar, an LA-based film critic. “People want to watch the movie that everyone’s talking about, whether it’s an Obsession or The Odyssey,” Aguilar says.That communal experience may be key, especially at a time when daily life feels incredibly expensive. “I think about the Great Depression and how that was one of the belle epoques of cinema, because people needed hope and a place to go because the economy was in crisis,” says Beandrea July, a critic, culture writer and host of the culture podcastAnnotations. “I think many people are feeling the crunch of inflation, of there not being enough work, of wages being stagnant, and movies provide an escape from that.”The rosy box office news comes with a bit of cognitive dissonance: while it’s a good year for filmgoers in LA, times remain difficult for the people making those movies. Box office figures are “only one indicator” of the industry’s health, July says. “I work with a lot of different film-makers, mostly independent film-makers, and it’s just been extremely tough for even really celebrated, Oscar-nominated film-makers to get their films made,” July says.That’s in part because studio gatekeepers are often risk-averse, preferring to invest in a sure bet like The Odyssey over an independent film. Meanwhile, much production has moved elsewhere, fora number of reasonsincluding the cost of shooting in LA, tax incentives in other cities, regulatory challenges and the simple fact that technology has made it easier to work anywhere. Shooting days in LAfell 20%from early 2024 to early 2025.But some critics see reason for hope in a shifting industry, pointing, for instance, to thesuccess of Obsession, made for $750,000, compared with The Odyssey’s $250m. As of Tuesday, Obsession had grossed more than $263m worldwide, according to Box Office Mojo.“I do think that we’re in a time where all the common wisdom about what it takes to make a successful movie is over,” Nicholson says. “The idea that you need to have a gigantic production budget with a ton of special effects, I think that’s ending. I think the idea that you have to have one of this small group of 30 movie stars to open a movie, that’s ending too.”Still, she says, “it’s going to take studios a long time to trust the idea that audiences will show up for good stories”. Film, Aguilar notes, remains a “gate-kept art form”.Despite the industry’s struggles, LA remains a city of cinephiles where those audiences do show up.“As much as people want to believe or think that movie theaters are on the way out, they continue to challenge that,” Aguilar says, referring to cinephiles. “Even if we have all the streaming and access to content all the time, people still want to go to the movies.”Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesWest CoastCaliforniafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kindness of strangers: The day of my mum’s funeral, the saleswoman at the stationery store made me feel less alone | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Because I’d visited so often to print things, she made me feel that someone had witnessed the journey I was on, all the way through to its difficult conclusion
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: Because I’d visited so often to print things, she made me feel that someone had witnessed the journey I was on, all the way through to its difficult conclusion
Content: Illustration: Alamy/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alamy/Guardian DesignKindness of strangersAustralian lifestyleKindness of strangers: The day of my mum’s funeral, the saleswoman at the stationery store made me feel less aloneBecause I’d visited so often to print things, she made me feel that someone had witnessed the journey I was on, all the way through to its difficult conclusionRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesHelen as told toKatie CunninghamSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 18.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMum’s disease progressed slowly at first, and then in a really big rush. After years of battling early onset Parkinson’s, in 2015 we were suddenly told she only had six months left.I was living in Brisbane, Australia, and Mum was in a care home 600km away in Taree, so I began flying down every second weekend to visit. At the time, it was still common to print out your boarding pass – or at least, it was for me; I was a bit late to the tech game.So every weekend I visited, I’d go to the local Officeworks to print my pass for the flight home. Every time, I was served by the same person, a friendly lady who asked why I was flying down so often. I told her what was going on. Whenever I saw her, she’d enquire about how Mum was going and we’d have a nice chat.When Mum became really ill, I drove down and stayed with her for a month until she passed, one terrible day two weeks after Christmas. The day of her funeral, on our way to the chapel, I went to Officeworks to print out the eulogy I had written. It had been a really dry summer but that day the skies ripped open and it was pouring down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKindness of strangers: Leo drove us home in a blizzard, and his parting words have stayed with meRead moreAgain, I was served by the same lady. When I told her what I needed to print, she came out from behind the counter and gave me a huge hug – a long, proper chest-to-chest embrace that wrapped me up and held me close. Then, because I didn’t have an umbrella, she insisted I take one off the shelf for free.That was the last time I went to Officeworks Taree, so I never saw that woman again, but I will always remember her care and support. Flying up and down every fortnight by myself had been an isolating experience. She made me feel that someone had witnessed the journey I was on, all the way through to its difficult conclusion. She made me feel less alone.I noticed in losing my mum how many people get awkward around grief. They don’t know what to say, or how to sit with it. This woman didn’t shy away from it at all. She could have stayed behind her register and offered me condolences. Instead, she came right around that counter and squeezed me tight. Her warm hug made me feel as if I could face the day.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.What is your name?Where do you live (city, state and country)?Tell us a bit about the kind act you've experienced?Where and when did this encounter take place?Can we publish your response?Yes, entirelyYes, but contact me firstYes, but please keep me anonymousNo, this is information onlyAre you comfortable with a journalist contacting you about this story for potential publication?YesNoWhat is your phone number?OptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. title: Which plants will survive and can I use grey water? Gardening as UK summers get drier  | Gardens | The Guardian
description: As parts of Beth Chatto’s visionary drought-tolerant gardens in Essex turn brown, the head gardener offers advice
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: As parts of Beth Chatto’s visionary drought-tolerant gardens in Essex turn brown, the head gardener offers advice
Content: Giant scabiosa at the Beth Chatto Gardens south of Clacton in Essex, the UK’s driest county.Photograph: Lisa O'CarrollView image in fullscreenGiant scabiosa at the Beth Chatto Gardens south of Clacton in Essex, the UK’s driest county.Photograph: Lisa O'CarrollGardensWhich plants will survive and can I use grey water? Gardening as UK summers get drierAs parts of Beth Chatto’s visionary drought-tolerant gardens in Essex turn brown, the head gardener offers adviceLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHer debut book, in 1978, was titled The Dry Garden. Since then, the late Beth Chatto createda rich legacywith her expertise as a plantswoman and by setting up one of the oldest unwatered public gardens in England.Once a car park but transformed in 1992 into an experiment to test what plants were drought-tolerant inEssex, the driest county in the UK, Chatto’s gravel gardens south of Clacton are being visibly tested this year.Desiccated and brown foliage carpets are a sorry sight in parts of the gardens greeting visitors familiar with bursts of Mediterranean colour in rockeries and beds.Dry, cracked soil, stunted growth and dead or dying plants are familiar to everyone in northern Europe this harsh summer, and particularly in southern England, where there has beenzero or low rainfallsince the middle of June.View image in fullscreenChatto pioneered the ‘right plant, right place’ concept in her garden in Essex but took a particular interest in dry gardening.Photograph: Beth Chatto GardensBut what lessons are being learned that can help gardeners respond as the UK suffers worsening climate crisis-driven heatwaves each summer?First, says the head gardener at Beth ChattoGardens, Malin Andersson, observe what is going on. Stunted growth, lack of flowering, leaf drop and leaf curls do not necessarily mean a plant is dead. It might be using mechanisms to cope with the stress not just of the direct sun, but the unrelenting heat that increases transpiration from leaves and evaporation of watered soil.“That stunted growth and the premature leaf drop on trees and shrubs or leaves curling up or just shrivelling is a sign of stress. They do it to protect themselves. They drop the leaves because they can’t supply them with water and then hopefully, when we eventually get water, they’ll recover,” she says.Chatto pioneered the “right plant, right place” motto of all good gardening, and the tried and tested drought performers are here in abundance: euphorbia, Gaura lindheimeri (now renamedOenothera lindheimeri), lavender, origanum and even roses, whose deep roots can reach lower water tables.View image in fullscreenAndersson says switching to Mediterranean plants may not be the answer as UK winters may be wetter.Photograph: Beth Chatto GardensBut switching to Mediterranean plants may not future-proof British gardens in climate breakdown. “We don’t know whether this is the new normal or not. It’s so unpredictable because we just had a really wet winter, so if everyone goes for the Mediterranean free-draining plants, or the ones that want free-draining conditions, then if you get a really wet winter, they might rot off,” she says.The last time the gardens endured zero rainfall in July was in 2022, but a blackboard charting rainfall at the entrance to the gardens underlines her point: this January the garden had 177mm of rain, compared with 19mm in 2022.View image in fullscreenA board charting rainfall at the gardens over the last four years, showing there was no rain in July.Photograph: Beth Chatto GardensAt Beth Chatto, the gardeners cut back the damaged areas on some plants after observing what worked, and kept others with their roots in shade. “We know that almost every year, we can give things a hard cut in the middle of summer and then expect it to maybe come back again or even flower again later in the summer,” Andersson says.But this year, she says plants “haven’t really come back”. They won’t discard plants, however, because they are hoping the roots will survive into next year.While many plants, including hydrangea, are not flowering in shade this year as they would normally, others are still going – albeit stunted in size.So which plants have weathered this record drought at Beth Chatto?View image in fullscreenBlue trumpet flowers of the hardy deciduous agapanthus ‘Northern Star’.Photograph: John Richmond/AlamyLily of the Nile(agapanthus)Flowers may be smaller but this South African adores the sun – six to eight hours a day, ideally – and their fleshy leaves and rhizome roots help retain moisture.View image in fullscreenCalifornia fuchsia surviving and thriving at Beth Chatto Gardens.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollCalifornia fuchsia(Epilobium canum ‘Dublin’)The tangerine trumpet-shaped flowers of California fuchsia are star performers at Beth Chatto, popping out from the browny foliage of plants less able to cope with the sun and heat.View image in fullscreenHeatwave survivor: Althaea cannabina.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollPalm-leafmarshmallow(Althaea cannabina)A tall upright plant related to hollyhock with simple pink flowers that last right through even the hottest summers.View image in fullscreenThe Russian sage is growing majestically at Beth Chatto.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollRussiansage(perovskia, renamed Salvia yangii)One of the wonders of the heatwave, still producing its lavender-coloured spikes in municipal gardens throughout the country.View image in fullscreenCatmint thrives in this year’s heatwave, but cats also love to sit in it.Photograph: Zoonar GmbH/AlamyCatmint(nepeta)This, too, is thriving at Beth Chatto. But cats also love to sit in it and nibble at it, so it might be an idea to plant one or two extra as sacrificial plants.View image in fullscreenSpanish broom, offering a swathe of bright yellow flowers at height.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollSpanishbroom(Spartium junceum)A tall shrub with dark stems and sheaths of yellow fragrant flowers reminiscent of gorse, it is native to the Mediterranean and is unsurprisingly towering majestically among its weaker brethren.Grasses have become more prevalent in gardening in the last 10 years, partly down to the new perennial movement pioneered by the Dutch designers Piet Oudolf and Henk Gerritsen.View image in fullscreenGrasses earning their keep in the Beth Chatto gravel garden.Photograph: Julie SkeltonMexican feather grass(Stipa tenuissima)A short tufty sheaf of grass, greenish at the bottom and fading to golden, they encircle some of the borders.View image in fullscreenStipa gigantea towering over the beds at Beth Chatto.Photograph: Julie SkeltonGiant feather grass(Stipa gigantea)Its tall upright arches dancing in the breeze are also earning their keep towering over swathes of what look like scorched beds.Calamagrostis grasses are also working hard, with the tall tufts offering movement with just as much interest as colour in a dry garden.View image in fullscreenGiant scabious, almost 2 metres tall, at Beth Chatto.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollGiant scabious(Cephalaria gigantea)Also paying their bills are these tall yellow upright flowers, cousins of the more common blue scabiosa found in the wild as well as in horticulture.And the ones struggling?View image in fullscreenHeatwave just-about survivor: elephant ears curling in the heat at Beth Chatto.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollDrifts of elephant ears (bergenia) in the parts of the gravel garden most exposed to the harsh sun are struggling, browned or dying.“I’ve never seen them do this before. They are usually good in drought because their waxy leaves tend to hold on to water. They are looking quite sad, but that’s not one we would cut, as we think that might come back,” says Andersson.WateringView image in fullscreenPeople are advised to use washing-up water for garden plants during the UK summer drought.Photograph: Gillian Pullinger/AlamyWithhosepipe bansacross much of the England, watering also becomes a challenge, with experts urging people to use grey water – water from showers, baths and dishwashing.Some recommend bringing a plastic bowl to the shower to catch the water before it warms up.TheRoyal Horticultural Society(RHS) says soil and potting composts are effective at filtering out the soap and detergent, but warns that to minimise bacterial growth you should only save grey water for 24 hours.‘Lawns don’t need watering!’ How to garden in a heatwave, from recycling bathwater to making the most of shadeRead moreNicholas Cryer, the senior water scientist at the RHS, said: “With prolonged drought becoming an ever more frequent feature of British summers, we must learn to manage water more efficiently. The estimated 60 litres of grey water produced per person within the home each day can be recycled in our gardens, reducing demand on mains water.“Plants can be safely watered with shower, bath, kitchen and washing-machine water. While gardeners should avoid using water containing bleach, disinfectants, dishwasher salt or harsh cleaners, soil and potting composts are effective at filtering out small amounts of soap and detergent, and RHS research indicates that when used over short periods, these residues do not significantly affect the function of many common garden plants.”Cryer added: “Grey water should not be used on edible salad crops, but it is a suitable choice for ornamental plants.”Explore more on these topicsGardensDroughtGardening advicePlantsExtreme heatWaterClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kinz, London W11: ‘No bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Home cooking, but in the most complimentary sense
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Home cooking, but in the most complimentary sense
Content: Kinz, London W11: ‘There’s something cinematic about this elegant setting.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKinz, London W11: ‘There’s something cinematic about this elegant setting.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewKinz, London W11: ‘No bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride’ – restaurant reviewHome cooking, but in the most complimentary senseGrace DentSun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome developers would rip the soul out of a 1930s banking hall, butKinz, a new all-day Lebanese brasserie housed in a former Lloyds Bank in Notting Hill, instead makes a feature of its chunky vault door. Where W11 residents once kept their cash, diners can now take a seat and sip Lebanese wine from theBekaa valley. After all, what visit to the bank wouldn’t be improved by a cold glass ofChateau Musar Jeune?This triple-height room with mezzanine seating is a very different proposition from all those tiny, homespun Lebanese restaurants typically anchored around Edgware Road since the 1970s. Kinz may offerkibbehnayyeh(finely minced raw lamb and beef with bulgur, spices and pine nuts),shish barak(tiny lamb and herb dumplings in yoghurt sauce) andwarak enab(lamb-stuffed vine leaves and baby courgettes), as do many places in pockets across west London, but there is something altogether more cinematic about this elegant setting.I sat with my pot of mint tea thinking that the place has all the hallmarks of a 1980s Duran Duran video, in which the boys pitch up somewhere sophisticated in Lebanon for mysterious hijinks. Kinz’s mezzanine seems almost built forJohn Taylorto sip ababunajnegroni (Hayman’s gin,Lillet Blanc,Suzeand chamomile) under his tousled fringe. Large-format photographs of Lebanese life line the walls, including one of an impressive matriarch on a visit to the hair salon.View image in fullscreen‘Home cooking in the most complimentary sense’: Kinz’s spiced chicken with rice.Even so, Kinz is far from showy – in fact, it feels a bit like an upmarket but still everyday Lebanese canteen. Pop in for a plate of spinachfatayerand end up staying for the Sunday specialmolokhiye–slow-simmered jute mallow with chicken, rice, pitta and a sharp, mignonette-style sauce.Fans of Akub,the well-loved modern Palestinian restaurantjust a few streets away, may well recognise the name of that formidable restaurateur,Rasha Khouri Bruzzo. Here, she has joined forces with brothers Jad and Karim Lahoud, both Londoners raised by Lebanese chef parents. The result is a deeply personal space, where the chocolate cake is the Lahouds’ mother Elene’s recipe – she’s even been known to turn up in the kitchen of a morning simply to test that this gooey, dark chocolate sponge is up to her standards.The vibe across much of the menu, meanwhile, is elegant sparseness: nothing is over-garnished or served with frippery. Mint tea comes in tiny, functional, stainless-steel pots. Cheeserikakat(filo pastry cigars) arrive on a plain plate looking for all the world like M&S party food … until you bite in and find them hot, crisp and delicately seasoned with fresh mint. I reckon I could eat at least 17 of these things in one sitting. It would not be pretty, but it would be a testament to their beige deliciousness.View image in fullscreen‘I could eat at least 17 of these in one sitting’: Kinz’s cheeserikakat.Rich hummus comes topped with tahini, with the option of adding pine nuts orawarma, a spiced, slow-cooked minced lamb. There isbaba ganoush, obviously, but alsomoutabal,or smoky chargrilled aubergine with tahini. Cod fillets come with walnuts and tahini sauce. All are understated, yet effective: no bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride and an urge to be accurate.The staff are a genuine delight – warm, knowledgable, unhurried – and the food is definitely decent. You might even mistake thefattetaubergine, baked in tomato sauce and served on yoghurt with broken toasted pitta, for parmigiana, but they are very different beasts. Parmigiana is rich, oily, cheesy and baked into submission. Fattet, however, which in Arabic means “crumbs”, is built on crisp bread soaked in yoghurt, and as a result is much lighter, sharper and altogether more refreshing.View image in fullscreen‘Light, sharp and refreshing’: Kinz’sfattetaubergine.The slow-cooked spiced chicken with rice is a standout: home cooking in the most complimentary sense, with properly stewed bird, roast almonds, a sharp sourness running through the rice, and a rich gravy served from a long-handled, copper-coloured pan.For pudding, we orderedosmalieyeh, or crispkataifi pastrylayered withashtaclotted cream and orange blossom syrup, which is delicate, not over-sweet and a gentle way to end. But it is Elene’s chocolate cake that is the real star of the dessert show: dense, dark, damp and oozing. We even ordered a second piece to take home, complete with specific instructions not to refrigerate it or Elene would be cross. I’ve never met the woman, but I was suitably chastened.Kinz was busy as heck on the lunchtime we visited, and it’s plain to see why. I’ve been recommending it to anyone with a large group to feed in west London. There is a very real sense that this re-loved bank and its new inhabitants are here to stay. Kinz will get my trade any time I’m passing – and I willalwaysorder that chocolate cake.View image in fullscreenKinz’sosmalieyehpudding is ‘delicate, not over-sweet and a gentle way to end a meal’.Kinz50 Notting Hill Gate, London W11, 020-4637 5068. Open all week, noon-11pm (midnight Fri & Sat). From about £40 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make quesadillas – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A cook-your-own adventure meal, with all manner of fillings and servings to explore
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: A cook-your-own adventure meal, with all manner of fillings and servings to explore
Content: Felicity Cloake’s quesadillas.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Johnny Bentham.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s quesadillas.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Johnny Bentham.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make quesadillas – recipeA cook-your-own adventure meal, with all manner of fillings and servings to exploreFelicity CloakeSun 16 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Mexican equivalent of a cheese toastie, but even quicker to make, these are the perfect summer holiday or weekend lunch, because everyone can choose their own fillings and help cook. Plus, this recipe is just a jumping-off point – once you’ve mastered the method, you can fill them with anything you like … grated chocolate and mashed banana are pretty good!Prep5 minCook4 min eachMakes880g blockcookingmozzarella50g halloumi, or mild cheddar, monterey jack or havarti, grated2 fresh green jalapeños, cut into rounds or a jar of them (optional, see step 4)Oil, to grease8 corn or flour tortillas, about 15cm in width1 tsp dried epazote or oregano, preferably Mexican (optional)To serveTomato salsaIceberg lettuce, shreddedAvocado, cubed or slicedBlack beansSoured creamView image in fullscreen1 Choosing your cheesesYou need something that melts well, and cooking mozzarella – the kind that comes in big rectangular blocks – is ideal (the kind that comes in balls is a bit too wet). You could just use all mozzarella, but I like to mix it with something with a bit more flavour, like a mild cheddar, or salty halloumi.2 Weigh out and grate the cheeseIt doesn’t have to be precisely the amount I’ve suggested, and you might like to add more of one than the other. Use the coarse side of a grater to shred both cheeses (unless they’re already grated, of course). Put the cheese in a bowl and stir until well combined.3 Prep the jalapeños …View image in fullscreenIf you like chilli, then carefully cut the jalapeños into thin rings. Use a knife, or a teaspoon to scoop out any seeds from the middle. Make sure you wash your hands well after touching them, and don’t rub your eyes or any bits of skin while you’re doing this!4 … unless you’re chilli-averseIf you don’t like chillies, there are lots of other things you can put in instead eg bite-size pieces of pepper, cherry tomatoes cut in half with the seeds scooped out, drained tinned sweetcorn, cubes of cooked potatoes or squash, finely chopped broccoli, defrosted spinach with all the water squeezed out, cooked chorizo, shredded ham or chicken etc … even pineapple!5 Ready your panBrush the base of a heavy frying pan with very little oil; just enough to make the inside look a bit darker, but not so much that it moves around when you tip the pan. Put on a medium-low heat and leave to heat up for about two minutes.View image in fullscreen6 Load up your tortillasLay a tortilla into the pan; look for the slightly smaller ones, about 15cm in diameter because they’re easier to fold. Sprinkle with about two generous tablespoons of the cheese (but don’t go right up to the edge, leave a gap) and then add a scattering of any extra ingredients and the dried herbs, if you’re using them.7 Cook the quesadillasWhen the cheese begins to melt, use a spatula to carefully fold the tortilla in half so the cheese is now on the inside; it will be hot. Press down around the edge with the spatula to help seal it. (Alternatively you can just add another tortilla on top if that feels easier.)View image in fullscreen8 Get them goldenContinue to cook until, when you carefully lift up the tortilla to look underneath, it’s golden on the bottom, then turn it over and cook until golden on the other side. Eat them as soon as they’re cool enough; I like them with tomato salsa , shredded iceberg lettuce, avocado, black beans and soured cream.9 (Maybe) make your own salsaWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appTo make an easy tomato salsa, carefully cut a quarter of a small red onion into little pieces. Put in a bowl and squeeze over the juice of half a lime. Chop four medium tomatoes, or eight cherry tomatoes and add to the bowl. Roughly chop a small bunch of coriander, if you like it, and stir in too.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassMexican food and drinkCheeseHerbs and spicesBreadVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘Sex was our glue – now if we fight, we can’t just screw and come out glowing’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Pam and Mike couldn’t keep their hands off each other when they met. But as aging and biology have taken their toll, their sex life has suffered
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: Pam and Mike couldn’t keep their hands off each other when they met. But as aging and biology have taken their toll, their sex life has suffered
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘Sex was our glue – now if we fight, we can’t just screw and come out glowing’Pam and Mike couldn’t keep their hands off each other when they met. But as aging and biology have taken their toll, their sex life has sufferedHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toOlivia LadanyiSun 16 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePam, 69double quotation markWe haven’t had sex in two years. Mike says it’s because his dick is deadWhen I first spotted Mike across a crowded hookah bar, I was gobsmacked. His hair was wild and his clothes were crazy. He was exactly my type. Our relationship was built on that initial attraction, and it’s still there, but we haven’t had sex in two years. Mike says it’s because his dick is dead. Sometimes that makes me feel insecure, and I tell him: “You just don’t think I’m beautiful anymore”.In our late 50s/early 60s, we were at it like rabbits. Once, on a hike, we were making out and a young couple came up to us to say they thought it was beautiful. I think it gave them hope that we can all hold on to that side of ourself as we age.I’ve internalised society’s expectations of me as an “older woman”. Society desexualises you and you absorb that. Mike and I stopped prioritising sex until it eventually fell off the table: four days without it became two weeks; two weeks became six months. You can see it happening, but you stop talking about it because it feels too shameful. Then before you know it, it’s been two years.double quotation markI’m going to find something sexy to wear to Burning Man, where everything pulses with sexWithout sex, every touch is more meaningful. Because it’s not a prelude, it is the thing. But sex was once our glue – if we were in a fight, we’d have sex and get over it. Now we can’t just screw and come out the other side glowing, we have to work harder at our relationship.Sex made me softer, and I liked that side of myself. Without it, my exterior is harder.Sexbrought out my playful, imaginative side. I miss that. I’m thinking about how I can reclaim those parts of myself – I used to put on Marvin Gaye, wear a sexy outfit and dance for Mike. Who told me I had to give that up?I’m going to find something sexy to wear to Burning Man this year, where everything pulses with sex and Mike is more attracted to me. Maybe we’ll get our mojo back then. When Mike tells me my ass looks great or he licks me on the cheek, I feel wanted – it tells me that I’m still a vibrant, attractive, sexy woman. I want to hold on to that for as long as I can.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreMike, 71double quotation markViagra can give me an erection but it can’t give me desireWhen I met Pam 11 years ago, I was going through a divorce and had been celibate for five years. We hit it off instantly. I liked everything about her: she was cute, smart and fun to be around. We couldn’t keep our hands off each other. I’d grab her ass or kiss her whenever she walked past, and we had sex several times a day.That sexual connection kept us together in the beginning. But now my dick is dead, we don’t have sex any more, which is a sad thing to say out loud. I wish it hadn’t fallen off a cliff, but maybe we’re not meant to have sex at this age. Viagra can give me an erection but it can’t give me desire. My brain just isn’t connected to my penis the way it used to be.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThe last time we had sex, I thought to myself: this isn’t fun any moreThe last time we had sex, I struggled to stay hard and it was painful for Pam. I thought to myself: this isn’t fun any more. It’s difficult to feel sexual when you’re hurting your partner. And sex can’t be spontaneous any more – for me to be hard enough and Pam to be wet enough, now it has to be planned with lube and Viagra.This is how we do it: ‘I could have sex every day, but he says no about 80% of the time’Read moreI still desire Pam but I don’t show it any more. Sometimes I think about going up to her and giving her a hug, but something stops me. Maybe it’s laziness. I’d like Pam to touch me more. It doesn’t have to be a sexual touch – just anything that says she wants me.Without sex, the intimacy has gone. And without intimacy, the relationship feels difficult. I always seem to be pissing her off, and she doesn’t think I’m as funny. We give each other pecks on the cheek and a kiss goodnight, but we don’t fool around or even kiss properly (a real spit-swapping kiss).I feel as if I’m letting Pam down by not keeping my end of the bargain. I’d like us to have sex again, maybe we’ll try at Burning Man. But even if that doesn’t happen, I hope we can find other ways to feel close.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I haven’t dated for years and want to try again. How do I prepare for the storm? | Family | The Guardian
description: Do you really want to date, or do you just feel you should? Be kind to yourself, and maybe try real-world dating and avoid the apps for now
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Do you really want to date, or do you just feel you should? Be kind to yourself, and maybe try real-world dating and avoid the apps for now
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyI haven’t dated for years and want to try again. How do I prepare for the storm?Do you really want to date, or do you just feel you should? Be kind to yourself, and maybe try real-world dating and avoid the apps for nowAnnalisa BarbieriSun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 05.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI haven’t been on a date in eight yearsandwant to startnext year. How can I prepare for the storm?I want to love and care forsomeone. I long for a supportive, funny life partner. Should I say that to a man?And is that too much in a dating profile?I vowed off relationships until I couldpermanentlyfix my anxiety.An expat temporarily settled in Singapore,I’m still making friendsand feel nervous around unfamiliar people.I am embarrassed that I’m a broke writer andstudent. I love what I do, but many Singaporeans arecareer-focused.How can I restart dating in the most emotionally supportive way? How do I stay brave when the lightning strikes?The question to ask is if you reallywantto date or feel youshould? I wonder why this feels like a huge deal to you: the abstaining until things are “just right”, saying you’ll date “next year”. We often do this if we’re not ready for something but feel we should be. Dating, like any relationships beyond childhood, is most successful when one feels comfortable in oneself, so the relationship becomes an addendum rather than a substitution for something.UK Council for Psychotherapy (UKCP) accredited psychotherapist Hannah Jackson-McCamley and I both found your use of language really interesting: “storm”, “lightning strikes”. Jackson-McCamley wondered if your “relational experiences, dating or otherwise, might associate relationships with being tumultuous and something one has to prepare for or defend against”. Early experiences can influence how we expect interpersonal relationships to be.Jackson-McCamley thought it was “beautiful you want to be so generous with your love … but I wonder if being a caring person is part of your script and perhaps redolent of the role you take in relationships? It’s also great that you are able to articulate what you want from a partner and are considering making it clear from the start. However, not everyone may be used to such clarity or be looking for a life partner.”The thing to remember is that you’ve abstained from dating – and that’s OK. But people you meet might not have. So they may, at least initially, treat it less seriously than you might. And that’s OK too – you are both allowed your different takes.double quotation markI want you to feel reassured that no one is ‘fixed’, we are all works-in-progressYou mention anxiety and Jackson-McCamley said anxiety was “a totally normal response to a perceived stress or danger, so it isn’t something you need to permanently fix. But I’d be keen to explore your experience of anxiety in relation to dating – and beyond. I want you to feel reassured that no one is ‘fixed’, we are all works-in-progress.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy partner’s mother dominates him and it makes me feel helpless | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreYou said nothing else of your life, and we wondered what has gone on/is going on for you. “Give yourself grace,” said Jackson-McCamley, “for trying to make friends and confronting your nerves around new people. I wonder if this is the first time you’ve felt different or like an outsider?”She also urged you not to discount what you might bring to a relationship “beyond traditional accoutrements of status: money, job title, etc”. You say you want a supportive, funny life partner, so your ‘wants’ are not material, and those of others might not be, either.Falling in love has risks, some real, some imagined. It sounds as if you see people daily in your student life, which is great. This is the best environment to meet people, both for friendship and romance. I wonder if by “dating” you meant using apps, but perhaps a more real-world, softer approach that starts by making friends and seeing where it goes might actually suit you better.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions.
