title: ‘We detected unusual activity’: the scam that uses AI to exploit your holiday photos | Scams | The Guardian
description: Fraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account details
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Fraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account details
Content: Common AI tools can accurately detect where a photo was taken more than 90% of the time.Photograph: Sean Pavone/AlamyView image in fullscreenCommon AI tools can accurately detect where a photo was taken more than 90% of the time.Photograph: Sean Pavone/AlamyScam watchScams‘We detected unusual activity’: the scam that uses AI to exploit your holiday photosFraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account detailsShane HickeySun 16 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou are on a short break in Porto and post some pictures of your family on Instagram or Facebook. With a small section of the Douro river in the background, you think it could have been taken anywhere.A few days later, you get a text saying that your card was compromised. “We detected unusual activity while you were travelling in Porto – please verify immediately,” says the message.You click on the link to confirm your bank details. Since you have not put any details of your trip on any of your social networks – bar the indistinct pictures – you don’t suspect there is anything suspicious about the messages.But the text was a fraud designed to extract your financial details. The criminals behind it figured out where you had been on holidays – lending credibility to their text – by using AI to analyse the image for the most sparse signs of where it was taken.View image in fullscreenImage showing how AI identifies the location where holiday pictures were taken.Photograph: McAfee LabsNew research has shown that by picking up on details in the picture – such as the background, the architecture, the signage or the light – the AI agent can pinpoint where it was taken. For criminals, this information gives attempts to defraud by text message or email an added legitimacy.McAfee, the producer of anti-virus software, used two freely available AI models to test more than 21,000 travel images. One of the models identified 91% of images accurately while the other got 87%. Staff were then asked to replicate the experiment with their own pictures and became uncomfortable with how easy their travels were pinpointed.The company says that it shows that computers don’t need photos to be tagged or attached metadata to identify where they are taken.“What AI does is give context … so that makes the scam [and] makes the threats credible,” says Vonny Gamot, the head of EMEA at McAfee.What it looks likePictures are more likely to be identified by AI if they have recognisable landmarks, skylines, signage and street markings. Food stalls and storefronts can also pinpoint quickly where the picture was taken.If the picture is taken on a beach or a hotel room, the accuracy of the AI is lowered. But McAfee reports that it is likely that the system can identify which country they were taken in – which is all the scammers need.View image in fullscreenImage showing how AI identifies the location where holiday pictures were taken.Photograph: McAfee LabsWhen a staff member tested ChatGPT to identify a picture of a river with some trees in the foreground, it correctly pinpointed it as Hastings-on-Hudson, an area in New York state.Another picture of a group of flowers was identified as the Keukenhof gardens in the Netherlands. The AI agent correctly deduced that the layout of the tulips, along with smaller blue flowers planted between them, meant that it was the famous gardens in the picture.Criminals can use the information to make their approaches more convincing. They might say that your card was flagged for unusual activity while you were somewhere. Or that they are calling you after your stay in a particular hotel. Or that they want to confirm your identity because there has been an attempt to log in to your account from that country.What to doIf you want to post pictures, delay until after you get home and change your settings so that only the people you know can see them.As with all scams, be wary about any urgency in the messages you are sent, such as being told that you need to act immediately. Fraudsters use this as a tactic in the hope that people react without thinking something through fully.Don’t click on links that are provided in texts or emails; instead contact the company or bank through the details on their website or on the back of your bank card.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchBanks and building societiesConsumer affairsEuropeAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: How is it physically possible to continue breaking sporting records? | Sport | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: Greece’s Kristian Gkolomeev was the only athlete to best an official world record at the Enhanced Games in Las Vegas in May.Photograph: Darko Bandić/APView image in fullscreenGreece’s Kristian Gkolomeev was the only athlete to best an official world record at the Enhanced Games in Las Vegas in May.Photograph: Darko Bandić/APNotes and queriesSportReaders reply: How is it physically possible to continue breaking sporting records?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical conceptsThis week’s question:Is it inevitable that consumerism will literally fill up the planet?Sun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleObviously, progressions in sports clothing technology must make a small difference to the abilities of an athlete – but how on earth is it physically possible that we continue to break world records, year on year? Are humans really faster or stronger than they were decades ago?Jennifer Michaelson, NewlynSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyI think it’s partly because there is a larger pool of athletes. In the past, competing athletes would have primarily been from western countries. Now, they’re from all over.SfddesOne reason for better results is 3 billion extra people on Earth just since 1990. The chance of a “special one” in there improves significantly.catchytitledThis is due to the advancements in nutrition and training. If you compare these with 20 years ago, there is a big difference. And added to this is the advances in sports equipment.MartWolvesSeveral pathways to advance performance have emerged. One is refined training, nutrition and equipment. That is partly enabled through the ability of athletes to turn professional. It allows them to construct their routines every day around improving at the sport; no need to separately earn a living, get an education or deal with other distractions.Another is higher levels of participation. A wider demographic can try the sport, which improves the chance of seeing some emerge as international-level prospects at an early age. How many Kenyans would have seen a path to earning a living through running a few decades ago? Now, it’s an ambition fora substantial number of young runners, who know it’s a realistic career.leadballoonRunning with the Kenyans: return to Iten - in picturesRead moreIt seems that while there remains scope for“marginal gains”in sports (asDave Brailsfordpursued in cycling), records will continue to fall, albeit by smaller and smaller amounts. Improvements in sports science and technology allow you to wring out gains in areas previously unavailable.Regarding cycling, I recall Mark Cavendish noting with scepticism that, due to advancements in science, monitoring and so on, some teams thought it made more sense to find someone with optimal physiology and teach them the sport from scratch than to identify a good young cyclist and train them to be better.DocRickettsIn a lot of Olympic sports, the competitor doesn’t have to break a world record by much – one-hundredth of a second faster or a centimetre longer will do the job. The pole-vaulterArmand Duplantis(andSergey Bubkabefore him) breaks his own world records 1cm at a time, almost as a party piece (and for a big cash bonus). In other events, such as track running or swimming, however, the main priority is to finish ahead of everyone else; if that results in breaking the world record, then all well and good.dfic1999Interesting that theEnhanced Gamesheld recently in the US produced so few new records [only Kristian Gkolomeev bested an official world record, forthe men’s 50m freestyle]. I think because it was more of a marketing exercise to sell more supplements, but “clean” athletes did as well or better than their drug-taking counterparts. Presumably, the “clean” athletes relied more on plain old hard work, consistency and healthily nurtured talent; those seem to be the areas where we continue to improve.fabulouswilsonsisterData, pure and simple.KiltedKiwiEdinAnd money.ThirdhandlukeExplore more on these topicsSportNotes and queriesWorld recordsAthleticsSports scienceDrugs in sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The weekend is 100 years old – but have ‘skiveday Fridays’ and hybrid working ruined it for everyone? | Work-life balance | The Guardian
description: In 1926, Henry Ford gave his employees both Saturdays and Sundays off – and the two-day chunk of time to party, pray or simply do nothing was born. Now it’s changed beyond recognition
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: In 1926, Henry Ford gave his employees both Saturdays and Sundays off – and the two-day chunk of time to party, pray or simply do nothing was born. Now it’s changed beyond recognition
Content: The introduction of the weekend gave rise to the minibreak – alongside plenty of other leisure activities.Composite: getty images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe introduction of the weekend gave rise to the minibreak – alongside plenty of other leisure activities.Composite: getty images/Getty ImagesWork-life balanceThe weekend is 100 years old – but have ‘skiveday Fridays’ and hybrid working ruined it for everyone?In 1926, Henry Ford gave his employees both Saturdays and Sundays off – and the two-day chunk of time to party, pray or simply do nothing was born. Now it’s changed beyond recognitionJess Cartner-MorleySun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor 11 years, from 1929 to 1940, the Soviet Union did not have weekends. Instead, to increase productivity citizens were allocated a day off in every seven at random. With 80% of the population at work on any given day, factories never had to power down.A letter from a disgruntled worker to Pravda newspaper, published soon after the implementation of this new working calendar, outlined the problems: “What is there for us to do at home if our wives are in the factory, our children at school, and nobody can visit us?” the letter-writer asked. “It is no holiday if you have to have it alone.” Parents found themselves at home while their children were at school, or with kids unsupervised while they were on shift. With no shared day off, extended family gatherings became impossible. The workforce became demoralised and listless, the projected spike in productivity never materialised, and the policy was first modified, then abandoned altogether.Eleven years, though. Is that not absolutely wild? A world without weekends feels impossible. A world without Saturday Night Fever, without Manic Monday. We may no longer go to church on Sunday, but we still worship the weekend. “The weekend looms large because it represents the triumph of collective time over market time,” says Brad Beaven, professor of social and cultural history at the University of Portsmouth. “It is not just about rest, but about reclaiming autonomy from the industrial clock.”View image in fullscreen‘We romanticise the weekend, even the prosaic bits – like the distant roar of a lawnmower.’Photograph: Cavan Images/Liz DeGroff/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFSaturday and Sunday, sacred to the dignity and humanity of working people, are laden with mythology and ceremony. From Cilla Black to Gary Lineker, the main characters of our weekends become giants of the culture. We romanticise the weekend, even the prosaic bits – the distant roar of a lawnmower, the rattle of classified football results on the radio. Everyone knows what a weekend means. The snap of a laptop cover at 4.58pm on a Friday. The clink of the first pint glass and the smell of chips on the way home. The slow-motion pace of a weekend pavement, the gear change from hustle to meander. The rituals have changed with the times, of course, and people-watching at brunch on Saturday is now as much of a tradition as cooking a roast at home on Sunday. A weekend changes shape as you move through life stages, but in each iteration it remains a shared experience between you and your peers.“The weekend that I had when I was 20 was very different from the weekend that I have now, at 40 and with kids,” laughs Pedro Gomes, professor of economics at Birkbeck, University of London and author of the book Friday is the New Saturday. “When you are young, you are bonding with your friends, and then when you get older, you might be with your family. Eventually, you might be with grandchildren. We move through different manifestations of the weekend, in our lifetimes.”But it can be hard to pin down, these days, where a weekend begins and ends. Laundry gets done on a work-from-home Friday, but emails are answered on Sunday. A shopping splurge is as likely to be a cheer-up treat on your phone after a tough Wednesday as a Saturday outing. The traditional Saturday 3pm football kick-off has been stretched across the television schedules all the way to Monday evening. The four-day week – first predicted by Richard Nixon, of all people, in 1956 – has become a reality in the Netherlands, with people working an average of 32.1 hours. Friday is forging ahead with a quiet secession from the working week without anyone signing off the paperwork. It raises the question: what even is “the weekend” in 2026?Remarkably, the concept of the weekend as we know it is only 100 years old. In 1926, Henry Ford changed the shape of the week, announcing that the workers at his factories would now do five eight-hour days instead of six, with no cut in pay. Ford did not invent the weekend – the idea had been bubbling under for a century, in campaigns by trade unions, religious groups and progressive employers – but by putting his considerable industrial weight behind it, the two-day chunk of freedom was born.“It is high time to rid ourselves of the notion that leisure for workmen is either lost time or a class privilege,” Ford wrote in his company’s Ford News in October 1926. Ford’s innovation was in part a response to his earlier invention: the assembly line, which had increased productivity but exhausted workers, with absenteeism up to 10% in factories; in his article he did not disguise that there was self-interest involved. “People who have more leisure require more transportation in vehicles,” he continued. The new fashion for day trips was an effective marketing device to sell cars. Meanwhile, his factories maintained a steady level of productivity despite the reduced hours. In 1938, faced with rising unemployment levels in the Great Depression, the five-day week was officially adopted across the US.View image in fullscreenThe weekend used to start after work at around 5pm on a Friday …Photograph: fotoVoyager/Getty ImagesOn this side of the Atlantic, Boots the Chemist was the pioneer. In 1933, the company opened a new factory in Nottingham, which proved so efficient that there was soon a surplus of stock. Reluctant to lay his staff off with unemployment running at 25%, John Boot ended the Saturday morning shift, reducing hours for the 5,000-strong workforce without cutting wages. It was commercially successful, resulting in lower rates of absenteeism, and was adopted as Boots policy in 1934. A government inquiry led by Richard Redmayne – great-grandfather, fun fact, of actor Eddie – published a “review of the experimental working of the five days week”, which noted “an improvement in stamina and animation of the employees arising from the physiological and psychological effects of a long weekend’s rest and relaxation”. Slowly, the weekend gathered momentum. In the UK, “the early 20th-century version of the weekend was generally recognised as a half-day Saturday and Sunday off,” says Beaven. “The full two-day weekend only really became widely adopted after the second world war.”Before industrialisation, there was little concept of consecutive days of leisure, because animals and crops could not be so long neglected. Work was dictated by the weather and the seasons, the clock mattering less than the sun. Factories, with their whistles and watches, changed the way time worked. A mechanised drumbeat of shifts and paydays drowned out the old rhythms of seasons and saints days.As work became more rigidly organised, the possibility emerged that leisure could be, too. Time off wasn’t merely a concession to workers, but also an engine of consumer capitalism. People with weekends would go to sports stadiums, buy picnic baskets and new clothes, need cinema tickets. By the late 20th century, with the arrival of cheap flights, this hadevolved into the minibreak: a miniature holiday, designed to fit into a weekend. Leisure time, once the opposite of the economy, became part of it.For generations, the British weekend revolved around one immovable appointment: the 3pm Saturday kick-off. “The weekend is about rest, but it is also about passion,” says Gomes. “Most of us are not lucky enough to be passionate about our jobs, but at the weekend we can follow our passions.” The link between football and the best day of the week is intrinsic to the national love affair with the sport. It is probably partly because football symbolised the best bit of the weekend that we ended up so obsessed with it.Morals – and the absence of them – have always been a theme of the weekend. When Sunday, a time of worship, was the only day off, skilled workers developed a habit of extending their free time into “Saint Monday”, by not turning up for work after a particularly enthusiastic day of drinking. Saturday afternoons off – and then the whole day – were granted by employers partly in the hope of bringing the hangovers forward by a day. Victorian reformers, obsessed with drunkenness, hoped that free Saturdays would encourage respectable recreation: organised sport, gardening, family outings. Ford, a vehement supporter of Prohibition, believed that the illegality of alcohol made his move towards a two-day weekend safe. (“A day off is no longer a day drunk,” he said.)The reality has never been quite so clean-cut. Weekends are naughty and nice, both bad behaviour and Sunday best. These are the days for shopping splurges and drinking sprees and hook-ups, but also for penance, whether by parkrun, DIY or actual prayer. Though perhaps less so the prayer bit:around one in three Britons attended church regularly in 1900, according to the National Centre for Social Research; now, this is number is around one in 20. Two moments stand out in the story of how Sunday lost its special place as a day, if not of worship, then of higher purpose. In 1994, the Sunday Trading Act allowed large shops in England and Wales to open on Sundays. Then, a quarter of a century later, pandemic lockdowns broke the now-fragile bonds between churches and their communities, and left many older parishioners with a wariness of gathering in ill-ventilated churches that might be bad for the health, even if good for the soul.View image in fullscreenPeople taking part in a parkrun on Coldham Common, Cambridge.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe late, great Maggie Smith had, as she so often did, the best line. “What is a weekend?” she asked, in Downton Abbey, with the entitled bewilderment of a dowager countess for whom income is spoonfed in silver from birth, not doled out in a brown envelope on a Friday night. The weekend is time carved out of, and in tension with, someone else’s ownership of your time. Not to mention that for aristocrats, who had servants for everything from laying fires to buttoning their dresses, every day was a day of leisure. The weekend feels like a cornerstone of civilisation, of democracy, because it matters most to those who spend the majority of the week following orders instead of giving them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaturday EditionAn exclusive roundup of the week's best Guardian journalism from the editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, free to your inbox every SaturdayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese days, the upstairs-downstairs division is between the hybrid workers and those whose work can never be done remotely. An age-old division between shift work and the relative flexibility of white-collar jobs has deepened. Thinkers like Liselotte Lyngsø, founding partner of the Copenhagen-based consultancy Future Navigator, have argued that the workforce is splitting into “time owners” – knowledge workers who increasingly choose where and when they work – and “time slaves”, whose jobs, like healthcare, manual shift work or gig economy roles like Amazon or Deliveroo driving, remains stubbornly tied to the clock.For the “time owners”, Friday is rapidly turning into the modern Saint Monday. It is an increasingly open secret that the last day of the working week has become, for remote workers, an unofficial half shift: calendar technically open, but both brain and laptop mostly on standby. When Gomes rana six-month trialof four-day-week working in Portugal in 2023, with more than 41 public and private firms involved, “organisations that can’t reduce hours – a nursery, for example – worked in shifts with a different day off within each week. Other firms made the decision to cut Friday out. Whenever their weekday off was, we found that many employees approached that day a little differently, using it to get ‘life admin’ done so that they could have their Saturdays and Sundays free. The weekend isn’t just about the number of hours, it is also a coordination device for communities to connect.”‘Cruel hoax’ or ‘work-life balance nirvana’: whatever happened to the four-day work week?Read moreAs with Saint Monday, “Skiveday Friday” has proved in the UK to be stubbornly, if silently, adhered to. In 2024, Transport for London rana three-month trialscrapping peak fares on Fridays explicitly in order to lure commuters back into central London.It failed, Fridays remaining quiet, despite the discount. For the laptopped-classes, there has been a shift in what Friday is for. Several major rail companies, including LNER and Avanti, have now made Fridays an entirely off-peak day like Saturday and Sunday, acknowledging that the weekend now begins earlier for many.Though it should be noted that, for those same workers, Saturday and Sunday themselves are under constant siege from the mission creep of work emails and contactability outside working hours in the age of the smartphone. “These are two sides of the same coin,” says Gomes. Work intensifies, and the weekend expands in order to absorb the pressure. “The speed of communication means that we now live with constant interruptions, and it is hard to find space either for deep work or for real rest. And yet we continue to structure the work week in much the same way as we did 100 years ago. It is no surprise that this isn’t working.”Hence why a three-day weekend is being suggested as a way to balance the books. But is it all woke nonsense? A pie in the sky idea, dreamed up by a lazy workforce which no longer knows the meaning of hard work? The Green party supports a “move towards” a four-day week, but other politicians are wary. In 2025, the Liberal Democrat-led South Cambridgeshire council, which had been operating a four-day week for two years, was attacked by the then local government secretary, Steve Reed, who said thatlocal governments “should not be paying full-time wages for part-time work”.In April this year, James Cleverly announced that a future Conservative government would look to ban four-day weeks for council staff, denouncing the “push from the left of centre in British politics” towards a four-day week as “completely wrong”.The 4 Day Week Foundation, which is leading the drive for change in Britain, says that56 out of the 61 companieswho signed up for their four-day week pilot decided to stick with it after the scheme ended. They cite an average of 35% increased revenue, and 57% decline in staff leaving rates, during the trial. There are now 260 companies in the UK officially signed up to the four-day week.View image in fullscreen‘While Fridays have become an unofficial half shift, the weekend is under siege from work emails and calls.’Photograph: Getty Images /iStockphotoThe divide–between time sharers and time slaves, those working five-day weeks, four-day weeks or more ad-hoc, less weekend-friendly shift work–is problematic because the weekend is designed to be shared. It’s where British culture learned to gather, a collective experience. Every generation has its own shared rituals. Boomers love a Saturday night movie, generation X are obsessed with Sunday lunch, millennials love to flock to a farmers’ market, while gen Z, for some reason, get their kicks standing in line for baked goods that have gone viral on TikTok. Even the Sunday scaries are made manageable by the knowledge that everyone out there is feeling the same. As a gulf widens – between the time owners and time slaves, between inherited wealth and the increasingly weedy salary pipeline – the weekend starts to feel less like an experience, and more like a nostalgic memory.It is funny to think that, at first, technology expanded our horizons. Railways gave ordinary people access to the coast; mass production made bicycles and cars affordable. It is only recently that technology has mutated into the energy vampire it is today, sucking the life from the weekend.Only in the last decade has online autobiography become everybody’s unpaid side hustle, so that your friends have already seen your holiday photos before you meet them for brunch. It is a very modern phenomenon that our friendships have migrated online, this week’s boy drama or family quarrel already debated at length in text bubbles and voice notes without the need to meet in the pub. Add to this the post-pandemic normalisation of the “soft commitment”, in which making plans and cancelling them have become two parts of the same social ritual and “I’ll see how I feel” has become an acceptable RSVP, and we have become less good at a core element of the weekend, which is actuallyseeing other people.Perhaps we shouldn’t fret so much. Ever since we invented the weekend, we have been anxiously taking its pulse. The Victorians worried that workers would waste their precious leisure days drinking. Mid-century Britain feared television was keeping families indoors. Today’s concern is that we spend Saturday scrolling Instagram and Sunday answering emails. The rituals change; the suspicion that the weekend is being ruined remains. Yet the weekend survives, perhaps because it has never demanded perfection. The lie-in and the late night are equally valid forms of resistance. Its holiest rites – the greasy fry-up, the football terrace, Saturday-night shiny-floor television – are gloriously unrefined. The weekend is where a good time still trumps good taste.The Soviets discovered that a day off is not much use unless other people are off, too; Ford understood that workers needed time in which to become themselves again, even if he hoped they would spend it buying cars. At 100, the two-day weekend is fraying at the edges, leaking into Friday and nibbled away by Sunday night emails. The weekend will keep changing, because work keeps changing. But it will still always be the best thing work ever invented.Explore more on these topicsWork-life balanceFour-day weekWork & careersTravel & leisureZero-hours contractsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My electric toaster is more than 100 years old’: readers on their ancient appliances | Life and style | The Guardian
description: After news that a couple from Gloucestershire are still using an Electrolux fridge from the 1930s, we asked readers about their experiences. From a 50-year-old TV to a 75-year-old vacuum cleaner, here are the old faithfuls
Author: Guardian community team
Headline: After news that a couple from Gloucestershire are still using an Electrolux fridge from the 1930s, we asked readers about their experiences. From a 50-year-old TV to a 75-year-old vacuum cleaner, here are the old faithfuls
Content: Older than the TikTok generation … Jason Connolly’s 1974 Janex Batman and Robin wind-up talking alarm clock.Photograph: Courtesy of Jason ConnollyView image in fullscreenOlder than the TikTok generation … Jason Connolly’s 1974 Janex Batman and Robin wind-up talking alarm clock.Photograph: Courtesy of Jason ConnollyLife and style‘My electric toaster is more than 100 years old’: readers on their ancient appliancesAfter news that a couple from Gloucestershire are still using an Electrolux fridge from the 1930s, we asked readers about their experiences. From a 50-year-old TV to a 75-year-old vacuum cleaner, here are the old faithfulsGuardian community teamSun 16 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBatman and Robin alarm clockI have a 1974 Janex Batman and Robin wind-up talking alarm clock. Amazingly, it still works even though it’s more than 50 years old. It plays audio of Batman and Robin having a discussion on why should really get up and out of bed. I love it. Every time I see it, I smile.Jason Connolly,57, district nurse, Macandrew Bay, New ZealandHotpoint toasterView image in fullscreenCrumbs! … Heather Sebastian’s trusty toaster.Photograph: Courtesy of Heather SebastianI have a Hotpoint toaster that could be more than 100 years old and still toasts bread and bagels perfectly. It’s the same model my grandparents had. I recovered mine from a house that was being demolished. After cleaning it with baking soda and vinegar, it looks pretty good for its age.Heather Sebastian,retiredteacher,Vancouver, CanadaElectrolux vacuum cleanerView image in fullscreenDust might … Jane McCall’s vacuum cleaner.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane McCallWhen my husband and I moved in together 46 years ago, we bought a secondhand Electrolux vacuum cleaner. It’s been going strong ever since. It has never broken. We take it into the repair shop occasionally for a little TLC and they tell us to never get rid of it because we’ll never find anything better.Jane McCall, 67, retired,Vancouver,CanadaKenwood mixerView image in fullscreenMixing up the generations … Alick’s Kenwood Chefette.I inherited my grandmother’s Kenwood Chefette food mixer. I think she got it in about 1975. The plastic bowl gave up about 20 years ago, but the mixer is still going strong. Even my daughter uses it when she visits, so it has served four generations.Alick, 62,environmentalhealthofficer, Berkshire, UKNorge Customatic fridgeView image in fullscreenChilled out … Anne Hartman’s Norge refrigerator.Photograph: Courtesy of Anne HartmanMy parents bought a summer cottage in 1975 that came with an old fridge. It’s a Norge Customatic, made in Detroit, with an original inspection tag from 1956. I have it now and it worked like an absolute champ until it needed new wiring a couple of years back. Sure, I could have just found another more modern fridge but I always loved this one with its turquoise and gold sparkle interior. I found a business in nearby Quebec that specialises in antique kitchen appliances and they serviced it. It should be good for another 70 years.Anne Hartman,50,repairer and builder of musical instruments, Toronto, Ontario, CanadaTefal toasterView image in fullscreenA slice of history … Barry Lillis’s toaster.Photograph: Courtesy of Barry LillisDuring my first year at university in London, when I went home for Christmas, my mum had replaced her old Tefal Thick’n’Thin toaster with a new one. The old one hadn’t been binned and was still working, so I took it back to university. It came with me on my adventures in student and young professional house shares, and eventually found a permanent home when I managed to buy my own place. Last year, we had a nasty scare when my wife phoned to say that the main electricity fuse was tripping when she turned on the toaster. I feared the worst but got home to find that a big lump of burnt toast was jammed inside and causing a short circuit. Disaster averted, and the old boy lived to fight another day! Still making perfect toast after the 27 years I’ve had it.Barry Lillis,49,productdesigner, London, UKDigitron digital clockView image in fullscreenStill ticking over … Richard’s bedside clock.Photograph: Supplied imageI have a Digitron digital clock, which is about 50 years old. I bought it when I was 14 and it still sits by my bedside. I grew up in Surrey and I got it using my pocket money from being a golf caddie on Sundays, for which I got £1.10 per round. I think it cost £15, which was a lot of money for me then.Richard, Hong KongHome stereoView image in fullscreenMusic to David Dalle’s ears … his old stereo setup.Photograph: Courtesy of David DalleMy home stereo was bought, secondhand, in 1998. A large part of my life is built around music and the stereo gets used daily. Besides a cleaning of the power amplifier, it has never failed. I added a Technics turntable a few years ago. There is no technology of any sort built to last like this. It sounds far better than any phone.DavidDalle, 53, IT worker, Ottawa, CanadaHitachi TVView image in fullscreenRetro vision … Richard Rosing’s 1985 television.Photograph: Courtesy of Richard RosingOur television is a 1985 Hitachi colour TV console. It has outlasted every household appliance we have owned. We have turned down multiple offers from younger people, who weren’t even born when we bought it, and think it’s just the coolest retro piece of electronic gear they’ve seen.Richard Rosing, 71,writer and musician,Nashville, USSamsung microwaveView image in fullscreenCanny investment … Lin Cochran’s microwave.Photograph: Courtesy of Lin CochranIn 1985, we rebuilt our kitchen and bought a Samsung Classic microwave after seeing a review in Consumer Reports magazine. During the renovation, we used the microwave to cook in the garage. Since then it’s been in use almost every day. I wish all of our investments had been so successful.Lin Cochran,retired, Huntsville, Alabama, USSanyo fanView image in fullscreenA blast … Ted Hume’s Sanyo rotary fan (and cat).Photograph: Courtesy of Ted HumeBefore I became a journalist, I attended Australia’s Royal Military College, Duntroon, in Canberra, to embark on a four-year degree to become an army officer. It was very hot there during the summer. In 1979, my parents bought me a Sanyo rotating fan. I still have it and it works perfectly and has never needed repair. It has been with me since my late teens to now, my late 60s. It has become part of the family in a way – it’s always there through the ups and downs. I just hope it never breaks.Ted Hume, 65,journalist, Tasmania, AustraliaKenwood food processorView image in fullscreenColeslaw king … Ian Watson’s food processor.Photograph: Courtesy of Ian WatsonI have a Kenwood food processor that my mother bought in the mid-1980s. She gave it to me when she bought a newer model. It emigrated with me to New Zealand in 2000. I use it weekly to make coleslaw, hummus, pastry and mayonnaise, and to blitz soups. It shows some signs of age but everything works fine.Ian Watson,66, retiredprofessor, Auckland, New ZealandSony TVView image in fullscreenA pretty picture … Richard’s Sony Trinitron TV.Photograph: Supplied imageI have a 1973 Sony Trinitron 13in colour TV. I mostly use it for playing VHS tapes but I can also connect it to satellite TV using a device. It’s a real talking point when friends come to visit. The picture is great for its age.Richard, 54, audiovisual technician, The Hague, the NetherlandsVitantonio waffle-makerView image in fullscreenWaffling on … Laina’sVitantonio appliance.Photograph: Supplied imageOur Vitantonio waffle-maker was a wedding gift and is 31 years old. It is still going strong. It’s sturdy enough to toast cinnamon rolls that come in a tube and shape them into waffles. A funeral will be held on its demise.Laina,60, navy veteran, northern Virginia, USSunkist JuicitView image in fullscreenAge is no barrier … for Tom Bentley’s juicer.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom BentleyWho says you need to slow down after you reach 50? My Sunkist Juicit is a stalwart, born sometime in the 60s or 70s. We have a large lemon and lime tree in the back yard, but its profusion of fruit doesn’t intimidate the Juicit. I often make lemon or limeade. It’s a pleasure to drink the sweetly tart juice.Tom Bentley, 71, Watsonville, California, USHoover vacuum cleanerView image in fullscreenClean machine … Sheilah’s upright vacuum cleaner.I own a Hoover upright vacuum cleaner, bought in 1951. I have had to replace the plug and the on/off switch a couple of times. The motor gets cleaned at the same time. It is much more powerful than any of the ones owned by my friends. I inherited it from my mother and I expect it to outlive me.Sheilah, Toronto, CanadaPhilips egg whiskI have my mother’s Philips electric egg whisk. I remember her using it in the 1960s. It’s a bit noisy but still working perfectly.Gill, Kent, UKMaytag washing machine and Whirlpool tumble dryerView image in fullscreenOld workhorses … Eric Mintz’s Maytag washing machine and Whirlpool tumble dryer.Photograph: Courtesy of Eric MintzI still have a Maytag washing machine and Whirlpool tumble dryer, which we bought when we moved into our house in 1987. They have seen daily use, cleaning everything, including reusable cloth nappies. Modern appliances can’t come close.Eric Mintz, retired, Metuchen, New Jersey, USDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Trump’s midterm malaise: endless war and high prices could spell doom for Republicans in November  | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: ‘Complete unraveling’ of Trump and Republican project reflects attitude of not caring at all about governance
Author: David Smith
Headline: ‘Complete unraveling’ of Trump and Republican project reflects attitude of not caring at all about governance
Content: As Iran war ceasefire negotiations were ongoing, Donald Trump showed off the construction of his planned White House ballroom on 19 May 2026.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenAs Iran war ceasefire negotiations were ongoing, Donald Trump showed off the construction of his planned White House ballroom on 19 May 2026.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump’s midterm malaise: endless war and high prices could spell doom for Republicans in November‘Complete unraveling’ of Trump and Republican project reflects attitude of not caring at all about governanceDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 16 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe was always one step ahead.Donald Trumpwon the US presidency as a wildly unlikely outsider in 2016 and stagedan astonishing comebackto win it again in 2024. Even his foes grudgingly called him a political savant with an intuition for exploiting grievances that left so-called experts floundering.But now they are asking if the dark genius has lost his touch. Trump is trapped in the quagmire of an unpopular war, obsessing over monuments in Washington and looking for a new spokesperson after hisWhite House press secretary quit. If the 80-year-old was deliberately trying to sabotage his Republican party in November’s midterm elections, it is not clear what he would do differently.“He’s always had a reptilian political instinct for public opinion that has served him well,” saidCharlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster. “You’re not seeing that much any more. You’re not seeing his ability to read the room. He seems tone-deaf on issues like the cost of living, the war, and the optics of gilding everything in sight and enshittifying Washington and he doesn’t care.”Trump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln amid record deploymentRead moreTrump campaigned on promises to lower prices and keep the US out of foreign entanglements and forever wars. The opposite has happened. Voters say they are suffering a cost of living crisis, exacerbated by Trump’s sweeping tariffs. Buying food to eat at home has become 33% more expensive in US cities since the beginning of 2019,according to government figures.Gas prices are ata record highfor this time of year, in part thanks to the US war in Iran, which drags on with no end in sight. While Trump claims to have destroyed Iran’s military capabilities, it emerged this week that he wasforced to hide in a catering truckand secretly swap planes after a Nato summit in Turkey because of a possible Iranian assassination plot.The administration’s entanglement has metastasised into a gruelling, daily haemorrhage of resources, currently costing the taxpayer an estimated $1bn a day. Critics argue the administration has strengthened Iran’s resolve and provided it with global leverage, specifically over the strait of Hormuz. They see it as betrayal of the noninterventionist posture that fuelled Trump’s rise to power and attracted a generation of disaffected voters.Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said:“What we’re watching right now is the complete unraveling of everything that Donald Trump, Maga and Republicans said they were about. They were against endless conflicts in the Middle East and they started a conflict in the Middle East without an exit strategy.They were supposed to be about no more spending American dollars abroad;we’re spending a billion dollars a day on this war without an end.”Yet the president appears to have other, more aesthetic concerns. Since returning to power last year, the longtime property developer has invested much time and energy in construction projects across Washington, including a White House ballroom and helipad, a triumphal arch and an ill-fated makeover of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds up a model for a proposed arch at a dinner with ballroom donors at the White House on 15 October 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesBardella added: “As he continues this misadventure in the Middle East that has resulted in the cost of living going up, and continues to pour resources into putting his name on shit and building ballrooms and monuments to himself, the American people are going: what the fuck? That’s the only realistic reaction you could have when you objectively look at the circumstances.”Trump’s second term has been defined by thinking big – Greenland, Venezuela, Iran – and thinking small. The board he appointed to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts added his name to the complex, only for a judge to order that it be removed; this weekthe board voted to add“Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump” beneath the main sign.According to Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, written by New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, the president has beenseen with a tube of super gluetrying to stick golden decorations to the marble fireplace in the Oval Office.Haberman estimates that Trump now devotes 70% of his mental space to renovation projects and “monuments to self”. Shetold Axios’s Behind the Curtainvideo series that she and Swan visited Trump in the Oval Office in March. “You would think that on the 17th day of the war that he would have maps of the Middle East or maps of troop deployments – who knows,” she said. “He picks up these pictures, and [they’re] of maple trees, and he says: ‘I am choosing maple trees for the White House. I am good at picking trees.’ I’m paraphrasing here, but that is pretty much what he said.”The president’s preoccupation with whether columns for his ballroom are more evocative of Athens or Rome, and with other efforts to preserve his legacy in marble, come as little surprise to Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill and longtime Trump critic.She said: “Donald Trump has been an egomaniac, a narcissist his entire life. Even in the private sector he has slapped his name on buildings and a multitude of failed branding businesses from Trump steaks to Trump airline toTrump Universityto Trump water to Trump wine. Why is anyone surprised that he would take that same type of narcissism and bring it over to his role in his second-term as president when he’s spending other people’s money to do it?“The problem has been that the Republican party has enabled him to get away with this and to their own detriment, which is why more and more people in his inner circle are concerned about how this is going to impact the midterms and control of Congress.”Indeed, Republicans are said to be quietly panicking about Trump costing them the House of Representatives and putting even the Senate in jeopardy. A nationalQuinnipiac University Pollreleased late last month showed his job approval rating dropping to an all-time low of 32%, with 58% disapproval. It found six in 10 Americans oppose the US military action in Iran.Past presidents such as George W Bush in 2006 and Barack Obama in 2010 have faced challenging midterms but worked with their parties in an effort to at least stem the losses.Rick Wilson, co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, said: “In both those cases their efforts were not successful, but it’s nightmarish to think what that would have been if Barack Obama had been saying, ‘I’m going to build a basketball arena at the White House,’ or George Bush had said, ‘I’m gonna build a golf course.’“Instead you’ve got a very different visual from this White House and that visual is 'we don’t care about anything else except for the ballroom and the arch and all the throw-away ephemera that he wants to focus on. It’s a terrible political look and it’s quite dangerous for the party because they have nothing to run on right now.”The sense of malaise deepened this week when Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary, announced that shewill bestepping down at the end of the month. The official explanation was that the 28-year-old wants to spend more time with her young family but the timing was unfortunate for an administration struggling to spin its way out of one crisis after another.For a president whose entire self-image is built on winning, the realisation that he is facing electoral defeat at home and humiliation abroad could be cause for an existential crisis. Sykes observed that, while Trump’s historical literacy is notoriously thin, he has begun to obsess over the ghosts of presidencies ruined by foreign blunders.“It’s awfully interesting that in the Maggie Haberman bookhe’s comparing himself toNapoleon and Alexander the Great and Caesar but his deepest fear right now is that he’s going to be Herbert Hoover or Jimmy Carter,” he said.Trump’s cloud does have a golden lining, however. Hemade an estimated $2.2bnduring the first year of his second term thanks to cryptocurrency holdings, foreign interests and his Truth Social business.Sykes added: “He hasn’t lowered the cost of living, he hasn’t made America more respected, he hasn’t won the war but he has succeeded in making himself a billionaire many times over by abusing his office.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026RepublicansTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyUS domestic policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his way | Brazil | The Guardian
description: President, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: President, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’
Content: Lula said he would dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare, and go after organised crime bosses.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLula said he would dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare, and go after organised crime bosses.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesBrazilBrazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his wayPresident, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’Tom Phillipsin São Bernardo do CampoSun 16 Aug 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s leftwing president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has launched his campaign for a historic fourth term and vowed that as long as he lived he would not allow the “shameless” right to return to power.Addressing a sea of supporters in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, the 80-year-old politician reminded voters of the chaos and violence that unfolded duringthe 2018-22 presidency of his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whose sonFlávio Bolsonaro will face Lula in October’s presidential election.Lula recalled how hundreds of thousands of citizens died during a Covid outbreakJair Bolsonarowas accused of bungling with his anti-science policies. Gun ownership soared as laws were relaxed, allowing criminal groups to expand their arsenals. “They handed out … more than a million weapons,” Lula said, promising to dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare as well as developing Brazil’s rare-earth deposits, the world’s second largest after China’s.View image in fullscreenLula launched his re-election campaign at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his rise to the presidency began in 1979 as a union leader.Photograph: Sebastião Moreira/EPALula also said he would improve security by targeting the rich organised crime bosses who lived in luxury apartments. “It’s easy to kill a crook in a favela. But the guy running the show lives in a penthouse … and we need to stop this,” Lula said. He also told his far-right rivals to “show some shame”.Lula was speaking at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his astonishing rise to the presidency began in 1979 when, as 33-year-old union leader, he spearheaded two historic strikes that helped end the military dictatorship. Those strikes made Lula a household name and in 2002, after three failed attempts,he won a landslide victoryto become his country’s first working-class president.‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaignRead moreDuring Lula’s first two-terms, from 2002 until 2010, he was credited with fighting hunger, dramatically expanding social welfare programmes and access to higher education, and improving Brazil’s global standing, although his administration was blighted by corruption scandals. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, became Brazil’s first female president but led the country into a severe economic recession beforebeing controversially impeachedin 2016.In 2018, Lula was jailed for alleged corruption and he spent 580 days in prison before the supreme courtquashed his conviction. Lula’s imprisonment allowed Bolsonaro to win that year’s election, ushering in four years of environmental destruction and international isolation.In 2022 Lula won his third term, defeating Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin and vowing to rescue the country from “one of the worst periods in Brazilian history”. “This nightmare is over,” Lula declared at his January 2023 inauguration. A week later, far-right radicals rampaged through the capital, Brasília, ina botched attempt to bring Bolsonaro back.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro and his wife, Fernanda Bolsonaro, arrive for his campaign launch event at Rio’s Copacabana beach.Photograph: Silvia Izquierdo/APBolsonaro wasjailed in 2025 for 27 yearsfor plotting that failed post-election power grab. Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, launched his campaign on Sunday with an event on Rio’s Copacabana beach, previously the scene of huge rallies in support of his father. “I am going to be Brazil’s next president because I’m going to fight this system,” Bolsonaro, who wore a bullet-proof vest under a yellow Brazil shirt, told a crowd far smaller than those his father used to attract.Polls suggest Lula holds a slender advantage over Bolsonaro, with 43% of intended votes to his rival’s 40% in a run-off which will take place on 25 October if, as expected, no candidate secures 50% of the vote in the 4 October first round.André Pagliarini, the author of a book about Lula called A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, said the showdown would be “the single most important electoral contest this year in the world”.Pagliarini said he believed a Bolsonaro victory would be a significant boost for thepro-Trump “reactionary block”that has won elections across Latin America, from Argentina and Chile to Colombia, where the far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella recently took office.Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly asserted its leadership over the region, launching deadly military operations against alleged “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific,threatening to “take back” the Panama canaland, in January,abducting Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro. Last week, the US state department publishedan incendiary videodeclaring that “American dominance in the western hemisphere will never be questioned again”.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch event on Sunday. Donald Trump’s administration has increasingly asserted its leadership over the region and recently designated Brazil’s two biggest organised crime groups as terrorist organisations.Photograph: Bruna Prado/AP​In recent months Trump has turned up the heat on Brazil, designating its two biggest organised crime groups, the Red Command and the PCC, as terrorist organisations. That has kindled fears of a US military intervention on Brazilian soil or interference in Brazil’s presidential election.During a visit to a jungle training camp in Panama on Friday, Trump’s defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said Washington planned to use the military to “ruthlessly” pursue Latin American drug traffickers, “just like [they did with] Isis and al-Qaida” during the “war on terror”.The idea, Hegseth said, was to “do bad things to bad people – because for too long, bad people did bad things to good people inside the United States of America and across Central and South America”.There was anger at the US outside Lula’s campaign launch on Sunday, where some activists handed out stickers that read: “Fuck Trump.”Seixas Alves, a 33-year-old Lula supporter, said he worriedthe decision to classify Brazilian drug factions as terrorist groupscould be used as a pretext for a US attack. “Just like they [did with] Saddam Hussein,” Alves added, referring to the Iraqi dictator’s supposed development of weapons of mass destruction.In Rio, Flávio Bolsonaro praised Trump’s decision to target the Brazilian crime groups and said he was the only politician capable of “sitting down with the US”.In Vila Euclides, Simone Tebet, a centrist Lula ally, urged voters to do everything they could to stop Brazil falling back into the hands of far-right politicians who wanted “to kill Brazilian democracy” and create “a country of hate”.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan’s defence minister heads to Australia to meet Marles in wake of melon-gate controversy | Japan | The Guardian
description: Discussions to focus on Australia’s acquisition of Mogami-class frigate as Japan plays down Albanese’s podcast comments
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Discussions to focus on Australia’s acquisition of Mogami-class frigate as Japan plays down Albanese’s podcast comments
Content: Australian defence minister, Richard Marles (L), with Japanese defence minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, at a defence ministers meeting in Tokyo earlier this year.Photograph: Masatoshi Okauchi/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAustralian defence minister, Richard Marles (L), with Japanese defence minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, at a defence ministers meeting in Tokyo earlier this year.Photograph: Masatoshi Okauchi/ShutterstockJapanJapan’s defence minister heads to Australia to meet Marles in wake of melon-gate controversyDiscussions to focus on Australia’s acquisition of Mogami-class frigates as Japan plays down Albanese’s podcast commentsTom McIlroyPolitical editorSun 16 Aug 2026 00.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 00.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapan’s defence minister will visit Canberra this week, the highest level engagement with Australia after controversy over Anthony Albanese’s comments abouta gift of melonsfrom prime minister Sanae Takaichi.The defence minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, will meet his counterpart and deputy prime minister,Richard Marles, on Tuesday, with discussions focused on Australia’s acquisition of Japan’s Mogami-class frigates and enhanced security cooperation.Koizumi is considered a potential future prime minister ofJapan. His father, Junichiro Koizumi, was prime minister from 2001 to 2006.Koizumi’s visit comes after a week in which Albanese defended himself over comments made on the Bush Deep podcast, released last month.Melon-gate was a non-issue in Japan. How did it get elevated to a crisis in Australia? | Malcolm FarrRead moreHe was discussing a pair of Japanese melons presented by Takaichi during a visit to Canberra earlier this year, and, while appearing to make hand gestures in front of his chest, said “she brought two, as you do”.Host Nikki Osborne joked: “She came in looking like Pamela Anderson.”Facing days of criticism from the opposition and in the media, Albanese has insisted his hand gestures and a comment about melons were misinterpreted and were not innuendo about breasts.The opposition criticised Albanese for putting at risk close relations with one of Australia’s most important partners in Asia.Public comments from Japan’s ambassador to Australia on Wednesday suggested Takaichi’s government wanted to avoid a diplomatic incident over the comments, which were initially not controversial but soon sparked strong criticism, including by a former envoy to Australia.Japan’s government refrained from public comments on the issue until Wednesday, when its current ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki released a statement not raising any further issue with Albanese’s conduct.Suzuki noted Takaichi had visited Australia in May – shortly before the interview in question – and had been hosted for dinner by Albanese “in a very relaxed atmosphere, and we believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders”.Albanese had earlier apologisedfor comments about Australian signer Kylie Minogue made in the same appearance.A Japanese diplomatic cable sent in July, and leaked during the controversy,blamed “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media”and said Tokyo believed there was no “ill intention” in Albanese’s actions.The visit comes as part of a five-day trip which will include a stop in India.“Our relationship with Japan continues to go from strength to strength, and I look forward to welcoming my good friend, minister Koizumi back to Australia this week,” Marles told Guardian Australia.“Together we will progress efforts to enhance defence cooperation and support our shared commitment to regional security, building on the joint statement announced by our prime ministers in May.“This includes in the areas of co-developing and co-producing defence capabilities, advanced weapons testing, enhanced training and exercises, and increased information and intelligence cooperation.”Takaichi has faced mounting political challenges, including on policies to help with the cost of living, and has seen sliding support in opinion polls in recent months.Koizumi was criticised by China at the weekend for visiting the Yasukuni Shrine, dedicated to Japan’s war dead. Visits to the shrine by senior politicians are regularly criticised by Japan’s neighbours including China and South Korea, who suggest they are symbolic of a lack of remorse for Japan’s actions during the second world war.In August last year, Labor agreed to buy Japan’s Mogami‑class frigates for the Royal Australian Navy.Australia will spend$10bn over a decadeto buy three of the frigates, with the first expected to be delivered in December 2029.Explore more on these topicsJapanAnthony AlbaneseSanae TakaichiRichard MarlesAustralian politicsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rescue teams search for survivors in Indonesia after powerful earthquake | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Searchers dig through collapsed buildings and debris after 7.7 magnitude quake killed at least 53 people
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Searchers dig through collapsed buildings and debris after 7.7 magnitude quake killed at least 53 people
Content: A collapsed house in Nagekeo in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province after the 7.7 magnitude earthquake.Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPAView image in fullscreenA collapsed house in Nagekeo in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province after the 7.7 magnitude earthquake.Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPAIndonesiaRescue teams search for survivors in Indonesia after powerful earthquakeSearchers dig through collapsed buildings and debris after 7.7 magnitude quake killed at least 53 peopleAssociated PressSat 15 Aug 2026 23.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescue crews dug through collapsed buildings and landslide debris in eastern Indonesia on Sunday as they searched for bodies and possible survivors a day after apowerful earthquakekilled at least 53 people, injured more than 100 and displaced thousands.At least 24 people died in Manggarai regency and 17 in neighbouring East Manggarai, with additional fatalities reported in Sikka, Ngada and Ende regencies, the national disaster management agency said. Rescuers were still searching for people feared buried beneath landslides triggered by the quake across six regencies on Flores, a predominantly Catholic island in Muslim-majorityIndonesia.Powerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern IndonesiaRead moreThe magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck 68km (42 miles) north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province, the USGS said. The quake, at a depth of about 10km (6 miles) off the coast of Flores, rattled much of the island and sent residents fleeing in panic. Tremors were also felt in neighbouring West Nusa Tenggara and parts of southern Sulawesi.View image in fullscreenA crack in the road in East Nusa Tenggara after the quake.Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPAThe disaster agency said the quake destroyed more than 900 homes and damaged nearly 450 more, forcing about 5,000 people into temporary shelters. Thousands more spent the night outdoors, fearing strong aftershocks. At least 167 public facilities, including schools, health centres and churches, were also damaged.Relief workers have begun distributing rice, ready-to-eat meals, drinking water, blankets and medicine, while emergency shelters were being set up for displaced residents. Authorities said restoring electricity and communications as well as delivering aid to remote villages isolated by landslides remained among the biggest challenges.View image in fullscreenEarthquake victims are treated in a temporary medical tent amid fears of aftershocks in Ruteng.Photograph: Juni Kriswanto/AFP/Getty ImagesThe quake also struck Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo national park, one of Indonesia’s best-known tourist destinations. Landslides blocked sections of the Trans-Flores Highway, a roughly 700km (435 mile) road linking communities across the mountainous island.Many residents continued to sleep outside rather than risk returning to damaged homes.“The shaking was terrifying, so intense that my house nearly collapsed,” said Anastasia Imad, a farmer in Labuan Bajo, speaking from a makeshift green tent beside her damaged home. “We feared the aftershocks would bring it down on us while we slept.”View image in fullscreenPeople in the coastal village of Nangahale in Sikka regency spent the night in a field.Photograph: Arnold Welianto/AFP/Getty ImagesTeams resumed searches on Sunday in areas that had remained inaccessible since the quake, particularly in Manggarai, East Manggarai and Nagekeo regencies.“We have cleared most landslides and reopened roads to previously isolated villages, although communication disruptions and power outages continue to hamper search efforts,” said Fathur Rahman, head of the search and rescue office in Maumere, the capital of Sikka regency.He said rescuers were focusing on searching the rubble of collapsed homes and other buildings for possible victims.Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions because of its location on the Pacific “ring of fire”, a horseshoe-shaped arc of seismic faults and volcanoes.Flores has experienced some of the country’s deadliest disasters. A powerful earthquake and tsunami in 1992 killed about 2,500 people on the island.In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake triggered a tsunami on Sulawesi that killed more than 4,400 people. In 2004, a magnitude 9.1 quake off Sumatra unleashed a tsunami that killed about 230,000 people in a dozen countries.Explore more on these topicsIndonesiaEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nazi artefacts still being sold online years after trade outlawed across Australia | Australia news | The Guardian
description: One seller says second world war memorabilia containing banned Nazi symbols is legal under exemptions to the laws
Author: Stephanie Convery
Headline: One seller says second world war memorabilia containing banned Nazi symbols is legal under exemptions to the laws
Content: Nazi paraphernalia remain for sale on Australian websites.Composite: suppliedView image in fullscreenNazi paraphernalia remain for sale on Australian websites.Composite: suppliedAustralia newsNazi artefacts still being sold online years after trade outlawed across AustraliaOne seller says second world war memorabilia containing banned Nazi symbols is legal under exemptions to the lawsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastStephanie ConverySun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNazi artefacts bearing prohibited symbols are being openly sold in Australia three years after the federal government made it illegal to do so, with vendors saying they are doing so for “educational” reasons.The government in 2023outlawed the display and tradeof items bearing the Nazi Hakenkreuz (swastika) and double-sig rune that was the logo of the Schutzstaffel (SS), after multiple states passed similar laws that banned the display of Nazi symbols and the performance of the Nazi salute.The laws included exemptions for religious, academic, educational, artistic, literary or scientific purposes.Guardian Australia has identified Australian sellers of military antiques listing German military items – including helmets, badges, medals, officer’s caps, flags and more – that appear to be from the Nazi era and which bear the Hakenkreuz or double-sig rune.The vendors, which include longtime dealers of military collectibles and Nazi objects, claimed to be selling the items for “educational” or “research purposes”.Kurt Coleman Military Antiques, a business with a registered address in Queensland’s Sunshine Coast region, had 25 pages of Nazi-era German military and related items for sale on its website as of this week.The listings included military booklets, pins, badges, rings, officer’s tunics, officer’s caps and weaponry with visible swastikas and other Nazi imagery.One of the highest-priced items was a white porcelain vase with an embossed Nazi eagle for $2,500. A 2-metre x 3.5-metre Nazi warship “battle flag” was listed for $2,000 but was “out of stock”, while a German Hitler Youth knife was listed for sale for $1,820.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhile the site’s landing page said he was “ALWAYS BUYING Military Antiques Medals, Militaria, Edged Weapons”, the webpage title – a commonly used field for search engine optimisation – said “Nazi Militaria For Sale, German Militaria, WW2 Militaria, Nazi Medals Australia”.All the items listed for sale at the time of writing appeared to be Nazi-related.The website claimed: “All items offered for sale are for educational purposes only. The seller does not endorse or promote any political ideology, and the items are presented solely as historical artifacts. Buyers are expected to use the items responsibly and in accordance with applicable laws.”The site appeared to have been operating for at least a year. An eBay page by the same name was listed as active since 2019, having sold approximately 44,000 items over that time. Listings on the eBay page at the time of writing included German war-related items, along with unrelated antiques and ephemera.Coleman has been approached for comment.Henry’s Military Collectibles, based in Western Australia, also had multiple German Nazi-era military items listed for sale, including multiple war merit crosses, belt buckles, and a Luftschutz (civil air defence) helmet. The items appear in the listing images to have stickers placed over the offending symbols.The website says Henry’s Military Collectibles “only deals products with historical value for collectors, museums and research purposes. We do not, in any case, associate or have association with National Socialism, the Third Reich period, Political Parties and/or military organisations. If you do have any association with the above, we would like you to leave the website and we ask you not to contact us.”Prior to the federal laws coming into force,owner Henry Fijolek told Guardian Australiathat Nazi items were always “strong sellers” and that they were never sold to “Nazi sympathisers”.Fijolek said by email this week that he believed he was operating within the bounds of the law, and felt he was qualified in making that interpretation as “I served in the Army as an officer for 37 years with 17 Years posted to the Australian Army History [unit]”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As stated in my disclaimer on my website I trade in these items without displaying the banned symbols and my intent is to trade in them within the allowed scope,” Fijolek said.“I know that there is some in the community that would to totally ban and eradicate the items however this is history and history regardless should never be eradicated as it serves to educate for the future.”A spokesperson for the Australian federal police said: “The AFP has engaged with a number of auction houses in relation to the sale and public display of items containing prohibited symbols. However, the AFP will not confirm details in relation to ongoing assessments and investigations relating to these matters.“People need to be aware of their legal obligations in relation to the public display or trading of items containing prohibited symbols.”‘Avalanche’ of demand for Nazi artefacts ahead of Australian ban on sale of hate symbolsRead moreAssociate professor Romain Fathi, a military historian at the Australian National University, said the collection of military and war-related objects has occurred for a very long time, but that military objects “are not neutral”.“The same object can have vastly different meanings based on the hand that is holding it, and the motivations of keeping the objects,” Fathi said.Military objects have often been used and displayed as propaganda for regimes, but can also be displayed as historical records, and “where they are contextualised, analysed and critiqued, they can be a critical vector of historical knowledge”.“Collecting militaria becomes more problematic when there’s a real attraction for war, for violence,” Fathi said. “Most collectors would have a few objects, but some devote their lives and resources to it.”Nazi or Third Reich collecting had different implications to collecting items from, for example, the French Revolution, Fathi said. “These objects are not playthings, they are objects of death, by a regime characterised by death. When individuals find power and fascination in them, that becomes very dangerous.”He continued: “If a Jewish or Holocaust Museum acquires Nazi paraphernalia to contextualise and evidence the genocide, there’s a deep moral, ethical dimension to this. The same act of collecting from a far-right activist – generally male – would be, evidently, deeply problematic and express sympathies that are dangerous to democratic societies.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsNazismAntisemitismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian health experts fear US vaccine scepticism is catching on as ‘anything Trump says filters through’ | Health | The Guardian
description: Australia records 3% fall in one-year-olds fully immunised against hepatitis B as downward trend continues, expert says
Author: Nick Visser
Headline: Australia records 3% fall in one-year-olds fully immunised against hepatitis B as downward trend continues, expert says
Content: Experts say the effects of Donald Trump’s rhetoric are already being seen in Australia, with more and more parents having concerns about vaccination.Photograph: Phanie/Sipa Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenExperts say the effects of Donald Trump’s rhetoric are already being seen in Australia, with more and more parents having concerns about vaccination.Photograph: Phanie/Sipa Press/AlamyHealthAustralian health experts fear US vaccine scepticism is catching on as ‘anything Trump says filters through’Australia records 3% fall in one-year-olds fully immunised against hepatitis B as downward trend continues, expert saysFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNick VisserSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian medical experts have warned a shift in child vaccination advice in the US is not grounded in science and could undo decades of public health advances.The US president, Donald Trump, signedan unprecedented executive ordercalling for American children to be vaccinated against fewer diseases, suggesting a link to autism despite no evidence. The official number of recommended immunisations for children would drop to 11, compared with 18 at the end of 2024.Six of those shots would be recommended for all children in the US, while the five others would only be recommended for high-risk children, including hepatitis B.Australia currently recommends 15 childhood vaccinations, all of which health experts say are key to protecting children’s health.Prof Julie Leask, a social scientist at the University of Sydney and an expert on social behaviours surrounding vaccination, said Trump’s decision, and his broader embrace of the US health secretary and vaccine opponent, Robert F Kennedy Jr, are threats to vaccine uptake in Australia.double quotation markColleagues are worried that we’re kind of going back to the futureProf Julie Leask“Anything Trump says filters through to Australia,” Leask said. “Australian parents and caregivers hear it, and it does affect a minority of people and makes them wonder about vaccines and their safety.”Leask, a trained midwife, has studied vaccination rates for decades. She said health professionals are already seeing the impacts of Trump’s rhetoric in Australia, with nurses saying they hear from more and more parents who have concerns about vaccination.“Some of my colleagues are worried that we’re kind of going back to the future,” she said.A national survey of Australian parents released in February showedparents were less accepting of routine childhood vaccinationsthan they were in the previous year.Figures from the Australian immunisation register show full childhood vaccination rates peaking between 2020 and 2021. The coverage rate for all children at five years old is now 92.6%, short of the 95% target.Lucy Clynes, the chief executive of Hepatitis Australia, is extremely concerned about the effect Trump’s policies have had on Australian vaccine confidence. The group analysed search term trends over the past 12 months and found whenever the US government makes comments undercutting the effectiveness or safety of vaccines, Australians head online in greater numbers looking to bolster those claims.“There has been a 3% drop in the number of one-year-olds who are fully immunised for hepatitis B in Australia, a downward trend since about 2020,” Clynes said. “People here see something that the US government has said and they start searching on Google or Instagram, and the results that they get are often wrong. They’re very scary.“When people start doing their own research on vaccines, it means they haven’t immediately trusted what their healthcare provider has told them … And that worries us.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump signs executive order with plan to reduce number of recommended childhood vaccinesRead moreHepatitis B is a viral infection of the liver and the most common blood-borne virus in Australia. Most people who get infected will develop chronic, lifelong infection that can, after many years, damage the liver and cause diseases including liver cancer and cirrhosis.There is no cure, and more than 230,000 Australians live with chronic hepatitis B infection.Vaccination offers a high degree of protection.
