Infants in Australia are recommended to get a course of four vaccines to prevent hepatitis B, including one at birth, which can prevent infection even if a mother is positive herself.Prof Ben Cowie, director of the WHO Collaborating Centre for Viral Hepatitis, says vaccination efforts for hepatitis B have been an incredible boon for public health in Australia, saving thousands of lives.“We know that [vaccination programs are] having a profound impact, particularly in high prevalence countries, many of which are in our region,” Cowie said.But vaccine hesitancy is rising and there is a downward trend in childhood vaccination rates, despite an inoculation like the hepatitis B jab being given to billions of people and shown to be incredibly safe and effective.“We can’t ignore that,” Cowie said.The Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases issued a statement for parents stressing the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) is safe and there is no scientific rationale to change the way that kids in Australia and New Zealand should receive it. Trump’s executive order means the single-injection shot will be split into three appointments.The body attached 10 published studies to the release, showing the MMR vaccine is scientifically safe and effective as given.“ASID encourages parents who have questions about vaccination to speak with their GP, paediatrician, immunisation nurse or other trusted healthcare professional,” the group said.“The science has not changed: MMR vaccination is a safe and effective way to protect children from measles, mumps and rubella.”Explore more on these topicsHealthDonald TrumpVaccines and immunisationnewsShareReuse this content

title: The PM called Sally McManus a giant of the labour movement. Now she just wants to go birding | Sally McManus | The Guardian
description: After securing wage rises for low-paid workers, weathering death threats and working with three PMs – the ACTU secretary is ready for a break
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: After securing wage rises for low-paid workers, weathering death threats and working with three PMs – the ACTU secretary is ready for a break
Content: Sally McManus at a rally of childcare workers demanding better pay and conditions in Sydney in 2022.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenSally McManus at a rally of childcare workers demanding better pay and conditions in Sydney in 2022.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPSally McManusThe PM called Sally McManus a giant of the labour movement. Now she just wants to go birdingAfter securing wage rises for low-paid workers, weathering death threats and working with three PMs – the ACTU secretary is ready for a breakFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 20.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSally McManus started her job as the country’s most powerful trade union leader amid howls of criticism.Shouted down for suggesting union members were right to break “unjust” industrial laws in a live TV interview, McManus quickly adjusted to the high-decibel work of being secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions.Now, nearly a decade later, she is ready to turn the volume down.“I’m looking forward to having a break,” McManus told Guardian Australia before handing over the job at the end of the month.“It’s been 33 years as a union official, 22 of them as a leader, and nine-and-a-half as ACTU secretary. It never stops.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailMcManus announced her departure last month, on the same day the ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, revealed plans to step down as well.Anthony Albanesedescribed both – the first all-female leadership team in the ACTU’s 99-year history – as“giants of the labour movement”.McManus has helped reshape Australia’s industrial landscape, pushing the Albanese government and business on a worker-friendly agenda.Along with O’Neil, she has helped lead campaigns for same job, same pay protections, laws giving workers the right to disconnect, wage theft criminalisation and ensuring minimum pay, insurance and safety standards for gig economy workers.Her tenure has spanned the Turnbull, Morrison and Albanese governments, economic disruption from the Covid-19 pandemic, Labor’s jobs and skills summit, allegations of corruption and lawlessness by union leaders, including the CFMEU, and, a year ago this week, the productivity roundtable convened by the treasurer, Jim Chalmers.View image in fullscreenThe ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, and the secretary, Sally McManus, during an economic reform roundtable last year.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPMcManus says some of her closest held victories includewage rises for low-paid workers, help for women and children affected by domestic violence and helping strengthen key industries including early childhood education and aged care.But the high-profile role has brought pressures.Since that first ABC TV interview on the day she was elected in March 2017, McManus has faced the “inner most horribleness” of critics – online and in real life.She has received death threats and tirades, a darker side of the job McManus says she tries to ignore.About 3 million workers on minimum wage to receive 4.75% pay rise in Fair Work Commission rulingRead more“I would say it has become 10 times, maybe 20 times, worse, and that’s got a lot to do with what happened with X and also just the continued monetisation of social media.“Back 10 years ago … you could actually have communities of like-minded people on social media, and not have to experience all the horribleness.”The job isn’t done, McManus says.She points to the rapidly shifting reality of work, including AI threatening the rights of employees. Having long advocated for tax reform in Australia, McManus wants more work on intergenerational equity and help for vulnerable people.She nominates Pauline Hanson’s growing political support as a priority for the labour movement, warning the One Nation leader would end unfair dismissal laws if the party ever secured power.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcManus considers a four-day work week realistic in the future.“If, in the end, AI becomes a wonderful thing and we don’t have to work as much because it’s replacing jobs, well, people still need to live and to participate in society.“The way to do that is to cut working hours with no loss of pay … and that’s something that we could actually do in Australia.”Asked about allegations of criminal behaviour and corruption within the CFMEU, McManus says a series of leaders in the controversial construction union had betrayed members.1:48Minimum wage increase of 5.2% welcomed by Anthony Albanese - video“Somewhere along the line, it’s hard to actually know when, the previous leaders of the CFMEU in at least three of the states completely walked away from union values and what was acceptable, for not just the majority but 95% of unions,” she said.“That whole experience just caused the rest of the union movement to really sharpen what that line is that we say cannot be crossed, and that’s corruption and that’s violence.”Victoria is preparing to initiate a royal commission into corruption on the government’s Big Build infrastructure program, expected to include evidence about CFMEU activities.McManus is blunt about the personalities involved.“I don’t consider them unionists. I don’t consider them to have union values. It’s easy for people to be performative unionists, to wear the gear and to sometimes talk the talk. [It’s] that much harder to walk the walk.”The 55-year-old says she is not at all tempted to enter politics. Instead, McManus plans to go bird watching and undergo surgery for a cochlear implant to fix hearing loss.“I’m not undertaking that lightly. It takes some significant attention in terms of rehab, and I want to give myself the best chance of getting as much of my hearing back as I can.”The incoming ACTU secretary, Melissa Donnelly, now the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union,will succeed McManus on 31 August.Explore more on these topicsSally McManusAustralian trade unionsLabor partyAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Logies 2026: Sam Pang wins gold and Sam Neill wins posthumous best actor at Australia’s TV awards | Logie awards | The Guardian
description: Neill takes award for performance in legal thriller The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer, at a ceremony dominated by wins for the ABC
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Neill takes award for performance in legal thriller The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer, at a ceremony dominated by wins for the ABC
Content: Sam Pang accepts the Gold Logie award for most popular personality on Australian television at the Logie awards on Sunday night.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEKView image in fullscreenSam Pang accepts the Gold Logie award for most popular personality on Australian television at the Logie awards on Sunday night.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEKLogie awardsLogies 2026: Sam Pang wins gold and Sam Neill wins posthumous best actor at Australia’s TV awardsNeill takes award for performance in legal thriller The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer, at a ceremony dominated by wins for the ABCLogies 2026 ceremony: the best moments and red carpet looks – in picturesSian CainSun 16 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 20.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Neill has won a posthumous best actor award at Australia’s biggest television awards, the Logies, with comedian Sam Pang taking home the night’s top honour, the Gold Logie award for most popular personality.Neill, whodied in July, won his posthumous Logie for best lead actor in a drama for his performance in legal thriller The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer. His close friend, the actor Heather Mitchell, accepted the award on his behalf.Logies 2026 ceremony: the best moments and red carpet looks – in picturesRead more“I’m so sorry I’m not Sam,” she said. “I know how much it would mean to him. This is an indication of his connection with his audience.”Mitchell said The Twelve, which Neill starred in for three seasons, “meant a great deal” to him.“He really relished the character of Brett Colby. He talked about it a lot, and he thought [Colby] was a very clever man, and also a sort of 007 kind of person. And that was Sam as well,” she said.View image in fullscreenHeather Mitchell pays tribute to Sam Neill onstage at the Logies.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEKPang, who is a panellist on quizshow Have You Been Paying Attention? and hosts The Front Bar and Sam Pang Tonight, joked: “I’ve got lots of people to thank tonight and I’ll probably forget some names. If I do forget you, I’m sorry, but maybe also have a think about how much you did.”The 52-year-old congratulated his fellow nominees for the top award: A Current Affair host Ally Langdon, comedian Julia Morris, ABC presenter Lisa Millar, MasterChef judge Poh Ling Yeow, presenter Robert Irwin and Tipping Point Australia host Todd Woodbridge.Pang was presented the award by Magda Szubanski, who made a surprise appearance after recently announcing she was in remission afterbeing treated for cancer.View image in fullscreenMagda Szubanski in character as her Kath & Kim role Sharon Strzelecki with Robert Irwin onstage.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEKThe Logies have historically been unusual awards, with a mix of popularly voted awards – which celebrities have always actively campaigned to win – and peer-voted awards. Last year the voting system was overhauled so that the “best” categories – formerly called “most outstanding” – are now determined by a combined score: 50% of which is peer assessment and audience data supplied by the broadcasters, and 50% of which is by popular vote.The Gold Logie and the “most popular” award categories remain determined entirely by popular vote.Irwin, who hosted this year’s ceremony, won his first Logie, taking home the Bert Newton award for most popular presenter for his role on I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out Of Here, which was recently cancelled by Network 10. Irwin thanked his family, who he said were watching remotely from a crocodile research expedition in north Queensland, as well as Australia Zoo, where he has lived since childhood.“My heart beats for Australia Zoo,” he said. “I bleed khaki … This is for my Australia Zoo family – 500 back at home, who back me, who work towards a mission that my dad started.”Brooke Satchwell won best lead actress in a drama for her role in Stan seriesDear Life, while Claudia Karvan won best supporting actress in a drama for her role as the mother of a trans child in SBS showHomebodies. Karvan used her speech to pay tribute to trans children and their parents, saying: “May their voices always be heard.”Simon Baker won best supporting actor for his performance in The Narrow Road to the Deep North – his second Logie win after his first in 1993, which was “somewhere in the shed”, he said. He thanked director Justin Kurzel and his castmates, joking: “There’s not a bad performance in this thing and I can say that because I have just won an award.”View image in fullscreenLila McGuire accepts the Graham Kennedy award for most popular new talent for her role in Goolagong.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEKThe ABC had a strong night, winning eight Logies.Goolagong, the ABC drama about the two-time Wimbledon winner Evonne Goolagong Cawley, won best miniseries, while the show’s star, Whadjuk and Ballardong Noongar actor Lila McGuire, won the Graham Kennedy award for most popular new talent.ABC comedy Dog Park won two awards: best actress in a comedy for Celia Pacquola and best scripted comedy program. Muster Dogs took best structured reality program,The Assembly won best factual program, Australian Story won best current affairs program and Play School won best children’s program.RFDS won best drama program for the second time, beating the likes of Heartbreak High and Mystery Road: Origin.In an unexpected turn, Bruce McAvaney lost the inaugural Bruce McAvaney award for most popular sports presenter to the former tennis player Jelena Dokic, who won for her work presenting at the Australian Open, Melbourne Cup, Wimbledon, Roland Garros, US Open and Cross Court.A Current Affair presenter Ally Langdon won the Ray Martin award for most popular news or public affairs presenter, for the second year in the row. Karl Stefanovic, who was nominated for the category for his role on Today, was not present, having told the Daily Telegraph that attending would be a “tad awkward” after beingdumped from his $2.8m contractat Nine for embracing far-right activist Tommy Robinson on his podcast. Stefanovic was a popular, recurring topic onstage, with Irwin joking that an empty chair had been left for him “on the far right”.View image in fullscreenDeborah Mailman accepts the Logie Hall of Fame award.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEKActor Deborah Mailman became the first ever Indigenous Australian nominated into the Logies Hall of Fame. Mailman, who has won six Logies in her career, paid tribute to her parents, who “met my dream with nothing but love and encouragement” when she was a would-be actor growing up in Mt Isa.“Every time I made that 24 and half hour bus trip back to Mt Isa from Brisbane, my mum and dad were always there waiting for me, so this is for them,” she said in an emotional speech.In addition to Mailman, broadcaster and producer Andrew Denton and the show A Country Practice were also inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame.Logie awards 2026: the full list of winnersGold Logie for most popular personality:Sam PangBert Newton award for most popular presenter:Robert Irwin, I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out Of Here!, Network 10Graham Kennedy award for most popular new talent:Lila McGuire, Goolagong, ABCRay Martin award for most popular news or public affairs presenter:Ally Langdon, A Current Affair, The Great Debate and Election 2025: Australia Decides; Nine NetworkBruce McAvaney award for most popular sports presenter:Jelena Dokic, 2026 Australian Open, 2025 Melbourne Cup, Wimbledon 2025, Roland Garros 2025, US Open 2025 and Cross Court 2025; Nine NetworkBest lead actor in a drama:Sam Neill, The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer, Binge/FoxtelBest lead actress in a drama:Brooke Satchwell, Dear Life, StanBest supporting actor in a drama:Simon Baker, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, Prime VideoBest supporting actress in a drama:Claudia Karvan, Homebodies, SBSBest actor in a comedy:Steve Bisley, Deadloch, Prime VideoBest actress in a comedy:Celia Pacquola, Dog Park, ABCBest drama program:RFDS, Seven NetworkBest miniseries or telemovie:Goolagong, ABCBest entertainment program:Tipping Point Australia, Nine NetworkBest current affairs program:Australian Story, ABCBest scripted comedy program:Dog Park, ABCBest comedy entertainment program:Have You Been Paying Attention?, Network 10Best competition reality program:MasterChef Australia, Network 10Best structured reality program:Muster Dogs, ABCBest lifestyle program:Travel Guides, Nine NetworkBest news coverage or public affairs report:Bondi Terror Attack, 7NEWS and Sunrise, Seven NetworkBest factual or documentary program:The Assembly, ABCBest sports coverage:Australian Open 2026, Nine NetworkBest children’s program:Play School, ABCExplore more on these topicsLogie awardsAustralian televisionTelevisionAustralian mediaAustralian Broadcasting CorporationNetflixMagda SzubanskinewsShareReuse this content

title: Five teenagers killed after car driven on wrong side of Irish motorway  | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Head-on collision between two vehicles on M9 in County Kildare also injured four other people, say police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Head-on collision between two vehicles on M9 in County Kildare also injured four other people, say police
Content: Emergency services at the scene of the collision, which happened at junction 3 of the motorway near Athy.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenEmergency services at the scene of the collision, which happened at junction 3 of the motorway near Athy.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAIrelandFive teenagers killed after car driven on wrong side of Irish motorwayHead-on collision between two vehicles on M9 in County Kildare also injured four other people, say policeNadeem BadshahSun 16 Aug 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive teenagers have died and four other people have been seriously injured in a crash involving a car driving in the wrong direction on a motorway in the Republic ofIreland, police said.Gardaí confirmed the bodies of the youths, all male, had been removed from the scene of the two-vehicle collision, which happened at about 3am on Sunday on the M9 in County Kildare.The force said the occupants of the second vehicle involved, three women, two in their 30s and one in her 20s, and a boy, all remained in hospital with serious injuries.The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, described the head-on collision between the two cars as “horrific” and said “in some cases” vehicles were being driven on the wrong side of motorways for social media likes.Last weekend, nine people were injured in a head-on collision on the M50 in Dublin involving a car travelling in the wrong direction.Describing Sunday’s crash, Kelly said: “These family members were travelling innocently when they were struck by a vehicle being driven the wrong way down the motorway.“This horrific incident, after the recent collision on the M50, shows how irresponsible and dangerous driving on the wrong side of the motorway is.“That, of course, should be self-evident, but what makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes, regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves.”He added: “As this particular incident has been referred to Fiosrú, the police ombudsman, I am constrained in what I can say in detail about this incident, but I know that gardaí do what they can to stop such vehicles while also taking into consideration all other road users.“Gardaí are put in a really challenging situation dealing with such incidents.”Officers are investigating the circumstances of the crash, which happened at junction 3 of the motorway, near Athy, at about 3am on Sunday.Emergency services had been alerted to reports of a vehicle travelling southbound on the M9 northbound carriageway.Earlier, a Garda Síochána spokesperson said the female driver and front-seat passenger of the second car had been taken to Tallaght university hospital, and were in a critical condition.A female rear-seat passenger, in her 20s, was taken to St Luke’s general hospital in a serious condition.The third passenger, a child, was taken to the Children’s Health Ireland at Crumlin in Dublin, also in a serious condition.The bodies of the teenagers who died were taken to Naas general hospital, where postmortem examinations were due to take place.Gardaí appealed for anyone who witnessed the collision or has dashcam footage to come forward.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeRoad safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: Wildfires kill two in Greece and torch Belgian nature reserve | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Couple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near Liège
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Couple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near Liège
Content: A firefighting helicopter drops water over a wildfire on the island of Salamina, near Athens.Photograph: Yannis Panagopoulos/Eurokinissi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighting helicopter drops water over a wildfire on the island of Salamina, near Athens.Photograph: Yannis Panagopoulos/Eurokinissi/AFP/Getty ImagesWildfiresWildfires kill two in Greece and torch Belgian nature reserveCouple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near LiègeAngela Giuffridaand agenciesSun 16 Aug 2026 17.27 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn elderly couple died in fires on the Greek island of Salamis on Sunday and Belgium is battling its largest modern-day wildfire at an inaccessible area nearGermany, in the latest wave of European wildfires.The couple died outside their home in the Peristeria beach area of Salamis, Greece’s coastguard said. More than 500 people were ordered to evacuate.Map of Greek wildfireIn Spain, a soldier died on Sunday while helping efforts to extinguish a large wildfire in Aragon, authorities said. French reinforcements were due to help contain the wildfire in the north-eastern region, which has raged for a week and threatened a 1,000-year-old monastery.View image in fullscreenA wildfire in the area of Las Peñas de Riglos in Aragon, Spain.Photograph: UME/AFP/Getty ImagesInBelgium, a wildfire that broke out on Friday in the High Fens, a large nature reserve popular with hikers, had ravaged about 3,000 hectares (7,400 acres) of land and was encroaching on the border with Germany by early Sunday morning.About 600 people in the municipalities of Waimes and Bütgenbach, in Liège province, were told on Saturday to evacuate from their homes, and tourists were also advised to leave, as winds shifted and smoke spread.Of those who followed the order, about 20 spent the night in a sports hall, while others sought refuge with family and friends.Hervé Jamar, the governor of Liège, said more than 250 firefighters and emergency staff were involved in the operation, including firefighters from Germany.Map of Belgian wildfireFarmers have also been helping to battle the blaze, using their tractors to pull in water from Lake Robertville.Air support, provided by two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden and four helicopters – two from Belgium and two from the Netherlands – is crucial owing to the nature reserve’s complex and fragile terrain, which is made up of dense forest, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy firefighting vehicles risk sinking.Access to Lake Bütgenbach was prohibited on Sunday to allow the aircraft to refill.View image in fullscreenAir support in fighting the fire in the High Fens nature reserve is crucial owing to the complex terrain where heavy vehicles risk sinking.Photograph: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/ShutterstockAuthorities described the conditions as still challenging, although two fire fronts towards Jalhay and Monschau were now under control, said Belgium’s interior minister, Bernard Quintin, after visiting the crisis centre in Vottem on Sunday afternoon.“On this third day of fighting the fires, all resources remain mobilised on the ground,” he wrote on X, and he thanked all those involved.“We can also count on the solidarity of our European partners … thank you to everyone who mobilised to fight the fires. United, we are stronger.”Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?Read moreThe fire, described by officials as the largest in Belgium’s modern history, began in an area that in 1911 was badly affected by massive wildfires during a drought.In Portugal, hundreds of firefighters were battling a series of blazes. At a wildfire near Dine, a village close to the border with Spain, five firefighters were injured when their vehicle caught fire, local media reported. Other fires were burning near the Spanish border, including at Boticas and Chavez.Human-caused climate breakdown issupercharging extreme weatheraround the world, driving more frequent and deadlier disasters from heatwaves to floods to wildfires.Much of Europe is experiencing a new period of intense heat, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.On Friday a fire engulfed ⁠homes in a Croatian holiday resort, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of “very extreme” wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.Hundreds more people were evacuated from villages in western Germany and south-west France, while stranded holidaymakers were picked up from beaches threatened by flames in Greece and the army rescued historical relics in Spain.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresEuropeExtreme weatherGreeceBelgiumGermanynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow | Russia | The Guardian
description: Kyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capital
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Kyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capital
Content: 0:56Warehouse near Moscow on fire after Ukrainian drone attack – videoRussiaUkrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says MoscowKyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capitalDan Sabbaghin KyivSun 16 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine has launched one of its largest drone attacks since the start of the war, causing a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow and killing at least six people overnight, according to Russian authorities.The defence ministry in Moscow said it had shot down 1,478 Ukrainian drones in the past 24 hours – the highest ever total claimed – in an escalating air war in which seven Ukrainians were also killed asRussiabombed 13 locations inside the country.A huge fire engulfed a 250,000 sq metre building near Podolsk, 25 miles south of Moscow’s city centre, belonging to the Wildberries distribution company. The facility was disabled as a result, Ukraine’s military said.Sergei Sobyanin, the mayor of Moscow, said 600 drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, of which 201 were destroyed. One person was reported killed in the region, while Ukraine said a second warehouse at nearby Domodedovo was also targeted.MapThe Russian news agency RIA Novosti reported that the figure was the largest daily total claimed by the defence ministry, exceeding a record that had been set only the day before, though the figure is probably exaggerated and could not be verified.Experts said Russian numbers needed to be treated with caution but added that the scale of damage caused overnight nevertheless demonstrated how rapidly Ukraine had expanded its long-range attack capabilities in 2026.Serhii Kuzan, the chair of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a thinktank, said Russian authorities “deliberately inflate their figures” to make exaggerated claims about the effectiveness of their air defence.But he said that “against the backdrop of increased production of Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles, both the number of strikes and the scale of Ukrainian weaponry’s deployment are on the rise” as the war continues.Kuzan argued that it was “quite possible” it was the largest-scale attack on the Moscow region, and it was “at least on a par” with theMay strikes on an oil refineryin the Kapotnya area near Moscow.View image in fullscreenFirefighters try to extinguish a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesA rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including theFlamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing dronefrom Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles from its border.Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv faces missile barrage after Zelenskyy targets Russian satellite networkRead moreUkraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it still does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles fired frequently by Moscow.At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to a rise in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter.Kuzan said: “With every successful strike, Russia’s economic and military capabilities are diminished, and the Kremlin faces a new dilemma: how to counter this in a war of attrition.”In the past month, Kyiv has shifted focus to attacking facilities linked to Wildberries, used widely by businesses to support online retail. Ukraine says the warehouses are used by the military for logistics, though they also store stock sold by large and small Russian businesses.Ukraine’s military said on Sunday it had disabled seven out of 10 of the company’s largest warehouses in an effort to hurt the Russian economy and affect ordinary citizens financially, in a strike conducted with FP-1 drones.View image in fullscreenA Wildberries employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire.Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty ImagesFive people were reported to have been killed in Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, and the local governor said a further 150 incoming drones had been destroyed. Ukraine said it had targeted a factory that produced rocket fuel in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, causing a fire there.Russian drone and missile attacks killed two people in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, while a Spanish F-18 jet shot down what appeared to be a Russia drone that had crossed over the border into Romania.The Spanish fighter was part of a Nato patrol mission and shot down the drone at about 5am after it crossed into Romanian airspace. “The drone appears to be Russian,” a Nato military spokesperson said.Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region, said the assault on the region was “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory”. Video footage on social media showed a fast fire raging across the Wildberries warehouse complex.Russian attacks on Ukraine also killed two in the Sumy border region and three others across the country. A ballistic missile attack on Kyiv shortly before 3am injured six and caused several fires in the capital.A blaze caused by the attacks destroyed a large part of the Petrovka book market in the Obolonskyi district in Kyiv overnight, with some booksellers reporting they had lost their entire stock in the incident.View image in fullscreenFirefighters work to put out a fire at a book market in Kyiv.Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP“There is nothing. Nobody has anything left,” said Natalya, a bookstore owner who was interviewed by Ukraine’s Hromadske website. “Everything burned down. I was selling foreign language [textbooks] for schoolchildren. We were waiting for September so that everyone would have textbooks … But what happened happened.”Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, praised the work of the country’s emergency services and accused the Russians of attacking ordinary people. “Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” he said in a social media post.Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles at Ukrainian cities and communities over the past week, most of them ballistic missiles of various types.Though Ukraine is effective at stopping slower-moving drones, it has little to no defence against high-speed ballistics, its stock of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles – the only weapons capable of knocking them out – having been run down.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in small Polish village | Poland | The Guardian
description: Hundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa
Content: The 55.6-metre statue of the Virgin Mary towers over the village of Konotopie, Poland.Photograph: Adam Burakowski/East News/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe 55.6-metre statue of the Virgin Mary towers over the village of Konotopie, Poland.Photograph: Adam Burakowski/East News/ShutterstockPolandEurope’s tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in small Polish villageHundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech WałęsaAssociated PressSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe’s tallest was inaugurated on Saturday in a small Polish village, in the presence of the anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa.Hundreds of people took part in the consecration of the monument, which towers 55.6 metres (182ft) over Konotopie in centralPoland, a village of fewer than 150 people.While helicopters scattered miniature red roses over the crowd, priests in white robes celebrated mass and the Mazowsze folk ensemble sang and danced to traditional Polish music.The statue is taller – if less dramatically located – than the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which measures 38 metres including its pedestal. The Polish monument’s height includes a crown-shaped 15-metre pedestal.It also surpasses another large-scale religious monument in Poland, the Christ the King statue in the western town of Świebodzin, which was revealed in 2010 and, with the mound it stands on, is 52.5 metres tall.There is a taller statue of the Virgin Mary in the Philippines, which measures 98 metres. But the new one in Poland is believed to be the largest of its kind in Europe.View image in fullscreenThe statue was paid for by a wealthy couple who live nearby.Photograph: Agnieszka Bielecka/EPAWałęsa, who won the Nobel peace prize for his leadership of the Polish anti-communist resistance as the head of the Solidarity trade union and was later Poland’s president, had a front-row seat during the inauguration ceremony.“This is the end of my path,” said Wałęsa, 82, suggesting the causes he had long championed, including democracy and the Catholic faith, were now completed. “I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary.”During his Solidarity days, Wałęsa famously wore a Black Madonna pin and he has often credited his faith in God with giving him the strength to fight against communism.Most Poles identify as Catholic. The church played a powerful role in public life after the fall of communism in 1989, benefiting from the prestige it earned through its support of the anti-communist opposition.The country is the homeland of Saint John Paul II, who was pope from 1978 until his death in 2005. A huge statue of him – but much smaller than the one of Mary – was revealed more than a decade ago in the city of Częstochowa.The influence of religion in public life has gradually declined in recent years, particularly among younger people and in urban areas. However, the Catholic church remains influential, especially in rural communities and among older generations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWiesław Mering, a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who attended the ceremony, said: “I cannot help but notice the weakening of the institution of the church, a withdrawal of specific social categories from Catholicism, and this hurts me. The history ofChristianityhas ups and downs, but this place is a reminder that Mary won’t give up on Poland.”View image in fullscreenVisitors descend from the viewing platform inside the statue.Photograph: Adam Burakowski/East News/ShutterstockThe statue was commissioned by Roman Karkosik, a wealthy Polish businessman, and his wife, Grażyna. The couple live in a small palace a few miles from Konotopie.Roman Karkosik, an entrepreneur whose ventures included plastic bottle manufacturing in the 1990s, amassed a fortune through investments on the Warsaw stock exchange to become one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals.The couple have said the monument is an expression of their gratitude to God. “The statue will be for all people,” Grażyna Karkosik said. “Each of us coming to see it will think more deeply about their own lives, not only about God.”Local authorities hope the monument will become an important pilgrimage site and a tourist destination. The statue has a viewing platform built inside its pedestal.Explore more on these topicsPolandCatholicismChristianityReligionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina stolen from Sicilian museum | Art | The Guardian
description: Theft of four works on national holiday described as wound to historical memory and cultural identity of city of Messina
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Theft of four works on national holiday described as wound to historical memory and cultural identity of city of Messina
Content: The five surviving panels of Antonello’sPolittico di San Gregorio –three of which were stolen on Saturday.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe five surviving panels of Antonello’sPolittico di San Gregorio –three of which were stolen on Saturday.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/ReutersArtRenaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina stolen from Sicilian museumTheft of four works on national holiday described as wound to historical memory and cultural identity of city of MessinaLorenzo Tondoin PalermoSun 16 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour of the most important works of art by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.Thievesgained access to the Regional Museum of Messina, or MuMe, on Saturday evening, possibly capitalising on attention being focused on La Vara, a huge religious festival that takes place in the city on 15 August, when Italy marks the Ferragosto national holiday.Bypassing the alarm systems, the gang broke into a security display box and stole four wood panels painted by Antonello, who is widely credited withchanging the course of Renaissance art.Thieves took three of the five surviving panels that made up an altarpiece known as thePolittico di San Gregorio, one of the Sicilian painter’s most important works.View image in fullscreenThe fourth, smaller stolen work, which depicts Virgin and Child.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/Reuters“It is an extremely serious and significant loss,” said Marisa Mercurio, the director of the museum. “They have stolen works of enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance, not only for Messina but for Sicily as a whole. All we can do now is hope they are recovered as soon as possible.”Originally composed of six panels created for the Monastero di San Gregorio, which was destroyed in the 1908 Messina earthquake, the altarpiece was the only work by the Sicilian painter never to have left his home city.A fourth work was taken from a secure display case: a small double-sided painting depicting the Virgin and Child with a Franciscan monk on one side and Christ on the other.The painting had belonged to the Wilhelm Soldan collection and was sold by Christie’s to the Sicilian regional government in 2003, the year it was attributed to Antonello.The haul could have been even greater: six paintings were stolen in total, but, inexplicably, two of the panels were abandoned on a low wall outside the museum.Born around ​1430, Antonello trained in Naples where he studied the works of Provençal and Flemish artists, whose influence is apparent in his works.“Antonello was instrumental in bringing Flemish oil-painting techniques toItaly, making possible a new softness, delicate glazing and subtle shading,” said Valentina Certo, an art historian affiliated with the University of Messina and author of the illustrated children’s book The Workshop of Antonello da Messina. “Even on very small panels, he was capable of extraordinary precision and detail.”View image in fullscreenThe grounds of the Regional Museum of Messina.Photograph: Danilo Arnone/Reuters“The overnight theft is a wound inflicted on the historical memory and cultural identity of the city of Messina,” she added. “These were works that had survived the earthquake, destruction and five centuries of history. To see them taken from the public in this way makes the loss impossible to measure in purely economic terms.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn 28 December 1908, the city of Messina was struck by what is still considered the deadliest natural catastrophe in modern European history: a 7.1-magnitude earthquake lasting 37 seconds that killed half its population and levelled much of the city.Along with homes, churches and monuments, invaluable historical sources and documents were lost, including works by Antonello.In February, the Italian government secured a rare Antonello masterpiece at auction in New York,spending $14.9m (£11m) on his Ecce Homo. The painting, sold at Sotheby’s, is an intenselyhuman portrait of the suffering Christ, believed to have been completed in about 1460.Prosecutors in Messina have opened an investigation into the theft. Police sources said the museum was fitted with several surveillance cameras and that the works were protected by a sophisticated alarm system. Investigators are examining several lines of inquiry, including whether the paintings were stolen for the illicit art market.According to the state news agency Ansa, investigators are also considering the possibility that the theft was carried out on commission for an art dealer.The theft took place after Italian police on Friday hadrecovered three paintingsby the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that werestolen earlier this yearfrom a private museum near the northern city of Parma.Explore more on these topicsArtItalyEuropePaintingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jared Kushner meets with Hamas ahead of talks with Netanyahu on Gaza | Jared Kushner | The Guardian
description: Trump’s son-in-law and envoy held rare meeting with Hamas chief in Egypt in push for progress on ceasefire
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump’s son-in-law and envoy held rare meeting with Hamas chief in Egypt in push for progress on ceasefire
Content: Jared Kushner speaks during the 56th annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on 22 January 2026.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPAView image in fullscreenJared Kushner speaks during the 56th annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on 22 January 2026.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPAJared KushnerJared Kushner meets with Hamas ahead of talks with Netanyahu on GazaTrump’s son-in-law and envoy held rare meeting with Hamas chief in Egypt in push for progress on ceasefireAssociated PressSun 16 Aug 2026 18.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy,Jared Kushner, held a rare meeting withHamas’s political chief on Sunday inEgypt, in a new diplomatic effort to make progress in the stalled Gaza ceasefire. Kushner will meet on Monday with Benjamin Netanyahu, who is under pressure after rejecting the new 15-point, US-backed road map.The talks aim to salvage the plan for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw from the Palestinian territory shattered bywar.At stake are the lives of some 2 million people in Gaza and reconstruction of the crowded enclave now largely controlled by Israeli forces, more than 10 months since the ceasefire ended major military operations. Ameetingbetween Kushner, fellow envoy Steve Witkoff and Hamas leaders in Egypt last yearhelpedclinchthe ceasefire, whose progress until now had been stalled over the key issue of Hamas’s disarmament.The over two-hour meeting inEgyptwith Hamas’s political chief, Khalil al-Hayya, was confirmed by a regional official and a Hamas official, both speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to reporters. Kushner was one of a trio of envoys meeting with al-Hayya, with officials from mediating countries Egypt, Qatar and Turkey also there.Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his alliesRead moreHamas in a statement later called on mediators and the US-createdBoard of Peaceoverseeing the ceasefire to “compel” Israel to approve the road map for next steps.Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, last weekrejectedthe 15-point plan in a rare publicshow of defianceagainst the Trump administration, Israel’s closest ally.Kushner; Tony Blair, the former British prime minister; and Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace director, are to meet with Netanyahu on Monday, according to a source familiar with the plans and a diplomatic source. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.Several regional powers including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates issued a joint statement condemning Israel’s rejection of the road map, saying: “Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza.” Other signers included Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia and the ceasefire mediators.View image in fullscreenEgyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi receives Jared Kushner in New Alamein, Egypt, on Sunday, in the presence of foreign minister Badr Abdelatty and general intelligence service chief Hassan Rashad.Photograph: Egyptian President Office/APAImages/ShutterstockThe foreign ministers’ statement called on the Board of Peace and the US to take “immediate and concrete measures” to keep any party from obstructing the plan’s implementation.Kushner’s meeting with theHamasleader aimed at ensuring the militant group’s commitment to the road map, particularly disarmament, before his meeting with Netanyahu, the regional official said.The Hamas official said the group is committed and waiting for mediators to start the 14-day negotiation period to work out a timetable for implementation. That period requires all parties’ approval of the road map to begin.The Hamas official also said the Hamas leader demanded that Israel halt its attacks onGazaand withdraw to the so-called “yellow line” dividing the territory before beginning implementation. The yellow line was never precisely defined. Israeli forces have moved beyond it and now control about 60% of Gaza.In May, Netanyahusaidthe next step was to move to 70% control, with Israel “tightening the grip” on Hamas “from every direction”.Israel has killedmore than 1,200 Palestiniansin Gaza, and wounded more than 4,100 sinceagreeingto the ceasefire on 10 October 2025, according to Gaza’s health ministry.The White House referred questions about Kushner’s meetings to the Board of Peace, which did not immediately comment. The Tony Blair Institute did not comment.BBC seeks to subpoena Trump children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuitRead moreUnder the road map, Hamas would hand over weapons to the Palestinian technocratic committee meant to oversee daily operations in the territory. The committee has not yet entered Gaza. But Hamas has linked the surrender of its heaviest weapons to the creation of a Palestinian state, something Israel’s current government rejects.The road map involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. But Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed.That stance leaves other elements of the ceasefire on hold, including reconstruction and the deployment of international forces to separate Israeli forces from committee-controlled areas.Netanyahu faces a challengingelectionon 27 October as he tries to hold on to power with a coalition that includes ministers taking a harsh line on Gaza, and it’s not clear whether he will take decisive steps on the ceasefire before then. Also coming up is the three-year anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October.Netanyahu’s Likud party on Sunday responded to the statement by regional powers by claiming “Arab states want to topple” Netanyahu so that centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot and center-left party leader Yair Golan “will give them everything they want. That will not happen.”Robert Mackey contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsJared KushnerHamasIsrael-Gaza warTrump administrationGazaIsraelEgyptnewsShareReuse this content

title: Taliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identity | Afghanistan | The Guardian
description: UK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisals
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: UK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisals
Content: Hamid (not his real name) worked for the Afghan national police unit alongside the British military.View image in fullscreenHamid (not his real name) worked for the Afghan national police unit alongside the British military.AfghanistanTaliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identityUK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisalsHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by aMinistry of Defenceleak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in anaccidental 2022 leakby an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.Hamid said he had received a number of threats from theTaliban, including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements.View image in fullscreenTaliban security personnel in Kandahar. It is nearly five years since the group retook political power in Afghanistan.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty ImagesThe MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal.Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme.“Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.”Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on15 August 2021after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed.View image in fullscreenHamid lives in hiding and says the emotional impact has been ‘devastating’.Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said.Abbas fought the Taliban alongside US and Australian troops. Now exiled in Iran, he feels abandonedRead more“Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.”After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain”.“It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said.Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said.“The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship.“I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.”An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission inAfghanistan, and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria.“Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.”Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsAfghanistanTalibanMinistry of DefenceSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform accused of targeting the most vulnerable with £50bn benefit cut | Benefits | The Guardian
description: Robert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Robert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’
Content: Robert Jenrick said it was ‘just plain immoral’ to pay social security to non-British people.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert Jenrick said it was ‘just plain immoral’ to pay social security to non-British people.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesBenefitsReform accused of targeting the most vulnerable with £50bn benefit cutRobert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’Rowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 16 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been accused of excluding the most vulnerable from society and punishing non-Britons living in the UK as it prepared to outline £50bn of cuts to benefits for disabled people and foreign nationals.Robert Jenrick, Reform’s finance spokesperson, will detail the plans for £20bn of cuts to disability benefits overall, as well as another £21bn from stopping foreign nationals – including EU citizens with settled status – claiming almost any benefits, among other cuts.The party said the plans were aimed at reducing the welfare bill by a quarter, with personal independence payments (Pip) replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”.It said “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by councils and mayors.In relation to foreign nationals, the plans extendproposals set out by Nigel Faragelast year in which he claimed that banning migrants from claiming some benefits and scrapping indefinite leave to remain would save £234bn over several decades.Jenrick’s policy paper goes further by stopping foreign-born households claiming universal credit, housing benefit, pension credit, jobseeker’s allowance, child benefit, free childcare, free school meals or disability benefits.The paper says the change would save the taxpayer £21bn a year by the fifth year of the policy, and would also apply to those with EU settled status. However, foreign-born parents with British-born children would still be eligible for child benefit and free school meals.Best for Britain, the pro-EU campaign group, said denying benefits to those with indefinite leave to remain would tear up Britain’s EU withdrawal agreement.Tom Brufatto, the executive director of policy at the organisation, said: “Ourpollingshows that people do want to renegotiate our relationship with Europe, but by moving closer, not by damaging ties with vital allies and punishing our neighbours, colleagues and friends who have settled status here.”Disability benefits system ‘not working’ Timms review findsRead moreJenrick claimed paying benefits to non-British people was “plain immoral” – even though many would have paid into the tax system through working. He also wrote in the Telegraph over the weekend that the amount spent on disability benefits was “not generosity … it is suicidal empathy”.However, Jenrick was accused by campaigners of making life harder for disabled people and of not understanding that it would not save money.Rachael Maskell, the Labour MP who led the campaign against previous disability benefit cuts under Keir Starmer, said: “When Pip helps people go to work, play a role in our society and simply live, threatening to remove Pip demonstrates that Reform do not want disabled people to play a full role in our society.“Instead, Labour is working with disabled people throughthe Timms reviewto optimise the impact of Pip to ensure both taxpayers and disabled people get real value out of the system.“Instead of making it harder for disabled people, who already experience significant financial deprivation, they should spend time learning of the benefit it brings.”Linda Burnip, the co-founder of Disabled People Against Cuts, said previous attempts to replace disability benefits with cheaper options had not been successful.“Originally the Tories scrapped disability living allowance and replaced it with Pip, aiming to save 20% from the social security bill,” she said.“However, this obviously has failed and the major problem with Reform’s crude plans to save money by denying payments to disabled people is that they fail to understand that a relatively small payment, which supports someone, could result in a massive saving overall from the public purse.“It could, for example, mean someone with a mental health condition is able to remain living safely in the community rather than needing to spend weeks or even months in a hospital for which private firms often charge around £12,000 per person a week.”Labour described the plans to cut disability benefits as “fantasy economics” that would “strip support” from disabled people and shift the costs of employing people with sickness or a disability on to employers through an insurance-based model.Mothin Ali, the Green party deputy leader, said the “establishment parties are all trying to outdo each other when it comes to who can be the most xenophobic, who can punch down the hardest to the most vulnerable in our country, and who can cut the most support from disabled people”.He added: “It is cowardly to take from the most defenceless when we should be taxing the super-wealthy, including those who are in the privileged position of accepting £5m donations,” he added, referring to Farage, the leader of Reform UK.Meanwhile, the Conservatives, who are trying to show they are taking a tough stance on welfare, said Reform’s announcement was “cobbled together” and claimed only the Tories had a “credible plan to save £23bn from welfare alongside our root and branch review of sickness benefits”.Explore more on these topicsBenefitsReform UKDisabilityRobert JenrickNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s been very tough’: hope of progress in gruelling battle against south Wales wildfire | Wales | The Guardian
description: Efforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the future
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Efforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the future
Content: Military personnel cut fire breaks to minimise the spread of the flames.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMilitary personnel cut fire breaks to minimise the spread of the flames.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianWales‘It’s been very tough’: hope of progress in gruelling battle against south Wales wildfireEfforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the futureBethan McKernanWales correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than three weeks after it began burning and two days after the military deployed to the area, there is hope that the huge wildfire on the hillside above the Ebbw valley village of Blaenavon may finally be coming under control.Emergency workers and soldiers described a gruelling battle against the deep-seated peat fire that has spread over 4,000 hectares (9,800 acres), putting lives, farmland and property at risk.At least 13 other fires have blazed across the valleys this weekend, prompting SouthWalesfire and rescue service to ask for military support – the first UK military deployment to deal with wildfires since 2018.Nationally, approximately 36 fires are still burning, 11 of which have been declared major incidents. Extreme heat and a lack of rain, supercharged by the climate crisis, have made this summer the busiest on record for wildfires in the UK, placing significant pressure on crews and resources.Wildfire breaks out in Ebbw valley, south WalesJamie Windsor, a group commander at Ebbw Vale station, said underground layers of peat beneath the orange and purple heather on the Blaenavon hillside had made the fire harder to put out.“It burns very deep, the peat, and because it’s been so hot, it’s not cooling down at night. You think you’ve got a handle on it but it’s burning underground and it just pops up again somewhere else,” he said. “We’re got a lot of wildfire experience here in south Wales but I’ve never seen anything like it in 30 years.”During the Guardian’s visit to the scene on Sunday, soldiers from the Queen’s Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment tirelessly dug firebreaks and turned over smoking soil to minimise the spread of fire. Small flames licked around the base of blackened trees a few metres away as they worked, while in another part of the woods several trees lit up quickly with no warning.View image in fullscreenA helicopter drops water over the land.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianOn the ridge of the hill, a civilian-contracted helicopter picked up water from a huge plastic pool fed by a local dam and circled again and again to dowse reigniting pockets of the smouldering hillside.Smoke from the area has been visible as far away as Cardiff and Gloucestershire.Firefightersfrom services around the UK have come to help improvise how to get water to hard-to-reach places, using an old steel mill on the edge of town as a temporary headquarters. New thermal camera drones and specialised response vehicles designed by the South Wales fire service came online this summer.“Just in time,” said Darren Cleaves, the group manager for the service, as he radioed a colleague at the perimeter of the fire to report what he could see on the drone screen. “The drone means we can be much more accurate with pinpointing where we need to go, and it keeps our teams safer.”View image in fullscreenDarren Cleaves operating the drone.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe combined efforts have worked, saving houses in Blaenavon a few hundred metres away. For weeks, residents on Llanover Close, a road on the village boundary, have watched a steady stream of fire engines, water tankers, tractors and other emergency vehicles and equipment go back and forth to the forestry track above their homes.Cindy Rogers, 60, lives in the last house on the road where Blaenavon meets the hillside. A fire in 2004 that began on the top of the mountain almost reached her house, she said, pointing from her back garden to where the fire line is still visible.View image in fullscreenCindy Rogers: ‘It’s a worry that this is going to get worse with climate change.’Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian“It’s a worry that this is going to get worse in the future with climate change, but I wouldn’t move unless I really had to,” she said. “All it takes is the wind to change direction and that’s it.”By Sunday afternoon, the Blaenavon fire was showing signs it may be slowing, said Fin Monahan, the chief fire officer of South Wales fire and rescue.“It’s been very tough, but I’m so proud of the professionalism of these teams and how hard they are working,” he said. “Morale is still high, everything is calm and controlled … It’s just the scale of what we’re dealing with is unprecedented. We normally get about 1,000 999 calls a week, and at the moment it’s 7,000.”View image in fullscreenA fire engine hits the road.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianArson had been a major contributor to this summer’s fires, Monahan said. “Not every investigation has been completed yet but we can already see it’s been a significant issue this year in south Wales. Fire safety education is another key area we focus on … Driving home last night, I saw smoke and I went and found a guy burning tires and other stuff in his garden, under a tree. I had to tell him to put it out.”The cause of the Blaenavon fire is still unknown, but across the country arson arrests have been made in relation to this summer’s fires. On Saturday, four teenage boys from Porth in the Rhondda valley were detained on suspicion of arson and later released on bail.In Stoke-on-Trent, a man and woman have been arrested in connection to a fire that destroyed four homes, and a man in King’s Norton and another in east London have been arrested on suspicion of arson to endanger life.The UK has experienced multiple heatwaves this summer, as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The whole of Wales and almost three-quarters of England were declared officially in drought last month, and the Met Office said this week that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature.View image in fullscreenIt is hoped the fire may finally be coming under control.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe Blaenavon fire and many others across the country may only finally settle with cooler temperatures and rain, but the onset of autumn and more rainfall is not guaranteed to reverse the drought conditions, the Met Office said on Saturday.In Blaenavon, flash flooding has plagued residents in recent years. Asupercharged El Niñois now predicted to bring wet and stormy conditions to the UK this winter.An 89-year-old resident of Llanover Close, who did not want to give his name, said he had lived on the street since it was built. “It’s the flooding that worries me. My basement flooded last winter,” he said. “Fire and flood … I never thought it would come to this.”Explore more on these topicsWalesFirefightersMilitaryWildfiresUK weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Water companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during drought | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Suppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumption
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Suppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumption
Content: Thames Water are among the five companies looking into the new pricing model.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThames Water are among the five companies looking into the new pricing model.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesWater industryWater companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during droughtSuppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumptionJoanna PartridgeSun 16 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTFirst published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater companies could be allowed to raise bills for customers during periods of drought under proposals being considered by the sector’s regulator for England and Wales.Suppliers would be permitted to factor “water scarcity” into bills as part of efforts to reduce consumption under Ofwat’s plans, which are being likened to surge pricing – the practice where private hire firms raise taxi fares at times of higher demand.The proposals come just a few days after the prime minster, Andy Burnham,said he was angrywith water companies and accused them of treating their customers like a “blank cheque” after more than a dozen firms were given the green light to raise water bills even higher.It emerged last Thursday that five companies – Southern Water, Thames Water, Severn Trent, Wessex Water andSouth East Water– would be allowed to raise bills more than originally planned before the end of the decade to allow for billions of pounds of extra spending on repairs and infrastructure.The surge pricing proposals, first reported by the Sunday Telegraph, come after the 30 July conclusion of Ofwat’s consultation on changing the rules relating to wholesale charging, with the regulator due to share its final decision shortly.Public anger over the behaviour of water companies hassoared in recent yearsas bills have continued to climb even while sewage has flowed into the nation’s waterways andfirms have increased bosses’ payand handed out millions of pounds in dividends to shareholders.View image in fullscreenSurfers Against Sewage, seen here in Brighton, England last year, are one of many protest groups who have taken aim at the water industry.Photograph: Charlotte Coney/Getty ImagesDuring an exceptionally hot and dry summer, leading to almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales being declaredofficially in drought, suppliers have also come under fire for failing to save water lost through leaky pipes, whichcampaigners say far outstrips the amountthat could be saved through a nationwide hosepipe ban.An Ofwat spokesperson said: “The efficient use of water is in the best interests of everyone, including businesses. The options we are progressing would support greater consideration of water scarcity and efficiency by water companies when setting their charges, and encourage more tariff innovation.”Several water companies have beencarrying out charging trialsover the past few years aimed at making bills more affordable and, potentially, reducing demand.South West Water, which supplies water to about 1.8 million customers across south-west England, including Cornwall and Devon, is trialling a “rising block tariff”, where about 500 household customers are charged a cheaper rate for using a lower amount (or “block”) of water and progressively higher prices for higher consumption.The company said 90% of its customers would see lower bills on this trial, according to its assessments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUniversity spinout to launch water quality app for UK and US watersRead moreAnglian Water, which supplies 7 million customers across the east of England, the UK’s driest region, and South West Water are also trialling charging customers more for water used in the summer than in the winter months.The Guardian understands there are no government plans for nationwide surge pricing for water bills.A government spokesperson said: “Water companies are trialling new charging structures which must, as promised, make bills fairer and more affordable while encouraging greater water efficiency.”They added: “We have already ringfenced money earmarked for new infrastructure so it can only be spent on fixing the problems, and will go further by fundamentally reforming the water sector so that it works for the public, keeping bills as low as they can be.”Andy White, a senior lead for social policy at the Consumer Council for Water (CCW), a government-sponsored body that represents customers’ interests, said water companies were right to explore new tariff structures that could help manage demand and give customers more control over their bills.He said: “Any new approach must be fair and protect customers who are already struggling with rising water costs. None of the schemes currently being trialled are designed to generate additional revenue for water companies, and many are structured so that most customers will pay less overall.”White added that companies should give consumers smart meter data to give them a clearer picture of how they use water.A spokesperson for Water UK, the industry’s trade association, said companies were working to cut down on leaks, adding: “We also need to consider whether we could help people save water by rewarding people through their water bill. This might include eliminating standing charges or expanding discounts for customers who save water.”Explore more on these topicsWater industryUtilitiesWater billsHousehold billsThames WaterSevern TrentSouth East WaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Arron Banks hired private investigators to dig into Conservative party chair | Arron Banks | The Guardian
description: Revelation comes after it was disclosed that Reform UK backer had paid for spying on prominent journalist
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Revelation comes after it was disclosed that Reform UK backer had paid for spying on prominent journalist
Content: Arron Banks reportedly used Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he previously owned, to investigate the Tory chair.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/Zuma Press/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenArron Banks reportedly used Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he previously owned, to investigate the Tory chair.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/Zuma Press/Rex/ShutterstockArron BanksArron Banks hired private investigators to dig into Conservative party chairRevelation comes after it was disclosed that Reform UK backer had paid for spying on prominent journalistRowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 16 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe businessman and Reform UK backerArron Bankscommissioned a private intelligence firm to dig into the Conservative party chair, in addition to having paid for an investigation into a prominent journalist.Banks, a formerReform UKcandidate and leave campaign donor, appeared to confirm on Sunday that he was behind an investigation into Kevin Hollinrake.The use of private investigators to look into Hollinrake was first reported by the Mail on Sunday, which said Banks had used Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he previously owned.As party chair, Hollinrake has led the Conservatives’ response to revelations about Nigel Farage’s finances, asking questions about the £5m undeclared gift Farage received from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election.Hollinrake addressed Banks on social media on Sunday, saying: “When you can’t answer the questions, investigate the people asking them.
