The TRPB is examining the betting and broader integrity issues, including hidden ownership and race manipulation.Separately, Quirozwas chargedwith a banned-substance violation on Thursday after another horse he trained, Bonita Rough, tested positive for albuterol. Bonita Rough did not race on 9 August, and the result does not establish that any of that day’s runners received a prohibited substance.What happens next?Investigators will await laboratory results, trace the American and British wagers and try to establish who placed them and whether they had undisclosed connections to the horses. Hiwu says results from the recently tested horses will be disclosed under its anti-doping rules.The betting trail may prove harder to follow than the drugs tests because the US racing bodies investigating the horses have no jurisdiction over wagers placed in London shops. That part of the inquiry may depend on information shared by British bookmakers and regulators.Quirozhas denied any wrongdoing, arguing that he simply entered his horses and tried to win. For now, racing authorities have reached no conclusion. The question remains whether somebody was unusually clever, unusually lucky – or operating with information unavailable to the public.Explore more on these topicsHorse racingUS sportsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Claressa Shields eyes Britain’s Price after stopping Kaye Scott to reclaim titles | Claressa Shields | The Guardian
description: The undisputed heavyweight champion completed a 38lb descent to 160lb before overwhelming the Australian in the sixth round in Atlanta
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The undisputed heavyweight champion completed a 38lb descent to 160lb before overwhelming the Australian in the sixth round in Atlanta
Content: Claressa Shields reacts after defeating Kaye Scott of Australia with a sixth-round TKO early Sunday morning at Atlanta’s State Farm Arena.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClaressa Shields reacts after defeating Kaye Scott of Australia with a sixth-round TKO early Sunday morning at Atlanta’s State Farm Arena.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesClaressa ShieldsClaressa Shields eyes Britain’s Price after stopping Kaye Scott to reclaim titlesAmerican stops Sydneysider at 1:38 of sixth roundShields claims WBA and WBC belts after 38lb cutLauren Price identified as preferred next opponentGuardian sportSun 16 Aug 2026 01.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClaressa Shields completed a remarkable journey from heavyweight to middleweight on Sunday, stopping Australia’s Kaye Scott in the sixth round to capture the WBA and WBC titles.The five-division world champion and double Olympic gold medalist dominated her outclassed opponent from the opening bell at State Farm Arena in Atlanta before dropping Scott in the sixth and overwhelming her against the ropes after the action resumed. With Scott unable to defend herself from another sustained barrage, the 42-year-old champion’s corner threw in the towel.The victory improved Shields’s professional record to 19-0 with four knockouts while Scott fell to 5-2-1. It also returned the 31-year-old American to championship status at 160lb, a division she hadpreviously ruled as undisputed championbefore moving through light-heavyweight and into the heavyweight ranks.Shields, who remains the undisputed heavyweight champion, had not fought at middleweight since defeating Maricela Cornejo in June 2023. Her promoter billed her as only the second heavyweight champion in more than 120 years to win a world title in a lower division.The anticipated effects of that dramatic weight loss never materialized against Scott, a decorated amateur who entered the paid ranks at 39 as she approached the IBA’s upper age limit, yet remained a significant underdog in only her eighth professional bout.View image in fullscreenA towel flies in from the corner of Kaye Scott as Claressa Shields pummels away during the sixth round.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesAfter the first bell sounded around 12.30am local time, Shields spent the opening rounds taking the Sydneysider’s measure before steadily increasing the tempo. Her hand speed and accuracy repeatedly allowed her to land first and escape Scott’s counters, while a sustained body attack drained the champion as the fight progressed.Scott remained game but was increasingly outgunned. After stacking an advantage on the scorecards, Shields began sitting down on her punches in the fifth and ended the contest one round later, blasting Scott backwards with a left hook before pinning her against the ropes. The ropes held Scott up, prompting a count, and her corner intervened moments after the restart, sealing only Shields’s second stoppage win in nine years.“It was a hard camp,” Shields said. “I always tell myself that everything is easy work, but it was a really hard camp. I cut 38 pounds. I started 14 weeks ago at 198 and then I got down to 160. It was the most disciplined I’ve been since the Olympics, I feel like.”Shields insisted she had not entered the ring intent on forcing an early stoppage, mindful that the weight cut could affect her stamina and punch resistance.“I was actually just trying to figure her out,” she said. “She was stronger than what I thought. She was very strong. I knew that, with me cutting the weight that I cut, I didn’t want to exert too much early.View image in fullscreenClaressa Shields reacts after defeating Kaye Scott by a sixth-round TKO on Sunday morning in Atlanta.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty Images“I was trying to make sure I could deal with her strength and not get caught with nothing crazy, because I’m not as strong as I feel at 175.”The bout was the first women’s headliner in State Farm Arena history and marked Shields’s first fight outside of Michigan since 2022. Asked about performing before a crowd of around 16,000 spectators, Shields said: “I knew I could [draw a big crowd]. Atlanta loves Black excellence just like Detroit. I came out here and showed why I am pound-for-pound No 1.”Shields named fellow Olympic championLauren Priceof Britain as her preferred next opponent at 160lb and said she hoped the fight could be staged in December or January. She also raised the possibility of facing Mikaela Mayer or pursuing undisputed status at middleweight against Canada’s Tammara Thibeault, who won the IBF, WBO and Ring titles in her fifth professional fight last weekend in Orlando.“She’s only had five fights as a professional, but she’s got belts,” Shields said of Thibeault. “It’s not my fault these girls don’t have the experience that I have. She’s got a belt that I know belongs to me – and that’s the Ring belt.”Explore more on these topicsClaressa ShieldsBoxingUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s the standard’: Mikel Arteta hails Arsenal’s desire on blue day for Maresca  | Mikel Arteta | The Guardian
description: The champions delighted their manager by ‘winning the first trophy’ while Enzo Maresca wants Manchester City signings to arrive soon
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: The champions delighted their manager by ‘winning the first trophy’ while Enzo Maresca wants Manchester City signings to arrive soon
Content: Mikel Arteta lifts the Community Shield, the ‘first trophy’ win for Arsenal this season.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta lifts the Community Shield, the ‘first trophy’ win for Arsenal this season.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesMikel Arteta‘That’s the standard’: Mikel Arteta hails Arsenal’s desire on blue day for MarescaChampions delight manager by ‘winning the first trophy’Maresca wants Manchester City signings to arrive soonBen Fisherat the Principality StadiumSun 16 Aug 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta said his Arsenal players demonstrated their hunger to defend the Premier League title in theirCommunity Shield triumphover Manchester City. Arsenal, who ended their 22-year wait last season and are seeking to win back-to-back top-flight titles for the first time since 1934-35, beat City 3-0 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff in Enzo Maresca’s first significant match in charge.Riccardo Calafiori opened the scoring after 24 seconds, the fastest goal in the competition since Bobby Owen’s strike for City in 1968, before Kai Havertz doubled Arsenal’s lead and their captain, Martin Ødegaard, completed the scoring on 48 minutes. The 3-0 defeat represented the joint-heaviest loss for a City manager in their first game in charge, with Harry Newbould the most recent to suffer a three-goal opening defeat – 4-1, also toArsenal, in 1906. It is also Maresca’s joint-heaviest defeat as a manager in England.Calafiori’s fast start inspires Arsenal to big Community Shield win over Manchester CityRead moreArteta was delighted with Arsenal’s convincing display. “I am obviously extremely happy with the performance, the result and winning the first trophy,” he said. “We talked about the desire we have to start the season and to show ourselves how much we want it and I saw a lot of positive things against a top opponent. I’m very impressed in the manner that we played, in the manner that we competed. That’s the standard for us. If we drive the standards at this level, I’m sure that we’re going to be really, really competitive.”Asked about the desire displayed by his team, he said: “Because we want to go straight again. The desire comes [because] I want to live that moment again. I want to live other moments, even bigger than them … we know what it’s going to take. We know the difficulty of the task. We’ve never done it at this club, to win it again. We know that it’s going to demand something special and we are ready for it.”Arteta praised the performance of Christos Tzolis, who was involved in all three goals. “He is a really intelligent boy and he has a massive quality, which is when he is in the last 20-30m [of the pitch] he is so composed to pick people out in and around the box,” said the Arsenal manager. “And also to finish actions and he has shown that again two or three times. He was decisive.”View image in fullscreenNew signing Christos Tzolis was involved in all three of Arsenal’s goals.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPAØdegaard said the team’s performance was evidence they are capable of winning back-to-back titles. “We played some brilliant football,” said Arsenal’s captain. “[It was a] great performance and a great way to start the season. I always want to help the team as much as possible with goals and assists. I want to score more goals. We showed our level today. We’ve shown we’re ready. We’re serious and we want to do it again. We want to attack it. We want to do it again. When you get a taste of how nice it is you want to do it again. We want to win everything.”Maresca acknowledged City, who are closing on a deal to sign Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi as they prepare to sell Rodri to Barcelona, would welcome new arrivals before their league opener at home to Bournemouth on Sunday. Rodri did not travel to Cardiff, where Elliot Anderson started in midfield, and Jack Grealish arrived from the substitutes’ bench for his first City appearance since May 2025. “Any new signing, the sooner they arrive the better because we are starting the Premier League in one week and if they start to work with us as soon as possible it’s better that they can also understand the way we want to play,” he said.Maresca said he was not alarmed by the manner of the defeat. “In general I’m always concerned, even when we win games so imagine how [concerned] that we didn’t win the game,” said the Italian, who succeeded Pep Guardiola this summer. “It’s just the beginning, we have many things that we need to do better, I think the reaction was good after conceding the first goal and now try to reset and analyse the game and think from Tuesday about the next game.”Explore more on these topicsMikel ArtetaCommunity ShieldArsenalManchester CityEnzo MarescanewsShareReuse this content

title: Scotland appoint Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approach | Scotland | The Guardian
description: The Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli, sacked by Monaco in June, is Scotland’s second non-Scottish manager after Berti Vogts
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli, sacked by Monaco in June, is Scotland’s second non-Scottish manager after Berti Vogts
Content: Sébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAView image in fullscreenSébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAScotlandScotland appoint Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approachBelgian is the first non-Scot in role since Berti VogtsSFA welcomes ‘aggressive, front-foot style of play’Ewan MurraySun 16 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Scottish Football Association has appointed the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002 to 2004.Clarke’s abrupt departurecame afterScotland were knocked out of the World Cupat the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager with the Danes Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand being linked with the position.Pocognoli, a left-back who played for Brighton and West Brom, will probably be welcomed byScotlandfans seeking a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, including appearances at three major tournaments, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief football officer, said Pocognoli “will bring an aggressive, front-foot style of play that will excite supporters”.After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France. The former Everton and Belgum winger Kevin Mirallas is expected to join him in the dugout.Pocognoli said: “When I first heard of the interest, I was immediately excited about the opportunity. Scotland’s supporters are famous for their passion – most recently at the World Cup in the USA - and I have experienced it myself as a player for Belgium when we played in 2013.“Along with my coaching staff, I will do everything I can to give them a team to be proud of and build on the success that has been achieved already by my predecessor.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland begin their Nations League campaign with a trip to Slovenia on 26 September. Pocognoli’s first home game in charge will be Switzerland’s visit to Glasgow three days later.Explore more on these topicsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flemming’s dramatic Burnley double pegs back West Ham on Championship return | Championship | The Guardian
description: Zian Flemming’s two late goals pegged back West Ham to rescue a 2-2 Championship draw for Burnley in the battle between two relegated clubs
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Zian Flemming’s two late goals pegged back West Ham to rescue a 2-2 Championship draw for Burnley in the battle between two relegated clubs
Content: Zian Flemming gees up the Turf Moor crowd after equalising for Burnley in added-on time.Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenZian Flemming gees up the Turf Moor crowd after equalising for Burnley in added-on time.Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesChampionshipFlemming’s dramatic Burnley double pegs back West Ham on Championship returnWill Unwinat Turf MoorSun 16 Aug 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are many good reasons why Burnley and West Ham are performing as Premier League tribute acts, slumming it in theChampionshipwith the hope of a shot at the limelight once more. They are two flawed teams, relegated because of chronic defects, and plenty were on show as West Ham blew a two-goal lead to start life on the second-tier circuit with an entertaining draw.Zian Flemming’s late double secured a thoroughly deserved point for the hosts, who showed promise going forward but took far too long to find a clinical finish. Despite going two goals ahead through Maximilian Kilman and Manor Solomon, West Ham rarely looked comfortable as they sat back, something that eventually cost them.Amin Nabizada’s solo stunner edges Watford past SouthamptonRead more“We did a very good first half,” Nuno Espírito Santo said. “We created a lot of situations we were able to control and stopBurnley. Not so good in the second half, but after we scored the second goal, I think we should have done better to keep the result.”Nuno continued his career-long love of conservatism and his side were put under pressure early on, only surviving through Burnley’s poor decision-making and inept finishing. In addition to continuity in the dugout, West Ham can boast their captain, Jarrod Bowen, who committed to the club rather than seek a quick return to the top flight this summer. It was his corner that found Kilman at the back post after he lost Aaron Ramsey in the box.Considering West Ham are favourites to go back up, this fortuitous lead should have been a foundation to build on, but little attempt was made to seek a second. They were passive for long periods, composed in possession, but Burnley were able to counter at speed through the midfield and cause problems, only to lack the composure to make the most of those situations.Nuno tried to rectify the faltering midfield by sending on James Ward-Prowse for the anonymous Pablo, a player who has yet to find his level in England. It made no difference as Burnley came out the better side, pinning West Ham back repeatedly, but Flemming appeared destined to not score, finding the fans, goalkeeper, the inside of the post and Ollie Scarles on the line rather than the back of the net.West Ham reminded everyone that they possess Premier League quality as Mohamadou Kanté made light work of Marcus Edwards on the right wing before pulling the ball back to Solomon to slam home from close range. This was their second and final shot on target, both leading to goals. Despite being second best, the visitors must have believed they were out of sight, by accident rather than design.View image in fullscreenMaximilian Kilman gives West Ham the lead as he heads home Jarrod Bowen’s cross.Photograph: COLORSPORT/Alan Martin/ShutterstockFlemming had other ideas as things finally clicked, aided by Scarles crudely taking out Edwards in the box, allowing the striker to settle his nerves after 83 minutes of near misses and create tension in the West Ham ranks. It worked as the visitors failed to clear a corner which Flemming swept home in the second minute of added time, further explaining why he has attracted transfer interest. Asked if Flemming will stay the Burnley manager, Nicky Hayen, who is desperate not to lose his talisman, said: “It does not help that he scored twice today.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNuno will want more action in the transfer market after the record Championship signing of Arne Engels from Celtic on Saturday. A striker is much needed as Taty Castellanos made little impact, while the aforementioned Pablo does not give the impression of a man who will fire West Ham to promotion. The bench featured five academy graduates, none of who Nuno felt comfortable bringing on, which says a lot. “The club knows the targets and the needs of the team. [We are] working very hard and trying to get the bodies in as soon as possible,” Nuno said. “We need especially in the offensive part of the team.”Hayen, celebrating his 46th birthday, took his team on a lap of honour after his first league game in charge as he aims to build a relationship with supporters, who suffered through plenty of unwatchable football under his predecessor. “We showed resilience and that’s why I’m really satisfied for these boys because they worked really hard to change this game around and also how we did it,” Hayen said. “I’m pleased with the fans, how they supported us for 95 minutes. We invested a lot of time before this game into them because what we wanted was really to find the connection with them, that we made the promise that we bring energy into the stadium, that we keep on going for 95 minutes and this is exactly what we did.”Explore more on these topicsChampionshipBurnleyWest Ham Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 11: Hull City | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Hull , the playoff winners, are expected to go back down, but their owner is optimistic and is investing in the squad
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Hull , the playoff winners, are expected to go back down, but their owner is optimistic and is investing in the squad
Content: Oli McBurnie hoists the Championship playoff trophy high and Hull will need him to retain his scoring touch in the Premier League. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPlayoff winners are expected to go back down, but their owner is optimistic and is investing in the squadByLouise TaylorSun 16 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:20th (NB: this is not necessarily Louise Taylor’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:6th (Championship)ProspectsIt is no exaggeration to say thatHull’s playoff triumphin May was a shock. They had, after all, started the season as Championship relegation favourites and operated under a transfer embargo throughout the campaign. Moreover, they conceded 66 league goals, the fourth-highest, along the way. Now another minor miracle will surely be required if Premier League survival is to be secured.Much may hinge on Oli McBurnie, the scorer of 19 goals last season, succeeding where he has struggled in the past and retaining his scoring touch in the top tier, but there is no lack of optimism in East Yorkshire. “Think about us like a volcano,” says Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.”Hull intend following Sunderland’s template last summer by making 14 new signings, albeit on a significantly smaller budget. So far 11 – Jack Butland, Hidemasa Morita, Matt Targett, Óscar Zambrano, Jens Hjertø-Dahl, Elliot Stroud, Konstantinos Tzolakis, Lucas Herrington, Joe Gelhardt, Lucas Gourna-Douath and the club record buy, the central defender Nobel Mendy, who has arrived from Rayo Vallecano for just over £20m – have arrived.“The transfer market is very slow,” said the manager, Sergej Jakirovic, who covets the Sunderland striker Wilson Isidor and last season’s 23-goal Championship top scorer, Swansea’s Zan Vipotnik. “But, in the last seven days of the window, it will become very, very quick.”His cause has been hindered by pre-season injuries, with perhaps the biggest blow involving an arm problem suffered by Butland. It threatens to keep the former Rangers goalkeeper, who had impressed in friendlies, out until Christmas. The consensus is that Hull will have long since become a lost cause by then, but, much as the impressive Jakirovic needs new faces andPremier Leaguenous, he does hold one ace card. Hull boast an exceptionally powerful team spirit driven by exemplary on-field leaders, including the veteran central defender John Egan. Maybe, just maybe, it can, once again, transport them further than anyone believes possible.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureIn June, the playoff winners faced kicking off the new Premier League season handicapped by a near certain six-point deduction. A club that spent last season under a two-window English Football League transfer embargo avoided it by selling their goalkeeper Ivor Pandur and midfielder Aidon Shehu to Rangers and Panathinaikos respectively for a combined £8.5m. Access to the fruits of the top tier’s broadcast deal has since made Hull a whole lot wealthier, but Ilicali has pledged not to risk the club’s future by overspending and, at the time of writing, has invested around £78m on the new players.Owner-fan relationshipUnpredictable and slightly conflicted. Aidon Shehu, the Turkish sports reporter turned media mogul – who is on his fifth manager since taking control in early 2022 – was offered a wholesale welcome when he took over from the unpopular Allam family, but he now exerts much more of a polarising effect on supporters. If November 2022, when he treated 320 fans to an all-expenses-paid week’s holiday at a luxury resort hotel in Antalya represented a high point, a nadir arrived when late payments resulted in Hull being placed under a transfer embargo last season. Nonetheless, the playoff triumph ensures many are prepared to offer the 57-year-old the benefit of the doubt.The managerThe Mostar-born, 49-year-old Jakirovic has Bosnian and Croatian citizenship and says his life was shaped by the 1990s Balkan war that broke out when he was 14. “It was life or death,” he has said. “It has made me the person I am today.” Shortly after his arrival from Turkey’s Kayserispor, in June 2025, Hull were placed under a transfer embargo, but, defying widespread predictions of imminent relegation, he led the team to sixth place before beating Middlesbrough in the Championship playoff final. A central midfielder or central defender in his playing days, the former Bosnia and Herzegovina international led Dinamo Zagreb to the Croatian League and Cup double in 2024.Star signingView image in fullscreenHidemasa Morita applauds the Sporting fans during the Portuguese Cup final in May, his last appearance for the Lisbon club.Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo/AlamyThe Japan defensive midfielder Hidemasa Morita joined from Sporting Lisbon after four trophy-laden years in Portugal. A fans’ favourite in Lisbon, he played regular Champions League football last season as Sporting reached the quarter-finals and has 40 senior international caps. Morita could have stayed in Lisbon, but opted not to renew his contract in order to experience Premier League football. Hull fended off competition from Ipswich for the signature of the 31-year-old who was a key part of the Japan squad at Qatar 2022. Morita is the second Japanese player to represent Hull and his amalgam of experience and quality in a key position promise to prove invaluable.Stat attackThe strangest part of the Championship playoffs might not have been theSouthampton spying scandal. Hull were second-bottom for expected points, 53.1, and would have been relegated if underlying performances determined results. It was remarkable tthey won promotion and it will be even more surprising if they make a serious fist of staying up.StatSet for a breakthroughThe 22-year-old central defender Charlie Hughes was Hull’s young player of the year last season and his assurance in possession and excellent passing range are bound to catch all sorts of Premier League eyes. Helpfully, his ballplaying ability is matched by some equally impressive – and combative – defending. After spending his youth in the academies of Liverpool and Manchester City, Hughes joined Wigan, leaving for Hull last summer. An imposing blend of steel and silk, a defender also comfortable in central midfield will miss the start of the season after hernia surgery. Happily, Hughes is expected back by early autumn at the latest and appears integral to the team’s survival hopes.World Cup impactNot content with helping Hull win the most unexpected of promotions, the Canada winger Liam Millar headed across the Atlantic to the World Cup. He made three appearances at the tournament as they reached the knockout stage, losing toMorocco in the round of 16. Given his career seemed in real jeopardy when he suffered a serious knee injury shortly after joining Hull in 2024, inclusion in Canada’s squad represented the fulfilment of an unlikely looking dream. “It was an unbelievable experience,” said the 26-year-old. “I’ve never seen Canada the way it was, I’ve never seen so many red shirts in Vancouver and Toronto. We want to inspire the next generation and I think we did Canada proud.”Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Hull CityPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nabizada stunner edges Watford past Southampton as ‘Spygate’ still looms large | Championship | The Guardian
description: Amin Nabizada and Iker Bravo’s early goals helped Watford to a perfect start to the season as they beat Southampton 2-1 at Vicarage Road
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Amin Nabizada and Iker Bravo’s early goals helped Watford to a perfect start to the season as they beat Southampton 2-1 at Vicarage Road
Content: Watford players swarm Iker Bravo after he opened the scoring against Southampton.Photograph: Peter Tarry/PAView image in fullscreenWatford players swarm Iker Bravo after he opened the scoring against Southampton.Photograph: Peter Tarry/PAChampionshipNabizada stunner edges Watford past Southampton as ‘Spygate’ still looms largePaul MacInnesat Vicarage RoadSun 16 Aug 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouthampton will have to get used to being barracked as they travel theChampionshipthis autumn, the “Spygate” team set to be everyone’s favourite boo boys in the second tier. Certainly that was the case in Hertfordshire, with Watford fans and players alike beside themselves after a hard-fought victory, decided by two memorable first-half goals.Tonda Eckert, the Southampton head coach, remains under investigationfor his part in the Spygate affairand presented a subdued figure both during and after this contest. He insisted that his team were more united than ever after suffering the indignity of being removed from last season’s playoffs, “but it would be easier to say that after a victory”, Eckert acknowledged.Flemming’s dramatic Burnley double pegs back West Ham on Championship returnRead moreWatford paid tribute to Kenny Jackett before the match, the one-club legend and local boy hailed with two minutes of applause. This celebration of longevity and connection, with a Panini-inspired tifo tumbling down the stands, cut a contrast with the current operation, where Alessio Dionisi has become Watford’s 12th full-time manager in just the past five years.“I am very tired and my team was too by the end,” said the Italian who was coaching Empoli in Serie B last season. Dionisi praised the attitude of his team – “I liked the mentality of my players, in every moment I saw one team working together,” he said. He also benefited from the Pozzo family’s multi-club network and the local academy in digging out a victory.The Spain under-21 attacker Iker Bravo was one of several signings to make the familiar trek from “sister” club Udinese this summer, and he made his mark quickly, opening the scoring with a quite stunning solo goal in the 12th minute. It was all his own work and Bravo had to deploy a combination of skills to turn an innocuous situation into real danger. Looking to latch on to a long ball some 40 yards from goal, the 6ftplaymaker won the first header then, crucially, got a second touch with an outstretched toe to get the ball under control. Bravo then span immediately and drove at goal, pushing his way into the box before chopping right and getting off a low shot that Daniel Peretz got a hand to, butcould not keep out.View image in fullscreenWatford’s Amin Nabizada jumps for joy after scoring their second goal against Southampton.Photograph: Peter Tarry/PAA great way to start any season, the energy among the Vicarage Road crowd grew immediately and the home side went on to dominate the first half. They doubled their lead in the 29th minute with a moment to remember for 19-year-old academy graduate Amin Nabizada who exploited the same gaps on the left of theSouthamptondefence to run with the ball from his own half before finishing precisely from a tight angle. “Nabizada was emotional but after the first 10 minutes he played well,” Dionisi said. “When there is one mentality amongst the team, then it’s better for him too.”Southampton had the better of the second half, taking advantage of a drop in tempo from the hosts to assert their interests. A spell of concerted possession in the 56th minute ended with Kuryu Matsuki pulling out wide, the young midfielder Cam Bragg moving unmarked into the half space and his shift left finding the Canada World Cup star Cyle Larin to poke home from 10 yards out.Larin had a chance to equalise just two minutes later with a shot on the turn but Federico Ravaglia – another new signing to impress for the Hornets – turned the ball round the post. When Finn Azaz came on as a second-half substitute for the Saints he bought an inch to fire off a low drive that went just beyond the left hand post. As a succession of dangerous set pieces were sent over by Ryan Manning, Southampton fans were singing “we’ll score when we want”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut as the game passed through a flurry of substitutions Eckert’s team were unable to generate enough momentum to truly unsettle Dionisi’s men. Their only further chance came in added time and was scuffed wide by Taylor Harwood-Bellis.Eckert said he had been happy enough with his team’s performance beyond “two errors in possession”. He insisted his squad are “very close and united” as a group. “We had a different expectation for the result but the group looks united and we now need to turn that into results.”Opening matches rarely offer much insight into how a season will pan out. But Watford fans were able to enjoy both temperate weather and a decent performance. If Southampton want to transform the negative energy of Spygate into something positive, meanwhile, they will have to start again next week.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWatfordSouthamptonmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo says this year is ‘probably’ his last as a footballer | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: The Al-Nassr and Portugal forward Cristiano Ronaldo is expected to retire soon after scoring more than 950 goals for club and country
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Al-Nassr and Portugal forward Cristiano Ronaldo is expected to retire soon after scoring more than 950 goals for club and country
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo reached the last-16 with Portugal in the World Cup this year.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo reached the last-16 with Portugal in the World Cup this year.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesCristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo says this year is ‘probably’ his last as a footballerAl-Nassr and Portugal forward expects to retire soonRonaldo has more than 950 goals for club and countryAFPSun 16 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo believes this year is “probably” his last as a professional footballer, the 41-year-old Portugal captain said in an interview with Vogue magazine published on Sunday.Ronaldo, who has established his place among football’s all-time greats with more than 950 goals for club and country, had previously spoken of retiring “soon” or within “one or two years”.‘I go with a clear conscience’: Cristiano Ronaldo confirms he has played his last World Cup gameRead more“This is probably my last year of football, and I want to leave a spectacular legacy,” theAl-Nassrforward told Vogue, saying his future after football was “all mapped out”.“I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard,” he said, listing travel and padel among his favourite activities. “Because football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ways, not just one.”Ronaldo married his partner, Georgina Rodríguez, in an intimate ceremony in the Portuguese resort of Cascais on Tuesday. The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player told Vogue he wanted to “continue to enjoy what I’ve earned – what we’ve earned. Because after all it’s been 25 years with a lot of sacrifice.”After being part of the Portugal side whichreached the last 16of the World Cup this summer, Ronaldo is due to link up with Al-Nassr for the new Saudi Pro League season.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalAl-NassrnewsShareReuse this content

title: Leicester learn harsh reality of life in League One but youngsters provide silver lining | League One | The Guardian
description: Uncertainty about Leicester’s future was matched by some on the pitch in 1-1 draw with Notts County
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Uncertainty about Leicester’s future was matched by some on the pitch in 1-1 draw with Notts County
Content: The Leicester manager, Russell Martin, said his side could learn a lot from their draw against Notts County on the opening day of the League One season.Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Leicester manager, Russell Martin, said his side could learn a lot from their draw against Notts County on the opening day of the League One season.Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockLeague OneLeicester learn harsh reality of life in League One but youngsters provide silver liningUncertainty about the club’s future was matched by some on the pitch in 1-1 draw with Notts CountyWill Unwinat Meadow LaneSun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Leicester thought this season was going to be the footballing equivalent of a gap year, visiting new places and learning some life lessons before returning home, then they were mistaken. Being outfought and outperformed byNotts County, a well-organised and energetic team promoted from the fourth tier, brought the harsh reality of life to the fore on Saturday.Russell Martin’s desire to play out from the back provided the fragile foundation of a dispiriting performance for a team tipped to storm back up. Ollie Cooper charging down the ponderous Alex McCarthy before seeing the ball bounce back off the crossbar welcomed Leicester toLeague Onewithin six minutes. McCarthy or the confused centre-back pairing of Caleb Okoli and Harry Souttar repeatedly gave the ball away in and around the penalty area as the team created their own problems. Things went so badly that a compilation of their slapstick defending quickly gained traction on social media.League One 2026-27 preview: the contenders, hopefuls and strugglersRead moreJayden Joseph gave Leicester an undeserved lead, but it did not ignite an improvement and they inevitably gave away an equaliser through further ineptitude at the back as no one reacted quickly enough to a dangerous situation, allowing the unmarked Conor Grant to pounce in the six-yard box.With most of the sell-out crowd of 17,172 celebrating their own uplift, and the rapid demise of their rivals, Leicester struggled to cope with the intensity. “We’ve got loads of learning to do and we’ll be better for that, much better,” Martin said.This was the first league meeting between the clubs since 1994 because they have been on very different paths over the past 32 years. There was plenty of passion for this rare East Midlands derby with County back at this level for the first time since 2014-15 and Leicester fans making the short trip to prove devotion is not determined by trophies and success. They also showed displeasure at the ownership that has overseen the slide and earned the right to boo as their viewing journeyed between subpar and unacceptable.“A bit of anxiety crept in, the atmosphere changed in the stadium, and that’s the biggest learning for us,” Martin said. “If we don’t look after each other with the ball, like we didn’t towards the end, then it doesn’t suit us.”View image in fullscreenJayden Joseph put Leicester ahead in their 1-1 draw against Notts County at Meadow Lane.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesWhenLeicester won the Premier Leaguea decade ago, County finished 17th in League Two and went on to spend four years in the National League. Leicester may think their reputation should mean they are playing on the other side of the River Trent at the City Ground, but that scenario is a long way off on this evidence.The uncertainty among the Leicester defence was in tune with the club’s overall situation. A sale brochure has been created to market the club for a takeover, but Martin has not received word that Leicester are officially for sale, despite reports of the owner, King Power, wanting more than £200m. It would seem difficult to reach such a figure based on the distressed nature of the asset, despite a £100m training ground and players such as Oliver Skipp, who cost £20m. For comparison, County train at the local university and their most expensive summer signing was £200,000.Among the misery, the silver lining is that dropping down the pyramid and selling off assets opens up opportunities for young players. Will Alves, Joseph and Sammy Braybrooke started and looked the most adept in difficult circumstances, while their more illustrious colleagues hid from battle. The trio spent last season on loan in either the third or fourth tier and that experience among those relegated from the Championship was an ideal fit. The expensive Premier League signings Okoli and Skipp were not representative of their CVs, while the forwards were blunt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTeamwork, tactics and data: behind the scenes at Wigan’s pre-season trainingRead more“I said to people it’s not going to be easy,” Martin said. “The first day of the season, we get some crazy results. This was not an easy fixture on Sky; early kick-off; a team that got promoted last year, just down the road. We take it and we move on. And we have to improve next week.”It cannot be easy being in the Leicester ranks, with their best players being quickly sold after relegation to bring in funds and questions remaining over others. Stephy Mavididi and Wout Faes missed the match after receiving bids, while the captain, Souttar, has interest from Championship sides. Given the unsettled and youthful nature of the squad, some pragmatism would not go amiss, but that is not Martin’s style.One of Leicester’s key selling points is, according to the brochure, their “140-year storied history”, but their efforts here will not even make a footnote. Leicester cannot assume previous success will mean either promotion or a quick sale. It is a club in a state of flux, lacking certainty on and off the pitch. If they hoped the trip to Meadow Lane would be the start of the uplift, they were sorely misguided.Explore more on these topicsLeague OneNotts CountyLeicester CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: End of an era? South Korea’s sun sets in the Premier League but Japan rise | Japan | The Guardian
description: After the glory days of Park Ji-sung and Son Heung-min, there is a real prospect of the new Premier League season being Korean-free for the first time since 2005
Author: John Duerden
Headline: After the glory days of Park Ji-sung and Son Heung-min, there is a real prospect of the new Premier League season being Korean-free for the first time since 2005
Content: Son Heung-min left Spurs for Los Angeles in 2025 after a long successful spell in the Premier League.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAView image in fullscreenSon Heung-min left Spurs for Los Angeles in 2025 after a long successful spell in the Premier League.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAJapanEnd of an era? South Korea’s sun sets in the Premier League but Japan riseAfter glory days of Park Ji-sung and Son Heung-min, the new season could be Korean-free for first time since 2005John DuerdenSun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 06.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been a cruel summer for South Korea. The national team crashed and burned at the World Cup, the police are investigating the football association, reports have emerged aboutbribes paid to foreign refereesin 2011 and 2012 and there is a real prospect of the English Premier League being Korean-free for the first time since 2005.That was when Park Ji-sung signed for Manchester United, to start a love affair between the Land of the Morning Calm and England’s top tier that has continued ever since. Park won four titles and his mantle was taken over in 2015 by Son Heung-min at Spurs.Japan the example to follow but this has been a dismal World Cup for Asia | John DuerdenRead moreSon ended his successful decade, during which he became a club captain, by lifting the Europa League in 2025. There are other Taegeuk Warriors who are fondly remembered such as Ki Sung-yueng, Lee Young-pyo and Lee Chung-yong, and then those that would be tougher quiz questions. Cho Won-hee, Yun Suk-young and Park Chu-young barely featured for Wigan, QPR and Arsenal respectively.Others have cult hero status.Ji Dong-won’s last-minute winneragainst Manchester City will never be forgotten by Sunderland supporters while Lee Dong-gook, who had a long and successful career, could not hit a barn door with Middlesbrough. While there have inevitably hits and misses, overall, the exports have been a source of pride.Now, though, those who stayed up late or got up early to watch their compatriots are going to have more free time. AfterSon left London for Los Angeles, Hwang Hee-chan was the sole participant, but the forward went down with Wolves. There are three Koreans on Premier League books, but Yang Min-hyeok of Spurs, Brentford’s Kim Ji-soo and Park Seung-soo of Newcastle are likely to be once again loaned out.There was talk of Lee Kang-in leaving Paris Saint-Germain for England, but in July the 25-year-old attacker joined Atlético Madrid to take Antoine Griezmann’s No 7 shirt. The former child TV reality star, introduced to the nation at the age of six and at Valencia’s academy four years later, is now perhaps Asia’s biggest name, but is going to play in England only in Champions League games. At the moment, there are not many other Koreans who look capable of becoming established Premier League players.That is not the case forJapan, with the Land of the Rising Sun taking the mantle from its eastern neighbour. Last season, Kaoru Mitoma shone with Brighton while there was also Daichi Kamada at Crystal Palace, joined at Selhurst by Takehiro Tomiyasu, Ao Tanaka at Leeds and Wataru Endo with Liverpool.View image in fullscreenHwang Hee-chan was relegated with Wolves last season.Photograph: Anna Gowthorpe/ShutterstockThe new season will see more. As Lee was signing for Madrid, Hull snapped up Hidemasa Morita, last seen in England playing for Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League quarter-final against Arsenal in March. Shortly after, Daizen Maeda became Ipswich’s first Japanese player. The forward, who joins after a successful Celtic spell with five league titles, was last in action forJapan against Brazilat the World Cup.While that game, with the five-time champions coming from behind to win in the 96th minute, was a frustrating one for the Samurai Blue, the team at least did OK. Korea’s World Cup campaign was, however, a disaster with a2-1 win against Czechiafollowed bya 1-0 loss by Mexicoand a truly dismal defeatby the same scoreline to South Africa. Thehead coachof the national team and the president of the FA have resigned and Park Ji-sung has been roped in head a new “reform football committee”. It’s a mess.Park has talked of the need to follow Japan’s long-term philosophy to close the gap with what is clearly Asia’s best team. Increasingly, Japanese players, who have historically headed to Germany first, want to play in England. It is perhaps not a coincidence that two of the promoted Premier League teams have recruited Samurai Blue as there are plenty who have impressed in the Championship in recent years.Continental clash: where world football stands on Fifa and Infantino – explainedRead moreIt all leads to growing Japanese interest in the Premier League and the opposite in Korea. In 2022, AIA, Tottenham’s shirt sponsor, commissioned a report that claimed there were 12 million fans of the club in the country. Even given Son’s undoubted popularity, wild European claims of fan numbers in Asia have been a feature since before Park arrived at Old Trafford 21 years ago. There are certainly nowhere near 12 million now, with one Korean TV executive saying viewing figures for Spurs games are nowhere near what they were.That is hardly surprising as widespread Premier League interest in Korea, like Japan, not a historic lover of English football, is still largely player driven. During his time in London, Son’s smiling face would appear in the top corner of the television screen when he was on the pitch to keep casual viewers from turning over. In Park’s time, Manchester United games were often the only one shown all weekend.When City and the rest of the world were witnessingthe Agüero moment in 2012, in Korea, fans had to watch the entirety of United at Sunderland. That was the final sighting of Park in a red shirt and it looks as if Hwang’s appearance against Burnley in May will be the last Korean representation in England’s top tier for some time.Explore more on these topicsJapanSouth KoreafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Elena Rybakina leads call for changes to 2028 calendar after schedule chaos | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Elena Rybakina said of the schedule: ‘It’s just crazy … hopefully something will change’ after news the LA28 tennis event begins three days after Wimbledon
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Elena Rybakina said of the schedule: ‘It’s just crazy … hopefully something will change’ after news the LA28 tennis event begins three days after Wimbledon
Content: Elena Rybakina wants tennis’ governing bodies to make things ‘more convenient’ to players.Photograph: Wally Nell/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenElena Rybakina wants tennis’ governing bodies to make things ‘more convenient’ to players.Photograph: Wally Nell/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockTennisElena Rybakina leads call for changes to 2028 calendar after schedule chaosOlympic tennis event begins three days after WimbledonRybakina: ‘It’s crazy … hopefully something will change’Tumaini CarayolSun 16 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina and a number of top tennis players have called for changes to the calendar in light of the “crazy” and “ridiculous” news that the tennis competition in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics will begin just three days afterWimbledonends.The LA28 Olympics announced last month that the tennis event will take place between 19 and 28 July. With the Wimbledon 2028 men’s final on 16 July, the best performers at the tournament will have minimal time to fly to a different continent and adapt from grass to hard courts.Asked whether she thinks adjustments should be made to the tennis calendar, Sabalenka said: “That’s definitely something that we can consider doing because three days after the men’s Wimbledon final, it’s ridiculous,” she said. “And an Olympics is something huge. It’s something that you play once in four years. So I feel like we should try to like open up the schedule a little bit and make sure that we have a bit like at least a week because it’s too much of a stress on the body.”Rybakina agreed: “It’s just crazy to know that it’s just a couple of days after Wimbledon, but I think this year the dates were moved at the beginning of the year, so who knows? Hopefully something will change for next year so it’s more convenient for everybody.”An Olympic summer is always a busy time in the tennis schedule, with the Games positioned between Wimbledon and the North American hard-court swing, but this will be a far tighter turnaround than Paris in 2024, which began 13 days after the end of Wimbledon.Daniil Medvedev said he was not aware of the tight schedule but he also believes there should be changes to the timetable: “Now that I hear this, it would be great if something can be done. You tell me three days, make it at least six. I don’t know, even six is not good. But make it at least six, seven, try to do something.”Iga Swiatek, meanwhile, said this is just one example of many where player welfare is not prioritised with tournament scheduling: “Overall, you can see that the schedule is crazy. I’ve been talking about that for years. At the beginning, everybody said I’m just a crybaby, but now more players are talking about it. It’s tough. This situation is going to be really difficult for the person that plays the final and then needs to get on hard courts and play on the other side of the world.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDjokovic’s medical malaise in Cincinnati exposes fraying edges of ageing great’s gameRead moreExplore more on these topicsTennisWimbledonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt’s ‘dream comes true’ with fourth European Championships gold | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The British sprinter became the first to win four titles at a single event while Dina Asher-Smith hit a record 11 European medals total
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British sprinter became the first to win four titles at a single event while Dina Asher-Smith hit a record 11 European medals total
Content: Amy Hunt is in dreamland after winning her fourth gold medal of the European Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt is in dreamland after winning her fourth gold medal of the European Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAmy Hunt’s ‘dream comes true’ with fourth European Championships goldBritish sprinter first to win four titles at single eventDina Asher-Smith hits record 11 European medals totalSean Ingleat Alexandra Stadium, BirminghamSun 16 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf there was any remaining doubt that this has been Amy Hunt’s summer, it was dispelled over 10 seconds of controlled fury at the European Championships, as Britain’s newest sporting superstar completed an unprecedented quadruple.When the baton was slapped into the 24-year-old’s hand on the anchor leg of the mixed 4x100m relay, she was a fraction behind Gina Lückenkemper of Germany. But then Hunt became the hunter, and a record-breaker.European Championships security scare keeps fans and athletes stuck at stadiumRead moreIn no time those long legs began to whir, her vast stride started to widen, and she found her wings. First Lückenkemper was chased down. Then Hunt ran into history.As she crossed the line, she stuck her tongue out, stretched her arms in triumph, then held four fingers to the camera. And just like that the Cambridge graduate had completed the quadruple.“It’s just a dream come true – I’ll remember this week for the rest of my life,” said Hunt after becoming the first athlete in the 92-year history of the European Championships to win four gold medals in a single event.To make things even sweeter, Britain’s time was a European record 39.97sec, with Germany taking silver in 40.11 and Spain claiming bronze.“I think it surpassed my expectations for myself at these champs,” Hunt said. “Not in terms of not just the goals, but how I’ve handled myself, how I’ve handled the pressure, the attention, the recovery, the discipline of it all.”“It was a bit like when you’re queueing for a rollercoaster and you’re a little nervous and you’re seeing the drops and stuff,” Hunt said when asked about the craziness of her past week. “Then when you get off you want to do it again. So it was that adrenaline kick certainly. I loved the event.”To run seven races in seven days is difficult enough. To win all seven, across heats and finals, not only takes talent and guts but a hefty dose of chutzpah too.But while Hunt certainly has main character energy she quickly ensured that her teammates – Jeremiah Azu, Dina Asher-Smith and Zharnel Hughes – were hailed as well.“To do it all together is incredible, especially because that was the first time we did that changeover about an hour ago in warm-up,” said Hunt. “And look how smooth it was. Such professionals.”View image in fullscreenDina Asher-Smith, with Amy Hunt, Zharnel Hughes and Jeremiah Azu, also made history with her record 11th European gold.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesIt was hard to argue with that. This was the first time the mixed 4x100m relay has taken place at these championships and with the men and women alternating changeovers the difficulty level was increased to the highest. No wonder the Netherlands and Italy were disqualified. But Britain looked smooth throughout – at least to the untrained eye.“I’m going to be completely frank with you, I was absolutely terrified,” said Asher-Smith. “When the gun was going, I was like ‘Dina, please relax, it’s only going to go well if you relax’. When I gave that baton to Zharnel, I was so happy, I can’t lie. That’s exactly how I feel. Very unfiltered. I was just like ‘get this out of my hand – bye’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHunt was not the only record holder on the night as Asher-Smith made it a record 11 European medals in total – surpassing Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska – with this victory.“It hasn’t sunk in at all,” she said. “I just don’t think it’s something that when you start your career you ever think is going to be attached to you. Just want to run faster and get better. So I feel very humbled and blessed.”“At this point in my career, I’m just having fun,” Asher-Smith said. “I’m just seeing what can be maxed out because I’m fortunate enough to stand on the line, and I don’t really have much to prove. I’d like an Olympic gold, but that’s kind of the only thing that’s on my bucket list.”Earlier on Sunday there was more British success in the women’s marathon, as Abbie Donnelly overcame bringing different sized running shoes to Birmingham to take a surprise bronze medal.However her race was saved when her boyfriend Shane dashed up in the morning with the right shoe. “I actually bought two different size shoes by accident to this race,” said Donnelly, who became the first British woman to win a European Championships marathon medal.“I tried them on last night and I was like ‘the right one does not feel right’”, added Donnelly, whose time of 2:27.33 was just over five minutes behind Finland’s Alisa Vainio, who set a championship record.“So then I had to call my parents and my boyfriend. It was half an hour beforehand that my boyfriend Shane put the [tracking] chip on because I was so flustered.”Britain also won the women’s team event through Donnelly, Rose Harvey, Louise Small and Clara Evans-Graham, while Germany’s Amanal Petros took the men’s marathon in a championship record 2:09.11.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s Georgia Hunter Bell surges to emphatic 1500m European gold | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Georgia Hunter Bell raced clear on the final lap to win the women’s 1500m in 4:07.78sec, with Klaudia Kazimierska in second and Patricia Silva third
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Georgia Hunter Bell raced clear on the final lap to win the women’s 1500m in 4:07.78sec, with Klaudia Kazimierska in second and Patricia Silva third
Content: Georgia Hunter Bell crosses the finish line to win the women's 1500m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell crosses the finish line to win the women's 1500m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsBritain’s Georgia Hunter Bell surges to emphatic 1500m European goldHunter Bell races clear on final lap to win in 4:07.78secKlaudia Kazimierska claims silver; Patricia Silva bronzeSean Ingleat Alexandra Stadium, BirminghamSun 16 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgia Hunter Bell’s glorious summer continues to take her to fresh summits. The 32-year-old was simply sublime as she demolished a decent European 1500m field to add another title to her swelling collection.It proved to be the final gold British medal of these championships, as Britain agonisingly missed out on coming top of the medal table to Italy by the slimmest margins.Birmingham 2026: Final night of European Athletics Championships: Hunt seals fourth gold medal – liveRead moreFirst Jazmin Sawyers failed to win long jump gold by a centimetre to Larissa Iapichino of Italy. Then, in the final race of the championships, Italy’s Lorenzo Benati held off Britain’s Charlie Dobson by 0.03sec in the men’s 4x400m relay.It meant that Italy finished top with 10 gold medals, one ahead of the British team, but it still marked an excellent effort on a thrilling final day.Hunter Bell led from the front. As expected, the women’s 1500m turned into a slow and tactical race. But in the last lap burn up, Hunter Bell truly ignited. Her 58.44sec final 400m took her 10 metres clear as she crossed the line in 4:07.78.No wonder when she crossed the line she applauded herself for a job well done.“That last 150m is always my favourite part of the race, and it was really nice to come down the home stretch and know that I had it,” said Hunter Bell, who finished a second clear of Poland’s Klaudia Kazimierska, with Portugal’s Patricia Silva taking a surprise bronze.Over the past five months, Hunter Bell has wonworld indoor 1500m gold,800m Commonwealth Games gold, and the European title. She now believes she can add a fourth to her collection at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest next month.Soon afterwards Sawyers jumped an outdoor long jump personal best of 6.99m to win silver against a high-quality field. It was all the more impressive given that she sustained a serious achilles injury 18 months ago. But she fell tantalising short of Iapichino, who jumped seven metres. France’s Hilary Kpatcha finished with a leap of 6.98m.Two more silvers for Britain quickly followed in the women’s and men’s 4x400m as Britain finished with 19 medals.As seven days of action in Birmingham came to an end with Mondo Duplantis taking pole vault gold in 6.15m, Jack Buckner, the chief executive of UKAthletics, hailed the European Championships as a huge success.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell shows off her gold medal after 1500m success in Birmingham.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APBuckner said that he was particularly pleased that Friday night’sepic 800m finalstarring Keely Hodgkinson, Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol had attracted around four million viewers on BBC One as he insisted his sport had cut through into the mainstream.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Everyone is absolutely delighted with the BBC numbers,” he said. “I heard it was 3.8m but that was without iPlayer. So they’ve been talking over four million on Friday night, which is really strong. So we are absolutely delighted and everyone is buzzing.“This is a big sport that cuts through with big stars and that’s what we want. We want big heroes and big names doing amazing things.”“Another star emerged here in Amy Hunt, which is fantastic for the sport,” he added. “Keely, in the way she conducts herself and the way she handles herself, is a role model. And then you look at all of them in the 4x100m relays and you just go ‘that’s what we want this country to be’.Buckner also hinted that Britain was tempted to bid again in the near future, with the rebuilt stadium at Crystal Palace a potential option. “It’s been absolutely fantastic,” he said. “We loved doing it. We learn a lot. We think we could do it better and we’re going to do it again.”Buckner also defended the struggles with ticket sales at the start of the week – and said that UKA had sold nearly three-quarters of all tickets in the 23,000-capacity Alexander Stadium.“In the buildup we did work with schools and we did work with community groups, and overall we’ve sold 73% of the tickets,” he said.“In any other country in the world, if they’ve delivered that result in ticketing, they’d have been jumping up and down with excitement. But our expectations are higher and we’re OK with that. We’ve sold out the last four days so it’s been a world-class ticketing result, but we want better.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Seifert demolition job sets up Manchester Super Giants for maiden men’s Hundred title | The Hundred | The Guardian
description: Manchester Super Giants triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Manchester Super Giants triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets
Content: Manchester Super Giants’ captain Jos Buttler (centre) holds the men’s Hundred trophy aloft at Lord’s.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester Super Giants’ captain Jos Buttler (centre) holds the men’s Hundred trophy aloft at Lord’s.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThe HundredSeifert demolition job sets up Manchester Super Giants for maiden men’s Hundred titleManchester Super Giants, 162-5 beat Trent Rockets, 158-8 by five wicketsOld Trafford-based side win men’s final at third attemptTaha Hashimat Lord'sSun 16 Aug 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new name has done the trick. The Manchester Super Giants – once known as the Originals, now part of the tournament’s IPL-ification – triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets. Tim Seifert set up victory with 72 off 38 balls; Liam Dawson completed it with two balls remaining, a six to seal it.New Zealand’s Seifert turned Jos Buttler, his captain, into a support act in a chase of 159, his scarily high backlift producing seven sixes and a 23-ball half-century. The 31-year-old launched far higher than any of the Rockets, their innings defined by useful cameos. Noor Ahmad fizzed the ball down for the Super Giants, taking three for 33, but this was Seifert’s night as the Manchester side won the tournament for the first time after two previous runners-up finishes.Trent Rockets soar over Sunrisers Leeds to bring home maiden women’s Hundred titleRead moreThe Rockets, who were going for a doubleafter their women’s side had triumphedearlier in the piece, did offer a scare at the close. Seifert departed with 22 balls remaining, 23 still required – and the Super Giants stumbled. Mohammad Amir removed Heinrich Klaasen and Michael Bracewell and, with three required off the last over, Dawson struck air with his first two balls. It would be third time lucky, Ben Sanderson sent over deep midwicket to finally finish it.It closed a season defined by team reboots and a drop in overall attendance. There has been Jude Bellingham in the ground, the introduction of the illogical name that is MI London and the persistence of a key problem: the cricket is yet to dominate conversation. Of course, a final allows the actual sport to breathe a little and a last-over end was welcome after Seifert had threatened to complete it much earlier. “It was a little bit [more] stressful than it needed to be,” said a relieved Buttler.Lord’s was a psychedelic place before the start. Ella Eyre had the thankless task as musical guest while the two sides warmed up yards away, daytime fireworks in full flow. This was a second consecutive men’s final for the Rockets but they had just the one survivor from last year: Sanderson. Ben Duckett’s runs had helped on their progress to this point while the Super Giants had enjoyed the fruits of an England pace triumvirate: Josh Tongue, Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson. With Buttler deciding to bowl, Duckett against the quicks – what felt like the key battle at the start of the day – was first up.View image in fullscreenManchester’s Liam Dawson (right) celebrates hitting the game-winning shot, a six over midwicket, with teammate Leus du Plooy (left).Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesDuckett got the scoop out against Atkinson and Baker, and was grateful for a drop; the left-hander reverse-swept the ball to Tongue, who erred at short third. Duckett looked on for a big one, having hit 141 against India at this ground last month.Ahmad decided otherwise. The left-arm wrist-spinner struck with his first ball, to Finn Allen, and the delivery to Duckett moments later would not have been out of place in a red-ball game. A wrong’un caught the inside-edge before finding Buttler’s gloves, Duckett gone for 31. Another Ahmad googly later in the innings accounted for Australia’s Tim David, whose difficult tournament – 90 runs from eight knocks – ended with a first-ball edge to the sharp Buttler, leaving the Rockets on 91 for four after 59 deliveries.In a match packed with internationals it was the uncapped Aneurin Donald who gave the Rockets their biggest lift. His 19-ball 38 included a mix-up with Sam Billings, prompting the captain’s run-out, but the Rockets could call upon a strong lower order for the finish. Mitchell Santner’s unbeaten 20 took him to a season’s batting average of 146. Lewis Gregory was brutal with a 16-ball 32.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt looked like a decent score but Seifert was in a hurry, taking 14 off Amir’s first over and pulverising the leg-side. He appeared a goner on 33 after finding Allen by the leg-side rope; the Rockets man leaped beyond the boundary before flicking it back into play for Calvin Harrison to complete the catch. The decision went upstairs and was adjudged not out due to Allen brushing the rope in the buildup.Seifert moved to his half-century by slogging Harrison into the Mound Stand, with the Super Giants reaching 87 for one off 50 balls. Their control grew when Buttler went stratospheric against Harrison with back-to-back sixes, but an attempt at a third cost him when he found long-off. Would this be a gamechanging moment? It was nearly the case, but Dawson got it right at the end.Explore more on these topicsThe HundredCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: American Kate Douglass breaks 50m freestyle world record twice in one day  | Swimming | The Guardian
description: Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the women’s 50m freestyle for the second time Saturday, winning the final in 23.19 seconds
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the women’s 50m freestyle for the second time Saturday, winning the final in 23.19 seconds
Content: Kate Douglass reacts after setting the world record for the women’s 50m freestyle for the second time in one day on Saturday at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, California.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APView image in fullscreenKate Douglass reacts after setting the world record for the women’s 50m freestyle for the second time in one day on Saturday at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, California.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APSwimmingAmerican Kate Douglass breaks 50m freestyle world record twice in one dayAmerican clocks 23.19sec to win final at Pan PacsDouglass had first broken record with 23.49sec in heatsAgenciesSat 15 Aug 2026 23.08 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 18.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKate Douglass lowered her own world record in the women’s 50m freestyle for the second time in one day, winning the Pan Pacific Championships final in 23.19sec.In the morning preliminaries, the 24-year-old American swam 23.49 to take the mark away from teammate Gretchen Walsh, who finished second in the evening final in 23.74. Australia’s reigning world champion Meg Harris was third in 23.89.Lani Pallister dethrones Katie Ledecky to claim Pan Pacs 400m freestyle crownRead moreDouglass returned 25 minutes later to finish second in the 200 breaststroke. She rallied down the stretch but couldn’t catch Alexanne Lepage of Canada, who led the entire race and touched in 2:21.73. Douglass finished in 2:22.57.Walsh had owned the 50 free record of 23.55 since setting it in June at an international meet in Rome.It is the third time Douglass has lowered the world mark in the sprint race. She first did it on June 19 at the TYR Pro Swim Series meet in Indianapolis, posting a time of 23.59. Nine days later, Walsh lowered it again.Douglass is a five-time Olympic medallist. She earned silver in the 50 free at the 2024 world championships but didn’t compete in the event at the 2024 Paris Games.It was the second individual world record set at the meet that includes swimmers from the US, Australia, Canada, Japan and China, among others.View image in fullscreenDouglass looks on before Saturday’s 50m freestyle heat.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesThe men’s 50 free was won by Jamie Jack of Australia in a championship record of 21.35. American Jack Alexy took silver in 21.42.Yu Yiting of China defeated a strong field including world record-holder Summer McIntosh to win the 200 individual medley.Yu was under world-record pace on the opening butterfly leg before American Regan Smith took over the lead on the backstroke. Yu moved back in front on the breaststroke and held off McIntosh in the closing meters. Yu’s time of 2:07.45 set a championship record in the outdoor pool in Irvine.McIntosh, the Canadian star whose lone individual victory of the week was in the 400 IM, took silver in 2:07.47. American Alex Walsh, the older sister of Gretchen Walsh, earned bronze in 2:07.66. Smith finished fourth.McIntosh claimed silver in the 200 freestyle and bronze in the 4 x 200 freestyle relay. She surprisingly failed to qualify for the 400 free championship final, but finished first in the ‘B’ final.“It wasn’t a horrible swim, but getting touched out is something that is never a good thing to feel,” she said. “Overall, the meet didn’t go the way I wanted it to, so there’ll definitely be a lot of reflection.”In the men’s 200 IM, Tomoyuki Matushita of Japan won in 1:56.02 over American Carson Foster.Explore more on these topicsSwimmingUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We detected unusual activity’: the scam that uses AI to exploit your holiday photos | Scams | The Guardian
description: Fraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account details
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Fraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account details
Content: Common AI tools can accurately detect where a photo was taken more than 90% of the time.Photograph: Sean Pavone/AlamyView image in fullscreenCommon AI tools can accurately detect where a photo was taken more than 90% of the time.Photograph: Sean Pavone/AlamyScam watchScams‘We detected unusual activity’: the scam that uses AI to exploit your holiday photosFraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account detailsShane HickeySun 16 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou are on a short break in Porto and post some pictures of your family on Instagram or Facebook. With a small section of the Douro river in the background, you think it could have been taken anywhere.A few days later, you get a text saying that your card was compromised. “We detected unusual activity while you were travelling in Porto – please verify immediately,” says the message.You click on the link to confirm your bank details. Since you have not put any details of your trip on any of your social networks – bar the indistinct pictures – you don’t suspect there is anything suspicious about the messages.But the text was a fraud designed to extract your financial details. The criminals behind it figured out where you had been on holidays – lending credibility to their text – by using AI to analyse the image for the most sparse signs of where it was taken.View image in fullscreenImage showing how AI identifies the location where holiday pictures were taken.Photograph: McAfee LabsNew research has shown that by picking up on details in the picture – such as the background, the architecture, the signage or the light – the AI agent can pinpoint where it was taken. For criminals, this information gives attempts to defraud by text message or email an added legitimacy.McAfee, the producer of anti-virus software, used two freely available AI models to test more than 21,000 travel images. One of the models identified 91% of images accurately while the other got 87%. Staff were then asked to replicate the experiment with their own pictures and became uncomfortable with how easy their travels were pinpointed.The company says that it shows that computers don’t need photos to be tagged or attached metadata to identify where they are taken.“What AI does is give context … so that makes the scam [and] makes the threats credible,” says Vonny Gamot, the head of EMEA at McAfee.What it looks likePictures are more likely to be identified by AI if they have recognisable landmarks, skylines, signage and street markings. Food stalls and storefronts can also pinpoint quickly where the picture was taken.If the picture is taken on a beach or a hotel room, the accuracy of the AI is lowered.
