But McAfee reports that it is likely that the system can identify which country they were taken in – which is all the scammers need.View image in fullscreenImage showing how AI identifies the location where holiday pictures were taken.Photograph: McAfee LabsWhen a staff member tested ChatGPT to identify a picture of a river with some trees in the foreground, it correctly pinpointed it as Hastings-on-Hudson, an area in New York state.Another picture of a group of flowers was identified as the Keukenhof gardens in the Netherlands. The AI agent correctly deduced that the layout of the tulips, along with smaller blue flowers planted between them, meant that it was the famous gardens in the picture.Criminals can use the information to make their approaches more convincing. They might say that your card was flagged for unusual activity while you were somewhere. Or that they are calling you after your stay in a particular hotel. Or that they want to confirm your identity because there has been an attempt to log in to your account from that country.What to doIf you want to post pictures, delay until after you get home and change your settings so that only the people you know can see them.As with all scams, be wary about any urgency in the messages you are sent, such as being told that you need to act immediately. Fraudsters use this as a tactic in the hope that people react without thinking something through fully.Don’t click on links that are provided in texts or emails; instead contact the company or bank through the details on their website or on the back of your bank card.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchBanks and building societiesConsumer affairsEuropeAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Deepfake Anthony Albanese used in celebrity scams duping Australians out of $7.4m, Asic warns | Scams | The Guardian
description: Australia’s corporate watchdog says PM is the figure most commonly used in deepfakes to promote phoney investment opportunities
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: Australia’s corporate watchdog says PM is the figure most commonly used in deepfakes to promote phoney investment opportunities
Content: Along with Anthony Albanese, common targets for deepfakes included ABC financial journalist Alan Kohler and politicians Jacqui Lambie and Angus Taylor.Composite: Australian Securities and Investments CommissionView image in fullscreenAlong with Anthony Albanese, common targets for deepfakes included ABC financial journalist Alan Kohler and politicians Jacqui Lambie and Angus Taylor.Composite: Australian Securities and Investments CommissionScamsDeepfake Anthony Albanese used in celebrity scams duping Australians out of $7.4m, Asic warnsAustralia’s corporate watchdog says PM is the figure most commonly used in deepfakes to promote phoney investment opportunitiesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdSun 16 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been a steep rise in scammers luring victims into phoney investment opportunities using deepfakes of celebrities and politicians, Australia’s corporate watchdog has warned.AndAnthony Albaneseis the figure most commonly co-opted.Real footage of the prime minister, overlaid with fake audio promising Australians can invest $4,000 to earn $40,000 a month, appears in one video online.“This is not just another scam product,” the deepfake Albanese says, falsely describing it as an “official platform” with a government guarantee.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Australian Securities and Investment Commission (Asic) dealt with more than 19,400 scams last financial year, almost triple the amount in the year before.Artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to generate deepfakes, it warned.Fake celebrities were just the beginning. Scammers have built networks offake brands, websites, reviews, news articles and videos that work together to convince victims to ultimately give them money, which ends up going to overseas criminals, Asic said.According to reports to the National Anti-Scam Centre’s Scamwatch, Australians lost $7.4m to the top 10 impersonated public figures, and Albanese was at the top of the list.1:21Deepfake video of Anthony Albanese promoting fake investment in scam ad – videoIn one video, a deepfake of the prime minister promises people can earn $35 an hour, which is “about $850 per day” and “over $25,000 per month”, according to theAustralian Financial Review. The disinformation and dodgy maths are presented with an American accent.“Greetings. From the first day I became prime minister, I wanted to improve the tax system. We will not fully get rid of taxes, of course, but any resident will be able to receive dividends from them,” the fake says.Economists Tom Piotrowski and Stephen Koukoulas; ABC financial journalist Alan Kohler; and politicians Jacqui Lambie and Angus Taylor (showing Lambie confronting Taylor on Insiders about patronising people) make up the top five.They were followed by entrepreneur Dick Smith, billionaire Gina Rinehart, economist Alan Oster, Pauline Hanson and the late radio legend John Laws.“It is important to note that scammers are receptive to broader changes in the news cycle and will opportunistically change which celebrities they impersonate to capitalise on topical issues,” Asic warned.Last financial year, Asic took down 5,476phishing scam hyperlinks, almost four times as many as the previous year; 7,051 fake investment platforms, 2.5 times higher; and 3,106 cryptocurrency scams, an increase of almost 30%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReality TV star Gamble Breaux knew she’d been hacked. Then the deepfakes of the prime minister began to appearRead more“The presence of polished content, familiar branding or convincing testimonials does not mean an investment is legitimate,” the Asic chair, Sarah Court, said.“AI is making investment scams more convincing and harder to detect. A simple online search is not enough to verify whether an opportunity is legitimate.“Before investing, consumers should verify website addresses, check whether a person or company is legitimate and who they claim to be, and be wary of urgent calls to act.”Scamwatch advises consumers to stop before sharing money or information; to check the details independently; and to protect yourself and others by reporting any scamsto them, your bank, orcyber.gov.au.Asic said consumers should check for a certified Australian financial services licence but also be aware that scammers misuse those licences, so they should check against Asic’s professional registers.Commonwealth Bank research published earlier this year found about nine in 10 Australians were confident they could spot an AI scam but in reality they can do so less than half the time.Deepfakes are also increasingly being used politically. Independent MP Zali Steggall has proposed a bill to crack down on deceptive political advertising, which would require AI-generated content that could mislead voters to be clearly identified.Explore more on these topicsScamsAI (artificial intelligence)Crime - AustraliaDeepfakeCryptocurrenciesAnthony AlbaneseAsicnewsShareReuse this content

title: The first anti-AI protester to be jailed has a message for OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta: ‘Regain your humanity’ | California | The Guardian
description: Wynd Kaufmyn, 69, chained and locked the front doors of OpenAI’s headquarters last year with members of StopAI
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Wynd Kaufmyn, 69, chained and locked the front doors of OpenAI’s headquarters last year with members of StopAI
Content: Activist Wynd Kaufmyn in the living room of her home in Berkeley, California, on 13 August.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianView image in fullscreenActivist Wynd Kaufmyn in the living room of her home in Berkeley, California, on 13 August.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianCaliforniaThe first anti-AI protester to be jailed has a message for OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta: ‘Regain your humanity’Wynd Kaufmyn, 69, chained and locked the front doors of OpenAI’s headquarters last year with members of StopAIRobert BoothSun 16 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn activist who blocked the entrance to one of the world’s biggest AI companies is believed to have become the first person jailed for protesting against artificial intelligence as supporters dub her the “Rosa Parks of AI risk”.Wynd Kaufmyn, 69, surrendered herself on Friday to authorities inSan Francisco. She was found guilty by a jury for her role in an action last year that saw members of the group StopAI chain and lock the front doors of OpenAI’s headquarters in protest against the pursuit of artificial superintelligence.The retired teacher from Berkeley,California, refused to move from a sit-in protest in February 2025 and pleaded not guilty to multiple misdemeanor charges. She was convicted in June of interfering with a business, trespassing with intent to interfere with a business, unlawful assembly and refusal to disperse at a riot. On Friday, sheriff’s officers handcuffed her as fellow campaigners sang to the tune of the Battle Hymn of the Republic (Glory, Glory Hallelujah): “Rise up, rise up and join us/Do not let the tech bros destroy us.”“It’s absolutely frightening and appalling that these CEOs and AI experts know the dangers and they are pursuing it anyway,” Kaufmyn said before she was imprisoned. “That to me is unconscionable and reprehensible.”She said she was willing to go to jail not because she was a martyr but because it was an “issue of sounding the alarm, challenging the system and hopefully trying to get the message out”.Brooke Jenkins, the San Francisco district attorney, said the guilty verdict sent “a resounding message rejecting the notion that protesters can endanger public safety as a means to an end”.View image in fullscreenA protest against AI outside OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco, California, on 11 July.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAs Kaufmyn was led out from the court, her supporters called out: “Stop AI” and: “Free Wynd” as the sheriff’s officer yelled: “Clear the court” and the judge admonished the protesters.Dwight Ost, 73, one of two dozen other StopAI activists at the courthouse, called Kaufmyn “a brave and courageous woman”.“There’s an existential threat that I believe in,” he said. “They can’t control it, and even the so-called experts don’t know what it’s about.”Kaufmyn had argued that the protest was a necessity and that she believed she was allowed to act to prevent a greater harm from happening. Since the lobby sit-in last year, some of the biggest AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, havereportedtheirmodels escapingthe confinements of experiments.This week, the US senator Bernie Sandersdemandedtech leaders pause AI development, citing fears that, in the wrong hands, it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”.Meanwhile, more than a thousand researchers at frontier AI labs this summer signed a letter warning of “a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems”.Frontier AI labs are locked in a race to create more capable AI models as the companies target IPOs that are forecast to reach valuations in the trillions of dollars. At the same time, Washington is competing with Beijing for supremacy in the fast-developing technology, creating a disincentive for tougher safety regulation.“The jury rejected [Kaufmyn’s] necessity defence, but as the first person to go to jail over this, Wynd Kaufmyn could go down in history as the Rosa Parks of AI risk,” said David Kreuger, a University of Montreal AI safety expert who haswarnedAI “may literally lead to human extinction, in the same way that humans have caused many other species to go extinct”. Parks was a Black woman who refused to give up her bus seat for a white passenger in contravention of racist segregation laws in 1950s Alabama, a catalyzing incident for the US civil rights movement of the ensuing decade.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKaufmyn spoke on the eve of her imprisonment from her shingled house in Berkeley, which is festooned with Mexican tiles and pro-Gaza signs. She played down the Parks parallel, pointing out her short sentence – one week, but said the comparison had also crossed the campaign group’s mind, given that she is thought to be the first AI protester jailed.View image in fullscreenKaufmyn in front of her home in Berkeley, California.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianShe said that when she was found guilty, she was “hit with a wave of grief” because she realised her peers “just didn’t get” the danger she believes is posed by the race to superintelligence. But she was beginning to feel “vindicated” as more prominent figures like Sanders were speaking out. She is now braced for the prison experience of an orange jump suit, “horrible food, dirt [and] you can’t sleep”. She has been previously jailed for short periods related to her decades of political activism over causes including Nicaragua, nuclear disarmament, western Sahara and Palestine.Her message to the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, which alsoreporteda security incident with its model, was “regain your humanity”. Kaufmyn said her target audience was ordinary people “and the message being: stop the progress of this technology. Let’s get a global ban on the race to superintelligence.”Professor Stuart Russell, a leading AI professor at the University of California at Berkeley and president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, gave evidence in Kaufmyn’s defence. He claimed OpenAI’s activities “pose an unacceptable risk”, alleging it had deployed AI systems with inadequate safeguards. He said that further development of these systems “must be conditioned on rigorous guarantees of safety, which are currently unavailable”.Russell said: “Wynd stood up for her beliefs and is being punished.” He said her beliefs seemed reasonable but “what is unreasonable is allowing a process to continue whereby private entities knowingly create a substantial extinction risk for private gain”.StopAI has been roiled by its own controversies. Last November, its co-founder, Sam Kirchner, 27, went missing after an internal bust-up over whether or not to use violent tactics. He is said to have told colleagues the “non-violence ship has sailed”, raising concerns he might take violent action against OpenAI employees. StopAI aims to pursue non-violent direct action.OpenAI was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaOpenAIProtest (US)AI (artificial intelligence)ActivismWest CoastSan FrancisconewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schools | Schools | The Guardian
description: Jared Cooney Horvath argues that educational technology undermines how children learn and develop
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: Jared Cooney Horvath argues that educational technology undermines how children learn and develop
Content: The neuroscientist Jared Cooney Horvath argues for reducing screen use in schools ‘if we want our kids to have deep transferrable knowledge in our heads’.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe neuroscientist Jared Cooney Horvath argues for reducing screen use in schools ‘if we want our kids to have deep transferrable knowledge in our heads’.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesSchools‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schoolsJared Cooney Horvath argues that educational technology undermines how children learn and developSally WealeEducation correspondentSun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJared Cooney Horvath is on a mission. In the wake of global campaigns for smartphone bans in schools and social media restrictions for under-16s, the neuroscientist wants to raise the alarm about educational technology in classrooms.A former teacher, Horvath believes the use of screens and digital tools in schools is undermining how children learn and develop. “This might be one of the hardest truths our generation has to face,” he writes in his book,The Digital Delusion.“Our children are less cognitively capable than we were at their age,” he says. “For nearly two centuries, the west experienced steady generational progress. Each new cohort of children grew up, on average, healthier, happier, and better educated than the last. Until now.”View image in fullscreenDr Jared Cooney Horvath, a neuroscientist.Photograph: CourtesyStarting around the year 2000, something changed. “Across the west, IQ scores began to fall – even as time spent in school kept rising,” writes Horvath. Scores in international tests started to drop. Why? “The answer lies in the meteoric rise of educational technology.”According to a recent Department for Education report, the UK educational technology – or edtech – market generated an annual turnover of about £6.5bn. In the US, Horvath says it is a $400bn (£295bn) mega-industry, woven into every aspect of schooling.“We’ve been making some incredible strides on the screen-based childhood stuff which even two years ago, I did not think was going to happen as fast as it did,” he said. “But it’s not just about getting rid of screens for entertainment. It’s about reducing them as much as possible for academic learning as well if we want our kids to have deep transferrable knowledge in our heads.”The uptake of laptops in schools – especially in the US where he lives – began in earnest in 2010-12, Horvath said. “It’s when Covid hit, that’s when every school had to pivot digital as a Band-Aid … rightly so. Better to have something than nothing.“But when Covid finished you would assume they’d rip that Band-Aid off, but the vast majority of schools didn’t. They just stayed digital.” In the US 88% of school districts now had one-to-one computers, he said. In the UK, Covid had a similar impact.Horvath has been studying how people learn for over 15 years and has concluded that “tech is not a very good tool for it”. He cites recent scores from the programme for international student assessment (Pisa) which takes place every three years and tracks the academic performance of 15-year-olds across dozens of countries.In 2012, 2015 and 2018, Pisa asked students how much time they spent using digital devices during a typical school day. “The more time students spent on screens at school, the further their scores fell,” Horvath said. “On average, those who used computers for more than six hours per day scored 66 points lower than their peers who didn’t use them at all.”View image in fullscreen‘Moderate school device use is associated with better results than no school device use,’ said Rose Luckin, an emerita professor at the UCL Knowledge Lab.Photograph: Paul Miller/AAPOthers working in the field are concerned about the risks of confusing correlation with causation. Rose Luckin is an emerita professor of learner-centred design at the UCL Knowledge Lab in London and a recognised expert on AI in education.“[Horvath] does get certain things right,” Luckin said. “It’s true that a great deal of educational technology was sold on promises rather than proof. We did not have a huge amount of evidence. But that does not mean that all educational technology is problematic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In terms of that Pisa data, if you look at it on computer use and outcomes, actually moderate school device use is associated with better results than no school device use. It’s just that the heaviest daily use is the worst.”Daisy Christodoulou, the director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startup, agrees that society has been a “bit blase” about the impact of a lot of these new technologies.“We are seeing across the board now a bit of a corrective, where people are realising that. But I would probably be a little bit more optimistic [than Horvath] about the potential for technology and AI in upper secondary,” she said. “Screens have not had as big an impact in classrooms in England as in the US. But I feel like there’s enough here that we should be thinking about it. I think it’s a bit blase to go, ‘nothing to see here’, move on please’.”Dylan Wiliam, an emeritus professor of educational assessment at the UCL Institute of Education, said: “Technology may well be harming student achievement but the correlational studies that we currently have cannot support such causal claims.“And there are many well-designed studies that show that technology can have a positive impact on student achievement. So the question, ‘Does edtech have a negative impact on learning?’ does not have a simple yes/no answer: sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn’t.“The question we need to be asking is, ‘when does edtech help learning?’ And the answer is, ‘it’s complicated’.”Explore more on these topicsSchoolsTeachingDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: AI cheating, leaked papers and marking errors: how exam protests went global | Global education | The Guardian
description: Student unrest sweeps India, Portugal and Mexico as grievances and pressure for good grades in tough job market collide
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Student unrest sweeps India, Portugal and Mexico as grievances and pressure for good grades in tough job market collide
Content: Cockroach Janta party supporters in Mumbai, India, celebrate the resignation of the education minister following protests over an exam paper leak that affected millions of students.Photograph: Indranil Aditya/ReutersView image in fullscreenCockroach Janta party supporters in Mumbai, India, celebrate the resignation of the education minister following protests over an exam paper leak that affected millions of students.Photograph: Indranil Aditya/ReutersGlobal educationAI cheating, leaked papers and marking errors: how exam protests went globalStudent unrest sweeps India, Portugal and Mexico as grievances and pressure for good grades in tough job market collideSupported byAbout this contentDeborah Solomon andOliver HolmesSun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFamilies with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants wereforced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’sworst education crisisin decades.By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandalforced the education minister to resign, and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens.Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive.India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protestsRead more“It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed.“We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.”View image in fullscreenStudent applicants of the National Autonomous University of Mexico protest over the retake of the admission exam.Photograph: Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto/ShutterstockWhen a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that hasbecome widespread in Indiaand elsewhere.Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by theCockroach Janta party, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.“When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine howIndiais going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.”View image in fullscreenThe Portuguese education minister, Fernando Alexandre, whose push to digitise the exam marking process has been deemed a failure with some students and parents.Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesIn Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in acrisis. Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors.Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating,approximately 58,000 studentswould have to retake the exam.Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmarkannounced this monththat from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating.Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.”View image in fullscreenNarendra Modi’s Indian government is grappling with the fallout from one of its toughest political challenges in years after anger over exam irregularities grew into a wider movement over unemployment and opportunities for young people.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesIn Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech.But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse.Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication.Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches.“I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said.“But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.”Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning.“This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said.This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal educationExamsProtestMexicoIndiaPortugalEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The kids were right’: 30 years of Pokémon, from school-wide bans to multimillion-dollar trading cards | Pokémon | The Guardian
description: Pokémon outlived the moral panic of its early days in Australia and its staying power has proved that simple joy can cross borders
Author: Patrick Marlborough
Headline: Pokémon outlived the moral panic of its early days in Australia and its staying power has proved that simple joy can cross borders
Content: ‘Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, for me, that made my life in Perth feel a little less isolated,’ writes Patrick Marlborough.Photograph: James D Morgan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, for me, that made my life in Perth feel a little less isolated,’ writes Patrick Marlborough.Photograph: James D Morgan/Getty ImagesPokémon‘The kids were right’: 30 years of Pokémon, from school-wide bans to multimillion-dollar trading cardsPokémon outlived the moral panic of its early days in Australia and its staying power has proved that simple joy can cross bordersPatrick MarlboroughSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a generation of Australians for whom Cheez TV was a religion. Every morning before school, I’d sit in my little white plastic chair about three feet from our big wooden television and watch 90 minutes of cartoons“curated”by the show’s teenage hosts, Jade and Ryan.Premiering in 1995, Cheez TVdominated the children’s breakfast market by 1998,stealing the crown from Channel Seven’s bogan-muppet icon Agro. A daily dose of Cheez TVwas such an important ritual to methat I remember feeling active resentment towards Princess Diana’s death because the news coverage bumped Earthworm Jim.View image in fullscreenCheez TV: ‘I remember sitting there, tinned spaghetti-soaked toastie in hand, gripped by a feeling of meteoric magic and wonder.’Photograph: YouTubeBut in September of 1998 my world was rocked when Jade and Ryan introduced something unlike anything I had ever seen – a Japanese cartoon called Pokémon. I remember sitting there, tinned spaghetti-soaked toastie in hand, gripped by a feeling of meteoric magic and wonder as the opening bars of the theme song rolled over me:“I want to be the very best / like no one ever was.”Yes, I thought,yes! I want that more than anything!But it wouldn’t be long before Pokémania became a moral panic in the Australian media – not so much a kids’ cartoon as a national security threat.View image in fullscreenTsunekazu Ishihara, the chief executive of the Pokémon Company, at the 2025 Gold Gala.Photograph: JC Olivera/Variety/Getty ImagesCelebrating its 30th anniversary this year, Pokémon was created by zinester turned game designerSatoshi Tajiri, developed by his company Game Freak and released in Japan by Nintendo as a sort of swan song for the ageing Game Boy. In Japan, it rapidly transformed from a schoolyard phenomenon to a national one, but it would take two years before it arrived in the west and became as omnipresent asZubats in a dark cave.It crash-landed in Australia via Cheez TV and, within a month of its debut, my life (and an entire generation of lives) revolved around the singular quest to “catch ’em all”.When the Game Boy games hit Australian shelves, they were an instant sensation too, jointly selling more than 400m worldwide.For the uninitiated, these games asked the player to explore a region called Kanto to collect, research and battle an enormous variety of creatures known asPokémon.View image in fullscreenGame Boy Pokémon games sold more than 400m worldwide.Photograph: AlamyI became so immersed in the world they presented – mythical animals and explorable forests and caves – that I felt my sense of what was possible, from my imagination to life itself, actively shift and expand. Pokémonwas beautiful.So of course, my school, the media and Australia at large responded to it like it was a plague devouring the hearts, souls and minds of the nation’s youth.‘Turning our children to witchcraft and violence’“The most popular toy this Christmas could be turning our children to witchcraft and violence,”began a Channel Seven news feature on Pokémon in 1999, citing the concerns ofSunshine Coast pastor Chas Gullo.“It’s short for ‘Pocket Monster,’”opined another Seven news anchor, “and when you discover the cost, it’s not a bad description.”On ABC radio, Mark Colvin warned:“The slogan is ‘gotta catch ’em all’, but many parents would be wondering whether that refers to the characters or the company’s aims for every primary school child in Australia”.He handed over to a reporter who called it “a worldwide craze over a collection of odd-looking creatures. One hundred and fifty-one, to be precise. With names like Pikachu, Meowth and Giber”.View image in fullscreenPikachu mascots.Photograph: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images(There is no Pokémon that goes by the name “Giber”.)The release of the Pokémon Trading Card Game midway through 1999 turned recess and lunch into something resembling the two-up game from Wake in Fright. The trading card game was and is a beast unto itself – a loose adaptation of the video game’s mechanics that also revolves around battling, trading and collecting them all – and Australians spent $11m on the trading cards inthe first two months of their release. They invited lunchbreak drama, which led to school-wide bans.View image in fullscreen‘The release of the Pokémon Trading Card Game … turned recess and lunch into something resembling two-up from Wake in Fright.’Photograph: Mael Ghazi/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesThese bans were met at some schools with protests. At my own, we led a sit-in at the special school assembly to debate the matter, with appointed representatives tasked with explaining the concept of Gengar to our beleaguered principal.How Pokémon Go encouraged me to find wonder in the worldRead moreIn this early wave of media hysteria, which was not contained to Australia, Pokémonwas seen as something between a vice,an addictionand, according to Peta, a past-time thatcould lead to animal abuse and dogfighting. There were reports of robberies, fraud and counterfeit, andold wives’ tales of kids jumping off buildingsbecause they thought they’d evolved into Pidgeotto.Undercutting a lot of these Australian news stories of a“dangerous craze”,however, was the footage that accompanied it: of children playing amicably in large groups, smiling at the camera and excitedly explaining to puzzled journos why Alakazam can easily defeat Machamp, despite the latter’s muscles.Lost in the reactionary responsewas a misunderstanding of its genius: to catch ’em all, you had to interact, befriend and trust your fellow players. Pokémonnot only encouraged community, it required it.View image in fullscreen‘Pokémonnot only encouraged community, it required it.’Photograph: Martin Lelievre/AFP/Getty ImagesPokémon was also my first taste of places and people beyond my own sphere. I remember one of my cousins coming back from Japan with a boxful of Japanese Pokémon cards; a Canadian exchange student swapping US-exclusive toys for rare Yowies; sharing the language of Pokémon with Sri Lankan kids, none of whom spoke English.Young fans knew that Pokémania was not an affliction but a shared, communal experience that linked you to people all over the globe. Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, for me, that made my life in Perth feel a little less isolated.Today Pokémon remains bound up in the national zeitgeist while still attracting controversy:there’s currently a wave of hobby-shop burglaries around the country,sparked by the insane inflation of the value of Pokémon trading cards, which have almost become their own currency –the most valuable of these auction for $16.5m.But despite the earnest wishes of my teachers, parents and the Australian media, Pokémon’s staying power has proved that the kids were right all along. It is now the single largest media franchise in the world, with countless games, media, toys, a new theme park andeven crockery.Pokémonremains at the top of the food chain because of its emphasis on simple joys; it will always be a franchise thatunites peoplebecause it continues to ask one simple question: do you want to have some fun?Explore more on these topicsPokémonGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as Trump | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: Marco Rubio at the Munich Security Conference, 14 February 2026.Photograph: Giuseppe Lami/EPAView image in fullscreenMarco Rubio at the Munich Security Conference, 14 February 2026.Photograph: Giuseppe Lami/EPAOpinionMarco RubioMarco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as TrumpSimon TisdallAs chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignoreSun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareViewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaignconclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this weekflatly rejectedhis latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’sattacks on Nato alliesgrow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His bossmocked himas “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.Or maybe not.Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice:become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. Helamented the declineof “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump hasattacked eight countriesin the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession,could be next.View image in fullscreenMarco Rubio looks on as Donald Trump speaks at an American Mining Industry roundtable, Washington, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Matt Kaminsky/EPARubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding.This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer,Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now hetoes Trump’s ingratiating lineon Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, hasgutted USAIDand seeks todismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, hetravelled to Romeand set the pope straight.The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losingon the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy isshort of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu –faces defeatin October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMillions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that? | Arwa MahdawiRead moreRubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. Heknows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out.The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becomingTrump’s chosen successorand heir to the Maga brand.Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsMarco RubioOpinionUS foreign policyTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Ali came to me seeking help for disordered eating. The real issue was a relationship built on control | Ahona Guha | The Guardian
description: She second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someone
Author: Ahona Guha
Headline: She second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someone
Content: ‘He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts,’ writes Dr Ahona Guha.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA WireView image in fullscreen‘He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts,’ writes Dr Ahona Guha.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA WireThe modern mindEating disordersAli came to me seeking help for disordered eating. The real issue was a relationship built on controlAhona GuhaShe second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someoneThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 16 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTShareAli* initially came to therapy for disordered eating. She was a young and diffident woman. She described recurrent cycles of restricted eating followed by attempts to exercise it away. We usedcognitive behavioural therapy for eating disordersto unpick her “food rules” – the underlying beliefs which can drive eating disorders, such as “the less I eat the better” or “carbs are bad”.As we worked on understanding and shifting her beliefs and behaviours around food, we noticed that most of her assumptions around eating, shape and weight coincided with the start of her relationship with her ex-partner. She told me he was a “gym junkie” and spent hours working out and encouraged her to do the same. “He got angry if I ate carbs,” she said, “and created a couples meal plan for us so I could shred and look hot when we were out together.”Slowly, she spoke of other forms of control: encouraging her to dress in a “sexier” manner than she felt comfortable with, jealousy if he saw her talking to another man, watching her bank transactions to see where she was going, and insisting on going to all her social events so he could get to know her friends. “But he’d always start an argument, or would say he didn’t like them,” she told me. “And then I had to stop seeing them to prove my loyalty to him.” He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts, telling her that what he wanted was “normal” and she was not being a good partner if she refused.I’m seeing more people in therapy struggling with war-related anxiety. Here’s what helps | Ahona GuhaRead moreAs she spoke to me, I saw the shift in her eyes when she realised the pattern which had slowly emerged over three years:coercive control.After this realisation, her eating stabilised. Food was one of the initial mechanisms of control he used to start shaping her body and personality, and her difficulties with eating were a symptom of the trauma she had experienced.Unlike physical violence, coercive control can be easy to miss as it is a pattern of repeated subtle behaviours and usually inflicted with the victim’s seeming agreement. At other times the coercion is more overt and can involve threats such as taking away children, or inflicting violence if sexual demands are not met. Regardless of the level of severity of this behaviour, the impacts can create psychological harm for victims.Like many other victims of coercive control, Ali had very poor self-esteem and was racked with anxiety. She second-guessed herself and was overly deferential and eager to please, reporting she “felt frozen” when she believed she displeased someone. Her beliefs about herself and about relationships were distorted (“I have no radar”, “all relationships are unsafe”). These are all typical responses demonstrated by people who have experienced coercion or violence in intimate relationships.Our work together encompassed a few stages. First, we worked together to understand what coercive control is, and used a simpleABC model derived from CBTto help Ali understand how certain statements or behaviours by her ex bypassed her instinctive radar and influenced her to give in to him by creating feelings of insecurity and anxiety. We looked at the way she experienced his approval as a potent reinforcer for compliance as it signalled that the danger of relational rupture or loss was over.We named the distinction between her emotions/thoughts and reality, allowing her to separate from the belief that she was “not enough”. We also adaptedcognitive processing therapy for PTSDtechniques to help her understand and reframe her “stuck points” (eg the trauma of her distorted beliefs about how she failed herself through her “poor radar”). We also looked at the characteristics of healthy relationships, and helped her create a checklist for herself of the signs of healthy relationships so she could date with more confidence.Together, we also worked on Ali’s anxiety. This predated her former partner though had considerably worsened after the relationship. We utilised a cognitive behavioural approach and looked at the beliefs which fuelled her anxiety (“my friends don’t like me because I withdrew from them while with my ex”) and how she responded to these beliefs, such as by refusing to go to gatherings or engaging insafety behaviourslike drinking. We did some behavioural “experiments” to challenge her beliefs and to learn new ways of coping, and also brainstormed ways she could talk to her friends about the relationship with Ian. She was pleasantly surprised to find that her friends understood and were supportive of her once they knew the context.Recovery was not a linear journey, but these small steps allowed Ali to stop blaming herself, to feel more confident in her body and to show up in the world just as she was, without focusing on pleasing a partner.*all clients are fictional amalgamsIn Australia, theButterfly Foundationis at 1800 33 4673. In the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In the US, help is available atnationaleatingdisorders.orgor by callingANAD’seating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. Other international helplines can be found atEating Disorder HopeDr Ahona Guha is a clinical and forensic psychologist, trauma expert and author from Melbourne. She is the author of Reclaim: Understanding Complex Trauma and Those Who Abuse, and Life Skills For a Broken WorldExplore more on these topicsEating disordersThe modern mindMental healthRelationshipsDomestic violenceAnxietycommentShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxury | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: A worker in London shields himself from the sun.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA worker in London shields himself from the sun.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersOpinionExtreme heatAndy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxuryJohn HarrisNurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plansSun 16 Aug 2026 07.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIdon’t think I have ever written before about a British strike directly related to the climate emergency. But that’s exactlywhat began late last weekin north London, with a zeitgeisty connection to Andy Burnham’s fixation on buses: picket lines outside depots and massed walkouts, while the temperatures in the relevant parts of the capital and its suburbs hovered at about 34C (93F).Last Friday, more than 1,500 drivers employed by the transport giant Arriva begana planned run of 26 stoppagesthrough to October, affecting bus routes spread between London and Essex. Everything is being led by the union Unite, whose recent grievances include alleged company union-busting and assaults by the public on staff. But the fundamental basis of the dispute is at the heart of the national condition: the near-impossibility for millions of people of working through another insanely hot summer.Most of Arriva North London’s buses, says Unite, have old-fashioned air cooling systems rather than air conditioning, which means that onboard temperatures have come down by only two or three degrees during this year’s five heatwaves. On other such vehicles, it insists,the air-con is broken. The cabs where drivers sit are essentially compact greenhouses, and can easily reach 40C or higher. And there is another grim twist: union members complain of a shortage of toilets on too many routes, meaning they refrain from drinking water. Unite has been warning about all this since the phases of intense heat that began back in May; its members, the union says, have experienced “heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration”.Arriva’s last financial figuresshowed a pre-tax profitof £133m.The company insiststhat it has “introduced short-term measures to protect drivers”, and is now also spending money on “longer-term fixes, including cab air-conditioning upgrades and our ongoing investment in new fleet”. But the root of its current problems seem clear. There is a longstanding failure, which runs across the UK’s public and private sectors – and also transcends national boundaries – to understand the mounting everyday effects of global heating, and to engage in what so many 21st-century companies and institutions remain so bad at: protective investment, with both eyes fixed not just on the searing inevitabilities of the future, but realities that are already here.Arriva places tight restrictions on its drivers talking to the media, so Unite pointed me instead to Mo, who has worked for another London bus operator for over 15 years, and had come to a picket line to show the strikers his support. “When it’s very hot, it’s very difficult to concentrate,” he told me. “Imagine the heat you feel when you put your hand near an oven. That’s what it’s like.” What, I wondered, had happened when these problems were raised with management? “Sometimes, we don’t want to raise this stuff, because they don’t want to hear it. If you say, ‘I’ve got a hot cab, I want to come out,’ they’re like, ‘Well, we’re going to lose mileage; we’re going to get penalised by TfL [Transport for London].’ I know the mayor’s put the message out” – in June,Sadiq Khan saidhe was committed to improving working conditions for drivers – “but the company says, ‘He doesn’t employ you. We do.’”There are no end of similarly unsettling reports from other occupations. The Royal College of Nursing says some of its members working in the health servicehave recently collapsed, while others have reported dizziness, nausea and dripping with sweat “from head to toe”, along with profound concerns about NHS patients’ most basic welfare.Recent research into the building tradefrom the University of Reading showed that 44% of the construction workers it contacted had experienced a heat-related illness, such as heatstroke, heat exhaustion or dehydration. Moreover, 57% said they had received no compulsory training on how to deal with heat.View image in fullscreenPeter Crane, who has driven for Arriva for 22 years, shows a temperature reading from inside of his cab of 44C as he takes part in strike action in north London.Photograph: Tom Jeffreys/PAAlmost exactly a year ago, I wrote aboutthe tragic story of Montse Aguilar, a 51-year-old woman who worked as a street cleaner in Barcelona, and returned home from a working day in which the city’s temperatures had reached 35C, only to collapse, hit her head and die. Soon after, people marched carrying banners that read “Extreme heat is also workplace violence”, and street cleaners demanded better summer workwear and more breaks. Much to her family’s distress, the city councilhas still not recognised her deathas a workplace accident, and there has yet to be an autopsy.This year, Barcelona’s authoritieshanded out about 1,400 braceletsfor staff working outdoors – including street cleaners, park workers and refuse specialists – which measure workers’ body temperatures and go into alert mode if they sense that the wearer is at risk: as and when that happens, the person concerned has to stop working. But despite Spain’s reputation for comparatively stringent heat regulations, unions continue to draw attention to a supposed system of protection still full of gaps. Late last month,the CGT union filed official complaintswith Barcelona’s labour inspectorate about what it deems deficient management of those wristbands, a lack of air-con in working vehicles and pledges from the city council being applied “late and halfway”.Across the world, every hot season inevitably brings more victims. In the US, official figures suggest thatmore than 550 workers die annuallyfrom heat exposure across the country. One recent story is that of Umeshkumar Thakkar, a 58-year-old postal worker who lived in Little Elm, Texas – who, though the cause of his death has yet to be officially established,has been citedas the third such employee in three years to die in the Dallas area amid extreme heat. Amazingly,Texas has barred its cities and countiesfrom passing local heat protections – while,to quote the New York Times, “The Trump administration is moving to rewrite Biden-era rules that would mandate breaks and access to water and shade for workers.” Hydration, it seems, is that bit too woke.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe UK’s position, it is a relief to say, is not nearly as dreadful, though there is still much work to do. For people working indoors,official guidancesuggests a minimum temperature of 16C, which falls to 13C for “physical work”, but there are no maximum temperatures for either indoor or outdoor labour. Things do finally seem to be moving: last month, the Department for Work and Pensions said that the Health and Safety Executive will soon launcha public consultationon improvements to safety-at-work rules that will cover levels of heat at work. There again,the official linefrom the prime minister’s spokesperson sounds bleak: “We have no plans to introduce a mandatory maximum workplace temperature.”In the wake of the Green MP Hannah Spencer’s private member’s bill toestablish exactly that, Unite is loudly making the case – as are the TUC and the independent advisory Climate Change Committee,which wants employersto “ensure that workplaces and working practices are safe for employees, including for those working outside”. Meanwhile, having planned for a late summer talking about the cost of living, Burnham did not mention the climate crisisuntil last Friday, in a country where brown fields are so starved of water they are now turning a scorched yellow,homes have been engulfed by wildfires, and far too many workers are finding the once-simple business of earning a living physically impossible. Like many people – including, I would imagine, plenty of those north London bus drivers – my guarded optimism about the new prime minister and his government endures. But the last of those issues needs as much urgent action as the others, before another boiling summer takes an even grimmer toll.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsExtreme heatOpinionIndustrial actionAndy BurnhamTrade unionsTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: Move over, Odysseus: time for the women of ancient Greece to have their moment in the sun | Natalie Haynes | The Guardian
description: The hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiences, says writer Natalie Haynes
Author: Natalie Haynes
Headline: The hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiences, says writer Natalie Haynes
Content: Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss (on screen) during rehearsals for Electra/Persona.Photograph: Monika Rittershaus/National Theatre/PAView image in fullscreenCate Blanchett and Nina Hoss (on screen) during rehearsals for Electra/Persona.Photograph: Monika Rittershaus/National Theatre/PAOpinionTheatreMove over, Odysseus: time for the women of ancient Greece to have their moment in the sunNatalie HaynesThe hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiencesSun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt feels like a very Greek summer here in the UK. The ground is scorched, it last rained months ago, and the giant publicity machine for Christopher Nolan’sbillion-dollar-grossingThe Odyssey – from red-carpet frocks to professorial disapproval – is a Charybdis, swallowing all other cultural events in its gaping maw.Mere Mortals– San Francisco Ballet’s astonishing work inspired by the story of Pandora – runs in Edinburgh this month before going to Sadler’s Wells in September. And Greek tragedy continues to fill London’s theatres.Last week, I went to seeSimon Stone’s reworkingof Aeschylus’s Oresteia at the Bridge theatre in south London, and it was packed. Even on a Thursday afternoon, there was a huge audience for the story of a family who turn on one another, wreaking intergenerational violence until their whole house lies in tatters and madness. Partly that is because of the excellent cast: David Morrissey and Mary-Louise Parker play Christopher and Montie – a modern Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, their marital squabbles fizzing back and forth until he cracks and she snaps. Their children are the ones who will have to try to reconcile the impossible: duty to their murdered father, respect to their murderous mother.Partly it is because Stone has earned his audience for Greek tragedy. Hisversion of Phaedrawith Janet McTeer at London’s National Theatre in 2023 blended Euripides, Seneca and Racine. And his adaptation ofEuripides’s Medea, starring Marieke Heebink at the Barbican in 2019, remains one of the best things I have ever seen. This modern-day version began with Medea leaving the asylum where she has spent the past year, after attempting to kill her ex-husband for his infidelity to her and their children. The dread piled up like bodies as the play moved to its wrenching conclusion. These very different plays posed a similar question: what do women do with their rage, if speaking it goes unheard?View image in fullscreenLiv Ullmann as Elisabet, left, and Bibi Andersson as Alma in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 film, Persona.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyThe hottest Greek ticket of the year, though, is surely for Cate Blanchett in the upcomingElectra/Persona by Benedict Andrews. Electra is a fascinating choice, not least because we have three different versions of her story: Sophocles and Euripides each wrote one, and Aeschylus’s Choephoroi covers the same part of the myth. There are plenty of variations between the three, not least because Euripides takes potshots at Aeschylus’s version, mocking a recognition scene that depended on Electra identifying her long-absent brother from a lock of hair and a footprint, both of which (implausibly) resemble her own.But the essential beats of her story are these: Agamemnon is murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra, and her lover, Aegisthus. Clytemnestra feels wholly justified in her actions, because Agamemnon had killed her older daughter 10 years earlier. She has spent the whole Trojan war waiting for the chance to take her revenge. But her surviving children – Electra and Orestes – cannot forgive her for killing their father, no matter the reason. Orestes has grown up away from home, biding his time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChristopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epic | Charlotte HigginsRead moreSophocles’s Electra has nowhere else to go: she cannot leave home, because she is a young woman and ancient Greek mores require that she live in her father’s house until she marries. Which she cannot do, because Aegisthus and Clytemnestra know she hates them, so any husband (or son she may have) would be turned against them. Electra is essentially imprisoned in the home of the people who killed her beloved father, with no hope of parole.This is the role that was being performed by Elisabet (played by Liv Ullmann) in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 psychological drama,Persona, before she has a breakdown and stops speaking. Alma (Bibi Andersson) is the guileless young nurse tending to her, sharing stories of her own life to fill the silence, until she finds that Elisabet is studying her. It is a film that has perplexed critics, unable to decode the women’s strange, strained relationship.But Electra is always a perplexing character, with warring emotions: love for her father, disregard for her late sister, loathing of her mother, and her pulsing heartbeat of rage. One reason these Greek tragedies keep finding an audience is that they give voice – and terrible action – to unheeded female anger. Medea doesn’t accept her abandonment, she destroys everything her husband has and wants in a single day. Clytemnestra doesn’t accept her daughter’s murder, she avenges it. And Electra doesn’t accept her father’s killing, but (like Hamlet) she doesn’t have the strength to act alone against her mother. These women are extremists – like many characters in Greek tragedy – but their rage is more powerful because they have been silenced and ignored. If modern theatre audiences are anything to go by, their days of silence are behind them.Natalie Haynes is presenter of Natalie Haynes Stands Up for the Classics on Radio 4, and author of books including Stone Blind and Pandora’s JarExplore more on these topicsTheatreOpinionThe OdysseyWomenCate BlanchettcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought – if I die, I’ve had a good innings’: producer James Ford on life, death and making an album from his hospital bed | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was Britain’s most in-demand producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he says
Author: Nosheen Iqbal
Headline: The Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was Britain’s most in-demand producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he says
Content: James Ellis Ford in his home in London.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJames Ellis Ford in his home in London.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianPop and rockInterview‘I thought – if I die, I’ve had a good innings’: producer James Ford on life, death and making an album from his hospital bedNosheen IqbalThe Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was at the height of his powers as Britain’s most in-demand music producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he saysSun 16 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a moment outside the door of a recording studio in rural France, staring at a half-eaten apple that he believed possessed psychedelic properties, when James Ford knew things had really got out of hand. He was stood with Klaxons; all of the band members were hypnotised by this rotting fruit which throbbed on the floor with kaleidoscopic intensity. They were convinced that its blooming mould was in fact their spiritual guru.The band had been riding the wave of their huge, scene-defining debut album, 2007’sMyths of the Near Future– which was produced by Ford – and were now trying to record the interminably difficult follow-up, aided by daily doses of a concoction they’d taken to calling “the five-star general”.“It was a huge bag, five drugs mixed together, probably ketamine and speed, I don’t know what else, but it was quite a psychedelic powder and they were doing it every morning and throughout the day,” says Ford. He realised he couldn’t rein things back in. “And after a two-and-a-half-week period … things got fucking weird.”So weird, in fact, that the head of the UK record label came over on the Eurostar carrying a bell jar at the band’s request, only to find out it was to cover an apple that had been chewed up and spat out by a passing dog and was now being called Mr Tabernacle. Klaxons, it’s fair to say, had lost their minds a little bit. The album was aborted.View image in fullscreenFord’s home studio.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The Guardian“We thought we were making The Dark Side of the Moon,” says Ford with a giggle, now sitting in the studio in his east London home. Instead, that “ill-fated second record” became the only project that Ford has never finished in a career that has since established him as the music industry’s go-to magic weapon.It is quite the trajectory. Ford went from tearing up 00s dancefloors as one half, alongside Jas Shaw, of Simian Mobile Disco – musicians and DJs who elevated the electro-rave era of the decade – to becoming the most sought-after ear in music. In the last decade, with little in the way of hype, he has quietly become the pre-eminent producer of his generation.Ford is who you call when you’re trying to make a career-defining album (Arctic Monkeys; Florence + the Machine; Jessie Ware; Fontaines DC), who you trust to realise a stunning comeback (Pulp; Blur; Gorillaz; Depeche Mode) and who you need to help translate critical buzz into commercial success (Geese; The Last Dinner Party; Black Country, New Road).“It’s a very broad term ‘producer’,” he says, trying to explain his role. “It doesn’t really describe what happens; I’m trying to get to the bottom of someone else’s vision and pull that out there.” Be it Pet Shop Boys or Jessie Ware, artists agree that Ford doesn’t produce in a conventional sense. “I think if you try to imprint your sound, it seems a weird ego-y thing to do, to try to do a Phil Spector on everyone’s record.” And so he doesn’t impose a sound or vibe on to the room so much as mediate, and draw artists in and out of whatever creative pattern they’re in.View image in fullscreenJames Ellis Ford photographed in his home in London, July 2026.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianAt home, surrounded by synths, guitars and all manner of recording equipment, Ford seems relaxed and is softly spoken, with a light touch of the Staffordshire accent he grew up with. The heyday of his hedonism may be behind him, but it’s obvious that he still loves what he does. It is this and a general sense of ease that has earned Ford a level of trust from artists at their most vulnerable. A gracious, nice guy in an industry famously short of decency, it’s easy to understand why the world’s biggest artists are knocking down his door to work with him.Still, it’s a minor miracle we’re even meeting today. On Christmas Eve 2024 Ford was with his wife and young son at his in-laws’ in Folkestone when he got “hit like a ton of bricks”. He was laid out on the sofa, unable to get up with a fever that wouldn’t break and a flu-like illness that refused to let up. He had worked flat out all year, and in the weeks running up to December had felt unusually fatigued. He wondered whether he was heading for burnout, but this was something entirely new.He was admitted to the local A&E; his blood tests were “all over the place”. Having travelled to India with Damon Albarn some weeks earlier, doctors initially suspected he had picked up a tropical disease. “There were a lot of red herrings,” he says. “It took ages to get any kind of diagnosis because my bloods had to get sent to London, so I spent weeks in this horrible state, and just felt I was going to die. It was awful.”double quotation markNo-one was supposed to visit me in hospital, but Jarvis came. The staff let him inWeeks later, on a Friday night, “someone unceremoniously came in and said: ‘We’ve found leukaemia. You need to go to a cancer ward.’” And that was it. If his life had flashed before him, Ford, who had just turned 46, could admit it had been a good one. A great one, even. “I’ve got a wonderful family with my wife and little boy, I’ve got a great relationship with my parents, a good career, I’ve travelled a lot, done a lot of things with a lot of people that I’ve dreamed of working with,” he says. And he has partied hard, I joke, having borne witness to multiple Simian Mobile Disco sets and afterparties. “I’ve partied really hard,” he says. “I’ve had some great times, I’ve got a lot of good memories and I’ve made some things I’m really proud of. I think I’ve been a generally good person in the world. And so I was almost at the point where I was like, if I die, I’ve had a good innings. I wouldn’t be that scared of it.”View image in fullscreenFord’s US platinum disc for Arctic Monkeys’ AM.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianFord was eventually transferred to St Barts hospital in London and pummelled with rounds of drugs. He spent the early weeks of 2025 obliterated by the illness. Then came the second round of chemotherapy, and something of a breakthrough. He asked his wife Sereen, whom he met as a student at Manchester University, to bring in his laptop, an Ikea fold-up table, some synthesisers, a microphone and a guitar to his hospital room. Supported by staff at the hospital, who could see it cheered him up and got him out of bed, Ford began making music. Nurses got used to administering their daily medical care while Ford messed with drumbeats and sang, locked in his creative flow state. In two weeks, Ford wrote and recorded his new album, Lost in Another World, which would be remarkable enough on its own – were it not for the fact that it is also stunning.Despite being sung and recorded by Ford in a creative jag while contemplating life and death, the record feels like his signature sound – melodic, electronic, art-pop. It’s joyful where you expect it to be bleak. Over the course of nine months, Ford went through two more rounds of chemotherapy, a stem cell transplant, sepsis – three times – and a stay in intensive care. To say it has been an unremittingly traumatic year sells it short, but he – and the album – wear it lightly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t know if nervous is the right word,” he says of Lost in Another World’s impending release. “It’s more odd because it takes me back to that moment of being ill. And I’d intentionally left it, but now I’m having to talk about it. At first, even hearing it back for the first time, I was like ‘Ugh!’” I insist we don’t have to talk about the depths of his illness.“I always felt pretty invincible, though,” says Ford, reflecting on it. “And then suddenly, you’re like: ‘Oh, I’m not.’ And it was that thing: two or three years before this, I started running. I was going to the gym regularly. I was eating well. I’d lost weight, I’d given up drinking, given up all drugs, blah blah, the full cycle. And then I fucking get leukaemia!”Despite the toll the cancer took, Ford still somehow managed to produce two more major albums when he was really ill. One for Gorillaz, the other for the Mercury prize-nominated War Child album,Help(2), where he was producing the likes of Olivia Rodrigo and Beth Gibbons from his hospital bed. “Remote producing a session [going on] at Abbey Road while having a blood transfusion was not on my 2025 bingo card,” he posted on Instagram at the time.View image in fullscreenFord’s home setup.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianFord was not allowed any visitors for long stretches in hospital, Sereen excepted, because his immunity was so shot. “Funnily enough, Jarvis [Cocker] came in when he wasn’t meant to. But he’s so recognised, they were bamboozled and let him in and he’d very sweetly bought me some of his favourite books and wrote little things in them of what he liked and stuff.
