It was wonderful but I was a bit: ‘Wow, OK!’”Mentally at least, music saved him. “It was amazing to have something to focus on that made me feel good, to get into that zone where I shut down everything else on the outside. The lyrics [for Lost in Another World] literally just fell out. Obviously I had a bunch of stuff to process, but it was the easiest music-making process I’ve ever had.”‘Some artists thought it was too political’: can Jarvis, Damon, Olivia Rodrigo and Arctic Monkeys reboot the biggest charity album of the 90s?Read moreHow is he doing now? “I’m still not fully out of it.” Ford will have his bloods closely monitored for the next few years and attend regular checkups to track whether the cancer comes back. For now, he is gearing up for a number of live shows following the album’s arrival into the world and rehearsals are under way.“The obvious thing that has come out of all of this is that it does make you recognise what and who the important things in your life are and that life is exceptionally fragile,” he says of his renewed work-life balance. “Not to spend any time with people who aren’t worth spending time with and on projects that aren’t worth spending time on. Just being really selective and intentional about every choice you make. And that can be as simple as ‘spend more time in nature’, ‘spend more time with my family’, ‘maybe not work so hard’.”He smiles at the last one. “None of that is particularly groundbreaking. It’s stuff you see every day on the internet, but it’s different when you live through it. I definitely had read about the value of gratitude and all of those things, but I could never really take it on board in a way that I have now.”Lost in Another World by James Ellis Ford is out now; he plays Rough Trade East, London,17 August; and the Horse Hospital, London, 17 September.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Abby Govindan: Pushing 30 review – playful comic makes the case for marriage as a side quest | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Govindan’s confident debut takes aim at patriarchal stereotypes with pranks, PowerPoint and easygoing storytelling
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: Govindan’s confident debut takes aim at patriarchal stereotypes with pranks, PowerPoint and easygoing storytelling
Content: A funny heart to heart … Abby Govindan.Photograph: Kathleen Nicole SorianoView image in fullscreenA funny heart to heart … Abby Govindan.Photograph: Kathleen Nicole SorianoEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAbby Govindan: Pushing 30 review – playful comic makes the case for marriage as a side questPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghGovindan’s debut takes aim at patriarchal stereotypes with pranks, PowerPoint and easygoing storytellingArusa QureshiSun 16 Aug 2026 05.31 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn south Asian culture, marriage continues to be paramount, with women still largely bearing the brunt of this societal pressure. Tonight, the few south Asian women in the audience that US comedian Abby Govindan calls upon – myself included – verify this, one explaining how her parents have given up now that she is in her mid-30s.For Govindan, who is nearing 30, it’s a familiar conversation she has had with well-meaning relatives, and one that creates an internal paradox. While she loves her south Asian identity and her Indian heritage, it can be difficult to reconcile this with the patriarchal stereotypes and archaic values that tend to hold women back.View image in fullscreenA show with heart … Abby Govindan.Photograph: Varun MummadiIn a confident fringe debut, Govindan explores the reductive nature of conversations around marriage and ageing, and the value that is placed on dating and relationships over simply living life to the full. She regales the audience with stories of her many wins in life, from that time she managed to convince the internet that she was the creator ofEmily in Paris, to when she scammed the KKK.Slides on a screen behind her show screenshots proving her penchant for pranks, with tweets that have unexpectedly gone viral and led to the dreaded Notes app apology, and even a playfully contentious Venn diagram illustrating her flawed reasoning for only dating Indian men. Discussions around misinformation and the impact of big tech’s stranglehold on our lives add an interesting through-line. But the show loses momentum a little with the general over-reliance on PowerPoint, which occasionally takes us out of the narrative and away from Govindan’s easygoing and conversational storytelling.Even so, in a show with heart, Govindan details her desire to shatter generational and gendered expectations, placing emphasis on her right to just be her silly self. As she notes, patriarchy is not just a south Asian problem – but in her actions and achievements, it’s up to her to break free from the confines that every generation of women in her family has faced.In the end, through the recreation of a funny heart-to-heart with a young family member, we see that it’s about not wanting to perpetuate the same harms, choosing to view marriage as a side quest and not necessarily the main event.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Have I tried having sex to my own music? God, no!’: Natalie Imbruglia’s honest playlist | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The singer was wooed with some knocked-off Joni Mitchell and might even be persuaded to sing Torn at karaoke. But what fan comment winds her up the most?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer was wooed with some knocked-off Joni Mitchell and might even be persuaded to sing Torn at karaoke. But what fan comment winds her up the most?
Content: Natalie Imbruglia … ‘I’m not the most confident party playlist DJ.’Photograph: RankinView image in fullscreenNatalie Imbruglia … ‘I’m not the most confident party playlist DJ.’Photograph: RankinHonest playlistPop and rock‘Have I tried having sex to my own music? God, no!’: Natalie Imbruglia’s honest playlistThe singer was wooed with some knocked-off Joni Mitchell and might even be persuaded to sing Torn at karaoke. But what fan comment winds her up the most?As told toRich PelleySun 16 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withMy dad gave me California Dreamin’ by the Mamas & the Papas on vinyl for my fifth birthday. I said: “Oh thanks, Dad,” but really, I thought: “Who is this weird bunch of people?” Obviously, the present was really for him.The first single I boughtI remember begging my mum to buy me Beat It by Michael Jackson at a record shop in the ’burbs of Sydney. I mean – he’s Michael Jackson.The song I do at karaokeWhen you’re a singer, it’s really awkward: you don’t want to throw a tantrum, sound too good or show off, because then everyone is like “Ugh.” I might do Torn, but only at parties, when I’m drunk and my friends make me.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toYou’re the Voice by John Farnham – because it’s a bit of a tour bus anthem after a show and a couple of gins.The song I can no longer listen toWhen I was 17, this guy wrote out the lyrics to Coyote by Joni Mitchell and told me he’d written a poem about me. I thought: “My God, he’s a poet.” But years later, I was listening to this album and thought: “I recognise those words!” So now I just think: “What a creep!”The best song to play at a partyAny time it’s afters at mine, I always think: “What am I gonna put on?” I’m not the most confident party playlist DJ. But, no matter the mood or the crowd, I can put on Genius of Love by Tom Tom Club, and everyone loves it.The best song to have sex toPass! Have I tried my own music? God, no!The song that changed my lifeI have to say Torn, don’t I? Even though it’s a cover, which I’ve been tortured over ever since. People say: “You didn’t write Torn.” I think: “So what? I know I didn’t.” There was a meme that said: “The way you feel when you find out Torn’s a cover,” and it all started again! I thought: “For fuck’s sake, I just got over that!”The song that gets me up in the morningI’m not good in the mornings, so it has to be something gentle, like Little Blue by Jacob Collier.The song that makes me cryA Song for You by Donny Hathaway is just the most incredible love song. The tone of his voice is so pleasing.The song I’d like played at my funeralAnother One Bites the Dust by Queen, segued into Don’t Stop Me Now.Natalie Imbruglia’s album Algorithm is out on 4 September.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockHonest playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blackbox review – a legendary escape from slavery is told with magic tricks | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The story of Henry ‘Box’ Brown, who succeeded in mailing himself out of bondage, is recounted rather than fully dramatised
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: The story of Henry ‘Box’ Brown, who succeeded in mailing himself out of bondage, is recounted rather than fully dramatised
Content: Jada Evelyn Ramsey and Josiah Alpher in Blackbox at Underbelly, Edinburgh.Photograph: Jason SullivanView image in fullscreenJada Evelyn Ramsey and Josiah Alpher in Blackbox at Underbelly, Edinburgh.Photograph: Jason SullivanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBlackbox review – a legendary escape from slavery is told with magic tricksUnderbelly, EdinburghThe story of Henry ‘Box’ Brown, who succeeded in mailing himself out of bondage, is recounted rather than fully dramatisedMark FisherSun 16 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry “Box” Brown is wrapped up in chains when he has an idea to claim his freedom. As inspiration hits him, actor Josiah Alpher flexes his muscles and, miraculously, the chains appear to pass through his neck. Magic!It is a neat visual metaphor for a true story that seems miraculous in itself. In 1849, Brown made a break to flee slavery near Richmond, Virginia, by posting himself in a wooden crate to Philadelphia, a state where ownership of human beings had been phased out by the Gradual Abolition Act of 1780. Alpher describes a painful journey, squashed, upturned and knocked about, beforeBrown’s happy delivery.Rickerby Hinds’s staging of his own play uses the language of stage magic, from the glamorous magician’s assistant (Jada Evelyn Ramsey) to the knotted rope trick, to emphasise how extraordinary this escape was. Brown gets into the box as if he were Harry Houdini performing a stunt.Hinds shows too how the bonds of US slavery were not just represented by physical chains: they extended to a church that sanctioned the practice and to the constant threat of whipping, a nagging psychological burden.Not for Glory review – folk dance and bagpipes, but not as we know themRead moreAll this is duly itemised in a script that tells Brown’s story before his break for freedom, not only the callous treatment at the hands of his owner, but also accounts of conditions even worse than his own.It is weighty material but it is lessened in three ways. The story is recounted rather than dramatised and were it not for the magic tricks would seem theatrically flat. The actors hit an impressively breakneck speed, but perform without tonal variation, making it hard to keep up. And the story ends where you might expect it to begin, with Henry “Box” Brown’s entry into a new life.At Underbelly, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalFestivalsMagicSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Four Walls and a Roof review – fascinating tale of Brecht, the red scare and today’s émigrés | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Rabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie explore the playwright’s life, and their journey from Beirut to Berlin, in an absorbing show at the Edinburgh international festival
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Rabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie explore the playwright’s life, and their journey from Beirut to Berlin, in an absorbing show at the Edinburgh international festival
Content: Pointed parallels to today … Four Walls and a Roof.Photograph: KFDA Sybille CornetView image in fullscreenPointed parallels to today … Four Walls and a Roof.Photograph: KFDA Sybille CornetEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFour Walls and a Roof review – fascinating tale of Brecht, the red scare and today’s émigrésStudio Theatre, EdinburghRabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie explore the playwright’s life, and their journey from Beirut to Berlin, in an absorbing show at the Edinburgh international festivalMark FisherSun 16 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBertolt Brecht termed it “cold execution”. He was thinking of the way the US government, in the era of theHouse Un-American Activities Committee(Huac), could murder its opponents not by directly killing them but by cutting them off from what kept them alive. Where the cold war was waged without bullets, these cold executions were enacted, for example, on any blacklisted artist who could no longer work in Hollywood.It is an idea picked up by Lebanese artists Lina Majdalanie and Rabih Mroué who use the story of the playwright in exile as a way of thinking about displacement in our own era. Brecht, no doubt seeing the writing on the wall, got out of his native Germany soon after the burning of the Reichstag in 1933. It took him several countries, eight years and a journey across land and sea to reach the US. As Majdalanie and Mroué wryly point out, getting back to Europe after the US questioned his communist affiliations took only a day.View image in fullscreenAn absorbing illustrated lecture … Rabih Mroué in Four Walls and A Roof.Photograph: KFDA Sybille CornetIn an absorbing illustrated lecture, accompanied by pianist Henrik Kairies singing songs by Brecht and Hanns Eisler, the pair use the playwright’s life away from home as a way of asking questions about place and identity. As émigrés from Beirut to Berlin, they have a personal interest in the idea of homeland: however you define it, it means more than the four walls and a roof of the title.Reading from their script in a casual, un-actorly way, they gently prod Brecht’s story towards today. The Huac wanted yes-or-no certainty and did not allow the playwright to readhis prepared statement. Had they heard his commentary on the early Nazi crackdown on free speech perhaps they would have spotted parallels with their own intolerance. With the far right on the rise again, they are parallels that speak to us ever more pointedly.AtStudio theatre, Edinburgh, until 17 August.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalBertolt BrechtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jonno: Here Comes Mr Funny review – Sheeps comic leaves flock for revelatory solo | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Saturday Night Live UK writer, who is one-third of the sketch troupe Sheeps, balances sincerity and shtick in a show with big laughs
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The Saturday Night Live UK writer, who is one-third of the sketch troupe Sheeps, balances sincerity and shtick in a show with big laughs
Content: Hitherto hidden … Jonno.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHitherto hidden … Jonno.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewJonno: Here Comes Mr Funny review – Sheeps comic leaves flock for revelatory soloMonkey Barrel, EdinburghThe Saturday Night Live UK writer, who is one-third of the sketch troupe Sheeps, balances sincerity and shtick in a show with big laughsBrian LoganSun 16 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are reasons to take up standup, and then there’s Daran “Jonno” Johnson launching this new career aged 38 as a form of exposure therapy for anxiety. At least we have an explanation for why this prodigiously funny and talented man hasn’t gone solo before. As one-third of thesketch-group-of-their-generation, Sheeps, and now head writer on the hitSaturday Night Live UK, he doesn’t lack credentials for a tilt at standup.And, while Here Comes Mr Funny has its teething problems, it’s a bright start to Jonno’s singular life, and gave me some of my biggest laughs of this fringe. What’s surprising about it, and arguably part of what works least well, is that Jonno – a man hitherto hidden behind tiers of irony in his performing career – reveals so much of himself. He admits to being nervous. He talks about envying watching his peers on TV, half expecting to see himself appear on screen and join them.View image in fullscreenNajo ditties … Jonno.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSome of this material is delivered from Jonno’s “stool of sincerity”, to which he repairs (or so he tells us) when wishing to speak from the heart. In fact, things aren’t as clear cut as that. One of the great charms of this performer is his impishness, a delight in gambolling one step ahead of his audience. The line does blur here between sincerity and shtick – but as Jonno gains standup confidence, it could fruitfully do so more.Joseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70 review – a dork’s last day at school is one to rememberRead moreIn the meantime, the shtick is summoned forth from a grab-bag of comedy styles, that includes banjo ditties (the smutty and surreal songs will be catnip to fans of Sheeps’cult-hit Christmas album), a one-man staging of a supposed new Lloyd Webber musical, and an improvised rap that refuses very sillily to proceed as intended. A particular highlight is the Bond themes sequence, in which Jonno glories to lead us up musical garden paths before slamming lyrical gates in our faces. I would classify this experiment in confronting his fears as a qualified success – but here’s hoping his therapist adjudges the work incomplete, and requires of Jonno repeated returns to solo standup.AtMonkey Barrel, Edinburgh, until 30 August.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a remarkable Bafta-winning film gets a vital update | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The story of Mir Hussein in Afghanistan, who cameras have now followed for 25 years. Plus: a comedy from the director of Colin from Accounts. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The story of Mir Hussein in Afghanistan, who cameras have now followed for 25 years. Plus: a comedy from the director of Colin from Accounts. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: A remarkable feat … Mir Hussein in 25 Years in Afghanistan on ITV1.Photograph: ITVView image in fullscreenA remarkable feat … Mir Hussein in 25 Years in Afghanistan on ITV1.Photograph: ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a remarkable Bafta-winning film gets a vital updateThe story of Mir Hussein in Afghanistan, who cameras have now followed for 25 years. Plus: a comedy from the director of Colin from Accounts. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Graeme VirtueandJack SealeSun 16 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google25 Years in AfghanistanSunday, 11.15pm, ITV1Mir Hussein was eight years old when he first saw a camera in 2002. Documentary-makers Phil Grabsky and Shoaib Sharifi filmed him and his family in Afghanistan when US troops arrived, and followed him for two decades as he grew up and became a cameraman himself in Kabul. The Bafta-winning film My Childhood, My Country: 20 Years in Afghanistan was released in 2021. This is an updated version that revisits those years and adds new insight into what has happened in the half-decade since, after the US and its allies left and the Taliban regained control. It’s a remarkable feat, showing everyday life – including joyous moments such as filming a football match – in the context of the regime.Hollie RichardsonForce of Nature7pm, ITV1Stunningly shot by a director who presents the creatures as if they’re Marvel superheroes, this must-watch nature series continues. Episode four looks at how animals who live in colder climates are adapting to the climate crisis, including a snow leopard in the Himalayas who is edged out of his homestead by a rival male.Priya ElanVan Der Valk8pm, ITV1When a young genome scientist making great leaps in cancer research takes a flier off the roof of an Amsterdam club, it falls to Marc Warren’s insomniac cop to doggedly untangle what really happened. But with a leather-clad female assassin and a smarmy pharma billionaire in the mix, it’s going to be a tough nut to crack.Graeme VirtueRichard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey8pm, Channel 4Grant’s jaunt around Odysseus haunts reaches the Tunisian island of Djerba, where he soaks up the energy of Arabic markets and the ancient know-how of Jewish craftsmanship. In Homeric terms this is lotus-eating country, but there’s no danger of our guide sinking into an amnesiac stupor: he’s soon off to the west coast of Italy in search of history’s worst dinner party host, Circe.Jack SealeDebuts at the Proms9pm, BBC FourA celebration of Proms history with its premieres and debuts. There’s the Spanish National Orchestra, who debuted this year on the same night Spain won the World Cup, plus superstar soprano Angel Blue, and the first accordion soloist.HRSunny Nights10.15pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenDream team … Will Forte and Vicki D’Arcy Carden in Sunny Nights on ITV1.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/ITVDirected by Colin from Accounts’ Trent O’Donnell, this crime comedy drama follows two American chancers who land in Australia and get into all types of trouble. Siblings Martin (Will Forte) and Vicki (D’Arcy Carden) are trying to set up a spray tan business when Martin has a one-night stand that ends up in blackmail.HRLive sportCricket: The Hundred, 2pm, BBC TwoThe women’s final at Lord’s, followed by the men’s final at 6pm.Community Shield Football: Arsenal v Man City,2pm, TNT Sports 1The new season curtain-raiser , at Principality Stadium in Cardiff.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Angels in America review – Tony Kushner’s five-hour fever dream predicts and reflects the US at 250 | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: People, ideas and scenes wash over each other in Ivo van Hove’s masterly staging at the Edinburgh international festival
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: People, ideas and scenes wash over each other in Ivo van Hove’s masterly staging at the Edinburgh international festival
Content: Exemplary cast … Minne Koole and Krisjan Schellingerhout in Angels in America performed by Internationaal Theater Amsterdam.Photograph: Jess Shurte/Edinburgh international festivalView image in fullscreenExemplary cast … Minne Koole and Krisjan Schellingerhout in Angels in America performed by Internationaal Theater Amsterdam.Photograph: Jess Shurte/Edinburgh international festivalEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAngels in America review – Tony Kushner’s five-hour fever dream predicts and reflects the US at 250King’s theatre, EdinburghPeople, ideas and scenes wash over each other in Ivo van Hove’s masterly staging at the Edinburgh international festivalMark FisherSun 16 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCould Tony Kushner’s sprawling fever-dream of a play now have come of age? It is 35 years since the two-part epic had its premiere in San Francisco when the memory of its Aids-crisis setting a few years earlier was still acute. Today, enough time has passed for us to see it in perspective: the historical moment in the mid 1980s when a new and initially untreatable virus was spreading, primarily among gay men, at the same time as reactionary conservative forces were in the ascendant under the two presidential terms of Ronald Reagan.In an Edinburgh international festival that is asking questions of the United States in the 250th anniversary year of the Declaration of Independence, Angels in America seems to predict and reflect the contradictory nation of today.Subtitled A Gay Fantasia on National Themes, the five-hour play lays out a set of competing ideologies as if psychoanalysing the country: the guilt of Judaism, the forgiveness of Catholicism, the repression of Mormonism, the liberation of being out and proud, the self-hatred of being closeted, and the law-of-the-jungle individualism that stokes right-wing thought.“America has rediscovered itself,” says Joe Pitt (Krisjan Schellingerhout), a Republican Mormon, believing that, under Reagan, his country has reclaimed a “sacred position among nations”. Such messianic idealism runs counter to reality. There is a hole in the ozone layer, points out Harper (Eefje Paddenburg), his wife, and only a particular type of sociopath, such as Joe’s idol Roy Cohn (Hans Kesting), would be proud that this is “no country for the infirm”.View image in fullscreenVisitations … Felix Schellekens and Hans Kesting in Angels in America.Photograph: Jess Shurte/Edinburgh international festivalJoe and Roy are symbols of a nation eating itself from the inside. Joe, because he cannot square his conservative values with being secretly gay. Roy, because he associates homosexuality with weakness: “Roy Cohn is a heterosexual man … who fucks around with guys.” The play does not mention it, but in the 70s and 80s, this real-life New York lawyer and kingmaker represented Donald Trump.So far so polemical, but the appeal of Kushner’s play is the way it blurs into the mythic with its feverish hallucinations. Characters end up in each other’s dreams, there are visitations from horny angels, Harper treats her Valium like a passport to faraway places and even the brutish Roy is haunted by Ethel Rosenberg (Marieke Heebink), a woman condemned to death as a result of his prosecution.It is this dreamlike quality that pervades Ivo van Hove’s masterly staging for Internationaal Theater Amsterdam, first seen in 2008 and performed here in Dutch, with English surtitles. Actors seem to appear out of nowhere on Jan Versweyveld’s edgeless set, empty but for a counter with a couple of turntables blasting out favourites by David Bowie, a musician whose stridency and vulnerability are a good match for the play. There are no doors, beds, tables or phones; just a fluid movement of people and ideas as scenes wash over each other.Leading an exemplary cast of eight, Kesting is at the play’s troubling heart as a Roy Cohn who is at once brutish and intellectually consistent. Even as his body decays, he dominates with alpha-male energy. His day is not over yet.At King’s theatre, Edinburgh, until 20 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalIvo van HoveTony KushnerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kinz, London W11: ‘No bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Home cooking, but in the most complimentary sense
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Home cooking, but in the most complimentary sense
Content: Kinz, London W11: ‘There’s something cinematic about this elegant setting.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKinz, London W11: ‘There’s something cinematic about this elegant setting.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewKinz, London W11: ‘No bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride’ – restaurant reviewHome cooking, but in the most complimentary senseGrace DentSun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome developers would rip the soul out of a 1930s banking hall, butKinz, a new all-day Lebanese brasserie housed in a former Lloyds Bank in Notting Hill, instead makes a feature of its chunky vault door. Where W11 residents once kept their cash, diners can now take a seat and sip Lebanese wine from theBekaa valley. After all, what visit to the bank wouldn’t be improved by a cold glass ofChateau Musar Jeune?This triple-height room with mezzanine seating is a very different proposition from all those tiny, homespun Lebanese restaurants typically anchored around Edgware Road since the 1970s. Kinz may offerkibbehnayyeh(finely minced raw lamb and beef with bulgur, spices and pine nuts),shish barak(tiny lamb and herb dumplings in yoghurt sauce) andwarak enab(lamb-stuffed vine leaves and baby courgettes), as do many places in pockets across west London, but there is something altogether more cinematic about this elegant setting.I sat with my pot of mint tea thinking that the place has all the hallmarks of a 1980s Duran Duran video, in which the boys pitch up somewhere sophisticated in Lebanon for mysterious hijinks. Kinz’s mezzanine seems almost built forJohn Taylorto sip ababunajnegroni (Hayman’s gin,Lillet Blanc,Suzeand chamomile) under his tousled fringe. Large-format photographs of Lebanese life line the walls, including one of an impressive matriarch on a visit to the hair salon.View image in fullscreen‘Home cooking in the most complimentary sense’: Kinz’s spiced chicken with rice.Even so, Kinz is far from showy – in fact, it feels a bit like an upmarket but still everyday Lebanese canteen. Pop in for a plate of spinachfatayerand end up staying for the Sunday specialmolokhiye–slow-simmered jute mallow with chicken, rice, pitta and a sharp, mignonette-style sauce.Fans of Akub,the well-loved modern Palestinian restaurantjust a few streets away, may well recognise the name of that formidable restaurateur,Rasha Khouri Bruzzo. Here, she has joined forces with brothers Jad and Karim Lahoud, both Londoners raised by Lebanese chef parents. The result is a deeply personal space, where the chocolate cake is the Lahouds’ mother Elene’s recipe – she’s even been known to turn up in the kitchen of a morning simply to test that this gooey, dark chocolate sponge is up to her standards.The vibe across much of the menu, meanwhile, is elegant sparseness: nothing is over-garnished or served with frippery. Mint tea comes in tiny, functional, stainless-steel pots. Cheeserikakat(filo pastry cigars) arrive on a plain plate looking for all the world like M&S party food … until you bite in and find them hot, crisp and delicately seasoned with fresh mint. I reckon I could eat at least 17 of these things in one sitting. It would not be pretty, but it would be a testament to their beige deliciousness.View image in fullscreen‘I could eat at least 17 of these in one sitting’: Kinz’s cheeserikakat.Rich hummus comes topped with tahini, with the option of adding pine nuts orawarma, a spiced, slow-cooked minced lamb. There isbaba ganoush, obviously, but alsomoutabal,or smoky chargrilled aubergine with tahini. Cod fillets come with walnuts and tahini sauce. All are understated, yet effective: no bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride and an urge to be accurate.The staff are a genuine delight – warm, knowledgable, unhurried – and the food is definitely decent. You might even mistake thefattetaubergine, baked in tomato sauce and served on yoghurt with broken toasted pitta, for parmigiana, but they are very different beasts. Parmigiana is rich, oily, cheesy and baked into submission. Fattet, however, which in Arabic means “crumbs”, is built on crisp bread soaked in yoghurt, and as a result is much lighter, sharper and altogether more refreshing.View image in fullscreen‘Light, sharp and refreshing’: Kinz’sfattetaubergine.The slow-cooked spiced chicken with rice is a standout: home cooking in the most complimentary sense, with properly stewed bird, roast almonds, a sharp sourness running through the rice, and a rich gravy served from a long-handled, copper-coloured pan.For pudding, we orderedosmalieyeh, or crispkataifi pastrylayered withashtaclotted cream and orange blossom syrup, which is delicate, not over-sweet and a gentle way to end. But it is Elene’s chocolate cake that is the real star of the dessert show: dense, dark, damp and oozing. We even ordered a second piece to take home, complete with specific instructions not to refrigerate it or Elene would be cross. I’ve never met the woman, but I was suitably chastened.Kinz was busy as heck on the lunchtime we visited, and it’s plain to see why. I’ve been recommending it to anyone with a large group to feed in west London. There is a very real sense that this re-loved bank and its new inhabitants are here to stay. Kinz will get my trade any time I’m passing – and I willalwaysorder that chocolate cake.View image in fullscreenKinz’sosmalieyehpudding is ‘delicate, not over-sweet and a gentle way to end a meal’.Kinz50 Notting Hill Gate, London W11, 020-4637 5068. Open all week, noon-11pm (midnight Fri & Sat). From about £40 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make quesadillas – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A cook-your-own adventure meal, with all manner of fillings and servings to explore
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: A cook-your-own adventure meal, with all manner of fillings and servings to explore
Content: Felicity Cloake’s quesadillas.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Johnny Bentham.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s quesadillas.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Johnny Bentham.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make quesadillas – recipeA cook-your-own adventure meal, with all manner of fillings and servings to exploreFelicity CloakeSun 16 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Mexican equivalent of a cheese toastie, but even quicker to make, these are the perfect summer holiday or weekend lunch, because everyone can choose their own fillings and help cook. Plus, this recipe is just a jumping-off point – once you’ve mastered the method, you can fill them with anything you like … grated chocolate and mashed banana are pretty good!Prep5 minCook4 min eachMakes880g blockcookingmozzarella50g halloumi, or mild cheddar, monterey jack or havarti, grated2 fresh green jalapeños, cut into rounds or a jar of them (optional, see step 4)Oil, to grease8 corn or flour tortillas, about 15cm in width1 tsp dried epazote or oregano, preferably Mexican (optional)To serveTomato salsaIceberg lettuce, shreddedAvocado, cubed or slicedBlack beansSoured creamView image in fullscreen1 Choosing your cheesesYou need something that melts well, and cooking mozzarella – the kind that comes in big rectangular blocks – is ideal (the kind that comes in balls is a bit too wet). You could just use all mozzarella, but I like to mix it with something with a bit more flavour, like a mild cheddar, or salty halloumi.2 Weigh out and grate the cheeseIt doesn’t have to be precisely the amount I’ve suggested, and you might like to add more of one than the other. Use the coarse side of a grater to shred both cheeses (unless they’re already grated, of course). Put the cheese in a bowl and stir until well combined.3 Prep the jalapeños …View image in fullscreenIf you like chilli, then carefully cut the jalapeños into thin rings. Use a knife, or a teaspoon to scoop out any seeds from the middle. Make sure you wash your hands well after touching them, and don’t rub your eyes or any bits of skin while you’re doing this!4 … unless you’re chilli-averseIf you don’t like chillies, there are lots of other things you can put in instead eg bite-size pieces of pepper, cherry tomatoes cut in half with the seeds scooped out, drained tinned sweetcorn, cubes of cooked potatoes or squash, finely chopped broccoli, defrosted spinach with all the water squeezed out, cooked chorizo, shredded ham or chicken etc … even pineapple!5 Ready your panBrush the base of a heavy frying pan with very little oil; just enough to make the inside look a bit darker, but not so much that it moves around when you tip the pan. Put on a medium-low heat and leave to heat up for about two minutes.View image in fullscreen6 Load up your tortillasLay a tortilla into the pan; look for the slightly smaller ones, about 15cm in diameter because they’re easier to fold. Sprinkle with about two generous tablespoons of the cheese (but don’t go right up to the edge, leave a gap) and then add a scattering of any extra ingredients and the dried herbs, if you’re using them.7 Cook the quesadillasWhen the cheese begins to melt, use a spatula to carefully fold the tortilla in half so the cheese is now on the inside; it will be hot. Press down around the edge with the spatula to help seal it. (Alternatively you can just add another tortilla on top if that feels easier.)View image in fullscreen8 Get them goldenContinue to cook until, when you carefully lift up the tortilla to look underneath, it’s golden on the bottom, then turn it over and cook until golden on the other side. Eat them as soon as they’re cool enough; I like them with tomato salsa , shredded iceberg lettuce, avocado, black beans and soured cream.9 (Maybe) make your own salsaWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appTo make an easy tomato salsa, carefully cut a quarter of a small red onion into little pieces. Put in a bowl and squeeze over the juice of half a lime. Chop four medium tomatoes, or eight cherry tomatoes and add to the bowl. Roughly chop a small bunch of coriander, if you like it, and stir in too.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassMexican food and drinkCheeseHerbs and spicesBreadVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content
